# Getting started

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/01-getting-started

This chapter installs `wf`, the WebFluent compiler, and runs a first
project in your browser. In about ten minutes you create the project, change
one line and see the page follow. The rest of the chapter covers optional
set-up: your editor, the other project templates, a site written from
scratch, and what a build writes.

## Before you start

You need:

- a terminal: macOS or Linux with `curl` and `bash`, or Windows with
  PowerShell (or, on any system, Rust's `cargo`);
- a web browser;
- a text editor. Any editor works; [Set up your editor](#set-up-your-editor)
  adds checks as you type, and [WebFluent Studio](#webfluent-studio) is an
  app made for WebFluent.

## Install

WebFluent is one binary, `wf`. Run the line for your machine. Each one
leaves `wf` on your `PATH`.

### macOS and Linux

```bash
curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/master/install.sh | bash
```

The script fetches the binary for your platform from the latest release.
You do not need Rust. It covers Apple Silicon and Intel Macs and x86_64
Linux.

### Windows (PowerShell)

```powershell
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/master/install.ps1 | iex
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> On Windows, type `webfluent` wherever this guide types `wf`.

Windows already has a `wf`: `C:\Windows\System32\WF.msc`, the Windows
Firewall console. System32 comes first on `PATH`, and `.MSC` is one of the
extensions Windows tries for a bare name, so typing `wf` opens the firewall
instead of WebFluent. For that reason the release zip, `install.ps1` and the
`.msi` install the compiler as `webfluent.exe` beside `wf.exe`, and the
`.msi` puts their folder on `PATH`. `webfluent build`, `webfluent serve` and
`wf.exe build` all work. After `cargo install webfluent`, use `wf.exe`.

### With Rust

```bash
cargo install webfluent
```

This builds `wf` from crates.io. It works everywhere Rust does, and it is
how to install on Linux arm64, which has no prebuilt binary yet.

### Packages

Each [release](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/releases) also
carries a `.deb`, an `.msi` and plain tarballs, for a machine where piping
a script to a shell is not an option.

## Check the install

Ask `wf` for its version:

```bash
wf --version
```

**You see** the release you installed:

```text
wf 6.0.0
```

If the shell says it cannot find `wf`, open a new terminal. The installer
adds its directory to your `PATH` in your shell's startup file, and the
terminal you ran it in read that file before the change.

## Create a project

Make a project called `hello` and move into it:

```bash
wf init hello
cd hello
```

**You see:**

```text
Created new WebFluent project: hello (template: spa)
  AGENTS.md is the language reference, for you and your coding agent
  .agents/skills/ and .claude/skills/ teach your coding agent to write it well

  cd hello
  wf build
  wf serve
```

`wf init` writes a small application so you have something real to read:
four pages (a dashboard, a task list, a profile and settings), three
components and two stores, with tests under `tests/`.

## Run the dev server

Start the dev server:

```bash
wf serve
```

**You see:**

```text
Building hello...
  4 pages, 3 components, 2 stores
  Output: ./build/
Build complete.
Starting dev server at http://localhost:3000/
```

Open `http://localhost:3000` in your browser. **You see** the app's
**Dashboard** page: a navigation bar, three task counts and a list of recent
tasks.

Leave the server running. It rebuilds when you save a file, reloads the page
when a build lands, and, when a build fails, draws the error over the page
until a save fixes it.

## Make a change

1. Open `src/pages/Home.wf` in your editor.
2. Find the line `Text("Welcome to your dashboard.").muted` and change the
   text to `Text("Welcome back.").muted`.
3. Save the file.

**You see** the browser reload by itself, and the dashboard now reads
**Welcome back.** under its heading.

To see what an error looks like, change `.muted` to `.mutd` and save. The
page shows error `E103` over it, with the file, the line and the hint
“Did you mean `.muted`?”.
Change it back, save, and the page returns.

You have a working project. Stop the server with Ctrl+C when you are done.
Run `wf build` to write the finished site to `build/`, ready for any static
host ([Deploy to GitHub Pages](/recipes/deploy-to-github-pages)).

The rest of this chapter is optional set-up. To keep learning, go to the
[tutorial](/learn/02-tutorial-shelf).

## Set up your editor

The language server, `wf-lsp`, gives your editor the same checks `wf build`
runs, as you type: diagnostics, completion of props, flags and cases, hover
with types and documentation, signature help, go to definition, references,
rename, formatting, inlay types, semantic highlighting and quick fixes.

`wf-lsp` is a second binary. Get it from the same
[release](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/releases) as `wf` —
`wf-lsp-<version>-<arch>-<os>.tar.gz` — and put it on your `PATH`, or build
it from a clone of the repository:

```bash
cargo install --path crates/wf-lsp
```

Then connect your editor:

- **VS Code** — the extension, [webfluent-vscode](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/webfluent-vscode), brings highlighting and
  the language server. Until it is on the Marketplace, install the `.vsix`
  from its latest release with **Extensions: Install from VSIX**.
- **Zed** — the extension, [webfluent-zed](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/webfluent-zed), brings Tree-sitter highlighting,
  the outline, snippets and the language server (found on `PATH`, or
  downloaded from the latest release). Install it with
  **zed: install dev extension**, pointed at a clone of it.
- **Neovim, Helix, Emacs, or any other editor with LSP** — run `wf-lsp`
  over stdio for the `webfluent` file type (`*.wf`, `*.wfx`).
  [Editors](/reference/cli#editors) has the configuration for each.

### WebFluent Studio

[WebFluent Studio](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/webfluent-studio) is
an app made for writing WebFluent. It puts a code editor, a live preview, a
visual designer, Git and GitHub, this guide and an agent in one window. It
does not use `wf-lsp`: the compiler runs inside the app, so it needs no
`wf` on your `PATH`, no terminal and no dev server. A project built in
Studio is byte-identical to the same project built with `wf build`, so you
can move between Studio and the command line at any time.

- **The preview** rebuilds as you type, and the build log and console link
  back to the source.
- **Diagnostics** have the compiler's own message and its fix, one click
  away; **Explain** opens the chapter of this guide for that code.
- **Design mode** edits the page on a canvas and writes the `.wf` you would
  have written.
- **The agent** builds its own change before you see it, then you accept or
  reject it one hunk at a time.

Studio is a separate, closed-source app at version 0.1, for Linux, macOS
and Windows; Android follows. Its builds are published on
[its releases page](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/webfluent-studio/releases).
You do not need it to use WebFluent: `wf` and any editor are the whole
toolchain.

## Change how `wf` is installed

Both installers read two environment variables:

| Variable | Effect | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `WF_INSTALL_DIR` | Installs the binary somewhere other than `~/.webfluent/bin` | `WF_INSTALL_DIR=/opt/wf/bin` |
| `WF_VERSION` | Installs that release instead of the latest | `WF_VERSION=v6.1.0` |

Running the installer again upgrades `wf` in place.

To build from a clone instead — for an unreleased change, or to work on the
compiler itself — run:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent.git
cd WebFluent && cargo install --path .
```

## Choose a template

`wf init` takes a template with `-t`:

| Template | Makes |
|---|---|
| `-t spa` (default) | An interactive application, routed in the browser |
| `-t static` | A marketing site, every page pre-rendered to HTML |
| `-t pdf` | A PDF document |
| `-t slides` | A PDF slide deck |

`--locales en,ar` starts an `spa` or `static` project translated: its text
is in `src/translations/`, one file per language, and the first locale is
the default ([Internationalisation](/recipes/translate-a-site#start-a-project-translated)).

This chapter starts with an `spa` because its starter is a small
application, with state, stores and tests to read. For a site of your own,
if you are unsure between `spa` and `static`, start with `static`. Every
page is real HTML before any script runs, which is better for search and for
the first paint, and the page is still fully interactive once the script
loads. [Static or single-page](/about/static-or-single-page) explains the
difference.

## Write a site from scratch

To see the smallest whole site, replace every file in `src/` except
`theme.wf` with the two below, and delete the starter's tests under
`tests/`, which test the pages you removed. Keep `src/theme.wf`: the
project's `webfluent.app.json` names the themes it declares (`Day` and
`Night`), and the build stops if they are gone.

`src/App.wf` is the shell every page shares, with the router in it:

```wf
app {
    Navbar {
        Navbar.Brand { Text("Hello").heading }
        Navbar.Links {
            Link("Home", to: "/")
            Link("About", to: "/about")
        }
    }
    Router
}
```

`src/pages/Home.wf` holds the pages, and each page names its own route:

```wf
page Home(path: "/", title: "Hello", description: "A first WebFluent site.") {
    state count = 0
    Container {
        Heading("Hello, world").h1
        Text("You have clicked {count} times.")
        Button("Click me").primary { on click { count = count + 1 } }
    }
}

page About(path: "/about", title: "About", description: "What this site is for.") {
    Container {
        Heading("About").h1
        Paragraph("Two pages, one shell, no framework.")
    }
}
```

Save, and the dev server shows a navigation bar with **Home** and
**About**. **Click me** counts your clicks. Here is what each part does:

- `app { … }` is the shell: what every page sits inside. `Router` is where
  the current page renders. There is no route table; each `page` names its
  own `path:`.
- `page Home(path: "/", title: …, description: …)` declares a page. `title`
  and `description` become the `<title>`, the meta description, the Open
  Graph and Twitter cards and the JSON-LD. If you leave them out, the build
  warns you.
- `state count = 0` is a signal. `Text("… {count} …")` reads it, so the text
  updates when it changes.
- In `Button("Click me").primary { on click { … } }`, the label is the one
  positional argument, `.primary` is a flag (a case of the button's `tone`
  prop), and the block holds the click handler.
- `Container`, `Heading`, `Text`, `Paragraph`, `Navbar` and `Link` are
  built-ins. The [components reference](/reference) lists
  all of them.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** There is no route table and no `import`. Each
> `page` names its own `path:`, and every file under `src/` is part of one
> program, so `App.wf` places pages and components it never imports. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

## What a build produces

`wf build` writes the finished site to `build/`. A static build with two
pages and a `path: "*"` page writes files like these:

```text
build/
  index.html          the page, pre-rendered (static) or the app shell (spa)
  about/index.html    one directory per route in a static build
  404.html            the `path: "*"` page, which a host serves for unknown paths
  app.js              the runtime this program needs, its stores and components
  pages/Home.js       each page in its own chunk, loaded when its route shows
  pages/Home.css      the styles only that page reaches
  styles.css          tokens, the built-ins you used, your stylesheets
  sitemap.xml         every indexable route (needs meta.site_url)
  robots.txt
  _headers            the security headers (build.csp), for hosts that read the file
  sw.js               the service worker, when the config names "offline"
  *.gz                pre-compressed copies a host can serve as they are
```

Do not edit anything in `build/`: the next build writes it again. Keep it
out of version control; the `.gitignore` that `wf init` writes already
does. The build copies `public/` to the root of `build/` as it is.

`app.js` carries only the parts of the runtime the program reaches. The
runtime is a set of feature modules — `each` for a `for`, `router` for a
second page, `net` for a `resource`, `icons` for an `Icon` — and the build
works out which ones the code it has written calls, then keeps only the
functions of those that the calls reach, with their names shortened. A
page of static text is an `app.js` of 1.9 kB gzipped. `wf build --stats`
shows what a build weighs, and [Performance](/about/what-a-build-ships)
explains how to read it.

## The project, in brief

A project's files are laid out like this:

```text
AGENTS.md             the language reference, for you and a coding agent
webfluent.app.json    the config
src/
  App.wf              the app shell (optional)
  pages/*.wf          pages
  components/*.wf     components
  stores/*.wf         stores
  *.css               your own stylesheets, bundled into styles.css
  translations/*.json translation files, with "i18n" in the config
public/               copied to the build's root (images, fonts, favicon)
tests/*.wf            `test "…" { }` declarations for `wf test`
```

The compiler reads every `.wf` or `.wfx` file under `src/` and merges them
into one program, so a page in one file uses a component from another
without importing it. The folders are a convention, not a rule.
[Project structure](/reference/project) covers naming, organisation
and the config, and the [configuration reference](/reference/config)
lists every key.

The config needs only a name:

```json
{ "name": "hello" }
```

## Common mistakes

A flag with a typo. A flag is checked against the element that takes it,
so `.mutd` is an error, not a style that quietly does nothing:

```wf expect=E103
page Home(path: "/", title: "Hello", description: "A first site.") {
    Heading("Hello").h1
    Text("Welcome back.").mutd
}
```

Use one of the flags the message lists, here `.muted`
([E103](/errors/E103)).

An `app` with no `Router`. The shell is drawn, but no page ever is:

```wf expect=R03
app {
    Navbar {
        Navbar.Brand { Text("Hello").heading }
    }
}

page Home(path: "/", title: "Hello", description: "A first site.") {
    Heading("Hello, world").h1
}
```

Put `Router` in the `app` where the current page should appear
([R03](/errors/R03)).

A link to a page you have not written yet. The compiler checks every
`to:` against the pages' paths:

```wf expect=R01
app {
    Navbar {
        Navbar.Links {
            Link("Home", to: "/")
            Link("About", to: "/about")
        }
    }
    Router
}

page Home(path: "/", title: "Hello", description: "A first site.") {
    Heading("Hello, world").h1
}
```

Add the page, `page About(path: "/about", …)`, or fix the address
([R01](/errors/R01)).

## Next

[Tutorial: Shelf](/learn/02-tutorial-shelf): build a reading-list site, start to finish.

# Tutorial: Shelf

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/02-tutorial-shelf

This tutorial builds **Shelf**, a small site that lists books worth reading
and lets a reader keep the ones they want. Each step adds one piece,
and ends with what you should see.

## What you will build

Shelf has a home page that lists books with a search box, a page for each
book, a **Your shelf** page with the books the reader saved, a form to
suggest a book, a theme with a dark mode, a test that clicks, and a deploy
to GitHub Pages.

Along the way you use most of what a real site needs: typed data read at
build time, a reusable component, a page per book, a store that keeps the
reader's choices, a validated form, a theme, a test and a deploy. Each step
links the chapter that covers its idea in depth.

It takes about half an hour, plus the deploy.

## Before you start

You need:

- `wf` installed and on your `PATH` ([Getting started](/learn/01-getting-started)).
  On Windows, type `webfluent` where this tutorial types `wf`.
- Chrome or Chromium on the machine, for the test that clicks
  ([step 9](#step-9-test-the-book-card)) and for `wf verify`
  ([step 10](#step-10-build-and-verify-the-site)). If it is installed
  somewhere unusual, point the `WF_CHROME` environment variable at it.
- For the deploy, a GitHub account and a repository called `shelf`.

You do not need to know WebFluent yet.

## Step 1: Create the project

Start from the `static` template, which pre-renders every page to HTML —
right for a site people find through search:

```bash
wf init shelf -t static
cd shelf
```

You write every file yourself, so delete what the template put in `src/`
and its tests under `tests/` (they test the starter's pages). Then replace
`webfluent.app.json` with:

```json
{
  "name": "shelf",
  "build": { "ssg": true, "csp": true },
  "meta": {
    "title": "Shelf",
    "description": "Books worth reading, and the ones you want to.",
    "lang": "en"
  }
}
```

`ssg` pre-renders each page. `csp` ships a Content-Security-Policy and makes
the build check its own output against it. [Configuration](/reference/config)
lists every key.

**Check it:** run `wf check`. It prints `IO Error: No .wf files found in src/` —
correct, because `src/` is empty until the next step.

## Step 2: Describe the books

The books are data, not code. Put them in `src/books.json`:

```json
[
  { "slug": "notes-on-the-analytical-engine", "title": "Notes on the Analytical Engine",
    "author": "Ada Lovelace", "year": 1843, "pages": 66,
    "summary": "The first published algorithm, and a view of what a machine might do beyond arithmetic.",
    "tags": ["computing", "history"] },
  { "slug": "the-design-of-everyday-things", "title": "The Design of Everyday Things",
    "author": "Don Norman", "year": 1988, "pages": 368,
    "summary": "Why doors confuse us, and what that says about everything else we make.",
    "tags": ["design"] },
  { "slug": "a-pattern-language", "title": "A Pattern Language",
    "author": "Christopher Alexander", "year": 1977, "pages": 1171,
    "summary": "Two hundred and fifty-three patterns for towns, buildings and rooms people want to live in.",
    "tags": ["design", "architecture"] }
]
```

Then describe the data's shape and read the file, in `src/types.wf`:

```wf
/// One book on the list.
type Book {
    slug: String
    title: String
    author: String
    year: Number
    pages: Number
    summary: String
    tags: [String] = []
}

data books: [Book] = "books.json"
```

`type Book` is a record that the type checker holds every use to: writing
`book.titel` is an error where you write it. `data books` reads the file **at
build time** and makes it a constant every page can read, so nothing is
fetched when the page loads. ([Types](/learn/12-types),
[Fetching data](/learn/15-data#read-a-file-at-build-time-with-data).)

**Check it:** run `wf check`. It prints `No problems in shelf.`

## Step 3: Keep the reader's shelf in a store

What the reader keeps must survive a reload and be the same on every page,
so it goes in a store, with its value kept by `persist`. Create
`src/stores/Shelf.wf`:

```wf
/// The books the reader wants to read, kept across visits.
store Shelf {
    persist saved: [String] = []
    derived count = saved.length

    action toggle(slug: String) {
        if saved.includes(slug) {
            saved = saved.filter(s => s != slug)
        } else {
            saved = [...saved, slug]
        }
    }
}
```

`persist` is a `state` that is kept in the browser's storage and read back on
the next visit; a change made in another tab arrives here too. `derived
count` recomputes whenever `saved` changes. ([Stores](/learn/11-stores).)

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** Shared state is not a context provider wrapped
> around the app, and saving it is not a `useEffect` that writes
> `localStorage`. A `store` is read by name wherever it is used, and
> `persist` does the saving. See [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

**Check it:** run `wf check`. It prints two `U04` warnings:
`` `Shelf.count` is declared but never read `` and the same for
`Shelf.toggle`. Nothing uses the store yet; the next steps do, and the
warnings go away.

## Step 4: Show a book with a component

Every book is shown the same way, so it is a component. Create
`src/components/BookCard.wf`:

```wf
// … reads what the other steps declare
/// A book at a glance, with the button that puts it on the shelf.
component BookCard(_ book: Book) {
    use Shelf
    Card.outlined {
        Stack(gap: .sm) {
            Link(book.title, to: "/books/{book.slug}")
            Text("{book.author} · {book.year}").muted.sm
            Text(book.summary)
            Row(gap: .xs) {
                for tag in book.tags { Tag(tag) }
            }
            Button(if Shelf.saved.includes(book.slug) { "On your shelf" } else { "Want to read" }).sm {
                on click { Shelf.toggle(book.slug) }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

- `_ book: Book` is the one prop a caller may pass without its name:
  `BookCard(book)`.
- `Card.outlined`, `Stack(gap: .sm)` and `Text(…).muted.sm` are built-ins
  with flags. The compiler knows each one's props and refuses a flag it does
  not take.
- `use Shelf` reads the store from step 3. The button's label is an `if`
  used as a value, and it follows the store: when the reader clicks, the
  label changes and nothing else re-renders.

([Components](/learn/10-components), [Elements](/learn/06-elements).)

**Check it:** run `wf check`. It reports two warnings and no error:
`` warning[U03]: `BookCard` is declared but never placed `` and
`` warning[U04]: `Shelf.count` is declared but never read ``. Nothing
places the card yet, and nothing shows the count; the next step does both.
The card also links to `/books/…`, a page that does not exist yet. The
compiler checks every link against the pages you declare, but only in what
the site draws, so it says nothing until the card is placed.

## Step 5: Add the home page and a page per book

The home page lists the books with a search box. Create
`src/pages/Home.wf`:

```wf
// … reads what the other steps declare
page Home(path: "/", title: "Shelf", description: "Books worth reading, and the ones you want to.") {
    state q = ""
    derived needle = q.trim().toLowerCase()
    derived found = books.filter(b => b.title.toLowerCase().includes(needle) || b.author.toLowerCase().includes(needle))

    Container {
        Stack(gap: .lg) {
            Heading("Books worth reading").h1
            Input(bind: q, label: "Search by title or author").search
            Text("{found.length} of {books.length} books").muted.sm
            Grid(columns: { base: 1, md: 2 }, gap: .md) {
                for book in found by book.slug { BookCard(book) }
            }
            if found.length == 0 { Text("Nothing matches “{q}”.").muted }
        }
    }
}
```

- `bind: q` keeps the input and the state in step, both ways.
- `found` is derived from `q`, so typing narrows the list as you go.
- `for … by book.slug` is a keyed loop: a card that stays in the list keeps
  its element instead of being rebuilt.
- `Grid(columns: { base: 1, md: 2 })` is one column on a phone and two from
  the `md` breakpoint. The pre-rendered HTML already has this layout, so no
  script is needed.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** A controlled input needs no `value` and no
> `onChange` that copies `e.target.value` back: `bind: q` does both. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

Then add a page for each book, `src/pages/BookPage.wf`:

```wf
// … reads what the other steps declare
page BookPage(path: "/books/:slug", slug: String, title: "Book", description: "One book on the shelf.", type: "article", paths: books.map(b => b.slug)) {
    derived book = books.find(b => b.slug == slug)
    head {
        meta(property: "og:title", content: book?.title ?? "Book")
    }
    Container {
        if let b = book {
            Breadcrumb {
                Breadcrumb.Item(to: "/") { Text("Books") }
                Breadcrumb.Item { Text(b.title) }
            }
            Heading(b.title).h1
            Text("{b.author}, {b.year} · {b.pages} pages").muted
            Paragraph(b.summary)
        } else {
            Heading("No such book").h1
            Link("Back to the list", to: "/")
        }
    }
}
```

- `:slug` in the path is a typed parameter of the page.
- `paths:` tells the static build which values to render: one HTML file per
  book, `books/a-pattern-language/index.html` and so on.
- `books.find(…)` may find nothing, so `book` is a `Book?` (a `Book` or
  `null`). `if let b = book` binds it only when it is there. Reading
  `book.title` without that check is a compile error (`T04`).
- `head { … }` adds tags to this page's `<head>` — here, the title that a
  shared link previews with.

([Pages and routing](/learn/05-pages-and-routing).)

**Check it:** run `wf serve` and open `http://localhost:3000`. You see
**Books worth reading**, `3 of 3 books` and three cards. Type `norman` in
the search box: one card stays, and the count reads `1 of 3 books`. Click **Want to read** on a card and its
label changes to **On your shelf**. Click a book's title and its page opens,
with a breadcrumb back to the list. `wf check` now reports only the `U04`
warning about `Shelf.count`; step 6 uses it.

## Step 6: Add the shelf page and the site's shell

The shelf page shows the books the reader saved. Create
`src/pages/ShelfPage.wf`:

```wf
// … reads what the other steps declare
page ShelfPage(path: "/shelf", title: "Your shelf", description: "The books you want to read.") {
    use Shelf
    derived mine = books.filter(b => Shelf.saved.includes(b.slug))
    Container {
        Stack(gap: .lg) {
            Heading("Your shelf").h1
            if mine.length == 0 {
                Text("Nothing yet. Pick something from the list.").muted
                Link("Browse the books", to: "/")
            } else {
                for book in mine by book.slug { BookCard(book) }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Add a page for addresses no other page claims, `src/pages/NotFound.wf`.
`path: "*"` matches anything, and the static build writes it as `404.html`:

```wf
page NotFound(path: "*", title: "Not found", description: "Nothing lives at this address.", noindex: true) {
    Container {
        Heading("Nothing lives here").h1
        Link("Back to the books", to: "/")
    }
}
```

Last, the shell every page shares, `src/App.wf`. `Router` is where the
current page is drawn:

```wf
// … reads what the other steps declare
app {
    Navbar {
        Navbar.Brand { Link("Shelf", to: "/") }
        Navbar.Links {
            Link("Books", to: "/")
            Link("Your shelf ({Shelf.count})", to: "/shelf")
        }
    }
    Router
    Footer { Text("Built with WebFluent").muted.sm }
}
```

**Check it:** `wf check` prints `No problems in shelf.` Every page now has a
navigation bar. Put two books on your shelf: the link reads
**Your shelf (2)**. Open it, then reload the page — the two books are still
there. Open `http://localhost:3000/nowhere` and you see **Nothing lives
here**.

## Step 7: Add a form to suggest a book

Readers can suggest books. Create `src/pages/Suggest.wf`:

```wf
page Suggest(path: "/suggest", title: "Suggest a book", description: "Tell us what belongs on the shelf.") {
    state title = ""
    state author = ""
    state why = ""
    state sent = false

    validate title { required "Which book?" }
    validate author { required "Who wrote it?" }
    validate why { maxLength(280) "Keep it under 280 characters" }

    Container {
        Stack(gap: .lg) {
            Heading("Suggest a book").h1
            if sent { Alert("Thank you — we will take a look.").success }
            Form(bind: form) {
                on submit {
                    sent = true
                    form.reset()
                }
                Input(bind: title, label: "Title")
                Input(bind: author, label: "Author")
                Textarea(bind: why, label: "Why it belongs here", rows: 4, maxLength: 280)
                Button("Send the suggestion", type: .submit).primary
            }
        }
    }
}
```

A `validate` block sits beside the state it guards, and the control bound to
that state shows its messages accessibly: the field gets `aria-invalid`, and
the message is announced. A submit that fails moves focus to the first field
with a problem and does not run `on submit`. ([Forms](/learn/14-forms).)

Then link the page from the shell. Add the third link to `src/App.wf`:

```wf
// … reads what the other steps declare
app {
    Navbar {
        Navbar.Brand { Link("Shelf", to: "/") }
        Navbar.Links {
            Link("Books", to: "/")
            Link("Your shelf ({Shelf.count})", to: "/shelf")
            Link("Suggest a book", to: "/suggest")
        }
    }
    Router
    Footer { Text("Built with WebFluent").muted.sm }
}
```

**Check it:** click **Suggest a book**, then **Send the suggestion** with
the form empty. The form does not send: **Which book?** appears under
**Title**, and **Who wrote it?** under **Author**. Fill in both and send
again. You see **Thank you — we will take a look.**, and the form is empty.

A real site sends the suggestion somewhere. You do not need a backend for
this tutorial, so this part is for later: describe the service once, in a
file of its own,

```wf
// … in src/api.wf, beside the pages
api Suggestions(base: env.PUBLIC_API ?? "/api") {
    post suggest(body: Map)
}
```

and call it from the form's handler:

```wf
// … in src/pages/Suggest.wf; the rest of the page is as above
on submit {
    await Suggestions.suggest(body: { title: title, author: author, why: why })
    sent = true
    form.reset()
}
```

([Data and APIs](/learn/15-data), [Environments and secrets](/recipes/environments-and-secrets).)

## Step 8: Give the site a theme

A theme changes the design tokens that every built-in is drawn with. Create
`src/theme.wf`:

```wf
theme Paper {
    color-primary: #6D28D9
    font-family: Charter, Georgia, serif
    radius-md: 10px
}

theme Ink {
    color-background: #111014
    color-surface: #1A1820
    color-text: #ECEAF2
    color-text-muted: #A8A3B5
    color-border: #2B2833
}
```

Then name the themes in `webfluent.app.json` — `Paper` as the theme and
`Ink` as the dark one:

```json
{
  "name": "shelf",
  "build": { "ssg": true, "csp": true },
  "theme": { "name": "Paper", "dark": "Ink" },
  "meta": {
    "title": "Shelf",
    "description": "Books worth reading, and the ones you want to.",
    "lang": "en"
  }
}
```

A reader whose system is set to dark mode gets `Ink`, before the first paint
and with no flash of the light theme. A token you do not name keeps its
baseline value. ([Styling](/learn/13-styling).)

**Check it:** the links and the **Send the suggestion** button are purple,
and the text is a serif face. Switch
your system to dark mode and the page turns dark. If the build stops with
``No `theme Paper` is declared in this project``, the config names a theme
that `src/theme.wf` does not declare: check the file name and the spelling.

## Step 9: Test the book card

Tests live in `tests/`. Create `tests/BookCard.wf`:

```wf
// … reads what the other steps declare
test "a card shows who wrote the book, and when" {
    BookCard(Book(slug: "x", title: "X", author: "Ada Lovelace", year: 1843, pages: 66, summary: "Notes."))
    expect "Ada Lovelace · 1843"
    expect "Want to read"
}

test "a book goes on the shelf, and comes off again" {
    BookCard(Book(slug: "x", title: "X", author: "Ada Lovelace", year: 1843, pages: 66, summary: "Notes."))
    click "Want to read"
    expect "On your shelf"
    click "On your shelf"
    expect "Want to read"
}
```

Run them:

```bash
wf test
```

The first test renders the card and reads what it shows. It also writes a
snapshot that the next run compares against. The second test **clicks**, so
it runs in a headless Chrome, with the same compiler and runtime a reader
gets. Buttons are found by their text, as a reader finds them.
([Testing](/learn/16-testing).)

**Check it:** the first run ends:

```text
  new   tests/BookCard.wf — a card shows who wrote the book, and when (snapshot written)
  ok    tests/BookCard.wf — a book goes on the shelf, and comes off again (in a browser)
2 passed, 0 failed, 1 snapshot(s) written
```

Run `wf test` again and the first line reads `ok`: the render matches its
snapshot.

If the second test says there is no browser, install Chrome or Chromium, or
set `WF_CHROME` to its path.

## Step 10: Build and verify the site

Stop the dev server, then build the site and load every page in a real
browser:

```bash
wf build
wf verify
```

`wf build` writes `build/`, a folder of HTML, CSS and JavaScript that any
static host can serve, and prints every warning, such as a missing `alt`, a
page without a description, or a state nothing reads. `wf verify` loads every
page in a real browser and fails on a script error, a failed request or a
blank page.

**Check it:** `wf build` ends with `Build complete.`, and `build/` holds
`index.html`, `shelf/index.html`, `suggest/index.html`, `404.html` and one
`books/<slug>/index.html` per book. `wf verify` lists six routes, each `ok`,
and ends with `6 page(s), 0 problem(s)`.

## Step 11: Deploy to GitHub Pages

Any static host serves `build/`. On GitHub Pages, a project site lives under
`https://<you>.github.io/shelf/`, so tell the build its sub-path and its
address. Add these keys to `webfluent.app.json`, keeping the others:

```json
{
  "build": { "ssg": true, "csp": true, "base_path": "/shelf" },
  "meta": { "site_url": "https://you.github.io/shelf" }
}
```

`base_path` prefixes every link and asset. `site_url` turns on canonical
links, the sitemap and absolute Open Graph URLs.

Then add a workflow that builds and publishes the site on every push to
`main`, `.github/workflows/pages.yml`:

```yaml
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/master/install.sh | bash
      - run: ~/.webfluent/bin/wf build
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: build
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
```

Push the project to your `shelf` repository. In the repository's
**Settings → Pages**, choose **GitHub Actions** as the source.

**Check it:** the **Actions** tab shows the **Deploy** workflow passing, and
`https://<you>.github.io/shelf/` shows **Books worth reading**.
The recipes cover [Netlify](/recipes/deploy-to-netlify),
[Vercel](/recipes/deploy-to-vercel),
[Cloudflare Pages](/recipes/deploy-to-cloudflare-pages),
[nginx](/recipes/serve-with-nginx) and other hosts.

## The whole program

Every `.wf` file above, as one listing. This is the program the steps built,
with the first of the two tests:

```wf
type Book {
    slug: String
    title: String
    author: String
    year: Number
    pages: Number
    summary: String
    tags: [String] = []
}

data books: [Book] = "books.json"

store Shelf {
    persist saved: [String] = []
    derived count = saved.length

    action toggle(slug: String) {
        if saved.includes(slug) {
            saved = saved.filter(s => s != slug)
        } else {
            saved = [...saved, slug]
        }
    }
}

component BookCard(_ book: Book) {
    use Shelf
    Card.outlined {
        Stack(gap: .sm) {
            Link(book.title, to: "/books/{book.slug}")
            Text("{book.author} · {book.year}").muted.sm
            Text(book.summary)
            Row(gap: .xs) {
                for tag in book.tags { Tag(tag) }
            }
            Button(if Shelf.saved.includes(book.slug) { "On your shelf" } else { "Want to read" }).sm {
                on click { Shelf.toggle(book.slug) }
            }
        }
    }
}

app {
    Navbar {
        Navbar.Brand { Link("Shelf", to: "/") }
        Navbar.Links {
            Link("Books", to: "/")
            Link("Your shelf ({Shelf.count})", to: "/shelf")
            Link("Suggest a book", to: "/suggest")
        }
    }
    Router
    Footer { Text("Built with WebFluent").muted.sm }
}

page Home(path: "/", title: "Shelf", description: "Books worth reading, and the ones you want to.") {
    state q = ""
    derived needle = q.trim().toLowerCase()
    derived found = books.filter(b => b.title.toLowerCase().includes(needle) || b.author.toLowerCase().includes(needle))

    Container {
        Stack(gap: .lg) {
            Heading("Books worth reading").h1
            Input(bind: q, label: "Search by title or author").search
            Text("{found.length} of {books.length} books").muted.sm
            Grid(columns: { base: 1, md: 2 }, gap: .md) {
                for book in found by book.slug { BookCard(book) }
            }
            if found.length == 0 { Text("Nothing matches “{q}”.").muted }
        }
    }
}

page BookPage(path: "/books/:slug", slug: String, title: "Book", description: "One book on the shelf.", type: "article", paths: books.map(b => b.slug)) {
    derived book = books.find(b => b.slug == slug)
    head {
        meta(property: "og:title", content: book?.title ?? "Book")
    }
    Container {
        if let b = book {
            Breadcrumb {
                Breadcrumb.Item(to: "/") { Text("Books") }
                Breadcrumb.Item { Text(b.title) }
            }
            Heading(b.title).h1
            Text("{b.author}, {b.year} · {b.pages} pages").muted
            Paragraph(b.summary)
        } else {
            Heading("No such book").h1
            Link("Back to the list", to: "/")
        }
    }
}

page ShelfPage(path: "/shelf", title: "Your shelf", description: "The books you want to read.") {
    use Shelf
    derived mine = books.filter(b => Shelf.saved.includes(b.slug))
    Container {
        Stack(gap: .lg) {
            Heading("Your shelf").h1
            if mine.length == 0 {
                Text("Nothing yet. Pick something from the list.").muted
                Link("Browse the books", to: "/")
            } else {
                for book in mine by book.slug { BookCard(book) }
            }
        }
    }
}

page Suggest(path: "/suggest", title: "Suggest a book", description: "Tell us what belongs on the shelf.") {
    state title = ""
    state author = ""
    state why = ""
    state sent = false

    validate title { required "Which book?" }
    validate author { required "Who wrote it?" }
    validate why { maxLength(280) "Keep it under 280 characters" }

    Container {
        Stack(gap: .lg) {
            Heading("Suggest a book").h1
            if sent { Alert("Thank you — we will take a look.").success }
            Form(bind: form) {
                on submit {
                    sent = true
                    form.reset()
                }
                Input(bind: title, label: "Title")
                Input(bind: author, label: "Author")
                Textarea(bind: why, label: "Why it belongs here", rows: 4, maxLength: 280)
                Button("Send the suggestion", type: .submit).primary
            }
        }
    }
}

page NotFound(path: "*", title: "Not found", description: "Nothing lives at this address.", noindex: true) {
    Container {
        Heading("Nothing lives here").h1
        Link("Back to the books", to: "/")
    }
}

theme Paper {
    color-primary: #6D28D9
    font-family: Charter, Georgia, serif
    radius-md: 10px
}

theme Ink {
    color-background: #111014
    color-surface: #1A1820
    color-text: #ECEAF2
    color-text-muted: #A8A3B5
    color-border: #2B2833
}

test "a card shows who wrote the book, and when" {
    BookCard(Book(slug: "x", title: "X", author: "Ada Lovelace", year: 1843, pages: 66, summary: "Notes."))
    expect "Ada Lovelace · 1843"
    expect "Want to read"
}
```

## What you built

Shelf is a whole site, and each part of it uses one idea of the language:

| You wrote | The idea | Read more |
|---|---|---|
| `type Book` and `data books` | Typed data read at build time | [Types](/learn/12-types), [Fetching data](/learn/15-data#read-a-file-at-build-time-with-data) |
| `store Shelf` with `persist` | Shared state kept across visits | [Stores](/learn/11-stores) |
| `component BookCard` | A reusable component with a positional prop | [Components](/learn/10-components) |
| `state`, `derived`, `bind:` and `for … by` on the home page | Reactivity and keyed lists | [State and reactivity](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity), [Control flow](/learn/09-control-flow) |
| `path: "/books/:slug"` with `paths:`, and `if let` | Route parameters, static paths and optional values | [Pages and routing](/learn/05-pages-and-routing) |
| `app { … Router … }` | The shell every page shares | [Pages and routing](/learn/05-pages-and-routing) |
| `validate` and `Form(bind: form)` | Validated forms | [Forms](/learn/14-forms) |
| `theme Paper` and `theme Ink` | Design tokens and dark mode | [Styling](/learn/13-styling) |
| `test "…" { … click … expect … }` | Tests that render and click | [Testing](/learn/16-testing) |
| `wf build`, `wf verify` and a workflow | Building, checking and deploying | [Deploy to GitHub Pages](/recipes/deploy-to-github-pages) |

To go further:

- Read the language properly, starting at [Language basics](/learn/04-language-basics).
- Talk to a real server: [Data and APIs](/learn/15-data).
- Make the site work offline: [Make a site work offline](/recipes/work-offline).
- Translate it: [Translate a site](/recipes/translate-a-site).
- Build a bigger project: [Tutorials](/learn/03-tutorial-todos).

## Common mistakes

Reading a value that may be missing. `books.find(…)` finds nothing when no
book has the slug, so `book` is a `Book?`:

```wf expect=T04
type Book { slug: String, title: String }

const books: [Book] = [Book(slug: "a-pattern-language", title: "A Pattern Language")]

page BookPage(path: "/books/:slug", slug: String, title: "Book", description: "One book.") {
    derived book = books.find(b => b.slug == slug)
    Heading(book.title).h1
}
```

Bind it with `if let b = book { Heading(b.title).h1 }`, as step 5 does, or
read it as `book?.title ?? "Book"` ([T04](/errors/T04)).

A field the type does not have. `type Book` names every field, so a typo
is an error where it is written:

```wf expect=T05
type Book { slug: String, title: String }

const books: [Book] = [Book(slug: "a-pattern-language", title: "A Pattern Language")]

page Home(path: "/", title: "Shelf", description: "Books worth reading.") {
    Heading("Books").h1
    for book in books by book.slug {
        Text(book.titel)
    }
}
```

Use the name the message suggests, `book.title` ([T05](/errors/T05)).

A store member the store does not declare. `Shelf` has `saved`, `count`
and `toggle`, and nothing else:

```wf expect=T06
store Shelf {
    persist saved: [String] = []
    action toggle(slug: String) {
        saved = if saved.includes(slug) { saved.filter(s => s != slug) } else { [...saved, slug] }
    }
}

page Home(path: "/", title: "Shelf", description: "Books worth reading.") {
    use Shelf
    Heading("Books").h1
    Text("{Shelf.total} saved")
    Button("Keep it") { on click { Shelf.toggle("a-pattern-language") } }
}
```

Read a member the store declares, or declare the one you need:
`derived count = saved.length` ([T06](/errors/T06)).

Going further: if you know React, Vue or Svelte, [Coming from React, Vue or
Svelte](/coming-from/react) maps what you know onto WebFluent.

## Next

[Tutorial: Todos](/learn/03-tutorial-todos): a single-page app, with a store and tests.

# Tutorial: Todos

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/03-tutorial-todos

This tutorial builds a todo list kept in the reader's browser, with a
store, a component, a filter in the address and tests that click.

It is the second of the book's tutorials, after Shelf. Two longer projects
in the recipes build on both. Todos and the two longer projects are
complete in the repository under `examples/tutorials/`, and none needs a
server: what a project keeps, it keeps in the reader's browser.

| Project | What you build | What it teaches | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Shelf](/learn/02-tutorial-shelf) (chapter 2) | A reading-list site: a page per book, a saved shelf, a form | Typed `data`, a component, `:slug` pages, a store with `persist`, a form, a theme, a test, a deploy | Half an hour |
| [Todos](/learn/03-tutorial-todos) (this chapter) | A list of things to do: add, tick, rename, filter | Types, a store with `persist`, a component, a keyed list, a filter in the address, tests that click | 20 minutes |
| [Field Notes](/recipes/build-a-notebook-site) (a longer project) | A notebook site, statically built, a page per note | `data` files, a layout, `:slug` pages with `paths:`, Markdown pages, search and tags, what a pre-rendered page can know | An hour |
| [Pocket](/recipes/build-a-budget-app) (a longer project) | A budget tracker with a dashboard, forms and two languages | `Money` and `Date`, derived totals, a `persist` migration, `validate`, a dialog and shortcuts, i18n and right-to-left text, a script of your own, offline | A couple of hours |

If you have not written WebFluent before, start with [the Shelf tutorial](/learn/02-tutorial-shelf): it is a gentler first half hour.

**What you will build.** A list of things to do, kept in the reader's
browser: add a todo, tick it, rename it, remove it, and show only the open
ones. It is one page, one store and one component. The finished project is
[`examples/tutorials/easy-todos`](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/tree/master/examples/tutorials/easy-todos).

**Time:** about 20 minutes.

## Before you start

You need:

- `wf` installed and on your `PATH` — `wf --version` prints `wf 6.0.0` or
  later ([Getting started](/learn/01-getting-started)).
- Chrome or Chromium on the machine, for the tests that click and for
  `wf verify`. Set `WF_CHROME` to its path when it is not in a usual place.
- Git, to fetch the finished projects.

Every code block whose first line names a file — `// src/stores/Todos.wf`
— is that file, or a run of lines from it, exactly as the project has it.
A test holds this chapter to the projects, so the code you read here is
the code that builds.

To start from a finished project instead, clone the repository and serve
one:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent
cd WebFluent/examples/tutorials/easy-todos
wf serve
```

**Check it:** the terminal prints `Starting dev server at
http://localhost:3000/`, and that address shows the project.

For this tutorial you need only `wf` and Chrome. You write every file
of this project yourself, and the blocks below hold each file whole, except
the tests, where one of six is shown.

## Step 1: Create the project

Make a single-page project and go into it:

```bash
wf init todos -t spa
cd todos
```

Delete everything the template put in `src/` and in `tests/`: you write
every file yourself, and the template's tests would fail without its pages.
Then replace `webfluent.app.json` with this:

```json
{
  "name": "todos",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "theme": { "name": "Paper", "dark": "Night" },
  "build": { "output": "./build", "output_type": "spa", "csp": true },
  "meta": {
    "title": "Todos",
    "description": "A small list of things to do, kept in your browser.",
    "lang": "en",
    "favicon": "/favicon.svg"
  }
}
```

- `"output_type": "spa"` makes a single-page app: one HTML shell, with
  pages swapped without a reload
  ([Static sites and SPAs](/about/static-or-single-page)).
- `"csp": true` ships a content security policy and holds the build to it
  ([Security](/about/security)).
- `theme` names two themes, `Paper` and `Night`, which you write in the
  next step.
- `favicon` is the icon in the browser's tab. A file in `public/` is served
  from the site's root, so put one at `public/favicon.svg`:

```bash
mkdir -p public
printf '%s' '<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 32 32"><rect width="32" height="32" rx="6" fill="#0F766E"/><path d="M9 16l5 5 9-10" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="3" fill="none"/></svg>' > public/favicon.svg
```

**Check it:** `wf check` prints `IO Error: No .wf files found in src/`.
That is expected: `src/` is empty until the next step.

## Step 2: Give it a look of its own

The config names a theme, so declare it first. A theme names only the
design tokens it changes; every other token keeps its default
([Styling](/learn/13-styling)). `Night` is the theme named as `"dark"` in the
config, and the page uses it when the reader's system is set to dark:

```wf
// src/theme.wf
/// Warm paper and ink, with one teal for what you can act on.
theme Paper {
    color-primary: #0F766E
    color-background: #F6F4EF
    color-surface: #FFFFFF
    color-text: #1F2328
    color-text-muted: #5E6670
    color-border: #E4E0D8
    font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif
    radius-md: 10px
}

/// The same page after dark.
theme Night {
    color-primary: #2DD4BF
    color-background: #14171A
    color-surface: #1C2024
    color-text: #ECEEF0
    color-text-muted: #A3ABB3
    color-border: #2C3238
}
```

The page you write in step 6 names classes — `card`, `todo`, `is-done`,
`filters` — and `src/todos.css` styles them. The build bundles every `.css`
file under `src/`, so the file needs no link. These are four of its rules;
copy the whole file from the
[finished project](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/blob/master/examples/tutorials/easy-todos/src/todos.css):

```css
.todo { flex-wrap: nowrap; padding: 0.6rem 0.25rem; border-top: 1px solid var(--color-border); }
.todo__title { flex: 1; }
.todo.is-done .todo__title { text-decoration: line-through; color: var(--color-text-muted); }
.filters a.is-on { background: var(--color-background); color: var(--color-text); font-weight: 600; }
```

Each colour is a token, `var(--color-border)`, so the dark theme recolours
the page with no rule of its own.

**Check it:** `wf check` prints `No problems in todos.`

## Step 3: Describe a todo

A `type` names the fields a value has, and the checker holds every use to
them ([Types](/learn/12-types)). An `enum` is a fixed set of cases:

```wf
// src/types.wf
/// One thing to do.
type Todo {
    id: Uuid
    title: String
    done: Bool = false
}

/// Which todos the list shows.
enum Filter { all, open, done }
```

- `Uuid` is one of the types the language brings; `uuid()` makes one.
- `done` has a default, so a new todo can leave it out.
- A case is written with a dot, `.open`, wherever a `Filter` is wanted.

Because the checker knows the fields, `todo.titel` is an error where it is
written, and the message names the field you meant.

**Check it:** `wf check` prints `No problems in todos.`

## Step 4: Write a store that remembers

A store holds state that any page or component can read
([Stores](/learn/11-stores)). This one keeps the list:

```wf
// src/stores/Todos.wf
/// The list, kept in the browser between visits.
store Todos {
    persist items: [Todo] = []

    derived open = items.filter(todo => !todo.done)
    derived done = items.filter(todo => todo.done)

    action add(title: String) {
        let text = title.trim()
        if text == "" { return }
        items = items.concat([Todo(id: uuid(), title: text)])
    }

    action toggle(id: Uuid) {
        items = items.map(todo => if todo.id == id { { ...todo, done: !todo.done } } else { todo })
    }

    action rename(id: Uuid, title: String) {
        let text = title.trim()
        if text == "" { return }
        items = items.map(todo => if todo.id == id { { ...todo, title: text } } else { todo })
    }

    action remove(id: Uuid) {
        items = items.filter(todo => todo.id != id)
    }

    action clearDone() {
        items = items.filter(todo => !todo.done)
    }
}
```

- `persist` is a `state` kept in the browser's storage. The list is still
  there after a reload, and a second tab follows the first, with no storage
  code written.
- A `derived` value follows what it reads: `open` is always the todos not
  yet done.
- An action is the one place state changes. `{ ...todo, done: !todo.done }`
  is the todo with one field changed.
- `rename`, `remove` and `clearDone` change the list in the same way.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from Vue?** A `derived` value is a `computed` with no function to
> write and no `.value` to read: `Todos.open` is the list itself. See
> [Coming from Vue](/coming-from/vue).

**Check it:** `wf check` prints seven `U04` warnings, such as ``warning[U04]:
`Todos.open` is declared but never read``. That is expected: nothing reads
the store yet. The page in step 6 reads every member, and the warnings go.

## Step 5: Build one row

A component is an element of your own ([Components](/learn/10-components)).
This one draws a single todo, and lets the reader rename it in place:

```wf
// src/components/TodoRow.wf
/// One row of the list: a box to tick, the title, and buttons to rename and
/// remove it.
component TodoRow(_ todo: Todo) {
    use Todos
    state editing = false
    state draft = todo.title

    action save() {
        Todos.rename(todo.id, draft)
        editing = false
    }

    Row(class: ["todo", if todo.done { "is-done" }], align: .center, gap: .sm) {
        Checkbox(checked: todo.done, aria-label: "Done: {todo.title}") {
            on change { Todos.toggle(todo.id) }
        }
        if editing {
            // `mount:` runs when the input is made: the cursor goes straight in.
            Input(bind: draft, aria-label: "New title for {todo.title}", class: "todo__edit", mount: (n) => n.focus()) {
                on key("Enter") { save() }
                on key("Escape") { draft = todo.title  editing = false }
                on blur { save() }
            }
        } else {
            Text(todo.title, class: "todo__title")
            IconButton(icon: "edit", label: "Rename {todo.title}", class: "todo__action").sm {
                on click { draft = todo.title  editing = true }
            }
        }
        IconButton(icon: "trash", label: "Remove {todo.title}", class: "todo__action").sm {
            on click { Todos.remove(todo.id) }
        }
    }
}
```

- `_ todo` is the component's one positional prop, so a call reads
  `TodoRow(todo)`.
- Its `state` belongs to each row: renaming one row does not put the others
  in edit mode.
- `class:` adds classes to the element's own. The list form may hold an
  `if`, which adds `is-done` only while the todo is done.
- Every control has an accessible name. The checkbox and the icon buttons
  say which todo they act on, so a screen reader — and the tests in step 7
  — can tell them apart ([Accessibility](/about/accessibility)).

**Check it:** `wf check` prints `U03` for `TodoRow` (nothing places it yet)
and four `U04` warnings. The store's `toggle`, `rename` and `remove` no
longer appear: the row calls them.

## Step 6: Write the page

The page holds the box for a new todo, the filters and the list. Here is
its first half:

```wf
// src/pages/Home.wf
page Home(path: "/", title: "Todos", description: "A small list of things to do, kept in your browser.") {
    use Todos
    state draft = ""

    // The filter lives in the address — `/?show=open` — so a reload or a
    // shared link keeps it.
    derived filter: Filter = if query.show == "open" { .open } else if query.show == "done" { .done } else { .all }
    derived shown = match filter {
        .open { Todos.open }
        .done { Todos.done }
        .all { Todos.items }
    }

    action add() {
        Todos.add(draft)
        draft = ""
    }

    Stack(class: "card", gap: .md) {
        Row(justify: .between, align: .baseline) {
            Heading("Todos").h1
            Text("{Todos.open.length} left", class: "count")
        }

        Row(class: "new", gap: .sm) {
            Input(bind: draft, placeholder: "What needs doing?", aria-label: "New todo") {
                on key("Enter") { add() }
            }
            Button("Add", disabled: draft.trim() == "").primary {
                on click { add() }
            }
        }
```

- `bind: draft` ties the input to the state both ways: typing changes
  `draft`, and `draft = ""` empties the box.
- `query` is the address's query string as a value, kept current. So
  `filter` follows the address, and `shown` follows `filter`.
- A `match` over an enum must cover every case. If you add a fourth case to
  `Filter`, this `match` is an error until it handles it.

The second half draws the filters and the list, and closes the page. Add it
below the first, after a blank line:

```wf
// src/pages/Home.wf
        Row(class: "filters", gap: .xs, align: .center) {
            Link("All", to: "/?show=all", class: { "is-on": filter == .all })
            Link("Open", to: "/?show=open", class: { "is-on": filter == .open })
            Link("Done", to: "/?show=done", class: { "is-on": filter == .done })
            Spacer
            if Todos.done.length > 0 {
                Button("Clear done").sm {
                    on click { Todos.clearDone() }
                }
            }
        }

        if shown.length == 0 {
            Text(if Todos.items.length == 0 { "Nothing yet — add your first todo above." } else { "Nothing here." }, class: "empty")
        }
        Stack(class: "list") {
            for todo in shown by todo.id {
                TodoRow(todo, animate: .fadeIn, exit: .fadeOut)
            }
        }
    }
    Text("Your list stays in this browser, and nowhere else.", class: "hint")
}
```

- `for … by todo.id` is a keyed list. When a todo is renamed, or the filter
  hides it, only its row changes; the other rows keep their elements, and
  the row being edited keeps its cursor ([Control flow](/learn/09-control-flow)).
- `animate:` and `exit:` fade a row in and out.
- A class map, `{ "is-on": filter == .all }`, turns a class on while its
  condition holds.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** The key goes on the loop, `by todo.id`, not as a
> `key` prop on the row. See [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

Last, the `app` declaration is the frame every page sits in. `Router`
marks where the current page is drawn:

```wf
// src/App.wf
// The frame every page sits in: a narrow column, centred.
app {
    Container(class: "shell") {
        Router
    }
}
```

Now start the development server in a second terminal, and leave it
running. Every save rebuilds the project and reloads the page:

```bash
wf serve
```

**Check it:** `wf check` prints `No problems in todos.`, and
<http://localhost:3000/> shows a card headed **Todos** with `0 left` and
*Nothing yet — add your first todo above.* Type a todo and press Enter: it
appears, and the count reads `1 left`. Reload the page, and the todo is
still there. Click **Open**, and the address becomes `/?show=open`.

If the server prints `No theme Paper is declared in this project`, you
probably skipped `src/theme.wf` in step 2. If a store member shows as
`U04` here, you probably left out part of the page.

## Step 7: Write tests

A test draws what it declares, then follows its steps in order. It types
into the control named **New todo** and clicks the button named **Add**,
the way a reader would ([Testing](/learn/16-testing)). Create
`tests/todos.wf` with this test:

```wf
// tests/todos.wf
test "adding a todo puts it in the list" {
    use Todos
    state draft = ""
    Input(bind: draft, aria-label: "New todo")
    Button("Add") { on click { Todos.add(draft)  draft = "" } }
    for todo in Todos.items by todo.id { TodoRow(todo) }
    Text("{Todos.open.length} left")

    expect "0 left"
    type "Buy bread" into "New todo"
    click "Add"
    expect "Buy bread"
    expect "1 left"
}
```

A test that clicks or types runs in a headless Chrome. The finished
project has six tests in
[`tests/todos.wf`](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/blob/master/examples/tutorials/easy-todos/tests/todos.wf):
two that only look at a row, and four that click — adding a todo, refusing
a blank one, ticking and clearing, and renaming that keeps one row for
each. Copy the file to have them all, then run them:

```bash
wf test
```

**Check it:** with the whole file, `wf test` ends with `6 passed, 0
failed, 2 snapshot(s) written`. The two tests that only look write a
snapshot of what they drew under `tests/__snapshots__/`, and later runs
compare against it.

If a test that clicks reports that no browser was found, Chrome is not
where `wf` looks: set `WF_CHROME` to its path.

## Step 8: Build it

Check, test and build the project:

```bash
wf check
wf test
wf build
```

`wf check` reports every finding and writes nothing. `wf build` writes
`build/`, which any static host serves: see the recipes for
[GitHub Pages](/recipes/deploy-to-github-pages),
[Netlify](/recipes/deploy-to-netlify),
[Vercel](/recipes/deploy-to-vercel) and
[Cloudflare Pages](/recipes/deploy-to-cloudflare-pages). To load the built page in a
real browser before you deploy, run `wf verify`: it fails on an error, a
missing file or a page that draws nothing.

**Check it:** `wf build` ends with `Build complete.`, and `build/` holds
`index.html`, `app.js` and `styles.css`.

## What you built

- A `type` and an `enum`, held to every use ([Types](/learn/12-types)).
- A store whose list survives a reload with `persist`, and `derived`
  values that follow it ([Stores](/learn/11-stores)).
- A component with state of its own, and accessible names on every
  control ([Components](/learn/10-components)).
- A keyed list, and a filter kept in the address with `query`
  ([Control flow](/learn/09-control-flow)).
- A theme with a dark variant, and the project's own stylesheet
  ([Styling](/learn/13-styling)).
- Tests that look and tests that click ([Testing](/learn/16-testing)).

## Common mistakes

A `match` that misses a case. A `match` over an enum must name every case,
so leaving out `.all` is an error:

```wf expect=T15
enum Filter { all, open, done }

page Home(path: "/", title: "Todos", description: "A small list of things to do.") {
    state filter: Filter = .all
    derived label = match filter {
        .open { "Open" }
        .done { "Done" }
    }
    Heading("Todos").h1
    Text(label)
}
```

Add the missing arm, `.all { "All" }`, or an `else` arm
([T15](/errors/T15)).

A list with no `by`. Without a key, a row that holds a control is drawn
again whenever the list changes, and a box the reader was using loses its
place:

```wf expect=U09
type Todo { id: String, title: String }

page Home(path: "/", title: "Todos", description: "A small list of things to do.") {
    state items: [Todo] = [Todo(id: "1", title: "Buy bread")]
    Heading("Todos").h1
    for todo in items {
        Checkbox(label: todo.title)
    }
}
```

Key the list by what identifies each item: `for todo in items by todo.id`
([U09](/errors/U09)).

A control bound to a `derived` value. `bind:` writes back to what it
names, and a derived value is worked out, never assigned:

```wf expect=F01
store Todos {
    state items: [String] = []
    derived open = items.length
}

page Home(path: "/", title: "Todos", description: "A small list of things to do.") {
    use Todos
    Heading("Todos").h1
    Input(bind: Todos.open, label: "Open")
}
```

Bind a `state`, as the page binds `draft`, and change the store through
its actions ([F01](/errors/F01)).

Going further: [Field Notes](/recipes/build-a-notebook-site) builds a
statically generated site on what this one taught.

## Next

[Language basics](/learn/04-language-basics).



---

# Language basics

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/04-language-basics

This chapter covers the shape of every `.wf` file. A WebFluent program is a
set of declarations: pages, components, stores and the rest, each a keyword
followed by a name and a body. Learn the thirteen kinds and the two kinds of
body, and you can read any `.wf` file.

In this chapter:

- the thirteen declarations, and the chapter that covers each
- how names are written
- comments, including the doc comments the editor shows
- render blocks and imperative blocks, and what goes in each
- the braced `.wf` layout and the indented `.wfx` layout
- the three ways to write a string, and how a string splices in values

## Declarations

A `.wf` file holds top-level declarations and nothing else. You cannot put an
element or a statement loose in a file; it belongs in the body of a
declaration. This file uses all thirteen kinds:

```wf
page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "The front page.") { Heading("Welcome").h1 }
component Pill(_ label: String, tone: Tone = .calm) { Badge(label) }
store Cart { state items = []  derived count = items.length }
theme Brand { color-primary: #0F766E  radius-md: 14px }
app { Navbar { Text("Shop").heading }  Router }
type Todo { id: String, title: String, done: Bool = false }
enum Tone { calm, loud }
api Backend(base: "/api/v1") { get todos() -> [Todo] }
const API = "/api/v1"
data posts = "posts.json"
image hero = "hero.jpg"
animation Pulse { from { opacity: 1 } to { opacity: 0.5 } }
test "pill shows its label" { Pill("Beta")  expect "Beta" }
```

Each keyword declares one kind of thing:

| Declaration | What it is | Read more |
|---|---|---|
| `page` | A route and what it shows | [Pages and routing](/learn/05-pages-and-routing) |
| `component` | A reusable element with typed props, events, slots and parts | [Components](/learn/10-components) |
| `store` | State shared across pages | [Stores](/learn/11-stores) |
| `theme` | Design tokens: colours, spacing, radii, fonts | [Styling](/learn/13-styling) |
| `app` | The shell every page renders inside, with the `Router` | [The app shell](/learn/05-pages-and-routing#the-app-shell) |
| `type`, `enum` | Records and enumerations the type checker enforces | [Types](/learn/12-types) |
| `api` | An HTTP service: its address, its endpoints and what they return | [Describe a service](/learn/15-data#describe-a-service-with-api) |
| `const` | A value read everywhere | [Constants](/reference/expressions#constants) |
| `data` | A JSON file read at build time, as a constant | [Read a file at build time](/learn/15-data#read-a-file-at-build-time-with-data) |
| `image` | A picture the build resizes and hands to `Image` | [Add a picture](/recipes/add-a-picture) |
| `animation` | Keyframes | [Keyframes](/recipes/keyframes) |
| `test` | A render held to expectations and a snapshot | [Testing](/learn/16-testing) |

Two other kinds of file under `src/` join the program. A `.css` file is a
stylesheet the build bundles. A `.js` file is a plain browser script, and its
top-level functions are in scope by name in your `.wf` code
([Call your own JavaScript](/recipes/call-your-own-script)).

Inside a body you write statements: `state`, `derived`, `effect`, `action`,
`persist`, `resource`, `validate`, `socket`, `if`, `for`, `match` and more.
The [grammar](/reference/grammar) lists every keyword and where it may appear.

### One program from many files

All the files under `src/` merge into one program. A component declared in
`components/Pill.wf` is usable from every page without an import. The
compiler reads `App.wf` (or `App.wfx`) first, then the other files in name
order, so a build is the same on every machine.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** There is no `import` or `export` between `.wf`
> files. A component, a store or a type declared in any file under `src/`
> is in scope in every other one. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

## Naming

Names follow fixed conventions, so you can tell what a word is from how it
is written:

- Declaration keywords are lowercase: `page`, `component`, `store`.
- The names they declare, and every element, are **PascalCase**: `Home`,
  `UserCard`, `Button`, `Table.Row`.
- State, props, actions, variables and flags are **camelCase**: `count`,
  `isOpen`, `save`, `.primary`.
- Enum cases start with a dot: `.calm`, `.md`.
- Design tokens start with a dollar sign: `$primary`, `$spacing-md`.

The compiler resolves every name. A name it does not know — a misspelled
element, a flag the element does not take, a case the enum does not have — is
an error with a hint, never a silent no-op.

## Comments

WebFluent has three kinds of comment. A `//` comment runs to the end of the
line, a `/* … */` comment may span lines, and a `///` comment documents the
declaration that follows it:

```wf
// A line comment.
/* A block
   comment. */
/// A person's initials, in a circle.
component Avatar(_ initials: String) { Text(initials).bold }
```

A `///` comment above a declaration, a prop or an event is its documentation.
The editor shows it on hover, and `wf docs` prints it in the component
gallery. Above a `state`, `persist`, `derived` or `action`, it documents that
member, and the editor shows it wherever the member is used.

## Bodies

A body is one of two kinds of block, and each holds different statements:

- A **render block** is the body of a page, a component or `app`. It holds
  elements, and the statements that shape them: `state`, `derived`, `if`,
  `for` and the like.
- An **imperative block** is the body of a handler or an action. It holds
  statements that do something: assignments, calls, `let`, `if`, `for`,
  `try`.

The two blocks have separate grammars. In this page, the `Text` is an element
in the render block, and the assignment sits inside an `on click` handler:

```wf
page Counter(path: "/", title: "Counter", description: "A number that goes up.") {
    state clicks = 0
    Heading("Counter").h1
    Text("Clicked {clicks} times")
    Button("Add one") {
        on click { clicks = clicks + 1 }
    }
}
```

> [!WARNING]
> An assignment written loose in a page body, such as `clicks = clicks + 1`
> next to the `Text`, is error `E105`. Its hint says where the line belongs:
> *"Code that does something goes in `on click { … }`, an `action` or an
> `effect`"*.

### Separating statements

Statements need no separator. You usually put one per line. To put two on one
line, separate them with `;` or with whitespace. Two spaces is the
house style, because it reads well:

```wf
page Score(path: "/", title: "Score", description: "Two teams, two numbers.") {
    state home = 1  state away = 2
    Heading("Score").h1
    Text("{home} – {away}")
    Button("Both score") { on click { home = home + 1; away = away + 1 } }
}
```

## Two layouts: `.wf` and `.wfx`

You can write the same grammar with braces or with indentation. A `.wf` file
opens a block with `{` and closes it with `}`. A `.wfx` file opens a block
with a line indented deeper than the one before it, and closes it when the
indentation returns.

This page is written in the braced layout:

```wf
page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "A panel that opens and closes.") {
    state open = true
    Heading("Home").h1
    Row(gap: .sm) {
        style {
            padding: 6px 0
            &:hover { background: $surface }
        }
        on click { open = !open }
        Text("Details").bold
    }
    if open {
        Spinner
    } else {
        Text("Closed")
    }
}
```

The same page in the indented layout:

```wfx
page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "A panel that opens and closes.")
    state open = true
    Heading("Home").h1
    Row(gap: .sm)
        style
            padding: 6px 0
            &:hover
                background: $surface
        on click { open = !open }
        Text("Details").bold
    if open
        Spinner
    else
        Text("Closed")
```

The indented layout follows these rules:

- A line indented deeper than the line before it opens a block. Indent with
  the same spaces or tabs as the lines around it; four spaces per level is
  the house style, and what `wf fmt` writes.
- A line whose indentation lines up with no enclosing block is error `E003`.
  The first line of a file is not indented.
- You may still write braces yourself, and everything inside them is laid out
  freely: `on click { open = !open }` on one line, or a map literal or an
  argument list across several lines. Inside parentheses and brackets,
  layout is free too.
- An empty block is written `{ }`.
- Blank lines and comment lines do not count.

Both layouts compile to the same output and every tool reads both, so a
project may mix them. `wf fmt --to wfx` converts a project to the indented
layout and `wf fmt --to wf` converts it back, without changing what any file
says. This guide writes `.wf`; every example has a `.wfx` spelling.

## Strings

A string is written in double quotes and splices in a value with `{expr}`:

```wf
page Greeting(path: "/", title: "Greeting", description: "A greeting that knows your age.") {
    state user = { name: "Sam", age: 41 }
    Heading("Hello, {user.name}!").h1
    Text("You are {user.age * 12} months old.")
    Text("A literal brace: \{ and \}")
    Text("A literal dollar: ${user.age}")     // `$` alone is plain text: "$41"
}
```

Spliced text is live: when `user` changes, the text changes with it. A splice
opens with a name, a `(` or a `[`, and closes on the same line; anything
else, such as `{key: value}` in prose, is plain text.

A splice may also say how to show its value: `{total:.currency}`,
`{when:.date(long)}`. This is
[formatting](/reference/expressions#showing-a-value-a-particular-way), written
where the value is read.

### Three ways to write one

A plain `"…"` string reads the escapes `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\"`, `\\`, `\{` and
`\}`, and splices `{…}`. For text that a plain string makes you escape over
and over, there are two other forms:

```wf
// Raw: no escapes, no splices. The text is what is written.
const SAMPLE = #"page Home(path: "/") { state n = 0 }"#

// As many # as the text needs, when it holds a `"#` of its own.
const TRICKY = ##"a raw string ends with "# — like that"##

// Block: over as many lines as it likes, escapes and splices on, and
// the indentation the source gave it removed.
const name = "Ada"
const LETTER = """
    Dear {name},
      thank you.
    """                       // "Dear Ada,\n  thank you."
```

Use each form for a different kind of text:

- A **raw string** (`#"…"#`) suits a sample of code, a regular expression or
  a Windows path: anything full of quotes, braces or backslashes.
- A **block string** (`"""…"""`) suits a paragraph, a template or a query.
  The closing `"""` sets how far the text was indented, and the compiler
  removes that much from every line.

## Quick reference

| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `page Name(path: "/…") { … }` | A declaration: keyword, name, arguments, body |
| `// …`, `/* … */` | Comments |
| `/// …` | Documentation for the declaration, prop, event or member below |
| `PascalCase`, `camelCase` | Declared names and elements; state, props, actions and flags |
| `.case`, `$token` | An enum case; a design token |
| `on click { … }`, `action save() { … }` | Imperative blocks, where assignments go |
| `a = 1; b = 2` or `a = 1  b = 2` | Two statements on one line |
| `.wf`, `.wfx` | Braced layout; indented layout ([grammar](/reference/grammar)) |
| `"Hi, {name}"` | A string with a live splice |
| `"{total:.currency}"` | A splice with a format |
| `#"…"#`, `"""…"""` | A raw string; a block string |

## Common mistakes

An assignment loose in a page body. A render block holds elements; code
that changes something belongs in a handler, an action or an effect:

```wf expect=E105
page Counter(path: "/", title: "Counter", description: "A number that goes up.") {
    state clicks = 0
    Heading("Counter").h1
    clicks = clicks + 1
    Text("Clicked {clicks} times")
}
```

Move the line into `Button("Add one") { on click { clicks = clicks + 1 } }`
([E105](/errors/E105)).

A comma between two statements. Commas separate arguments, never
statements:

```wf expect=E002
page Score(path: "/", title: "Score", description: "Two teams, two numbers.") {
    state home = 1, away = 2
    Heading("Score").h1
    Text("{home} – {away}")
}
```

Write each statement on its own line, or separate them with `;` or two
spaces: `state home = 1  state away = 2` ([E002](/errors/E002)).

A name the language already has. `query`, `env`, `format`, `now` and the
other built-in names cannot be a program's own:

```wf expect=E118
page Search(path: "/", title: "Search", description: "Find a book.") {
    state query = ""
    Heading("Search").h1
    Input(bind: query, label: "Search")
}
```

Choose another name, such as `term` ([E118](/errors/E118)).

## Next

[Pages and routing](/learn/05-pages-and-routing).



---

# Pages and routing

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/05-pages-and-routing

This chapter covers WebFluent's pages and routes: a page is a route and what
it shows. Each page names its own path, so there is no separate route table
to keep in step with your pages.

In this chapter:

- the attributes a page takes
- the `app` shell that frames every page, and the `Router`
- links, `navigate()` and how the active link is marked
- route parameters, query strings and fragments
- layouts, guards and per-page head tags
- a page in another language, with `lang:` and `translates:`
- the catch-all page
- what runs, and in what order, when a page opens

## Declaring a page

A page is a `page` declaration with a name, a `path:` and a body. This page
answers `/about`:

```wf
page About(path: "/about", title: "About us", description: "Who we are and why we build this.") {
    Container {
        Heading("About us").h1
        Paragraph("We are three people and a dog.")
    }
}
```

The page's header takes these attributes:

| Attribute | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `path:` | yes | The route: `"/"`, `"/about"`, `"/posts/:slug"`, or `"*"` for the catch-all |
| `title:` | strongly advised | The `<title>`, the history entry, and what a screen reader announces on arrival. It may name the page's parameters, `"{slug} — Blog"`, or splice an expression over them and the program's constants |
| `description:` | strongly advised | The meta description: the snippet a search result and a link preview show. Keep it under about 160 characters (`S03`) |
| `image:` | | The image a shared link previews with, site-relative or absolute |
| `image_alt:` | | What that image shows, for a reader who cannot see it (`og:image:alt`). `meta.image_alt` in the config describes the site's image |
| `type:` | | `og:type`: `"website"` (the default) or `"article"` |
| `noindex:` | | `true` keeps the page out of search results and out of the sitemap |
| `lang:` | | The language the page is written in, when it is not the site's: `"en"`, `"ar"`, `"pt-BR"`. It sets `<html lang dir>`, `og:locale` and the JSON-LD's `inLanguage` ([A page in its own language](/recipes/site-in-two-languages)) |
| `translates:` | | The page this one is a translation of, by name: `translates: Home`. Translations list each other as `hreflang` alternates |
| `layout:` | | The component that frames the page ([Layouts](#layouts)) |
| `guard:` | | An expression that must hold for the route to render ([Guards](#guards)) |
| `redirect:` | | Where the reader goes when the guard fails. The default is `/` |
| `paths:` | | The values a static build renders a `:param` page for ([Pre-render a page for each item](/recipes/pre-render-each-item)) |
| `name: Type` | | A route parameter, typed ([Route parameters](#route-parameters)) |
