A page without a `title:` builds with warning `S01`, and one without a
`description:` with warning `S02`. The compiler cannot write those for you,
and a page without them looks bare when someone shares or searches for it.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React Router, Vue Router or SvelteKit?** There is no route
> table and no `routes/` folder. Each `page` names its own `path:`, and the
> compiler builds the router from every page. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react#things-that-work-differently).

## The app shell

The `app` declaration is the shell: what every page renders inside, such as a
navbar and a footer. The `Router` marks where the current page goes:

```wf
app {
    Navbar {
        Navbar.Brand { Link("Acme", to: "/") }
        Navbar.Links {
            Link("Docs", to: "/docs").prefix
            Link("Pricing", to: "/pricing")
        }
        Navbar.Actions { Button("Sign in").sm { on click { navigate("/login") } } }
    }
    Router
    Footer { Text("© Acme").muted.sm }
}
```

The `Router` behaves like this:

- It is bare: it takes no children, and it may sit at any depth inside `app`
  (in a `Row`, a `Container`, a `Stack`).
- Its route table is built from every page's `path:`, ordered by
  specificity: static segments before `:params`, and `*` last. The order you
  declare pages in can never shadow a route.
- A project with no `app` declaration gets a bare router.
- `Router(transition: .fade, duration: "200ms")` animates page changes
  ([Motion](/recipes/route-transitions)).

## Links and navigation

A `Link` is an `<a>` whose clicks the router handles. To move from code, for
example after a button press, call `navigate(path)`:

```wf
page Start(path: "/", title: "Start", description: "Where the tour begins.") {
    Heading("Start here").h1
    Link("Home", to: "/")
    Link("Guide", to: "/docs").prefix           // also active on /docs/anything
    Button("Take the tour") { on click { navigate("/about") } }
}

page Guide(path: "/docs", title: "Guide", description: "The guide.") { Heading("Guide").h1 }
page About(path: "/about", title: "About", description: "Who we are.") { Heading("About").h1 }
```

### The active link

The link whose `to:` matches the current route carries the class `.active`
and `aria-current="page"`, so you can style it and a screen reader announces
it. Two rules widen or narrow the match:

- `.prefix` (the flag for `active: .prefix`) also makes a link active on the
  routes beneath it, which suits a section link such as **Guide**.
- A `to:` with a query, such as `"/?show=open"`, is active only when the
  address carries those values too. A row of filter links then marks the one
  that is on, and a plain link to the same path gives way to it.

### Paths under a sub-path

Write every path from the site's root, `"/about"`, even when the site is
served under a sub-path. With `build.base_path` set to `"/docs"`, the
compiler prefixes every `Link`, every `navigate()` and every asset for you.

### Static and single-page navigation

How a link moves depends on the build:

- In a static build, a link is a real page load, and so is `navigate()`.
- In a single-page app, a link swaps the page without a reload. Focus moves
  to the new page's heading, the scroll goes back to the top (or to the
  `#fragment` the address names), and the new title is announced.

## Route parameters

A `:name` segment in the path is a typed parameter of the page. You read it
as a plain name, or as `params.name`:

```wf
type Post { slug: String, title: String, body: String }

store Posts {
    state all: [Post] = [
        Post(slug: "hello", title: "Hello", body: "First post."),
        Post(slug: "again", title: "Again", body: "Second post.")
    ]
}

page PostPage(path: "/posts/:slug", title: "Post", description: "One post.", slug: String) {
    use Posts
    derived post = Posts.all.find(p => p.slug == slug)
    if let p = post {
        Heading(p.title).h1
        Paragraph(p.body)
    } else {
        Heading("No such post").h1
        Text("Nothing lives at /posts/{params.slug}.")
    }
}
```

A parameter is a `String` unless you declare another type, such as
`id: Number`. A static build renders a `:param` page once for each value its
`paths:` names ([Pre-render a page for each item](/recipes/pre-render-each-item)).

## Query strings and fragments

`query` is the URL's query string as a map, and `hash` is its `#fragment`.
The runtime keeps both current, so a page that reads them follows the
address:

```wf
page Products(path: "/products", title: "Products", description: "Everything we sell.") {
    derived tab = query.tab ?? "all"
    derived sort = query.sort ?? "name"
    Heading("Products").h1
    Row(gap: .sm) {
        Link("All", to: "/products?tab=all")
        Link("On sale", to: "/products?tab=sale")
    }
    Text("Showing {tab}, sorted by {sort}; section: {hash}")
}
```

A query string is not part of the route: `/products?tab=sale` is the
`/products` page. To change the query from code, call
`navigate("/products?tab=sale")`.

The *static paint* is the HTML the build pre-renders for a page. In it,
`query` and `hash` are unknown, so anything that depends on them is drawn
once the page is live in the browser.

## Layouts

A layout is a component that frames a page. You name it with `layout:`, and
the page renders in its default slot. Use a layout for one section's chrome,
such as a docs sidebar or an app rail; the `app` shell is for the whole
site's.

In this example, two docs pages share one sidebar and breadcrumb:

```wf
component DocsShell(_ crumb: String) {
    slot
    Row(gap: .lg) {
        Sidebar {
            Sidebar.Item(to: "/docs") { Text("Guide") }
            Sidebar.Item(to: "/docs/reference") { Text("Reference") }
        }
        Stack {
            Breadcrumb {
                Breadcrumb.Item(to: "/docs") { Text("Docs") }
                Breadcrumb.Item { Text(crumb) }
            }
            children
        }
    }
}

page Guide(path: "/docs", title: "Guide", description: "The guide.", layout: DocsShell("Guide")) {
    Heading("Guide").h1
}

page Reference(path: "/docs/reference", title: "Reference", description: "The reference.", layout: DocsShell("Reference")) {
    Heading("Reference").h1
}
```

A layout follows these rules:

- The compiler checks the layout's arguments like any component call
  (`DocsShell("Guide")`).
- The layout component must declare a default `slot`, and place `children`
  where the page goes. Without the `slot` line the build stops with error
  `E104`. A component that is only ever called, not named as a layout,
  needs `children` alone ([Slots](/learn/10-components#slots)).
- The page's skip link jumps past the layout's chrome to the page's first
  element. That element gets `id="wf-content"` when it has no id of its own.

## Guards

A guard keeps a route from rendering until a condition holds. `guard:` names
an expression, usually a store's derived value. When it is false, the reader
is sent to `redirect:` (by default, `/`):

```wf
store Auth {
    state user = null
    derived loggedIn = user != null
    action login() { user = { name: "Sam" } }
    action logout() { user = null }
}

page Account(path: "/account", title: "Your account", description: "Your account.", guard: Auth.loggedIn, redirect: "/login") {
    use Auth
    Heading("Welcome back").h1
    Button("Sign out") { on click { Auth.logout() } }
}

page Login(path: "/login", title: "Sign in", description: "Sign in.") {
    use Auth
    Heading("Sign in").h1
    Button("Sign in").primary { on click { Auth.login()  navigate("/account") } }
}
```

The browser evaluates the guard on every navigation.

> [!CAUTION]
> A guard is a gate in the browser, not a secret. A static build still
> pre-renders the guarded page's HTML, so keep anything private behind an
> API that the page fetches.

## Per-page head tags

A `head { }` block adds tags of the page's own to the document's `<head>`.
The build writes them into the static paint where it knows the value, the
live page keeps them current, and they are removed when the reader leaves
the page:

```wf
page Share(path: "/share", title: "Share", description: "A page with its own tags.") {
    state image = "/og-share.png"
    head {
        meta(property: "og:image", content: image)
        link(rel: "canonical", href: "https://example.com/share")
        script(src: "/analytics.js", defer: true)
    }
    Heading("Share").h1
}
```

A tag's `src:` and `href:` go through the same scheme check as every
address, at build time and on the live page, so a value never points one at
`javascript:` or `data:`. A `script(src:)` is written out, never read from a
value, and a `meta(http-equiv: "refresh")` may not take its address from
one (`E107`): whoever controls the value would choose what the page runs or
where the reader goes.

`title:` and `description:` are page attributes, not head tags. From them
and the config, the compiler writes the standard tags itself: charset,
viewport, description, canonical, Open Graph, Twitter card and JSON-LD.

## A page in another language

A page written in a language other than the site's says so with `lang:`, and
names the page it translates with `translates:`. This site is in English,
with its home page in Arabic at `/ar`:

```wf
page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "What we make.") {
    Heading("Welcome").h1
}

page HomeAr(path: "/ar", title: "الرئيسية", description: "ما نصنعه.", lang: "ar", translates: Home) {
    Heading("أهلاً بك").h1
}
```

What the two attributes do:

- **`lang:`** writes the page as `<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">`, with its
  `og:locale` and its JSON-LD's `inLanguage` to match. The router sets
  `lang` and `dir` when it shows the page, and puts the site's back on a page
  without one.
- **`translates:`** joins the pages. Each lists the others as `hreflang`
  alternates, each at its own address, with `x-default` for the one in the
  site's language, so a search engine finds every language.
- A `translates:` that names no page, or two translations of one page in one
  language, is `R05`.

This is different from `t()` and `setLocale`, which translate one address in
the browser. [Publish a page in each language](/recipes/site-in-two-languages)
compares the two.

## The catch-all page

A page with `path: "*"` answers every route no other page claims. The router
shows it in the browser, and a static host serves it as `404.html`:

```wf
page NotFound(path: "*", title: "Not found", description: "Nothing lives here.", noindex: true) {
    Container {
        Heading("Nothing here").h1
        Link("Back home", to: "/")
    }
}
```

## Set-up code: what runs when a page opens

A page's body is a render block: it declares state, derived values and
actions, and lists what to show. The top of the body runs once, when the page
renders. A call written there, such as `Deploys.load(id)`, is *set-up code*:
it runs once as the page opens.

```wf
store Deploys {
    state rows = []
    action load(id: String) { rows = [{ id: id, ok: true }] }
}

page Deploy(path: "/deploys/:id", title: "Deploy", description: "One deploy.", id: String) {
    use Deploys
    Deploys.load(id)
    Heading("Deploy {id}").h1
    for row in Deploys.rows by row.id {
        Text("{row.id}: {row.ok}")
    }
}
```

### The life of a page

A page goes through these stages, in order:

1. The route matches. In a split build, the page's chunk loads, and its
   stylesheet with it.
2. The body runs **once**: each `state` takes its initial value, set-up calls
   run, and the elements are created. Nothing re-renders after this; whatever
   reads a state updates on its own.
3. Each `effect` runs, and runs again when what it reads changes. Timers
   start.
4. The page is placed. In a single-page app, focus moves to its heading, the
   scroll goes to the top and the title is announced.
5. When the route changes, everything the page created is disposed of:
   effects, timers, listeners, connections and `.route` stores. Their
   `cleanup { }` blocks run.

There is no `onMount` to write. Set-up code runs at stage 2, an `effect` at
stage 3, and `after(0) { … }` once the page is on screen.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** A page's body is not a function called on every
> render; it runs once. Set-up code does what `useEffect(…, [])` did, and
> nothing re-renders after it. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react#things-that-work-differently).

## Quick reference

| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `page Name(path: "/x", title: "…", description: "…") { … }` | A page and its route |
| `path: "/posts/:slug"`, `slug: String` | A typed route parameter, read as `slug` or `params.slug` |
| `path: "*"` | The catch-all page, served as `404.html` |
| `app { … Router … }` | The shell around every page, and where the page goes |
| `Link("Docs", to: "/docs").prefix` | A link, active on its route and the routes beneath it |
| `navigate("/about")` | Move to a route from code |
| `query.tab`, `hash` | The query string and the fragment, kept current |
| `layout: Shell("Crumb")` | Frame the page with a component's default slot |
| `guard: Auth.loggedIn, redirect: "/login"` | Render only while a condition holds |
| `head { meta(…) link(…) script(…) }` | Tags of the page's own in `<head>` |
| `lang: "ar", translates: Home` | A page in another language, joined to the page it translates |

The [configuration reference](/reference/config) covers `build.base_path`,
and [Static or single-page](/about/static-or-single-page) covers how each build
serves pages.

## Common mistakes

**A route names a parameter the page does not declare.** Each `:name` in
the path is a parameter of the page, and the page must declare it:

```wf expect=R02
page Post(path: "/posts/:slug", title: "Post", description: "One post.") {
    Heading("A post").h1
}
```

Add `slug: String` to the page's header, beside `path:`, and read it as
`slug` ([R02](/errors/R02)).

**A link to a page that does not exist.** The compiler knows every route, so
a `Link` or a `navigate()` to a path no page answers stops the build:

```wf expect=R01
page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "The front page.") {
    Heading("Home").h1
    Link("About us", to: "/about")
}
```

Declare the page, `page About(path: "/about", …)`, or fix the path
([R01](/errors/R01)).

**A layout with nowhere to put the page.** A `layout:` component must
declare a default `slot` and place `children` where the page goes:

```wf expect=E104
component Shell(_ crumb: String) {
    Stack {
        Text(crumb)
    }
}

page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "The front page.", layout: Shell("Home")) {
    Heading("Home").h1
}
```

Add `slot` at the top of `Shell` and `children` inside its `Stack`
([E104](/errors/E104)).

## Next

[Elements](/learn/06-elements).



---

# Elements

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/06-elements

This chapter covers WebFluent's elements: everything a page shows, whether a
built-in such as `Button` or a component you declare. Every element is
written in the same shape, so once you can read one call you can read them
all.

In this chapter:

- the shape of an element call, and the order of its block
- props, enum cases and flags, and the props every element takes
- HTML attributes, and which element of a built-in receives them
- parts, such as `Card.Header`
- the text, heading and layout elements
- the families of built-ins, the HTML they render, and what the compiler
  checks on every element

## The call shape

Every element call has the same five pieces, each optional except the name:

```text
Name(positional, prop: value, prop: value).flag.flag { block }
```

- **`Name`** is PascalCase: a built-in (`Card`), a part of one
  (`Card.Header`), or a component of the project (`UserCard`,
  `Panel.Footer`).
- **One positional argument** comes first, unnamed. It is the element's main
  value: a button's label, a heading's text, an icon's name. You pass every
  other value by name.
- **Named props**, `name: value`, come in any order, and the value may be any
  expression.
- **Flags**, `.name`, are written tight against the closing parenthesis, or
  against the name when there are no parentheses: `Button("Save").primary.lg`,
  `Spacer.sm`, `Card.elevated { … }`. An element or a component called with
  no arguments needs no parentheses: `Spinner` and `Spinner()` are the same
  call, and this book writes the shorter one.
- **The block**, `{ … }`, holds its contents in a fixed order: `style { }`,
  then `transition { }`, then `on … { }` handlers, then slot fills, then
  children.

This button uses all five pieces, with its block in that order:

```wf
page Editor(path: "/", title: "Editor", description: "A save button, fully dressed.") {
    Heading("Editor").h1
    Button("Save", disabled: false).primary.lg {
        style { min-width: 120px }
        transition { background: 150ms ease-out }
        on click { log("saved") }
        Icon("check")
    }
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from JSX or a Vue template?** There are no tags and no string
> attributes: `<Button variant="primary" size="lg">Save</Button>` is
> `Button("Save").primary.lg`. A prop's value is an expression, never a
> string to be parsed, and children go in the block. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react#the-map).

## Props, cases and flags

Each prop has a type the compiler knows: `String`, `Number`, `Bool`, a state
binding, a path, or an **enum**, which is a fixed set of named cases. You
pass an enum prop a case, written with a leading dot:

```wf
page Toolbar(path: "/", title: "Toolbar", description: "Two labels, spaced apart.") {
    Heading("Toolbar").h1
    Row(gap: .md, align: .center, justify: .between) {
        Text("Drafts")
        Text("3 unsent")
    }
}
```

A **flag** is a short way to write one of two things: a `Bool` prop set to
`true`, or a case of one of the element's enum props. Each comment shows the
long spelling of the flags on its line:

```wf
page Search(path: "/", title: "Search", description: "A search box and two buttons.") {
    state term = ""
    Heading("Search").h1
    Button("Delete").danger                                // tone: .danger
    Button("Continue").full.outlined                       // width: .full, outlined: true
    Input(bind: term, label: "Search").search.required     // type: .search, required: true
}
```

The two spellings mean the same thing. `.md` on a `Row` means `gap: .md`,
because `gap` is the only prop of `Row` with an `md` case. A flag follows
these rules:

- When two enum props of an element share a case name, the flag is
  ambiguous. The compiler reports `E103` and asks you to name the prop.
- A flag the element does not declare is error `E103`, and the message lists
  the flags the element takes. There is no shared vocabulary of modifiers to
  guess from.
- A `Bool` prop may take a condition instead of a flag:
  `Button("Light", outlined: theme != "light")`.

### Universal props

Every element also takes the *universal props*. The reference does not
repeat them on each element:

| Prop | What it does | Read more |
|---|---|---|
| `class:` | Adds classes from your own stylesheets. It adds; it never replaces | [Styling](/learn/13-styling#classes-and-your-own-stylesheet) |
| `ref:` | Names a handle on the element: `box.focus()` | [State and reactivity](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity#element-handles) |
| `mount:`, `update:`, `cleanup:` | Hands the element to a script each time it is made, again when what `update` reads changes, and takes it back when it leaves | [Hand an element to a script](/recipes/hand-an-element-to-a-script) |
| `animate:` or a flag (`.fadeIn`) | The animation it enters with | [Animate in and out](/recipes/animate-in-and-out#animate-an-element-in) |
| `exit:` | The animation it leaves with | [Animate in and out](/recipes/animate-in-and-out#animate-an-element-out) |
| `delay:`, `duration:`, `speed:` (`.fast`, `.slow`), `easing:` | How the animation is timed | [Animate in and out](/recipes/animate-in-and-out), [Motion defaults](/recipes/motion-defaults) |
| `stagger:` | Inside a `for`, each item's delay grows by this much | [Animate a list](/recipes/animate-a-list) |
| `on:` | When the animation plays: `.mount` (the default) or `.enterView` | [Animate in and out](/recipes/animate-in-and-out#play-an-animation-when-it-is-scrolled-to) |
| `shared:` | A name the element keeps across a route change | [Shared element](/recipes/shared-element) |
| `count:` | A number in its text counts up or down to its new value | [Count a number](/recipes/count-a-number) |

The [components reference](/reference) lists every element's
own props.

## Attributes

A named argument that is not a prop becomes an HTML attribute. These
families are declared, so they draw no warning:

- the global attributes: `id`, `title`, `role`, `tabindex`, `lang`, `dir`,
  `hidden`;
- `aria-*` and `data-*`;
- the attributes of the element's kind: input, anchor, media, form and table
  attributes on the elements that take them.

Any other name is still written to the element, with warning `C04`. You write
a hyphenated name as it is:

```wf
page Signup(path: "/", title: "Sign up", description: "A name field and a menu button.") {
    state name = ""
    Heading("Sign up").h1
    Button("More", aria-expanded: "false", aria-controls: "panel", data-track: "more")
    Input(bind: name, label: "Name", id: "name", autocomplete: "name", maxlength: 40)
}
```

### Attribute values

An attribute's value follows these rules:

- A value that reads state is kept in step with it.
- `true` is written as the word: `data-open: true` renders
  `data-open="true"`, so the selector `[data-open="true"]` matches it.
- A boolean attribute such as `hidden` or `disabled` is either present or
  absent.
- `false` removes an attribute, except an `aria-*` one, which keeps the
  string `"false"` because it is a real ARIA state.

The same rules apply to an attribute you write on a call of your own
component, which passes it to the component's root.

### Where a built-in puts them

A built-in places your attributes and `on` handlers on the element it draws:

- On its root, for most built-ins: the scrolling box of a `VirtualList`, the
  handle of a `Splitter`, the box of a `Tabs` or a `Carousel`, the panel of a
  `Sidebar`, the `<nav>` of a `Breadcrumb`, the `<dialog>` of a `Modal`.
- On its input, for a control drawn inside a box (`Switch`, `Checkbox`,
  `Radio`, `Slider`, `DatePicker`, `FileUpload`). The input is the control,
  and its own handlers are already there. `hidden`, `lang` and `dir` belong
  to the whole control, so they stay on its box.

A `role:` or `aria-label:` you write takes the place of the one the built-in
gives itself: a `Splitter`'s `separator`, a `Switch`'s `switch`, a
`Breadcrumb`'s name. A `Sidebar`'s `id:` is the one its toggle points at.

This list box puts `role`, `tabindex` and `aria-activedescendant` on the
`VirtualList`'s scrolling box, and a `role` and `id` on each row:

```wf
page References(path: "/", title: "References", description: "A list box of references.") {
    state refs = [{ id: "a" }, { id: "b" }, { id: "c" }]
    state current = 0
    Heading("References").h1
    VirtualList(rowHeight: 24, label: "References", role: "listbox", tabindex: "0", aria-activedescendant: "ref-{current}") {
        style { height: 240px }
        on keydown(e) { if e.key == "ArrowDown" { current = current + 1 } }
        for r in refs by r.id { Text(r.id, id: "ref-{r.id}", role: "option") }
    }
}
```

The pre-rendered page and the template engine write the same attributes on
the same elements, as far as the build knows their values.

## Parts

Some built-ins are made of parts. You write a part under its owner's name,
inside its owner:

```wf
page Regions(path: "/", title: "Regions", description: "A card, a table, a select and tabs.") {
    state region = "fra1"
    Heading("Regions").h1
    Card.elevated {
        Card.Header { Heading("Frankfurt").h2 }
        Card.Body { Text("Our main region.") }
        Card.Footer { Button("Open").primary }
    }
    Table(caption: "Regions") {
        Table.Head { Table.Row { Table.Cell("Region").header  Table.Cell("Latency").header } }
        Table.Body { Table.Row { Table.Cell("fra1")  Table.Cell("34 ms") } }
    }
    Select(bind: region, label: "Region") {
        Select.Option("Frankfurt", value: "fra1")
        Select.Option("Iowa", value: "iad1")
    }
    Tabs {
        Tabs.Page("Summary") { Text("Two regions.") }
        Tabs.Page("Details") { Text("fra1 and iad1.") }
    }
}
```

A part belongs inside its owner. `Card.Body` outside a `Card` is error
`C03`. Your own components may declare parts too
([Components](/learn/10-components)).

A `Tabs` keeps the open tab in a state of yours with `bind:`, holding the
open page's `value:`. Only the open tab is in the Tab order; the arrow keys
move between tabs, the other way round in a right-to-left page:

```wf
page Account(path: "/account", title: "Account", description: "Your profile and billing.") {
    state tab = "profile"
    Heading("Account").h1
    Tabs(bind: tab, label: "Account") {
        Tabs.Page("Profile", value: "profile") { Text("Your name and photo.") }
        Tabs.Page("Billing", value: "billing") { Text("Your plan and invoices.") }
    }
    Text("Open: {tab}")
}
```

Any element of your own can move the same way: `roving: .x` makes a row
one stop for Tab, with the arrow keys inside it
([Events](/learn/08-events#moving-through-a-group-with-the-arrow-keys)).

## Text and headings

The typography elements cover inline text, headings, paragraphs, code,
quotations and Markdown:

```wf
page Article(path: "/", title: "Article", description: "Every kind of text.") {
    state count = 3
    Heading("Release notes").h1                // a real <h1>; .h2 is the default
    Text("{count} changes").bold.muted         // a run of text
    Paragraph("Prose, as a <p>.")
    Code("let x = 1").block
    Blockquote("A quotation.")
    Markdown("**Bold** and a [link](/docs)")   // Markdown, rendered as HTML
}
```

The compiler checks the outline the headings form: a page needs an `h1`
(`A12`), and a heading level may not be skipped, such as `h2` straight to
`h4` (`A11`).

[Render Markdown](/recipes/render-markdown) shows what `Markdown`
draws, and how to show text somebody else wrote.

## Layout elements

The layout elements arrange what is inside them. Each comment says what the
element is:

```wf
page Dashboard(path: "/", title: "Dashboard", description: "Every layout element at once.") {
    Header { Heading("Dashboard").h1 }
    Container {                                  // centred, with a max width
        Row(gap: .md, align: .center) {          // horizontal flex
            Column(span: 8) { Text("main") }     // a child of a 12-column grid
            Column(span: 4) { Text("aside") }
        }
        Grid(columns: 3, gap: .lg) { Card { Text("a") }  Card { Text("b") }  Card { Text("c") } }
        Stack(gap: .sm) { Text("one")  Text("two") }   // vertical flex
        Spacer.lg
        Divider
    }
    Section { Text("another region") }
    Footer { Text("the last region") }
}
```

`Header`, `Section` and `Footer` render real landmarks: `<header>`,
`<section>` and `<footer>`. Use them for the page's regions, so a screen
reader and a search engine can follow the page's outline. Inside a
`Document`, `Header` and `Footer` mean something else: they are drawn in
the margin of every printed page ([PDF and slides](/learn/17-pdf-and-slides#set-the-paper-headers-and-footers)).

## The families of built-ins

The built-ins fall into these families:

| Family | Elements |
|---|---|
| Layout | `Container`, `Row`, `Column`, `Grid`, `Stack`, `Spacer`, `Divider`, `Header`, `Section`, `Footer`, `VirtualList`, `Splitter` |
| Navigation | `Navbar`, `Sidebar`, `Link`, `Tabs`, `Breadcrumb`, `Menu`, `OnThisPage`, `Pagination`, `Stepper` |
| Data display | `Card`, `Table`, `List`, `Badge`, `Tag`, `Avatar`, `Tooltip` |
| Content | `Callout`, `Kbd`, `EmptyState`, `Stat`, `CodeBlock`, `Chip`, `Accordion`, `VisuallyHidden` ([below](#content-a-note-a-key-a-figure)) |
| Forms | `Form`, `Input`, `Textarea`, `Select`, `Checkbox`, `Radio`, `Switch`, `Slider`, `DatePicker`, `FileUpload`, `Field`, `Fieldset`, `InputGroup`, `RadioGroup`, `NumberInput`, `Calendar` ([Forms](/learn/14-forms)) |
| Feedback | `Alert`, `Toast`, `Modal`, `Dialog`, `Popover`, `Spinner`, `Progress`, `Skeleton` ([Events](/learn/08-events#overlays-modals-dialogs-toasts-and-menus)) |
| Actions | `Button`, `IconButton`, `ButtonGroup`, `Dropdown`, `CopyButton`, `ThemeToggle`, `LocaleSwitch`, `Toggle`, `ToggleGroup` |
| Media | `Image`, `Video`, `Audio`, `Frame`, `Icon`, `Carousel` ([Add a picture](/recipes/add-a-picture), [Video and audio](/recipes/video-and-audio)) |
| Typography | `Text`, `Heading`, `Paragraph`, `Code`, `Blockquote`, `Markdown`, `Unsafe.Html` |
| Somebody else's code | `Host`, `Element`, `Portal` ([Call your own JavaScript](/recipes/call-your-own-script), [Hand an element to a script](/recipes/hand-an-element-to-a-script)) |
| Documents and decks | `Document`, `PageBreak`, `TableOfContents`, `Background`, `Watermark`, `Chart`, `QrCode`, `Presentation`, `Slide`, `TitleSlide`, `SectionSlide`, `TwoColumn`, `ImageSlide` ([PDF and slides](/learn/17-pdf-and-slides)) |
| Routing | `Router` ([Pages](/learn/05-pages-and-routing#the-app-shell)) |

### Content: a note, a key, a figure

The content built-ins are the pieces a page of text and figures is made
of. Each is drawn the same on the live page, in the static paint and in a
PDF:

```wf
page Report(path: "/", title: "Report", description: "The month, at a glance.") {
    state tags = ["Rust", "Go"]
    Heading("Report").h1
    Callout("Figures are for the month to date.").note
    Row(gap: .lg) {
        Stat("Revenue", value: 48210, format: .currency, change: 0.124)
        Stat("Churn", value: 0.031, format: .percent, change: -0.02)
    }
    Text { Text("Search with ")  Kbd("mod+k") }
    for tag in tags by tag {
        Chip(tag).removable { on remove { tags = tags.filter(x => x != tag) } }
    }
    CodeBlock("wf build", language: "bash", title: "Terminal").copy
    Accordion.single {
        Accordion.Item("How is revenue counted?") { Text("Paid invoices, by the day they were paid.") }
        Accordion.Item("When does the month end?") { Text("At midnight UTC on its last day.") }
    }
    if tags.length == 0 {
        EmptyState(icon: "folder", title: "No tags", text: "Add one to group the report.")
    }
}
```

- **`Callout`** is a note set apart from the text, with its kind's icon
  and word: `.note`, `.tip`, `.important`, `.warning`, `.caution`, or a
  `title:` of its own.
- **`Stat`** says which way a figure moved, to a screen reader as well
  ("Up 12.4%").
- **`Kbd`** writes a key combination as this system does: `⌘K` on a Mac,
  `Ctrl+K` elsewhere.
- **`Chip`** can be pressed (`selected:`, a toggle button) and removed
  (`.removable`, its button named `Remove Rust`, firing `on remove`).
- **`CodeBlock`** adds a bar with the file name and a copy button, and
  `.lines` numbers the lines.
- **`Accordion`** is native `<details>`; `.single` keeps one open at a time.
- **`VisuallyHidden`** is words only a screen reader hears.

## What an element renders

Each built-in renders real, semantic HTML. A `Button` is a `<button>`, a
`Link` an `<a>`, a `Heading(…).h2` an `<h2>`, and a `Table` a `<table>` with
`<th scope="col">` cells in its head.

Each also carries a stable class named after it, with a modifier class for
each flag. For example, `Button("Save").primary.lg` renders:

```html
<button class="wf-btn wf-btn--primary wf-btn--large" type="button">Save</button>
```

These classes are part of the public surface and stay stable across
releases, so your own stylesheet may target them
([Styling](/learn/13-styling#classes-and-your-own-stylesheet)). The reference
names each element's class.

## What the compiler checks on every element

The compiler holds every element call to these rules:

| What it checks | When it fails |
|---|---|
| The name is a built-in, a part inside its owner, or a declared component | `E101`; a part outside its owner is `C03` |
| There is at most one positional argument, and the element takes one | A second is `E113`; one a built-in does not take is `C05` |
| Every named prop exists, with a value of its type, and an enum prop's case exists | A wrong type is `T01`; a missing case is `E103` |
| A named argument that is not a prop is a declared attribute | Any other is written as an attribute, with `C04` |
| Every flag resolves to exactly one prop | `E103` |
| A handler names a DOM event, or one of the component's declared events | `V09` for any other name, such as a misspelled `on clik` |
| A slot fill names a declared slot | `E103` |
| An `Icon("name")` or `icon:` names an icon the runtime draws ([the list](/reference#icons)) | `V08`; the name shows as a word |
| Accessibility: an `Image` has `alt:`, an `IconButton` a `label:`, a control a label, a `Modal` a title, a `Table` a `Table.Head` | `A01`–`A10` |

## Quick reference

| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Name(value, prop: value)` | An element with one positional and named props |
| `.flag` | A `Bool` prop set to `true`, or an enum prop's case |
| `prop: .case` | An enum prop, named |
| `{ style { } transition { } on … { } fills children }` | The block, in its fixed order |
| `aria-label: "…"`, `data-tone: "…"`, `id: "…"` | HTML attributes |
| `Owner.Part { … }` | A part, inside its owner |
| `class:`, `ref:`, `mount:`, `animate:` | Universal props, on every element |

The [components reference](/reference) lists each built-in's
props, flags, events, slots and parts; `wf registry --json` prints the same
data for a tool.

## Common mistakes

**A second positional argument.** Only the first argument may go without a
name, so a tone passed after the label does not build:

```wf expect=E113
page Trash(path: "/", title: "Trash", description: "Empty the trash.") {
    Heading("Trash").h1
    Button("Empty the trash", "danger")
}
```

Write the tone as a flag, `Button("Empty the trash").danger`, or name it,
`tone: .danger` ([E113](/errors/E113)).

**A flag the element does not have.** Flags are not a shared vocabulary; each
element takes its own, and a word it does not declare stops the build:

```wf expect=E103
page Save(path: "/", title: "Save", description: "A save button.") {
    Heading("Save").h1
    Button("Save").huge
}
```

The finding lists the flags `Button` takes; `.lg` is its largest size
([E103](/errors/E103)).

**A part outside its owner.** A part only means something inside the element
it belongs to:

```wf expect=C03
page Profile(path: "/", title: "Profile", description: "A profile card.") {
    Heading("Profile").h1
    Card.Body { Text("Sam, designer") }
}
```

Wrap it in its owner, `Card { Card.Body { … } }`, or use a plain `Stack`
([C03](/errors/C03)).

## Next

[State and reactivity](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity).



---

# State and reactivity

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/07-state-and-reactivity

This chapter covers state and reactivity in WebFluent. A `state` is a value
the page can change. Anything that reads it — a text, an attribute, a
`derived` value, an `effect`, a style splice — updates when it changes, and
nothing else does. This is *fine-grained reactivity*: there is no
re-render of a component tree, and you never subscribe or unsubscribe by hand.

In this chapter:

- `state`, `derived` and `effect` — the three kinds of reactive value
- actions and `let` locals — the code that changes state
- `persist`, timers and element handles
- how the runtime cleans up after a page, a branch or a list item
- the browser's own values: `viewport`, `query`, `now` and the rest
- where a name is looked up, and the mistakes people make

## `state`

You declare a state at the top of a page, component or store body, with an
initial value. This counter shows the whole idea — one state, a text that
reads it, and a button that writes it:

```wf
page Counter(path: "/", title: "Counter", description: "A state, read and written.") {
    state count = 0                  // inferred: Number
    state name: String = "Sam"       // declared
    state items: [String] = []       // a list of strings
    state selected: String? = null   // may be null
    state user = { name: "Sam", tags: ["admin"] }   // a map literal: its fields are its type

    Heading("Counter").h1
    Text("{name} has clicked {count} times")
    Button("+1") { on click { count = count + 1 } }
}
```

Each click sets `count`, and only the `Text` that reads it changes.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** `useState` returns a value and a setter, and a
> change runs the whole component again. A `state` is assigned directly,
> `count = count + 1`, and the body never runs again: only what reads
> `count` updates. A value that should follow a prop or a state is a
> `derived`. See [Coming from React](/coming-from/react#things-that-work-differently).

The type of a state is read off its initial value, or written after a colon.
[Types](/learn/12-types) has the type language. Assigning a value of another type
is an error (`T01`).

You write state only in an imperative block — a handler, an action or an
effect. You can:

- assign it: `count = count + 1`
- change a place inside it: `user.name = "Ann"`, `items[0] = "Pen"`
- call a method that changes it: `items.push("Pen")`, `items.sort()`

A change inside a value gives the state a new copy with that place changed, so
everything that reads it repaints, and a `persist` value is written.

The *static paint* — the HTML the build pre-renders for a page — seeds every
state with its initial value, so a pre-rendered page shows what the first
paint in the browser would.

## `derived`

A derived value is computed from state, and computed again when any state it
read changes. This cart works out its subtotal, total and whether it is empty:

```wf
page Cart(path: "/", title: "Cart", description: "Totals worked out from state.") {
    state items = [{ name: "Pen", price: 2.5, qty: 4 }, { name: "Pad", price: 6, qty: 1 }]
    state taxRate = 0.2
    derived subtotal = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0)
    derived total = subtotal * (1 + taxRate)
    derived empty = items.length == 0

    Heading("Your cart").h1
    Text("Subtotal: {format(subtotal, .currency)}")
    Text("Total: {format(total, .currency)}")
    if empty { Text("Your cart is empty.").muted }
}
```

The rules:

- A derived value may read state, other derived values and the browser's
  values, and may call an action that returns a value.
- It is never assigned to (`X01`), and an action it calls may not assign
  state (`X04`).
- The static paint seeds it from the initial state.

## `effect`

An effect runs once, then again whenever a state it read changes. Its
`cleanup { }` block runs before the next run, and when the page — or the
branch the effect lives in — leaves:

```wf
page Watch(path: "/", title: "Watch", description: "Effects that follow a search.") {
    state search = ""
    effect {
        log("search is now {search}")
    }
    effect {
        document.title = "Search: {search}"
        cleanup { document.title = "Search" }
    }
    Heading("Watch").h1
    Input(bind: search, placeholder: "Search")
}
```

Use an effect for the world outside the page: the document title, a
third-party widget, a subscription. Keep computation in `derived`.

> [!WARNING]
> An effect that writes what it reads — `effect { n = n + 1 }` — starts its own
> next run and never settles. The compiler refuses it (`X02`). Compute the
> value with `derived` instead.

## Actions and locals

An action is a named function of a page, component or store. Its body is an
imperative block: assignments, `let` locals, calls, `if`, `for`, `try`,
`return` and `await`. This to-do list adds, removes and loads items with
three actions:

```wf
page Todos(path: "/", title: "To-dos", description: "Actions that change a list.") {
    state items: [String] = []
    state draft = ""

    action add() {
        let text = draft.trim()
        if text == "" { return }
        items.push(text)
        draft = ""
    }

    action remove(index: Number) {
        items = items.filter((_, i) => i != index)
    }

    action load() {
        let r = await fetch("/api/todos")
        let { todos } = r
        items = todos
    }

    Heading("To-dos").h1
    Input(bind: draft, placeholder: "What needs doing?") { on keydown(e) { if e.key == "Enter" { add() } } }
    Button("Add").primary { on click { add() } }
    for item, i in items {
        Row { Text(item)  IconButton(icon: "trash", label: "Remove") { on click { remove(i) } } }
    }
}
```

What an action's body can hold:

- **Locals.** `let x = …` declares a local of the action or handler.
  `let { a, b } = m` and `let [x, y] = l` destructure a map and a list.
- **`await`.** Using it makes the action asynchronous, and `name.pending` is
  `true` while a call of it runs ([Forms](/learn/14-forms#show-that-a-request-is-running)).
- **Loops.** `for item in list { }`, `for item, i in list { }` and
  `for n in 1..=10 { }`.
- **Errors.** `try { } catch e { }` guards a call that may fail.
- **`return`.** `return` leaves the action; `return x` leaves with a value.

A `let` is the action's own. After `let list = items`, `list.push(x)` changes
`list` and leaves `items` as it was; assign it back with `items = list`, or
write `items.push(x)`, which gives the state a new list.

You call a page's action by name, `add()`, and a store's through the store,
`Todos.add()`.

## `persist`

`persist` declares a state kept in the browser's storage across visits. It is
read back on the next visit and written on every change. These two
preferences survive a reload:

```wf
page Prefs(path: "/", title: "Preferences", description: "Settings kept across visits.") {
    persist scheme = "light"
    persist perPage = 20
    Heading("Preferences").h1
    Select(bind: scheme, label: "Theme") {
        Select.Option("Light", value: "light")
        Select.Option("Dark", value: "dark")
    }
    Slider(bind: perPage, min: 10, max: 100, step: 10, label: "Rows per page")
}
```

How it behaves:

- The storage key is the owner's name and the state's (`Prefs.scheme`), so a
  page and a store may each have a value of the same name.
- It works in a store too, where every page shares it.
- When storage is blocked or full, the value falls back to its initial value.
- A block after the declaration can say which storage to use, give a version
  with migrations, and choose whether to follow other tabs. That block and the
  rest of the policy are in [Stores](/learn/11-stores#keeping-a-value-across-visits).

## Timers

`every(ms) { }` repeats, and `after(ms) { }` fires once. The interval is a
number of milliseconds or a duration: `every(5.seconds)`, `after(2.minutes)`.
This page counts the seconds it has been open and hides a welcome message
after three:

```wf
page Clock(path: "/", title: "Clock", description: "A timer and a one-off delay.") {
    state seconds = 0
    state toast: String? = "Welcome"
    every(1000) { seconds = seconds + 1 }
    after(3000) { toast = null }
    Heading("Clock").h1
    Text("{seconds}s on this page")
    if let message = toast { Alert(message).info }
}
```

Both stop when what declared them leaves the page: a branch that closes, a
list item that is removed, a route that changes.

## Automatic clean-up

Everything a body creates — effects, timers, listeners, element handles —
belongs to the *scope* it was created in: the page, branch, list item, `match`
arm or slot whose nodes it sits among. When that scope's nodes leave, the
runtime disposes of what it created:

- an `if` branch turns false, an item drops out of a `for`, a `match` arm
  changes, or the route changes;
- intervals are cleared, effects stop running, and `cleanup { }` blocks run.

You never unsubscribe by hand.

## Element handles

`ref: name` on an element gives you a *handle*: a name that reads as the
element itself. Here a button and the `/` key both put the cursor in the
search box:

```wf
page Search(path: "/", title: "Search", description: "A handle on an input.") {
    state q = ""
    Heading("Search").h1
    Input(bind: q, ref: box, placeholder: "Search")
    Button("Focus the box") { on click { box.focus() } }
    Button("Clear") { on click { q = ""  box.focus() } }
    on key("/") { box.focus() }
}
```

The `ref:` declares the name; you do not declare it anywhere else. Anything
the element has is there: `box.value`, `box.scrollIntoView()`.

A handle is filled once the element exists, so set-up code at the top of the
body cannot use it yet. Read it in a handler, an `effect` or `after(0) { }`.

## The browser as values

Some names are always in scope and kept current by the runtime, so a page
reads the browser the way it reads its own state:

| Name | Is | Updates when |
|---|---|---|
| `viewport` | `.width`, `.height`, and `.sm` `.md` `.lg` `.xl` — whether the window is at least that breakpoint | a breakpoint is crossed (through `matchMedia`, not on every pixel) |
| `query` | the URL's query string as a map: `query.tab` for `?tab=x` | the URL changes |
| `hash` | the URL's `#fragment`, without the `#` | the URL changes |
| `theme` | `"light"`, `"dark"` or `"system"` — the reader's choice ([Styling](/learn/13-styling#dark-mode)) | `setTheme(…)` is called |
| `now` | a `DateTime`, every minute; `now(every: 1.seconds)` for a finer clock ([Types](/learn/12-types#now)) | the clock ticks |
| `network` | `.online`, `.effectiveType`, `.saveData`, `.downlink`, `.queued` ([Real-time](/recipes/show-the-network)) | the connection changes |
| `update` | `.available` and `.apply()` — a new version of an offline site ([Offer a new version](/recipes/offer-a-new-version)) | a new build is installed |
| `locale`, `dir` | the current locale and `"ltr"`/`"rtl"`, with i18n configured ([Translate a site](/recipes/translate-a-site)) | `setLocale(…)` is called |

This page reads four of them:

```wf
page Where(path: "/", title: "Where", description: "The browser, read as values.") {
    Heading("Where am I?").h1
    Text(if viewport.md { "A wide window" } else { "A narrow window" })
    derived tab = query.tab ?? "all"
    Text("Tab: {tab}, section: {hash}")
    Text("Theme: {theme}")
    if !network.online { Alert("You are offline.").warning }
}
```

The rules:

- The breakpoints are the `screen-sm` … `screen-xl` design tokens: 640, 768,
  1024 and 1280px unless a theme moves them.
- They are the language's names, so a `state`, prop or `const` of the same
  name is an error (`E118`).
- Copy one into a `state` and you keep the value it had when the page
  opened: `state clock = now(every: 1.seconds)` never ticks (`X06`). Read it
  where it is shown, or in a `derived`.
- The static paint does not know them, so what depends on them is drawn once
  the page is live. For layout, prefer
  [responsive values](/learn/13-styling#responsive-values), which are right in
  the first paint.

## Where values come from, in order

When a body reads a name, the nearest declaration wins. The compiler looks
in this order, innermost first:

1. A `let` local, a lambda's parameter or a caught error, inside its block.
2. Loop variables and arm bindings (`if let`, a `match` arm), inside their
   block.
3. Route parameters and props (`slug`, `_ label`).
4. `state`, `persist`, `derived`, `resource` and actions of the body. A
   body member may not share a name with a parameter or a prop (`E102`).
5. A `use`d store's members, always through the store's name
   (`Cart.total`).
6. Constants, `data` and `image` declarations, `env.X`, and the browser's
   values above.
7. Browser globals: `window`, `document`, `localStorage`, `JSON`, `Math`,
   `Date`, `fetch`, `setTimeout`, `console`, `navigator`, `location`.

So with `state name = "outer"`, `for name in items by name { Text(name) }`
shows each item, and a `const name` is hidden by both.

## Summary

| You write | It is | Section |
|---|---|---|
| `state count = 0` | a value the page changes; its readers update | [`state`](#state) |
| `derived total = …` | a value computed from state, never assigned | [`derived`](#derived) |
| `effect { … cleanup { … } }` | code that runs when what it read changes | [`effect`](#effect) |
| `action add() { … }` | a named function that changes state | [Actions and locals](#actions-and-locals) |
| `let x = …` | a local of an action or handler | [Actions and locals](#actions-and-locals) |
| `persist scheme = "light"` | a state kept across visits | [`persist`](#persist) |
| `every(1000) { … }`, `after(3000) { … }` | a repeating timer and a one-off delay | [Timers](#timers) |
| `ref: box` | a handle on an element | [Element handles](#element-handles) |
| `viewport`, `query`, `hash`, `theme`, `now`, `network`, `update`, `locale`, `dir` | the browser, read as values | [The browser as values](#the-browser-as-values) |

[Grammar](/reference/grammar) and [Built-in functions](/reference/built-ins) are
the reference for each.

## Quiz

```quiz
A page shows `Heading("Counter")` and `Text("{count}")`. A click runs `count = count + 1`. What runs again?
- The page's body, which draws the heading and the text again -- A body runs once, when the page opens; nothing re-renders after it.
+ The `Text` that reads `count`, and nothing else -- Only what reads a state follows it; the heading reads no state.
- The page and every component inside it -- There is no component tree to re-render; a component's body runs once too.
```

```quiz
`items` is a state. Which `total` stays equal to the sum of `items` as items are added?
- `state total = items.sum()` -- A state takes its initial value once; adding an item leaves the total as it was.
+ `derived total = items.sum()` -- A derived value is worked out again whenever a state it read changes.
- `derived total = 0`, with `total = items.sum()` in each action that adds an item -- A derived value is never assigned (X01).
```

```quiz
Which of these clocks ticks every second?
- `state clock = now(every: 1.seconds)` -- A state takes `now` once, when the page opens (X06).
+ `derived clock = now(every: 1.seconds)` -- A derived value follows `now` as it ticks.
- `derived clock = now` -- This one ticks, but once a minute: `now` alone keeps minutes, and `now(every: 1.seconds)` asks for seconds.
```

## Common mistakes

**A state that copies `now` once.** A `state` takes its initial value when the
page opens and keeps it, so a clock or an "… ago" worked out from it never
moves:

```wf expect=X06
page Feed(path: "/", title: "Feed", description: "When this was posted.") {
    state posted = @2026-03-14T09:30:00Z
    state clock = now(every: 1.seconds)
    Heading("Feed").h1
    Text("Posted {posted.until(clock).minutes()} minutes ago")
}
```

Declare it `derived clock = now(every: 1.seconds)`. The same holds for
`viewport`, `query`, `hash`, `theme`, `network` and `update`
([X06](/errors/X06)).

**An effect that writes what it reads.** Each run changes `visits`, which
starts the next run, so the page never settles:

```wf expect=X02
page Visits(path: "/", title: "Visits", description: "A count that runs away.") {
    state visits = 0
    effect { visits = visits + 1 }
    Heading("Visits").h1
    Text("{visits} visits")
}
```

Change the state in a handler or an action, or work the value out with
`derived` ([X02](/errors/X02)).

**Assigning a derived value.** A `derived` is worked out from what it reads,
so nothing may set it:

```wf expect=X01
page Cart(path: "/", title: "Cart", description: "A total you cannot set.") {
    state items = [2.5, 6]
    derived total = items.sum()
    Heading("Cart").h1
    Text("Total: {total}")
    Button("Clear") { on click { total = 0 } }
}
```

Change what it reads instead, `items = []`, and `total` follows
([X01](/errors/X01)).

## Next

[Events](/learn/08-events).



---

# Events

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/08-events

This chapter covers events in WebFluent. An event handler is the code that
runs when something happens: a click, a key, a drop, a component saying it
changed. You write it as `on <event> { … }`
inside the block of the element it listens to, and its body can change state,
call actions and navigate.

In this chapter:

- handlers and the event object
- keys, and shortcuts for a whole app
- the events your own components fire
- overlays: modals, sheets, toasts, menus, popovers and tooltips, what closes them, and how they stack
- gestures: drag and drop, long-press, swipe and the splitter
- listening to the window and the document

## Handlers

A handler is written inside an element's block: `on <event> { … }`, or
`on <event>(name) { … }` when the body reads the event object. This page
counts clicks and logs what happens in a text field:

```wf
page Clicks(path: "/", title: "Clicks", description: "Handlers on a button and a field.") {
    state n = 0
    state last = ""
    Heading("Clicks").h1
    Button("+1") { on click { n = n + 1 } }
    Input(bind: last, placeholder: "Type here") {
        on input { log(last) }
        on keydown(e) { if e.key == "Enter" { log("submitted {last}") } }
        on focus { log("in") }
        on blur { log("out") }
    }
    Text("{n}")
}
```

A handler may name any DOM event. The common ones are `click`, `input`,
`change`, `submit`, `focus`, `blur`, `keydown`, `keyup`, `mouseenter` and
`mouseleave`. The rest — `dblclick`, `contextmenu`, `pointerdown`,
`pointermove`, `touchstart`, `wheel`, `scroll`, `paste`, `drop`, `dragover`,
`animationend`, `ended` and the others — work the same way. The
[components reference](/reference#on-every-element) lists
every one. On a call of your own component, the events it declares
([Components](/learn/10-components#events)) join them.

A handler's body is an imperative block, so it may assign state, call
actions, `await` and `navigate`.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React or Svelte?** A handler is not a prop: there is no
> `onClick={…}` and no `on:click={…}`. Write `on click { … }` inside the
> element's block. `onclick:` as an argument is an inline handler, and the
> compiler refuses it (`E106`). See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react#the-map).

A handler on a component call — `UserCard("Sam") { on click { … } }` —
attaches to the component's root element, so a styled button component is
clickable wherever it is used.

### The event object

To read the event, name a parameter: `on keydown(e) { … }`. It is the
browser's own event object, so `e.key`, `e.target.value`, `e.clientX`,
`e.preventDefault()` and `e.stopPropagation()` are all there.

Without a parameter, the event is still in scope as `event` — unless the
program has an `event` of its own (a loop's item, a state, an action), which
wins. Name the parameter to read the event there.

A DOM event sends one value, the event, so a handler names one name at most:
`on click(e, x)` is an error (`T22`). Read what you want from the event,
`e.clientX`. Several names are for a component's own events, which send what
they declare ([below](#emitting-events-from-components)).

This drop zone uses the event object twice — to allow the drop, and to read
the dropped files:

```wf
page Drop(path: "/", title: "Drop", description: "A place to drop files.") {
    state names: [String] = []
    Heading("Drop files here").h1
    Card {
        on dragover(e) { e.preventDefault() }
        on drop(e) {
            e.preventDefault()
            names = Array.from(e.dataTransfer.files).map(f => f.name)
        }
        Text(if names.length == 0 { "Nothing yet" } else { names.join(", ") })
    }
}
```

### How often a handler runs

An event can come far more often than its handler needs to run: a key per
letter, a scroll per pixel. Say how often in the handler's parentheses:

```wf
page Reader(path: "/", title: "Reader", description: "A search box and a long page.") {
    state typed = ""
    state q = ""
    state read = 0
    state loads = 0
    Heading("Reader").h1
    Input(bind: typed, label: "Search") {
        on input(debounce: 300.ms) { q = typed }
    }
    Stack {
        style { height: 300px; overflow-y: auto }
        on scroll(e, throttle: 100.ms) { read = e.target.scrollTop }
        Stack { style { height: 2000px; flex-shrink: 0 } Text("A long article") }
    }
    Text("Searching for {q}, scrolled {read}px")
    Text("End of the list") { on visible { loads = loads + 1 } }
}
```

- **`debounce: 300.ms`** runs the handler once the events have stopped
  coming for that long, with the last of them: a search asked when the
  reader stops typing.
- **`throttle: 100.ms`** runs it at once, then at most once in that long,
  and once more where the events stopped: a scroll position followed
  without running on every pixel.
- A wait still pending when the page, branch or item leaves is dropped.
- **`on visible`** runs each time the element comes into view: scrolled to,
  or drawn where the reader is looking. A "load more" row is an element
  with `on visible { feed.loadMore() }` at the end of the list.

## Keys

`on key("…")` answers to one key, with modifiers. On an element it fires while
that element has focus; at the top of a page or component it fires anywhere on
the page:

```wf
page Keys(path: "/", title: "Keys", description: "Keys on a field and on the page.") {
    state open = false
    state q = ""
    Heading("Keys").h1
    Input(bind: q, ref: box, placeholder: "Search") {
        on key("Escape") { q = "" }            // on the element: while it has focus
        on key("Enter", e) { log(e.target.value) }
    }
    on key("mod+k") { box.focus() }            // on the page: anywhere on the page
    on key("?") { open = !open }
    if open { Alert("Shortcuts: {keyLabel("mod+k")} to search, ? for this.").info }
}
```

How a combination is spelled:

- Modifiers are `mod`, `ctrl`, `shift`, `alt` and `meta` (or `cmd`), joined
  with `+`. `mod` is ⌘ on a Mac and Ctrl everywhere else, so one shortcut
  works on both; write `ctrl` or `cmd` only when you mean exactly that key.
- Then comes the key as the browser names it: `k`, `Enter`, `Escape` (or
  `esc`), `Tab`, `ArrowDown` (or `down`), `space`, `F2`.
- `on key("Enter", e)` names the event too.

How it listens:

- On an element, the handler listens on that element.
- At the top of a page or component, it listens on the document for as long as
  the page shows.
- Every modifier must match exactly, so `ctrl+k` does not fire on
  `ctrl+shift+k`.

A combination no keyboard sends — an unknown modifier, no key — is an error
(`E117`).

### Shortcuts for an app

To give an app shortcuts that work on every page, write them with `mod` and
declare them on `app`:

- **`mod`** is ⌘ on a Mac and Ctrl everywhere else.
- On **`app`**, a shortcut is heard on every page for as long as the app runs.
- A **chord** is its steps with a space between: `mod+k mod+s`. The second
  step must come within a second and a half of the first, and on its own it
  does not fire a shortcut of its own.

This app drives its shortcuts and its **View** menu from one table of
commands:

```wf
store Commands {
    state said = ""
    state table: [Command] = [
        { id: "palette", keys: "mod+shift+p", title: "Commands" },
        { id: "sidebar", keys: "mod+b", title: "Toggle sidebar" },
    ]
    action run(e) {
        for c in table {
            if keyIs(e, c.keys) {
                e.preventDefault()
                said = c.id
            }
        }
    }
}

type Command { id: String, keys: String, title: String }

app {
    on key("mod+s") { Commands.said = "saved" }
    on key("mod+k mod+s") { Commands.said = "shortcut help" }
    on keydown(e) { Commands.run(e) }
    Menu(trigger: "View") {
        for c in Commands.table {
            Menu.Item(shortcut: c.keys) { Text(c.title) }
        }
    }
    Text("Commands: {keyLabel("mod+shift+p")}")
    Router
}
```

The helpers and rules it relies on:

- **`keyIs(e, "mod+s")`** is whether a key event is that combination — a
  chord's too — so one table of commands can drive the shortcuts, the menus
  and a palette.
- **`keyLabel("mod+shift+p")`** is how this system writes it: `⇧⌘P` on a Mac,
  `Ctrl+Shift+P` elsewhere. A `Menu.Item`'s and a `Tooltip`'s `shortcut:` are
  written the same way, and the item — or the tooltip's control — tells
  assistive technology with `aria-keyshortcuts`.
- **Events outside any element.** A page, a component or `app` may handle
  `keydown` and `keyup`, and the window's `resize`, `scroll`, `hashchange`,
  `popstate`, `online`, `offline`, `message`, `storage` and
  `visibilitychange`, and the window losing and gaining focus (`blur`,
  `focus` — an editor saves on leaving, for example). Each listens for as
  long as its owner shows.
- **A letter is also the key in its place.** On a Mac `⌥⌘P` sends `π`, and
  `mod+alt+p` still matches it.

### Moving through a group with the arrow keys

A tab strip, a toolbar or a row of choices is one stop for Tab: Tab enters
it and leaves it, and the arrow keys move inside it. `Tabs` and `Menu` work
that way already. `roving:` gives any element of yours the same:

```wf
page Editor(path: "/", title: "Editor", description: "Format the text.") {
    state bold = false
    state italic = false
    Heading("Editor").h1
    Row(roving: .x, role: "toolbar", aria-label: "Format") {
        Button("Bold", aria-pressed: bold) { on click { bold = !bold } }
        Button("Italic", aria-pressed: italic) { on click { italic = !italic } }
    }
}
```

- `roving: .x` moves with ArrowLeft and ArrowRight, `.y` with ArrowUp and
  ArrowDown, `.both` with either.
- Across a right-to-left page the next item is to the left, so ArrowLeft
  moves forward there.
- Home and End go to the ends, and a letter goes to the next item whose
  name starts with it.
- Tab enters at the chosen item, the one marked `aria-selected`,
  `aria-checked` or `aria-pressed`, or the first. A disabled item is passed
  over, and a key held with Alt, Ctrl or ⌘ is left to the browser.

For a key of your own that follows the direction of the text, write
`on key("inline-start")` or `on key("inline-end")`: ArrowLeft and
ArrowRight in a left-to-right box, the other way round in a right-to-left
one.

## Emitting events from components

A component declares the events it fires with `event`, and fires them with
`emit`. The caller handles them like DOM events, with a name for each value
the event sends — `on change(v)`, `on menu(key, x, y)`.
[Components](/learn/10-components#events) covers the details. This counter tells
its page every time it changes:

```wf
component Counter(_ start: Number) {
    event change(value: Number)
    state n = start
    Row(gap: .sm) {
        Button("−") { on click { n = n - 1  emit change(n) } }
        Text("{n}")
        Button("+") { on click { n = n + 1  emit change(n) } }
    }
}

page Tally(path: "/", title: "Tally", description: "A component that reports its count.") {
    state total = 0
    Heading("Tally").h1
    Counter(10) { on change(v) { total = v } }
    Text("Now {total}")
}
```

## Overlays: modals, dialogs, toasts and menus

An *overlay* is something a page opens over itself: a modal that asks a
question, a toast that confirms, a menu of actions, a tooltip. Most are
opened by a state, so the page decides when they show. This page has one of
each:

```wf
page Overlays(path: "/", title: "Overlays", description: "What a page opens.") {
    state confirm = false
    state deleted = false
    Heading("Overlays").h1
    Button("Delete").danger { on click { confirm = true } }
    Modal(visible: confirm, title: "Delete this?") {
        Text("This cannot be undone.")
        Modal.Footer {
            Button("Cancel") { on click { confirm = false } }
            Button("Delete").danger { on click { confirm = false  deleted = true } }
        }
    }
    if deleted { Toast("Deleted").success }
    Menu(trigger: "More") {
        Menu.Item { Text("Rename") }
        Menu.Divider
        Menu.Item { Text("Archive") }
    }
    Tooltip("Copies the link") { IconButton(icon: "copy", label: "Copy link") }
}
```

- **`Modal`** and **`Dialog`** are real `<dialog>` elements, open while their
  `visible:` state is true.
  - The browser traps focus and makes the rest of the page inert. Escape or
    a press on the backdrop closes it, and the state is set back to `false`,
    so it never disagrees with what is on screen.
  - When it opens, the focus goes to what says `autofocus`, else its first
    control; when it closes, the focus goes back to what had it.
  - It fades out before it goes, however it was closed.
  - `on close` runs when it closes, however it was closed.
  - `title:` is its heading, which names it (`A08` without one).
    `Modal.Footer` is the row of actions, and `.closable` adds a close
    button. [`Modal`](/reference#modal) lists the rest.
- **`Toast`** shows the moment it is rendered and leaves after three seconds.
  It is announced politely to screen readers. Put it under a condition that
  turns true, or call `toast(…)` from a handler (below).
- **`Menu`** and **`Dropdown`** open a list from a button. Arrow keys move
  between items, Home and End jump to the ends, a letter jumps to the next
  item that starts with it, Enter and Space choose, Escape closes with focus
  back on the button, and a click outside closes it.
- **`Tooltip`** shows its text when its child is hovered or focused, and is
  linked to it with `aria-describedby`.

### What closes an overlay, and where the focus goes

`dismiss:` says what closes a `Modal`, a `Dialog`, a `Sheet` or a `Popover`
besides the page's own button: `.any` (Escape or a press outside, the
default), `.escape`, or `.none`, for a form that must be answered.
`initialFocus:` names, by its `ref:`, what takes the focus when it opens:

```wf
page Profile(path: "/", title: "Profile", description: "A modal that starts in a field.") {
    state editing = false
    state name = ""
    Heading("Profile").h1
    Button("Edit profile") { on click { editing = true } }
    Modal(visible: editing, title: "Edit profile", dismiss: .escape, initialFocus: nameField) {
        Input(bind: name, label: "Name", ref: nameField)
        Modal.Footer { Button("Save").primary { on click { editing = false } } }
    }
}
```

An **`AlertDialog`** asks before something that cannot be undone. A screen
reader hears an alert dialog, read with its body; Escape answers it, and a
press beside it does not. Put the answer that loses nothing first in its
footer.

A **`Sheet`** is a modal that comes in from an edge: `side: .bottom` (the
default), `.start` or `.end`, which swap in a right-to-left page. Dragged by
its handle or heading toward that edge, past 30% of its size, it closes; a
bottom sheet with `snap:` points opens at the first and settles at the
nearest one it is let go near:

```wf
page Shop(path: "/", title: "Shop", description: "Filters in a bottom sheet.") {
    state filters = false
    state sort = "new"
    Heading("Shop").h1
    Button("Filters") { on click { filters = true } }
    Sheet(visible: filters, title: "Filters", snap: [0.5, 1]).closable {
        Radio(bind: sort, value: "new", label: "Newest")
        Radio(bind: sort, value: "price", label: "Price")
        Sheet.Footer { Button("Show results").primary { on click { filters = false } } }
    }
}
```

On a narrow screen a `Sidebar` opens over the page as a drawer, which is a
layer like these: the focus goes in and stays there, Escape or a press
outside closes it, and the focus goes back to its toggle.

### Toasts, questions and announcements from a handler

Three functions open an overlay from code rather than from state:

```wf
store Mail {
    state archived: [String] = []
    action archive(id: String) {
        archived = archived.concat([id])
        toast("Conversation archived", action: "Undo", onAction: restore)
    }
    action restore() { archived = archived.slice(0, -1) }
}

page Inbox(path: "/", title: "Inbox", description: "Toasts, a question, an announcement.") {
    use Mail
    state gone = false
    Heading("Inbox").h1
    Button("Archive") { on click { Mail.archive("m1") } }
    Button("Delete everything").danger {
        on click {
            if await ask("Delete every message?", detail: "This cannot be undone.", yes: "Delete", danger: true) {
                gone = true
                announce("Every message deleted", .assertive)
            }
        }
    }
}
```

- **`toast(message, …)`** shows a toast above everything, a modal included,
  and says it to a screen reader. It takes `tone:` (`.success`, `.danger`,
  `.warning`, `.info`), `duration:` in milliseconds, and `action:` with
  `onAction:` for a button on it. It waits while the pointer is on it or the
  focus is in it, has a close button, and no more than three show at once.
  `toast.promise(p, loading: …, done: …, failed: …)` follows a promise.
- **`await ask(question, …)`** draws an alert dialog and is `true` for yes,
  `false` for no or Escape. It takes `detail:`, `yes:`, `no:` and
  `danger: true`; the focus starts on no. (`confirm` is the browser's.)
- **`announce(text)`** says something to a screen reader with nothing on
  screen moving; `announce(text, .assertive)` interrupts, for what cannot
  wait.

A program that names something `toast`, `ask` or `announce` of its own keeps
it; the function is then out of reach there.

### Layers: popovers, menus and tooltips above everything

A `Popover`, a `Menu`'s list and a `Tooltip` are drawn in the browser's *top
layer*, above everything else on the page, so a box with `overflow: hidden`
cannot clip them. Each is placed against its *anchor*, the element it
belongs to, and flips or slides to stay on screen.

This page opens a popover at a button and a context menu at the pointer:

```wf
page Editor(path: "/", title: "Editor", description: "Layers at a control and at the pointer.") {
    state branches = false
    state asked = false
    state point = { x: 0, y: 0 }
    state said = ""
    Heading("Editor").h1
    Button("main", ref: branch) { on click { branches = !branches } }
    Popover(visible: branches, anchor: branch, label: "Branches") {
        on close(reason) { said = "closed by {reason}" }
        Text("main")
        Text("feature/layers")
    }
    Card {
        on contextmenu(e) {
            e.preventDefault()
            point = { x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY }
            asked = true
        }
        Text("Right-click for the context menu")
    }
    Menu(visible: asked, at: point) {
        Menu.Item(shortcut: "F2") { Text("Rename") }
        Menu.Divider
        Menu.Item.danger { Text("Delete") }
    }
    Text(said)
}
```

- **`Popover`** is open while its `visible:` state is true, placed against
  `anchor:`, an element's `ref:`. Escape or a press outside closes it (as
  `dismiss:` allows), sets `visible:` back to `false`, and `on close(reason)`
  hears `"escape"` or `"outside"`. Its anchor says what it opens and whether
  it is open (`aria-controls`, `aria-expanded`), the focus goes to its first
  control, and `label:` is its name (`A18` without one).
- **`Menu`** without `trigger:` is a list that state opens, at an `anchor:`
  or `at:` a point. Choosing an item closes it.
- The open layers form one stack, newest on top. Escape closes the newest
  layer that can be dismissed — a popover, a menu, an open `Modal` or
  `Dialog` — and nothing behind it hears that key. A modal opened from a
  popover takes the first Escape; the popover takes the next.
- A tooltip keeps Escape only while focus is on its control. Otherwise the
  key goes on to the layer below, or to the element with focus.
- A layer takes the attributes and handlers any element takes — `role:`,
  `aria-*`, `ref:` — on the element it draws. A `Popover` is a `dialog`
  unless its `role:` says otherwise.

Every option of these — `placement:`, `offset:`, `.arrow`, a menu's
`checked:`, `disabled:` and `Menu.Sub`, a tooltip's `delay:` and
`shortcut:` — is listed under [`Popover`](/reference#popover),
[`Menu`](/reference#menu) and
[`Tooltip`](/reference#tooltip). To ask before a destructive
action, see [Build a confirm dialog](/recipes/confirm-dialog).

## Gestures: drag, long-press, swipe and the splitter

The runtime turns what the pointer does over time into one event that says
what it means. A mouse, a pen and a finger run the same code. A finger picks a
drag up with a long press, so a plain swipe still scrolls the page.

This list reorders its items by drag and drop:

```wf
page Tabs(path: "/", title: "Tabs", description: "Drag to reorder.") {
    state tabs = ["App.wf", "Home.wf", "Shell.wf"]

    action move(what: String, near: String, position: String) {
        let rest = tabs.filter((x) => x != what)
        let at = rest.indexOf(near)
        let i = if position == "after" { at + 1 } else { at }
        tabs = [...rest.slice(0, i), what, ...rest.slice(i)]
    }

    Heading("Tabs").h1
    Row {
        for tab in tabs by tab {
            Card(drag: tab, dragGroup: "tabs", dropAxis: .x) {
                on receive(d) { move(d.value, tab, d.position) }
                Text(tab)
            }
        }
    }
}
```

- **`drag: value`** picks an element up: a mouse moved a few pixels, or a
  finger held still. Escape puts it back, and the click a drag ends with is
  not a click.
- **`on receive(d)`** takes a drop: `d.value` is what was dropped, and
  `d.position` is `"before"` or `"after"` along `dropAxis:` (`.y`, down the
  page, unless you say `.x`), or `"inside"` on a target with
  `dropInside: true`.
- **`dragGroup:`** on a drag and its targets keeps groups apart, such as tabs
  and tree rows.
- **`on longpress(p)`** is half a second held still; **`on swipe(s)`** is a
  finger or a pen swept across, with `s.direction`.
- **`Splitter(bind: side, min: 160, max: 480, reset: 240, label: "Sidebar
  width")`** sizes the region beside it, by drag or by the arrow keys. A drag
  or a key starts from the region's size as it is drawn.

[On every element](/reference#on-every-element) lists the
drag props and the gesture events in full, `dropValue:` and
`on dragmove(d)` among them; [`Splitter`](/reference#splitter)
lists its props.

On a call of your own component, the drag, the drop and the gestures apply
to the one element it draws. A component whose body is an `if`, a `for` or
several elements has no one element for them, and the build says so
(`C07`): wrap what it draws in a `Stack` or a `Row`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> A drag has no keyboard of its own. Give what it does a menu item or a
> command too (`Move left`, `Move to…`), as the platform's accessibility rules
> ask of every pointer action.

## Listening outside the page's elements

A handler on an element hears that element. For the window, write the handler
at the top of the page, a component or `app`, outside any element — `resize`,
`scroll`, `hashchange`, `popstate`, `online`, `offline`, `message`, `storage`,
`visibilitychange`, `blur` and `focus` are heard there
([Shortcuts for an app](#shortcuts-for-an-app)). It listens for as long as its
owner shows:

```wf
page Scrolled(path: "/", title: "Scrolled", description: "How far down the reader is.") {
    state y = 0
    on scroll { y = window.scrollY }
    Heading("Scrolled").h1
    Text("{y}px down")
}
```

For any other target or event, use an `effect` with a `cleanup`, which removes
the listener when the page leaves. An action named without parentheses is the
function itself, so you can hand it to the browser:

```wf
page Selection(path: "/", title: "Selection", description: "What the reader has selected.") {
    state picked = ""
    action track() { picked = document.getSelection().toString() }
    effect {
        document.addEventListener("selectionchange", track)
        cleanup { document.removeEventListener("selectionchange", track) }
    }
    Heading("Selection").h1
    Text("Selected: {picked}")
}
```

For the viewport's size, the network and the URL, the language already keeps
values current — `viewport`, `network`, `query`, `hash` — so no listener is
needed ([State](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity#the-browser-as-values)).

## Summary

| You write | It does | Section |
|---|---|---|
| `on click { … }` | runs when the element fires the event | [Handlers](#handlers) |
| `on keydown(e) { … }` | names the event object | [The event object](#the-event-object) |
| `on input(debounce: 300.ms) { … }`, `on scroll(e, throttle: 100.ms) { … }` | runs once the events stop; at most once a while | [How often a handler runs](#how-often-a-handler-runs) |
| `on visible { … }` | runs when the element comes into view | [How often a handler runs](#how-often-a-handler-runs) |
| `on key("Escape") { … }` | answers to one key or combination | [Keys](#keys) |
| `on key("mod+k mod+s") { … }` on `app` | an app-wide shortcut, here a chord | [Shortcuts for an app](#shortcuts-for-an-app) |
| `keyIs(e, "mod+s")`, `keyLabel("mod+s")` | test a key event; write a combination for this system | [Shortcuts for an app](#shortcuts-for-an-app) |
| `event change(v: Number)`, `emit change(n)` | a component's own event | [Emitting events from components](#emitting-events-from-components) |
| `Modal(visible: open, title: "…")` | a dialog opened by state | [Overlays](#overlays-modals-dialogs-toasts-and-menus) |
| `Popover(visible:, anchor:)`, `Menu(visible:, at:)` | layers placed at a control or a point | [Layers](#layers-popovers-menus-and-tooltips-above-everything) |
| `drag: v`, `on receive(d)`, `on dragmove(d)` | drag and drop | [Gestures](#gestures-drag-long-press-swipe-and-the-splitter) |
| `on longpress(p)`, `on swipe(s)` | a held press; a sweep | [Gestures](#gestures-drag-long-press-swipe-and-the-splitter) |
| `Splitter(bind: side, min:, max:)` | a handle that sizes a region | [Gestures](#gestures-drag-long-press-swipe-and-the-splitter) |
| `on scroll { … }` outside any element | a window event | [Listening outside the page's elements](#listening-outside-the-page-s-elements) |

The [components reference](/reference) lists every event and
prop of each built-in.

## Common mistakes

**Naming more values than a DOM event sends.** A DOM event sends one value,
the event, so a second name has nothing to hold:

```wf expect=T22
page Spot(path: "/", title: "Spot", description: "Where the pointer clicked.") {
    state at = ""
    Heading("Spot").h1
    Button("Click me") { on click(e, x) { at = "{x}" } }
    Text(at)
}
```

Name the event alone and read from it: `on click(e) { at = "{e.clientX}" }`
([T22](/errors/T22)).

**A misspelled event.** A handler for an event the element never fires never
runs, so the compiler warns:

```wf expect=V09
page Clicks(path: "/", title: "Clicks", description: "A misspelled event.") {
    state n = 0
    Heading("Clicks").h1
    Button("+1") { on clik { n = n + 1 } }
    Text("{n}")
}
```

Spell the event as the browser does, `on click`
([V09](/errors/V09)).

**A key combination no keyboard sends.** Modifiers have fixed names, and a
word that is not one stops the build:

```wf expect=E117
page Search(path: "/", title: "Search", description: "A shortcut no keyboard sends.") {
    state q = ""
    Heading("Search").h1
    Input(bind: q, ref: box, placeholder: "Search")
    on key("command+k") { box.focus() }
}
```

Write `cmd+k`, or `mod+k` for ⌘ on a Mac and Ctrl elsewhere
([E117](/errors/E117)).

## Next

[Control flow](/learn/09-control-flow).

# Control flow

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/09-control-flow

This chapter covers the five statements that decide what a page shows: `if`,
`if let`, `for`, `show` and `match`. Each one follows the state it reads, adding and removing elements as
its condition changes, so you never update the page by hand. Each animates
