when you ask it to ([Animate an element in and out](/recipes/animate-in-and-out)).

In this chapter:

- `if`, `else if` and `else`, and `if let` for a value that may be null
- `for` over a list, with a key — and `VirtualList` for thousands of rows
- `show`, which hides elements without removing them
- `match`, which shows one arm by an enum's case
- `if` and `match` as values, and the same statements in actions

The statements in this chapter appear in a *render block* — the body of a
page, component or element, which says what to draw. The last section shows
them in an *imperative block* — a handler or an action, which runs code.

## `if` / `else if` / `else`

`if` shows a branch while its condition holds. This page shows one of three
messages, by how many times the button was pressed:

```wf
page Status(path: "/", title: "Status", description: "A message chosen by a count.") {
    state count = 0
    Heading("Status").h1
    if count == 0 {
        Text("Nothing yet.").muted
    } else if count < 10 {
        Text("A few: {count}")
    } else {
        Text("Many: {count}").bold
    }
    Button("+1") { on click { count = count + 1 } }
}
```

How it behaves:

- A branch's elements are created when its condition turns true, and removed
  when it turns false.
- State declared inside a component in the branch starts over each time the
  branch is created.
- A condition must be a `Bool`, or a value that may be null, which counts as
  `false` when it is null.
- A list or a record as a condition is an error (`T07`), since it would always
  be true.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** `{open && <Panel />}` and `cond ? a : b` inside JSX
> become statements: `if open { Panel }` and `if cond { a } else { b }`. A
> condition is a `Bool`, so test a list with `items.length > 0`. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

## `if let`

`if let name = value { }` binds the value inside the branch when it is not
null. It is the way to read a value of type `T?` (one that may be null)
without the type checker objecting:

```wf
type User { name: String, email: String? }

page Profile(path: "/", title: "Profile", description: "A user who may not be signed in.") {
    state user: User? = null
    Heading("Profile").h1
    if let u = user {
        Text("Signed in as {u.name}")
        if let mail = u.email { Text(mail).muted } else { Text("No email on file").muted }
    } else {
        Button("Sign in") { on click { user = User(name: "Sam", email: null) } }
    }
}
```

The rules:

- `if let x { }`, with no `=`, does the same for a name already in scope.
- The narrowing holds inside the branch only. `if x != null { }` and
  `if x && … { }` narrow `x` inside their branch the same way; the right-hand
  side of the `&&` is not narrowed:

  ```text
  if user != null && user.name == "x" { … }     // T04: `user` may be null
  if user != null && user?.name == "x" { … }    // reads through the null
  if let u = user { if u.name == "x" { … } }    // or bind it, then test it
  ```
- The binding follows the value. When `user` becomes another user, the branch
  shows the new one in place. It is drawn again only when the value goes to
  `null` and back.

## `for`

`for` draws its block once for each item of a list. This page loops three
ways — by key, with the index, and over a range:

```wf
type Todo { id: String, title: String, done: Bool = false }

page Checklist(path: "/", title: "Checklist", description: "Three kinds of loop.") {
    state todos: [Todo] = [Todo(id: "a", title: "Write"), Todo(id: "b", title: "Ship", done: true)]
    Heading("Checklist").h1

    for todo in todos by todo.id {                      // keyed: each item keeps its nodes
        Row(gap: .sm) {
            Checkbox(checked: todo.done, label: todo.title) { on change { todo.done = !todo.done } }
        }
    }
    for todo, i in todos {                              // with the index
        Text("{i + 1}. {todo.title}")
    }
    for n in 1..=3 { Badge("{n}") }                     // over a range
}
```

`by expr` names the *key*: the value that tells one item from another. With a
key:

- An item that stays in the list keeps its nodes. Focus, scroll position and
  animation state survive an insert, a removal or a move, and moves slide.
- An item keeps its nodes under a new value too — a refreshed response's rows
  are all new objects. Its body reads the item and the index live, so a
  changed row changes in place, and its components' state with it.
- Keys must be unique. The runtime warns once when two items share one.
- A key may read the index as well as the item
  (`for t, i in rows by "{t.id}-{i}"`).

Without a key, the list is rebuilt whenever it changes, and the build warns
(`U09`) when its items hold state, a control or a stateful component. Looping
over something that is not a list is an error (`T08`).

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React or Vue?** The `key` prop and `:key` become `by`, written
> once on the loop rather than on the element it draws: `for todo in todos by
> todo.id { … }`. See [Coming from React](/coming-from/react) and
> [Coming from Vue](/coming-from/vue).

> [!WARNING]
> Do not key by the index alone. A key of the index moves with the position,
> not the item: after an insert every item has another's key, and nothing is
> kept. Key by what identifies the item.

### Long lists

A list of thousands of rows — a project's files, a search's results, a long
diff — belongs inside a **`VirtualList`**. The box scrolls, and only the rows
in view and a few either side are drawn; two spacers stand for the rest, so the
scrollbar is the whole list's. Its body is one keyed `for`.

This page windows ten thousand file paths of a fixed height, and a list of
search hits whose rows are measured:

```wf
type Hit { id: String, heading: Bool, text: String }

page Search(path: "/", title: "Search", description: "Results, a window at a time.") {
    state rows = (0..10000).map((i) => "src/file{i}.wf")
    state hits: [Hit] = []
    state current = ""
    Heading("Search").h1
    VirtualList(rowHeight: 32, label: "Files") {
        style { height: 400px }
        for path in rows by path { Text(path) { style { height: 32px; margin: 0 } } }
    }
    VirtualList(estimate: 24, reveal: current, label: "Results") {
        style { height: 400px }
        for h in hits by h.id {
            if h.heading { Heading(h.text).h2 } else { Text(h.text) }
        }
    }
}
```

- **`rowHeight:`** says every row is that tall, which is the fast path.
  Without it, each row is measured once drawn, and **`estimate:`** stands for
  the rows not yet drawn.
- **`reveal:`** reads a row's key. When it changes, that row is scrolled into
  view — the selected file, the current match.
- **`label:`** is the box's accessible name.

A few rules keep it right:

- Give rows no vertical margins: a row's height is its box's.
- A tree is a list of the rows that are showing. Flatten it in a `derived`
  (each open folder followed by its children) and window that.
- With anything else in its body, or a `for` with no `by`, it draws every row
  (`V12`).
- The pre-rendered page paints the first 60 rows, and a list drawn before its
  box has a height waits for one, so its first frame shows the rows in view.

[`VirtualList`](/reference#virtuallist) lists its props, and
the box takes the attributes and handlers any element takes — a
`role: "listbox"`, an `on keydown`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The box needs a height that does not come from its rows — `style { height:
> 400px }`, a `max-height:`, or a grid cell or flex row that sets one. A box
> as tall as what it holds grows until every row is drawn.

## `show`

`show` keeps its elements in the page and toggles whether they are visible;
`if` creates and destroys them. Use `show` for something expensive to rebuild,
or whose state must survive being hidden. This panel keeps its card in the
page while it is hidden:

```wf
page Panel(path: "/", title: "Panel", description: "A panel hidden, not removed.") {
    state open = true
    Heading("Panel").h1
    Button("Toggle") { on click { open = !open } }
    show open {
        Card { Text("Still here when hidden; my state survives.") }
    }
}
```

## `match`

`match` shows one arm at a time. Over an **enum** it chooses by case, and a
case with a *payload* — values carried by the case — hands them to its arm.
This job moves through its cases as the buttons are pressed:

```wf
enum Status { idle, running(job: String), failed(reason: String), done(count: Number) }

page Job(path: "/", title: "Job", description: "One arm per case of an enum.") {
    state s: Status = .idle
    Heading("Job").h1
    match s {
        .idle { Button("Start") { on click { s = .running("build-42") } } }
        .running(job) { Row { Spinner.sm  Text("Running {job}")  Button("Fail") { on click { s = .failed("timed out") } } } }
        .failed(reason) { Alert("Failed: {reason}").danger }
        .done(n) { Text("Done, {n} steps") }
    }
    Text(match s { .idle { "waiting" } .failed(r) { r } else { "busy" } })   // as a value
}
```

Over a **resource** it chooses by the request's state — loading, error or
ready ([Fetching data](/learn/15-data)).

The rules:

- An arm binds one name per part of the payload: `.failed(reason)`.
- `else` covers every case without an arm of its own.
- Without an `else`, a `match` must give every case of the enum an arm, or it
  is an error (`T15`). That holds for a `match` statement and a `match`
  expression alike; an expression that covers every case needs no `else`.
- An arm is drawn again when the arm changes, not when its value does. A new
  payload of the same case — `.failed("refused")` after `.failed("timed
  out")` — reaches what the arm drew in place.

## Expressions that choose

`if` and `match` are also values, and `??` picks a fallback for a value that
may be null:

```wf
page Choose(path: "/", title: "Choose", description: "Values picked by a condition.") {
    state n = 5
    state nick: String? = null
    derived size = if n > 10 { "big" } else { "small" }
    derived label = nick ?? "anonymous"
    Heading("Choose").h1
    Text("{size} {label}")
}
```

An `if` value with no `else` is `null` when its condition fails.
[Expressions](/reference/expressions) has the rest.

## In actions and handlers

The same statements work in an imperative block — a handler or an action —
on values rather than elements, plus `try`/`catch`. This action fetches rows
and keeps the first hundred:

```wf
page Sync(path: "/", title: "Sync", description: "Control flow inside an action.") {
    state rows: [Map] = []
    state error = ""
    action pull() {
        try {
            let r = await fetch("/api/rows")
            let { items } = r
            rows = []
            for item, i in items {
                if i >= 100 { return }
                rows.push(item)
            }
        } catch e {
            error = e.message
        }
    }
    Heading("Sync").h1
    Button("Pull") { on click { pull() } }
    if error != "" { Alert(error).danger }
    Text("{rows.length} rows")
}
```

## Summary

| You write | It shows | Section |
|---|---|---|
| `if c { … } else if d { … } else { … }` | the first branch whose condition holds | [`if`](#if-else-if-else) |
| `if let u = user { … }` | a branch with the value, when it is not null | [`if let`](#if-let) |
| `for todo in todos by todo.id { … }` | the block once per item, keyed | [`for`](#for) |
| `for t, i in todos { … }`, `for n in 1..=3 { … }` | with the index; over a range | [`for`](#for) |
| `VirtualList(rowHeight: 32) { for … by … }` | only the rows in view | [Long lists](#long-lists) |
| `show open { … }` | its block, hidden rather than removed | [`show`](#show) |
| `match s { .idle { … } else { … } }` | one arm by case, or by a resource's state | [`match`](#match) |
| `if c { a } else { b }`, `match s { … }`, `a ?? b` | a value | [Expressions that choose](#expressions-that-choose) |
| `try { … } catch e { … }` | in an action: a guard on what may fail | [In actions and handlers](#in-actions-and-handlers) |

## Common mistakes

**A list used as a condition.** In JavaScript an empty array is truthy too, so
`if items` would always pass; WebFluent refuses it:

```wf expect=T07
page P(path: "/", title: "T", description: "D") {
    state items: [String] = []
    Heading("Items").h1
    if items { Text("{items.length} items") } else { Text("Nothing yet.") }
}
```

Say what you mean: `if items.length > 0`. See [T07](/errors/T07).

**A loop with no key over items that hold state.** Each `Input` starts again
whenever the list changes, so a field being typed in loses what was typed:

```wf expect=U09
page P(path: "/", title: "T", description: "D") {
    state rows = [{ id: 1, name: "Milk" }, { id: 2, name: "Eggs" }]
    Heading("Shopping").h1
    for r in rows { Input(bind: r.name, label: "Item") }
}
```

Key the loop by what identifies the item: `for r in rows by r.id`. See
[U09](/errors/U09).

**A `match` that misses a case.** Adding a case to an enum makes every
`match` on it without an `else` incomplete:

```wf expect=T15
enum Status { idle, running, failed }

page P(path: "/", title: "T", description: "D") {
    state s: Status = .idle
    Heading("Job").h1
    match s {
        .idle { Text("Waiting") }
        .running { Spinner }
    }
}
```

Give the missing case an arm, `.failed { Alert("Failed").danger }`, or add an
`else`. See [T15](/errors/T15).

## Next

[Components](/learn/10-components).



---

# Components

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/10-components

This chapter shows how to declare a *component*: a reusable element of your
own. It has typed
props, the events it fires, the slots its caller fills, the parts it
offers, and a body that draws it. The one thing to remember: the compiler
checks a call to your component exactly as it checks a call to a built-in
such as `Button`, so a missing prop or a misspelled flag is an error where
you wrote it.

**In this chapter**

- Declaring a component and calling it
- Props, including enum props
- Events, slots, scoped slots and parts
- A component's own state, and stores inside a component
- What a call puts on the component's root element
- How to design a component's interface

## A first component

This page declares a `Greeting` component and places it once:

```wf
component Greeting(_ name: String) {
    Text("Hello, {name}!")
}

page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "A greeting.") {
    Heading("Welcome").h1
    Greeting("Ada")
}
```

The page shows the heading **Welcome** and the line **Hello, Ada!**.

- `component Greeting(…)` declares the component. Its name is capitalised,
  as every element's is.
- `_ name: String` is a prop. The `_` lets a call pass it without its name,
  so `Greeting("Ada")` sets `name` to `"Ada"`.
- The block is the body: what the component draws each time it is placed.
- `Greeting("Ada")` in the page is a call, written like any built-in.

## Props

A *prop* is a value the caller hands to the component. This component takes
four, with a type and, for three of them, a default:

```wf
/// A person, at a glance.
component UserCard(_ name: String, role: String, active: Bool = true, avatar: String? = null) {
    Card.elevated {
        Row(align: .center, gap: .md) {
            if let src = avatar { Avatar(src: src, alt: name) } else { Avatar(initials: name.slice(0, 2)).primary }
            Stack {
                Text(name).bold
                Text(role).muted
            }
            if active { Badge("Active").success }
        }
    }
}

page Team(path: "/", title: "Team", description: "Three people, three cards.") {
    Heading("Team").h1
    UserCard("Monzer", role: "Developer")
    UserCard("Sam", role: "Designer", active: false, avatar: "/sam.png")
    UserCard("Ann", role: "PM").active
}
```

The rules for props:

- `_ name: Type` marks the one prop a call may pass positionally. It must be
  the first prop. Every other prop is passed by name.
- Every prop has a written type: `String`, `Number`, `Bool`, `Map`, `Any`,
  `[T]` (a list), `T?` (may be `null`), or a declared `type` or `enum`. See
  [Types](/learn/12-types) for the whole type language.
- `= expr` gives a prop a default, so a call may leave it out. A `T?` prop
  with no default defaults to `null`.
- A `Bool` prop is set with a flag, `.active`, or by name, `active: false`.
- A `///` comment above the component or above a prop is its
  documentation. The editor shows it on hover, and `wf docs` prints it.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** There is no `...rest` that forwards whatever the
> caller passed. A prop the component does not declare is an error (`C02`);
> `class:`, `aria-*`, `data-*` and a few others go to the root element (see
> [What a call puts on the root element](#what-a-call-puts-on-the-root-element)).
> See [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

A prop that reads the caller's state stays live inside the component: a
`Pill(pressed: isOn)` repaints when `isOn` changes. You do not need to pass
a callback or re-render anything yourself.

The checker holds every call to the declaration. Leaving out a prop that
has no default is `C01`; passing a prop the component does not declare is
`C02`; a second positional argument is `E113`. A positional argument to a
component whose first prop is not marked `_` is bound to that first prop,
with a `C06` warning asking you to add the `_`.

## Enum props

An *enum prop* takes one case of a declared `enum`. The caller picks the
case with a flag or by name:

```wf
enum Tone { calm, loud }

component Note(_ text: String, tone: Tone = .calm) {
    Text(text, class: "note") {
        style { padding: $sm; border-radius: $radius-sm }
    }
}

page Notes(path: "/", title: "Notes", description: "One note in each tone.") {
    Heading("Notes").h1
    Note("Quiet")
    Note("Loud!", tone: .loud)
    Note("Loud too").loud
}
```

`.loud` and `tone: .loud` mean the same. A flag the enum does not have, such
as `.huge`, is an error (`E103`) that lists the cases it does have.

The compiler writes a component's enum props to its root element as
`data-<prop>="<case>"` — here `data-tone="loud"` — so a stylesheet can
select on them: `[data-tone="loud"] { font-weight: 700 }`. See
[Styling](/learn/13-styling) for project stylesheets.

## Events

An *event* is how a component tells its caller that something happened. The
component declares it with `event name(param: Type)` and fires it with
`emit name(value)`. The caller handles it with `on name(value) { }`, as it
handles a click:

```wf
type Todo { id: String, title: String, done: Bool = false }

component TodoRow(_ todo: Todo) {
    event toggle(id: String)
    event remove(id: String)
    Row(align: .center, gap: .sm) {
        Checkbox(checked: todo.done, label: todo.title) { on change { emit toggle(todo.id) } }
        IconButton(icon: "trash", label: "Remove {todo.title}").sm { on click { emit remove(todo.id) } }
    }
}

page Todos(path: "/", title: "Todos", description: "Rows that report back.") {
    state todos: [Todo] = [Todo(id: "1", title: "Milk"), Todo(id: "2", title: "Eggs")]
    action toggle(id: String) {
        todos = todos.map(todo => if todo.id == id { Todo(id: todo.id, title: todo.title, done: !todo.done) } else { todo })
    }
    Heading("Todos").h1
    for todo in todos by todo.id {
        TodoRow(todo) {
            on toggle(id) { toggle(id) }
            on remove(id) { todos = todos.filter(todo => todo.id != id) }
        }
    }
}
```

The checker holds each `emit` to the parameters its event declares (`T09`).
A handler on a call must name a declared event or a DOM event; an `emit`
outside a component is `E114`. A DOM event handler written on a component
call, such as `on click`, attaches to the component's root element (see
[What a call puts on the root element](#what-a-call-puts-on-the-root-element)).
For events in general, see [Events](/learn/08-events).

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** A callback prop such as `onToggle={…}` becomes a
> declared `event toggle(id: String)`, fired with `emit toggle(id)` and handled
> on the call as `on toggle(id) { … }`. The checker holds both ends to the
> declaration. See [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

### An event with several values

An event may send several values. The handler names them in the order the
event declares them, and each name has the type declared for it. In this
example `key` is a `String`, and `x` and `y` are `Number`s:

```wf
component Entry(_ key: String) {
    event menu(key: String, x: Number, y: Number)
    Button(key) {
        on contextmenu(e) {
            e.preventDefault()
            emit menu(key, e.clientX, e.clientY)
        }
    }
}

page Files(path: "/", title: "Files", description: "A menu that knows where it opened.") {
    state at = "nothing yet"
    Heading("Files").h1
    Entry("notes.wf") { on menu(key, x, y) { at = "{key} at {x}, {y}" } }
    Text("Menu for {at}")
}
```

A handler may name fewer values than the event sends: `on menu(key)` reads
the key and ignores the rest. It may not name more. A name past the last
value would always be `undefined`, so the checker reports it (`T22`). You
handle an event that sends nothing with no names: `on close { }`.

## Slots

A *slot* is a place in the component where the caller's content goes. The
component places the caller's block with `children`, and may declare named
slots that the caller fills with `name { … }`:

```wf
component Panel(_ title: String) {
    slot trailing
    Card {
        Row(justify: .between, align: .center) {
            Heading(title).h2
            trailing
        }
        children
    }
}

page Keys(path: "/", title: "Keys", description: "A panel with a slot.") {
    Heading("Keys").h1
    Panel("API keys") {
        trailing { Badge("Beta").info }
        Text("Rotate every 90 days.")
        Button("Generate").primary
    }
}
```

- `children` places the call's block. It needs no declaration: a component
  that writes `children` takes a block.
- `slot trailing` declares a named slot, which the body places by its name.
- Anything in the call's block that is not a named fill goes to
  `children`. Here that is the `Text` and the `Button`.
- A bare `slot` line declares the default slot by name. You need it only on
  a component a page names as its `layout:`, where it is required
  (`E104`); see [Layouts](/learn/05-pages-and-routing#layouts).

A fill is compiled in the caller's scope: it reads the caller's state and
loop variables, and its handlers are the caller's. The component only
decides where the fill lands. A page's `layout:` is a component with a
default slot, called with the page as its block (see
[Pages and routing](/learn/05-pages-and-routing#layouts)).

### Scoped slots

A *scoped slot* hands values to its fill. The component declares what it
hands over, places the slot with those values by name, and the caller's
fill names them in order:

```wf
type Todo { id: String, title: String, done: Bool = false }

component TodoList(items: [Todo]) {
    slot row(item: Todo, index: Number)
    slot empty
    if items.length == 0 {
        empty
    } else {
        for it, i in items by it.id { row(item: it, index: i) }
    }
}

page Use(path: "/", title: "Todos", description: "A list that hands each row to its caller.") {
    state todos: [Todo] = [Todo(id: "1", title: "Milk")]
    Heading("Todos").h1
    TodoList(items: todos) {
        row(todo, i) { Text("{i + 1}. {todo.title}") }
        empty { Text("Nothing to do.").muted }
    }
}
```

The page shows **1. Milk**. The fill's names take their types from the slot
declaration: `todo` is a `Todo` and `i` a `Number`. The fill is drawn again
when a value it is handed changes.

## Parts

A *part* is a component of the component's own, called under its name —
the way `Card.Header` is a part of `Card`:

```wf
component Panel(_ title: String) {
    part Header(_ text: String) { Heading(text).h2 }
    part Footer { Divider  Text("End").muted.sm }
    Card { Text(title)  children }
    slot
}

page Parts(path: "/", title: "Parts", description: "A panel with parts of its own.") {
    Heading("Parts").h1
    Panel("Keys") {
        Panel.Header("Rotate")
        Text("Body")
        Panel.Footer
    }
}
```

You declare a part inside its component. A part has props, events and slots
of its own, but it cannot declare parts: a part inside a part is an error.
Calling a part outside its owner, such as `Panel.Header` with no `Panel`
around it, is `C03`.

## Local state and actions

A component may have its own `state`, `derived` values, `effect`s, actions,
timers and handles. Each placed instance gets its own copy, so the two
`Counter`s on this page count separately:

```wf
component Counter(_ start: Number, step: Number = 1) {
    event change(value: Number)
    state n = start
    derived even = n % 2 == 0
    action move(delta: Number) { n = n + delta  emit change(n) }
    Row(gap: .sm, align: .center) {
        Button("−").sm { on click { move(-step) } }
        Text("{n}").bold
        Button("+").sm { on click { move(step) } }
        if even { Badge("even").info }
    }
}

page Counters(path: "/", title: "Counters", description: "Two counters, two counts.") {
    state last = 0
    Heading("Counters").h1
    Counter(0) { on change(v) { last = v } }
    Counter(10, step: 5) { on change(v) { last = v } }
    Text("Last value: {last}")
}
```

What an instance creates — effects, timers, listeners — is disposed of when
the instance leaves the page. See [State and reactivity](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity)
for `state`, `derived` and `effect`.

## Stores inside a component

`use StoreName` brings a store into a component, as it does into a page.
Every instance reads and writes the same store:

```wf
store Cart {
    state items: [String] = []
    action add(name: String) { items.push(name) }
}

component AddToCart(_ name: String) {
    use Cart
    Button("Add {name}").primary { on click { Cart.add(name) } }
}

page Shop(path: "/", title: "Shop", description: "Buttons that share one cart.") {
    use Cart
    Heading("Shop").h1
    AddToCart("Pen")
    Text("{Cart.items.length} in cart")
}
```

Clicking **Add Pen** changes the page's text from **0 in cart** to
**1 in cart**. [Stores](/learn/11-stores) covers stores in full.

## What a call puts on the root element

A component's *root element* is the one element its body draws at the top.
Some of what you write on a call goes to that element rather than to a
prop:

- A DOM event handler: `Pill("x") { on click { … } }` attaches to the root,
  so a styled button component is clickable wherever you place it.
- `class:`, which is added to the root's own classes.
- A `style { }` block, which styles the root: `Tile(label: "a") { style {
  grid-column: 2 / span 2 } }` places that tile in its grid. Its rule's class
  joins the root's classes, as `class:` does.
- An attribute the component takes no prop for: `aria-*`, `data-*`, `id`,
  `role`, `title` and `hidden`. You write it as you would on an element:
  `data-open: true` is `data-open="true"`, and `false` writes no attribute,
  except for an ARIA state, which keeps `"false"`.
- `mount:`, `update:` and `cleanup:` (see
  [Hand an element to a script](/recipes/hand-an-element-to-a-script)).
- `drag:`, the `drop…:` props, `on receive`, `on dragmove`, `on longpress`
  and `on swipe`. These need one root element: on a component whose body is
  an `if`, a `for` or several elements they are `C07`.

When the component declares a prop of that name, it receives the value
instead and decides where it goes. Declare the prop when the root is not
the right element for it. This `Pill` takes the class and the description
as props and puts them on its `Badge`:

```wf
component Pill(_ label: String, extra: String = "", note: String = "") {
    Badge(label, class: extra, aria-description: note)
}

page Pills(path: "/", title: "Pills", description: "Styled by the caller.") {
    Heading("Pills").h1
    Pill("Beta", extra: "chip-beta", note: "Not finished yet") { on click { log("beta") } }
}
```

The `on click` still goes to the root, which here is the `Badge`.

## Designing components

A component's interface is its props, events, slots and parts. These
guidelines keep it clear to callers.

### A value down, an event up

A component does not take `bind:`. To make a control of your own, take the
value as a prop and fire an event when it should change. The caller decides
what to do with the new value:

```wf
component Counter(_ value: Number, label: String, min: Number = 0) {
    event change(value: Number)
    Row(gap: .sm, align: .center) {
        Button("−", disabled: value <= min).sm { on click { emit change(value - 1) } }
        Text("{label}: {value}")
        Button("+").sm { on click { emit change(value + 1) } }
    }
}

page Booking(path: "/", title: "Booking", description: "How many seats.") {
    state seats = 1
    Heading("Book").h1
    Counter(seats, label: "Seats", min: 1) { on change(v) { seats = v } }
}
```

Clicking **+** sets `seats` to 2, and the component shows **Seats: 2**
because its `value` prop reads `seats`.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from Vue or Svelte?** There is no `v-model` or `bind:` on your own
> component. Take the value as a prop and fire a `change` event; the caller
> assigns its state in the handler. `bind:` belongs to the built-in controls.
> See [Coming from Vue](/coming-from/vue) and
> [Coming from Svelte](/coming-from/svelte).

### Pick the right way in

Choose the part of the interface by what the caller wants to do:

| The caller wants to… | Use |
|---|---|
| configure it with a value | a prop |
| choose one of a few looks | an `enum` prop, set with a flag |
| put any content inside | the default slot, `children` |
| put content in a particular place | a named slot |
| render each item its own way | a scoped slot, `slot row(item: T)` |
| offer a sub-element with its own props | a part, `Panel.Header` |
| hear that something happened | an `event` |

### Keep state where it is read

A component's own `state` is right for what only that component cares
about, such as whether its menu is open or it is hovered. What the page or
other components care about comes in as a prop and goes out as an event —
or lives in a store.

### Document it

A `///` comment above the component, a prop or an event is shown on hover
in the editor and in the gallery `wf docs` writes.

## Other people's code

To use a JavaScript library — a chart, a map, an editor — call it from a
`.js` file under `src/` and hand it an element with `mount:` and
`cleanup:`. To place somebody else's custom element, use
`Element("tag-name", …)`. You can also publish your components as custom
elements for another framework to place. See [Call your own JavaScript](/recipes/call-your-own-script),
[Hand an element to a script](/recipes/hand-an-element-to-a-script),
[Place a custom element](/recipes/place-a-custom-element) and
[Publish components as custom elements](/recipes/publish-custom-elements).

## Components in the pre-rendered page

A static build pre-renders each page to HTML — the *static paint*. It
expands every component call into HTML at build time: props substituted,
slots filled, and loops and branches over the seeded state drawn. A page
built from components is therefore a complete page before any script runs.
See [Static sites and SPAs](/about/static-or-single-page).

## Quick reference

| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `component Name(_ a: T, b: T = v) { … }` | Declare a component; `_` marks the positional prop |
| `Name(x, b: y).flag` | Call it; a flag sets a `Bool` prop or picks an enum case |
| `/// text` | Documentation for the component, a prop or an event |
| `event name(p: T)` | Declare an event |
| `emit name(v)` | Fire it from the body |
| `on name(v) { … }` | Handle it on the call |
| `slot` · `children` | Declare and place the default slot |
| `slot name` · `name` | Declare and place a named slot; the caller fills it with `name { … }` |
| `slot row(item: T)` · `row(item: v)` | A scoped slot; the caller fills it with `row(x) { … }` |
| `part Name(…) { … }` · `Owner.Name` | Declare a part and call it |
| `use Store` | Read a store inside the component |

[Components reference](/reference) lists every built-in,
and [Diagnostics](/errors) every code named here.

## Quiz

```quiz
A page declares `state count = 3` and places `Panel("Totals") { Text("{count}") }`. `Panel` declares no `count`. What does the fill show?
+ 3, the page's `count` -- A fill is compiled in the caller's scope: it reads the caller's state, and the component only decides where it lands.
- Nothing, because `Panel` has no `count` -- The component never reads the fill's names; they belong to the caller.
- An error until `count` is passed to `Panel` as a prop -- A fill needs no prop to read the caller's state.
```

```quiz
`component Note(_ text: String)` is called as `Note("Saved", tone: "success")`. What happens?
- It builds, and `tone="success"` lands on the root element -- Only what *What a call puts on the root element* lists goes to the root without a prop, and `tone` is not on that list.
- It builds, and `tone` is ignored -- Nothing is ignored in silence: the compiler checks a call to your component as it checks a built-in's.
+ The build stops with `C02`: `Note` declares no prop `tone` -- Declare the prop, or correct its spelling.
```

```quiz
A page places `Counter(0)` twice, and `Counter` declares `state n = start`. You press **+** on the first. What does the second show?
+ 0 -- Each placed instance has its own copy of the component's state.
- 1 -- State shared by every instance belongs in a store, not in a component.
- It depends on which instance was drawn first -- No instance reads another's state, whatever the order.
```

```quiz
`for row in rows { Counter(row.start) }` draws three counters, and you press **+** on each. Then `rows` gains an item. What happens to the three?
- They keep their counts, matched by position -- Without `by` there is nothing to match an item by; the list is rebuilt.
+ They start again from `row.start`, since a list with no key is rebuilt when it changes -- Key it, `for row in rows by row.id`, and each keeps its state; the build warns of this (U09).
- The build refuses the loop until it has a key -- It builds; the missing key is a warning, U09.
```

## Common mistakes

**A required prop left out.** A prop with no default must be passed on every
call:

```wf expect=C01
component UserCard(_ name: String, role: String) {
    Card { Text(name).bold  Text(role).muted }
}

page P(path: "/", title: "T", description: "D") {
    Heading("Team").h1
    UserCard("Ada")
}
```

Pass it, `UserCard("Ada", role: "Engineer")`, or give it a default in the
declaration, `role: String = ""`. See [C01](/errors/C01).

**A prop the component does not declare.** Often a misspelling, or a prop
written as though the component forwarded what it was given:

```wf expect=C02
component Note(_ text: String, muted: Bool = false) { Text(text) }

page P(path: "/", title: "T", description: "D") {
    Heading("Notes").h1
    Note("Saved", tone: "success")
}
```

Declare the prop, or correct its name. See [C02](/errors/C02).

**A handler that names more values than its event sends.** An event sends
what it declares, and nothing else:

```wf expect=T22
component Counter(_ value: Number) {
    event change(value: Number)
    Button("+") { on click { emit change(value + 1) } }
}

page P(path: "/", title: "T", description: "D") {
    state seats = 1
    state last = 0
    Heading("Seats: {seats}").h1
    Counter(seats) { on change(next, previous) { last = previous  seats = next } }
    Text("Was {last}")
}
```

Name only what the event sends, `on change(next)`, or declare a second
parameter and `emit` it. See [T22](/errors/T22).

## Next

[Stores](/learn/11-stores).



---

# Stores

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/11-stores

This chapter covers *stores*. A store holds state that more than one page or
component shares: the cart, the signed-in user, the theme, a cache of what was fetched. It holds
`state`, `derived` values and actions, and every page that reads it sees
the same values.

The one thing to remember: **a store is built the first time something
reads it.** Declaring a store does nothing. The first `Cart.items`,
`Cart.count` or `Cart.add(…)` builds it, and every later read uses that
same instance. As a result, the order you declare stores in does not
matter — a `derived` value may read a store declared below it — and a store
nothing reads costs nothing, in time or in bytes.

**In this chapter**

- Declaring a store and reading it from pages
- How long a store lives: its scope
- Actions, including async actions
- Keeping a value across visits with `persist`, and changing its shape later
- Connections and data a store owns
- Inspecting and testing a store
- When to use a store, and when a page's own state

## A first store

This program declares a `Cart` store and reads it from two pages:

```wf
type Item { id: String, name: String, price: Number, qty: Number = 1 }

store Cart {
    state items: [Item] = []
    derived count = items.length
    derived total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0)
    action add(item: Item) { items.push(item) }
    action remove(id: String) { items = items.filter(i => i.id != id) }
}

page Shop(path: "/", title: "Shop", description: "Things to buy.") {
    use Cart
    Heading("Shop").h1
    Button("Add a pen").primary { on click { Cart.add(Item(id: "pen", name: "Pen", price: 2.5)) } }
    Text("Cart: {Cart.count}, {format(Cart.total, .currency)}")
}

page CartPage(path: "/cart", title: "Cart", description: "What you are buying.") {
    use Cart
    Heading("Cart").h1
    for item in Cart.items by item.id {
        Row(justify: .between) {
            Text("{item.name} × {item.qty}")
            Button("Remove").sm { on click { Cart.remove(item.id) } }
        }
    }
    if Cart.count == 0 { Text("Your cart is empty.").muted }
}
```

Clicking **Add a pen** changes **Cart: 0, $0.00** to **Cart: 1, $2.50**,
and the `/cart` page lists the pen.

- `store Cart { … }` declares the store and its members.
- `use Cart` in a page says the page reads the store. The page then reads
  members as `Cart.items` and `Cart.count`, and calls actions as
  `Cart.add(…)`.
- Everything that reads `Cart.count`, on any page, updates when it changes.

The checker knows every member and its type. `Cart.cont` is an error
(`T06`, with the nearest member it does have), and `Cart.add("pen")` is an
error because `add` takes an `Item` (`T01`).

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** There is no context provider to wrap the tree in,
> and no selector to write. Declare the store once and read `Cart.count`
> anywhere; only what reads `count` updates when it changes. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

## Store members

A store holds the same members a page does: `state`, `persist`, `derived`
values and actions. This fuller `Cart` adds a coupon kept across visits and
an action that raises the quantity of an item already in the cart:

```wf
type Item { id: String, name: String, price: Number, qty: Number = 1 }

store Cart {
    state items: [Item] = []
    persist coupon = ""

    derived count = items.reduce((n, i) => n + i.qty, 0)
    derived subtotal = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0)
    derived discount = if coupon == "SAVE10" { subtotal * 0.1 } else { 0 }
    derived total = subtotal - discount

    action add(item: Item) {
        if items.some(i => i.id == item.id) {
            items = items.map(i => if i.id == item.id { { ...i, qty: i.qty + 1 } } else { i })
        } else {
            items.push(item)
        }
    }
    action remove(id: String) { items = items.filter(i => i.id != id) }
    action clear() { items = [] }
}
```

`add` changes `items` itself: it assigns a new list with that one item's
quantity raised. Writing `let found = items.find(…)` and then
`found.qty = found.qty + 1` would change only the local copy that `let`
made ([chapter 7](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity#actions-and-locals)), and the
cart would stay as it was.

Inside the store you read its members by their bare names: `items`,
`count`. Outside it, a page or component reads them through the store's
name: `Cart.items`, `Cart.count`.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from Vue or Svelte?** `use Cart` is not Pinia's `useCartStore()`
> and makes no copy; there is no `$cart` prefix either. Every reader gets the
> one instance, by the store's name. See [Coming from Vue](/coming-from/vue)
> and [Coming from Svelte](/coming-from/svelte).

You may declare a store in any `.wf` file the build reads. By convention it
goes in `src/stores/`, and `wf generate store Cart` writes it there. A page
reaches a store by name from anywhere. `use` says which stores a page
reads, for the person reading the code and for the editor; it does not
limit what the page can reach, and a page that reads `Cart.count` without
it reads the same store.

## Store scope

A store's *scope* says how long it lives. You set it in the declaration;
these three stores live for the page, the tab and the route:

```wf
store Cart(scope: .app) { state items: [String] = [] }        // the default: as long as the page is open
store Session(scope: .session) { state step = 1 }             // this tab's
store Filters(scope: .route) { state search = "" }            // this route's
```

| Scope | Lives | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `.app` (the default) | as long as the page is open | the cart, the signed-in user |
| `.session` | as long as the tab; what it keeps goes in the tab's own storage, gone when the tab is | state for one tab |
| `.route` | until the route changes | the filters on a list, a wizard's step |

When the route changes, a `.route` store drops what it holds. The next read
builds it again from its initial values.

`store X(eager: true)` builds the store at boot instead of on first read.
Use it for the rare store whose set-up must run whether or not a page reads
it. If a `derived` value of yours has a side effect that used to run when
the page loaded, `eager: true` keeps it running then.

## Actions

A store's actions are its interface: pages change the store by calling
them. An action may be asynchronous — it uses `await` — and an async action
exposes `pending`, which is `true` while a call of it runs:

```wf
store Session {
    state user: Map? = null
    state error = ""
    derived loggedIn = user != null

    action login(email: String, password: String) {
        error = ""
        try {
            let r = await fetch("/api/login", { method: "POST", body: { email: email, password: password } })
            user = r.user
        } catch e {
            error = "Could not sign in: {e.message}"
        }
    }

    action logout() {
        user = null
        navigate("/")
    }
}

page Login(path: "/login", title: "Sign in", description: "Sign in.") {
    use Session
    state email = ""
    state password = ""
    Heading("Sign in").h1
    Form {
        on submit { Session.login(email, password) }
        Input(bind: email, label: "Email").email.required
        Input(bind: password, label: "Password").password.required
        Button("Sign in", type: .submit, disabled: Session.login.pending).primary
    }
    if Session.error != "" { Alert(Session.error).danger }
}
```

The **Sign in** button is disabled while `Session.login` runs.

Inside an action, a bare name is the store's own member — `items`, `error`
— unless something nearer declares it. A `let`, a parameter, a `for`
binding, a lambda's parameter or a caught error belongs to the action until
its block ends. So `let items = …` in an action reads and writes that local
variable and leaves the store's `items` alone.

An action may read other stores through their names. Stores are global, so
a store needs no `use`. A `derived` value may call one of the store's own
actions to compute a value, but not one that assigns state: that is `X04`,
because the derived value would change state every time it is read.

## Keeping a value across visits

`persist` declares a member whose value is kept in the browser's storage
and read back on the next visit. It is stored under the store's name and
the member's name, so a page and a store may each persist a `theme`.
`persist` works the same way at the top of a page or a component.

```wf
store Prefs {
    persist scheme = "system"
    persist density = "comfortable"
    persist recent: [String] = []
    action visited(path: String) {
        recent = [path, ...recent.filter(p => p != path)].take(5)
    }
}
```

By default the value goes in `localStorage`, and **a write in another tab
of the same site arrives in this one**. `localStorage` is shared between
tabs, and two tabs that disagree about the theme would be a bug.

### Options

A block after the declaration changes where and how the value is kept:

```wf
type Item { id: String, qty: Number = 1 }

store Cart {
    persist items: [Item] = [] {
        in: .local          // .local (default, across visits) · .session (this tab) · .app (the project's own)
        version: 2          // the version of the shape this build writes
        sync: false         // don't take what another tab wrote
        migrate 1 -> 2 { old.map(i => Item(id: i.id, qty: i.count)) }
    }
}
```

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `in:` | Where the value lives: `.local` (the default, kept across visits), `.session` (this tab), or `.app` (see [Storage the project provides](#storage-the-project-provides)) |
| `version:` | The version of the value's shape that this build writes |
| `sync:` | `false` stops this page taking a value another tab or window wrote |
| `key:` | Keeps one stored value per key (see [One stored value per instance](#one-stored-value-per-instance)) |
| `migrate n -> m { … }` | Brings a value written at version `n` forward to `m` |

### Versions and migrations

A version is a promise to returning readers. Once you declare a shape with
`version:`, the page brings a value written by an older build forward one
step at a time. Each `migrate n -> n+1` step reads the old value as `old`
and returns the new one. A reader who last visited two deploys ago keeps
their cart instead of finding it empty.

The build checks the chain:

- A gap in the chain is a `P01` warning: an older value would be discarded.
- A step above the declared version is a `P02` warning: it never runs.
- A value written by a *newer* build is left alone, and the page uses the
  initial value. This build cannot know what a later shape means.

The build also remembers the shape of every persisted value, in
`.wf-cache/persist.json`. When a shape changes and `version:` was not
raised, it warns (`D04`): a returning reader's browser still holds the old
shape, which the page would read as the new one.

> [!WARNING]
> A `persist` inside a `store(scope: .route)` does not reset with the route.
> The route change drops the store, and the next read builds it again — from
> storage, so the value comes straight back. The build reports this as
> `P03`. Use `state` for what the route owns, and a wider scope for what
> outlives it.

### One stored value per instance

A `persist` in a component uses one stored value for every place the
component is drawn. Three `Panel`s that each persist `open` share one
value, so opening one opens them all. `key:` names what tells the instances
apart, and each key gets its own stored value:

```wf
component Panel(_ title: String) {
    persist open = false { key: title }
    Button(title) { on click { open = !open } }
    if open { children }
}
```

The build warns (`D03`) about a component that persists a value with no
`key:` and is placed more than once, or in a loop.

### A key that follows state

`key:` is read as state. When what it reads changes, the member takes the
value kept under the new key, and writes go there. A desktop app keeps its
layout per project this way. A store's key may read the store itself, or
another store:

```wf
store Layout {
    state project = "halyard"
    persist side = 240 {
        key: project
        in: .app
    }
}
```

### Storage the project provides

`in: .app` keeps the value somewhere other than the browser's two storages:
a desktop app's store reached through its native bridge, or an extension's
storage. It reads `window.wfStorage.app`, which a script of the project's
under `src/` defines. The object has this shape:
`{ get(name), set(name, text), remove?(name), watch?(name, fn) }`.

- `get` answers at once or with a promise, so an IPC call is fine. Until it
  answers, the value is its declared initial value. A write made before the
  answer is not undone by it, and an answer for a key that has since
  changed is ignored.
- `set` receives the JSON text to keep.
- `watch(name, fn)`, when present, hears another writer, such as another
  window, and returns a function that stops it. `sync: false` turns it off.

If no `window.wfStorage.app` is defined, the value is kept in
`localStorage`, and `wf serve` says so on the console.

This script connects `.app` to Tauri's IPC:

```js
// src/app-store.js — Tauri's IPC, reached when a value is read or written
const call = (command, args) => window.__TAURI__.core.invoke(command, args);
window.wfStorage = {
  app: {
    get: (name) => call("store_get", { name }),
    set: (name, text) => call("store_set", { name, text }),
  },
};
```

See [Make a desktop or phone app with Tauri](/recipes/tauri-app) for the rest of a desktop project.

### Secrets are never persisted

`persist token: Secret = ""` is an error (`T12`). The point of the `Secret`
type is that its value never reaches a place any script can read, and the
browser's storage is such a place. Keep a session in an httpOnly cookie
instead (see [Security](/about/security)).

## A connection a store holds

A store may hold a connection — a `socket`, a `stream`, a `channel`, a
`peer` or a `worker` (see [Open a socket](/recipes/open-a-socket)) — for every page at
once. The connection opens when the store is first read and closes with the
store; a `.route` store's connection closes when its route leaves. The
store's actions and handlers name the connection as it is declared, and a
page reads it through the store:

```wf
store Live {
    state last = ""
    socket feed = ws("wss://example.com/feed") {
        on message(m) { last = m.text }
    }
    action say(text: String) { feed.send({ text: text }) }
}

page Feed(path: "/", title: "Feed", description: "One line for every page.") {
    Heading("Feed").h1
    match Live.feed {
        open { Text(Live.last) }
        else { Text("Reconnecting…") }
    }
    Button("Wave") { on click { Live.say("hello") } }
}
```

## Loading data into a store

A store can own a `resource` (see [Data and APIs](/learn/15-data)). It is asked
for the first time something reads the store, and lives as long as the
store does — not as long as the page that happened to read it first — so
another page that reads the store finds what has already arrived, and
nothing is asked for again. It is abandoned with the store: a `.route`
store's when its route leaves, to be asked for afresh when the route comes
back.

Inside the store it is `rows`, anywhere else `Deploys.rows`, and its
`state`, `data`, `error`, `refreshing` and `pending` follow it in both. Its
address and options read the store's own state, so an action that moves
one asks again:

```wf
type Deploy { id: String, status: String }

store Deploys {
    state page = 1
    resource rows: [Deploy] = fetch("/api/deploys?page={page}")
    derived failing = (rows.data ?? []).filter(d => d.status == "failed").length
    action next() { page = page + 1 }
    action refresh() { rows.reload() }
}

page DeploysPage(path: "/deploys", title: "Deploys", description: "Every deploy.") {
    Heading("Deploys").h1
    Text("{Deploys.failing} failing")
    match Deploys.rows {
        loading { Spinner }
        error(e) { Text(e.message) }
        ready(rows) {
            for d in rows by d.id { Text("{d.id}: {d.status}") }
        }
    }
    Button("Refresh", disabled: Deploys.rows.pending) { on click { Deploys.refresh() } }
    Button("Next page") { on click { Deploys.next() } }
}
```

A resource over a service's endpoint is owned the same way —
`resource list = Catalog.items(page: page, paginate: .page)` — and its
`loadMore()` moves the store's `page`. The resource is the store's to
replace: `Deploys.rows = …` is an `X01`, as it is inside the store.

When an action decides what is kept — a reply merged into rows already
held, a list built from several calls — fill the store's state from a
`fetch` instead, and call the action where the data is first wanted:

```wf
store Feed {
    state items: [Map] = []
    action more() {
        let r = await fetch("/api/feed?after={items.length}")
        items = [...items, ...r.items]
    }
}
```

## Stores in the pre-rendered page

A static build pre-renders each page to HTML — the *static paint*. The
static paint seeds each store's state from its initial values, so
`Cart.count` is painted as `0`, and a store seeded with rows paints the
rows. A value an action changes at run time is corrected once the page is
live.

## Looking at one while it runs

`wf serve` puts a **stores** button in the corner of the page. It opens on
what every store that has been built is holding, and a log of every action
that has run: the arguments it was given, and the state before and after
it. Clicking an entry puts the store back to what it held before that
action, which is usually enough to find a bug.

The same tools are on `window.WF`, for a console or a script:

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `WF.storeSnapshot()` | Returns what every built store holds |
| `WF.storeSnapshot("Cart")` | Returns what one store holds |
| `WF.restoreStore("Cart", values)` | Puts a store back to `values` |
| `WF.watchStores(fn)` | Calls `fn` for every action, and returns the function that stops it |

Nothing is recorded while nothing is watching, so a deployed site pays
nothing for any of it. See [Runtime API](/reference/runtime).

## Testing a store

`wf test` renders a test with the project's stores at hand, and a test's
`data` seeds a store by its name. This test seeds a cart with two of one
item and reads what `CartSummary` shows:

```wf
type Item { id: String, qty: Number = 1 }

store Cart {
    state items: [Item] = []
    derived count = items.map(i => i.qty).sum()
}

component CartSummary {
    use Cart
    Text("{Cart.count} items")
}

test "the cart shows what is in it"(data: { Cart: { items: [{ id: "a", qty: 2 }] } }) {
    CartSummary
    expect "2 items"
}
```

In a project the store and the component live under `src/` and the test
under `tests/`.

A test that clicks a button runs the store's actions in a real browser.
See [Testing](/learn/16-testing).

## When to use a store

Put a value where the code that reads it can reach it, and no wider:

| The value is… | Keep it in |
|---|---|
| read by more than one page, or must outlive a navigation | a store |
| owned by one screen, and should go when the screen does | `store X(scope: .route)` |
| read by one page and its components | the page's `state`, passed down as props |
| read by one component | the component's own `state` |

## Quick reference

| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `store Name { … }` | Declare a store, built on first read |
| `store Name(scope: .route)` | How long it lives: `.app` (the default), `.session` or `.route` |
| `store Name(eager: true)` | Build it at boot |
| `use Name` | Say a page or component reads it |
| `Name.member` · `Name.action(…)` | Read a member, call an action |
| `Name.action.pending` | `true` while an async action runs |
| `persist x = v` | Keep a member across visits |
| `persist x = v { in: …, version: n, sync: false, key: k }` | Where and how it is kept |
| `migrate n -> m { … old … }` | Bring an older stored value forward |

## Quiz

```quiz
A program declares a `Cart` store, and nothing has read it yet. When is the store built?
- When the app boots -- Only `store Cart(eager: true)` is built at boot.
- Each time a page says `use Cart`, as a fresh copy for that page -- Every reader shares one instance; `use` makes no copy.
+ The first time something reads one of its members or calls an action -- A store nothing reads is never built and costs nothing.
```

```quiz
A page reads `Cart.count` but has no `use Cart` line. What happens?
+ It builds and works: `use` says which stores a page reads, and does not limit what it can reach -- A store is reached by its name from anywhere.
- The build stops with `X05` -- `X05` is a `use` that names a store nothing declares, such as `use Carts`.
- It builds, but `Cart.count` is always `0` on that page -- Every reader sees the same instance, with or without `use`.
```

```quiz
`store Filters(scope: .route) { persist search = "" }`. The reader types a search, leaves the route and comes back. What is `search`?
- `""`, because a `.route` store is dropped when the route changes -- The store is dropped, but the next read builds it again from storage.
+ What they typed: the value comes back from storage, which the build warns about (`P03`) -- Use `state` for what the route owns, and a wider scope for what outlives it.
- An error: a `.route` store cannot hold `persist` -- It builds; `P03` is a warning.
```

## Common mistakes

**A member the store does not have.** A name guessed from what the store
ought to hold, rather than read from what it declares:

```wf expect=T06
store Cart {
    state items: [String] = []
    derived count = items.length
}

page P(path: "/", title: "T", description: "D") {
    use Cart
    Heading("Cart").h1
    Text("{Cart.total} items")
}
```

Read a member the store declares, `Cart.count`, or declare the one you need.
See [T06](/errors/T06).

**`use` with the store's name misspelled.** A store's name is capitalised,
and `use` must name it exactly:

```wf expect=X05
store Cart { state items: [String] = [] }

page P(path: "/", title: "T", description: "D") {
    use cart
    Heading("{Cart.items.length} in the cart").h1
}
```

Write `use Cart`. See [X05](/errors/X05).

**Assigning a store's `derived` value.** A `derived` value is worked out from
the state it reads, so nothing may set it:

```wf expect=X01
store Cart {
    state items: [String] = []
    derived count = items.length
}

page P(path: "/", title: "T", description: "D") {
    use Cart
    Heading("{Cart.count} items").h1
    Button("Empty") { on click { Cart.count = 0 } }
}
```

Change the state it reads, through an action: `action clear() { items = [] }`,
called as `Cart.clear()`. See [X01](/errors/X01).

## Next

[Types](/learn/12-types).



---

# Types

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/12-types

This chapter covers WebFluent's types and the checker that holds a program to
them. The checker runs in `wf build`, `wf check` and the
editor, before any output is written. It is *gradual*: a program that
declares no types still checks, because whatever the checker cannot work
out has the type `Any`, and `Any` agrees with everything. Every annotation
you add lets the checker say more. It is also *structural*: a value fits a
type when it has the right fields, whatever it was declared as. The checker
changes nothing in the output; it only reports.

**In this chapter**

- The type language, and the types that come with the language
- Records (`type`), enums and the shapes of map literals
- Where the checker gets a type from, and how it infers one
- Narrowing a value that may be `null`
- Typing data from the network
- The checks, and what the checker does not check

## A first type error

This page declares an `Invoice` record and builds one with the wrong kind
of value for `total`:

```wf expect=T01
type Invoice { id: String, total: Number, paid: Bool = false }

page Invoices(path: "/", title: "Invoices", description: "What is owed.") {
    state invoice: Invoice = Invoice(id: "INV-001", total: "120")
    Heading("Invoice {invoice.id}").h1
    Text("Owed: {invoice.total}")
}
```

The build stops, pointing at the field:

```text
error[T01]: `total` of `Invoice` is `Number`, but `"120"` is `String`
 --> src/App.wf:4:53
```

Writing `total: 120` fixes it. Had the invoice been an untyped map,
`{ id: "INV-001", total: "120" }`, the page would build, and
`invoice.total` would be a string at run time.

## The type language

| Type | Written | Values |
|---|---|---|
| String | `String` | `"text"`, `"with {interpolation}"` |
| Number | `Number` (`Int` and `Float` are accepted as other spellings of it) | `42`, `3.14` |
| Bool | `Bool` | `true`, `false` |
| List | `[String]`, `[Todo]` | `[a, b]` |
| Map | `Map` | `{ key: value }` — an object with unknown keys |
| Optional | `String?`, `Todo?` | a value or `null` |
| Record | the `type`'s name | `Todo(id: "a", title: "b")` |
| Enum | the `enum`'s name | `.case` |
| Any | `Any` | anything; what is not known |

You write a type after a colon on a `state`, a prop, an action parameter, a
`type` field, a route parameter, a `let` or a `resource`. This page uses
several:

```wf
page Typed(path: "/", title: "Typed", description: "State with declared types.") {
    state name: String = ""
    state count: Number = 0
    state tags: [String] = []
    state picked: String? = null
    state profile: Map = {}
    action greet(who: String, times: Number) { log("hi {who} × {times}") }
    derived pick = picked ?? "none"
    Heading("Typed").h1
    Text("{name} {count} {tags.length} {pick}")
    Button("Go") { on click { greet(name, count) } }
}
```

## The types the language brings with it

Eleven more types come with the language. Each is a **plain JSON value at
run time**, with no wrapper object, so it crosses a `fetch`, a `persist`,
the static paint (the HTML the build pre-renders for a page) and the
template engine unchanged. `.native()` hands a real platform object to a
library that wants one.

| Type | Carried by | Written as a literal |
|---|---|---|
| `Date` | `"2026-03-14"` | `@2026-03-14` |
| `Time` | `"09:30"` | `@09:30` |
| `DateTime` | ISO 8601 | `@2026-03-14T09:30Z` |
| `Duration` | milliseconds | `3.days`, `90.minutes`, `250.ms` |
| `Money` | `{ amount: 1299, currency: "EUR" }` | `€12.99`, `$9.99`, `£4.50` |
| `Url` | a string | `"https://example.com"` |
| `Email` | a string | `"ada@example.com"` |
| `Color` | a string | `#0F766E` |
| `Uuid` | a string | `uuid()` makes a fresh one |
| `File` | the browser's `File` | what a `FileUpload` yields |
| `Secret` | a string | — |

Money is held in **minor units** — cents, pence — so its arithmetic is
whole-number arithmetic and nothing drifts. A duration is milliseconds, so
it adds to a moment. `uuid()` is where a `Uuid` comes from: it uses the
platform's own generator where there is one, and otherwise builds a
version-4 UUID from the best randomness available.

This page books a stay with dates, money and a refined number:

```wf
type Booking {
    id: Uuid
    guest: Email
    from: Date
    nights: Number(1..=30)
    total: Money
}

page Stay(path: "/", title: "Stay", description: "One booking.") {
    state from: Date = @2026-03-14
    state nights: Number = 5
    state total: Money = €249.00

    derived checkout = from.plus(days: nights)
    derived late = now.date().isAfter(checkout)

    Heading("Your stay").h1
    Text("Out on {checkout:.date(long)}")
    Text("Due {format(total)}")
    if late { Alert("Checkout has passed").warning }
}
```

Everything the language **computes** is a call; everything the carrier
**already has** is a field. So `total.amount` and `total.currency` are
fields, and `from.plus(days: nights)` and `now.date()` are calls.

| Type | Methods |
|---|---|
| `Date` `Time` `DateTime` | `.year() .month() .day() .weekday() .hour() .minute() .second()`, `.plus(days: 3)` and `.minus(…)` (which take `years months weeks days hours minutes seconds ms`), `.isBefore(d) .isAfter(d) .isSame(d)`, `.until(d)` (a `Duration`), `.startOfDay() .startOfWeek() .startOfMonth() .endOfDay()`, `.native()`; `DateTime` also `.date() .time() .inZone("Europe/Berlin")` |
| `Duration` | `.days() .hours() .minutes() .seconds() .ms()`, `.plus(d)` |
| `Money` | `.plus(m) .minus(m) .times(n) .convert(rate, "USD")`; `format(m)` needs no style and no currency code |
| `Url` | `.host() .path() .query()`, `.with(query: { page: 2 })` |
| `Email` | `.domain()` |
| `Color` | `.mix(other, 0.2) .lighten(0.1) .darken(0.1) .alpha(0.5) .contrast(other)` |
| `File` | `.preview()` — an object URL, revoked when the scope that made it leaves; the fields `.name .size .type` |

Adding a month lands on a day that exists: `@2026-01-31.plus(months: 1)` is
the 28th of February, not the 3rd of March. All of these methods also run
at build time, so the static paint shows the answer instead of a blank that
fills in when the page hydrates.

### A literal is held to its type

A string written where one of these types is wanted is read as that type,
and checked where you wrote it. The second `state` on this page does not
build:

```wf expect=T01
page Links(path: "/", title: "Links", description: "A URL held to its type.") {
    state site: Url = "https://example.com"     // fine
    state bad: Url = "example"                  // T01: a URL has a scheme
    Heading("Links").h1
    Text("{site.host()} {bad}")
}
```

### `now`

`now` is a `DateTime` that keeps itself current. It updates every minute by
default, or as often as a page asks with `now(every: …)`:

```wf
page Feed(path: "/", title: "Feed", description: "What happened lately.") {
    state posted: DateTime = @2026-03-14T09:30:00Z
    derived age = posted.until(now)
    Heading("Feed").h1
    Text("{ago(posted)} — {age.minutes()} minutes")
    Text("ticking: {now(every: 1.seconds)}")
}
```

Read `now` where it is shown or in a `derived` value. A `state` takes its
initial value once, so `state clock = now(every: 1.seconds)` stays at the
moment the page opened (`X06`; see
[State and reactivity](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity)).

### A condition on a type

Any type may say what its values must be. The compiler holds every value it
can read to that condition, as it does to the three states on this page:

```wf
page Stay(path: "/", title: "Stay", description: "Values held to a condition.") {
    state nights: Number(1..=30) = 12
    state pass: String(minLength: 8) = "correcthorse"
    state start: Date(after: @2026-01-01) = @2026-03-14
    Heading("Stay").h1
    Text("{nights} nights from {start}, {pass.length} characters")
}
```

The conditions are `min`, `max`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `pattern`,
`after` and `before`, and a range for the two ends at once: `1..=30`
includes the end, `0..10` excludes it. A value that arrives at run time —
typed into a field, say — is refused by validation, from the same
condition, so a refined type needs no `validate` rule for it (see
[Forms](/learn/14-forms)).

### `Secret` is not a string

A `Secret` is a string the compiler will not let escape. This page lets one
escape four ways, and each is a `T12`:

```wf expect=T12
page Login(path: "/", title: "Login", description: "Four ways a secret escapes.") {
    state token: Secret = ""
    persist saved: Secret = ""                       // kept in the browser
    Heading("Signed in").h1
    Text(token)                                      // shown
    Text("Bearer {token}")                           // in text, which is how it ends up in a URL
    Button("Debug") { on click { log(token) } }      // in the console, and often in a log service
}
```

Joining it with `+` or handing it to a browser global such as `console`, a
storage or a `fetch` address is a `T12` too, and a secret has no string
members to read. Hold it in `state`, which ends with the visit; what must
outlive the visit belongs on the server.

### Your own name wins

A `type` the program declares takes the name back from the language. A
project with its own `type Color { name: String }` means that record
everywhere it writes `Color`.

## Records: `type`

A *record* is a value with named, typed fields, declared with `type`:

```wf
enum Tone { neutral, info, danger }

type Todo {
    id: String
    title: String
    done: Bool = false
    tone: Tone = .neutral
    note: String?
}

type Admin = Todo { owner: String }

page Records(path: "/", title: "Records", description: "A list of records.") {
    state todos: [Todo] = [
        Todo(id: "1", title: "Write the docs"),
        Todo(id: "2", title: "Ship", done: true, tone: .info, note: "Friday"),
    ]
    state special: Admin = Admin(id: "3", title: "Review", owner: "sam")
    Heading("Records").h1
    for todo in todos by todo.id {
        Row(gap: .sm) {
            Text(todo.title)
            if let n = todo.note { Badge(n).info }
        }
    }
    Text("{special.owner} owns {special.title}")
}
```

- You may separate fields with newlines or commas.
- You build a record by naming its fields: `Todo(id: "1", title: "x")`. A
  field with a default may be left out, and a `T?` field defaults to
  `null`. Leaving out a field with no default is `C01`.
- A record whose fields can all be left out is built with none given,
  `Offers()`, wherever a value goes: a prop's default (`component
  Card(offers: Offers = Offers())`), a field's default, a `const`, a
  `state`, an argument.
- `type Admin = Todo { owner: String }` extends a record: an `Admin` has
  every field of `Todo`, then its own.
- Records are structural: `{ id: "a", title: "b" }` given where a `Todo` is
  wanted is a `Todo`, and its fields are checked against the record's.
- A `Map` fits any record, and a record fits a `Map`. So JSON from `fetch`
  fits a `type` it was never declared as.

## Enums

An *enum* is a type with a fixed set of *cases*. A case may carry a
*payload* — values that travel with it:

```wf
enum Size { sm, md, lg }
enum Status { idle, running(job: String), failed(reason: String), done(count: Number) }

page Enums(path: "/", title: "Enums", description: "Enums with and without payloads.") {
    state size: Size = .md
    state s: Status = .idle
    Heading("Enums").h1
    Button("Bigger") { on click { size = .lg } }
    Button("Start") { on click { s = .running("build-42") } }
    Text(match size { .sm { "small" } .md { "medium" } else { "large" } })
    match s {
        .running(job) { Text("Running {job}") }
        .failed(reason) { Alert(reason).danger }
        .done(n) { Text("{n} done") }
        else { Text("Idle") }
    }
}
```

- You write a case as `.name`. On its own it is a case of an enum not yet
  known; where a `Size` is wanted it becomes a `Size`, and `.huge` there is
  `T02`.
- A case with a payload, `.failed("x")`, is checked like a call. A `match`
  arm binds the payload: `.failed(r)` gives `r` the type `String`.
- At run time a bare case is its name and a case with a payload is a list,
  `["failed", "timed out"]`, so `size == .lg` still compares cases.
- A `match` with no `else` must give every case an arm (`T15`).
- An enum prop is written to a component's root element as `data-<prop>`
  (see [Enum props](/learn/10-components#enum-props)).

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from TypeScript in React or Vue?** A union of strings such as
> `"idle" | "running" | "failed"` becomes an `enum`, and a field that only
> some states have becomes that case's payload: `.failed(reason: String)`. A
> `match` then has to give every case an arm. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

## Shapes of map literals

A map literal has the fields it was written with. `{ name: "", age: 0 }`
has the *shape* `{ name: String, age: Number }`, and reading `form.nam` is
`T05`, with the fields it does have. A shape fits a `Map`, a record with the
same fields, and any shape it agrees with. An empty `{}` and a literal with
a spread say nothing about their keys, so they are plain `Map`s.

```wf
page Shapes(path: "/", title: "Shapes", description: "A map literal with a shape.") {
    state form = { name: "", age: 0, tags: ["new"] }
    Heading("Shapes").h1
    Input(bind: form.name, label: "Name")
    Text("{form.name} is {form.age} with {form.tags.length} tags")
}
```

## Where types come from

The checker reads a type from five places.

**Declared:** annotations, a `type`'s fields, an `enum`'s cases, a page's
route parameters, an event's parameters, a component's props.

**Inferred:** a literal; a list of literals (`[1, 2]` is `[Number]`, `[]`
is `[Any]`); a record construction; a `derived` value from its expression;
a `state` from its initial value (one that starts as `null` is `Any?`); a
`for` binding from the list's item type; a `match` arm's binding; an
`if let` binding; a lambda's parameters from what the method expects
(`items.filter(item => …)` gives `item` the item type).

**From the registry:** the type of every built-in prop, and what a `bind:`
needs — `Checkbox` and `Switch` a `Bool`, `Slider` a `Number`, `Input` a
`String` or a `Number` by its input type.

**From the method tables:**

- On a `String`: `trim`, `toLowerCase`, `toUpperCase`, `replace`, `slice`,
  `padStart`, `repeat`, `capitalize`, `truncate(n)` → `String`; `length`,
  `indexOf` → `Number`; `includes`, `startsWith`, `endsWith` → `Bool`;
  `split` → `[String]`.
- On a list: `map` → `[U]` from the lambda; `filter`, `slice`, `concat`,
  `sort`, `sortBy`, `unique`, `take`, `flatMap` → `[T]`; `find`, `first`,
  `last` → `T?`; `some`, `every`, `includes` → `Bool`; `length`, `sum`,
  `indexOf`, `findIndex` → `Number`; `join` → `String`; `groupBy` → `Map`;
  `reduce` → the initial value's type.
- On a `Number`: `toFixed`, `toString` → `String`.

Any other method is `Any`. The full lists are in
[Built-ins](/reference/built-ins).

**From stores:** `Todos.items` has the type of the store's state, and
`Todos.add` the signature of its action.

Browser globals (`window`, `document`, `JSON`, `Math`, `Date`, …) are
`Any`.

A name keeps the type it was declared or inferred with: `state x = 1` stays
a `Number`, and assigning a string to it later is `T01`.

## Bidirectional inference

The checker works in both directions. When the context wants a type, it
checks the expression against that type; otherwise it reads the type off
the expression. The comments show what each `derived` value is inferred to
be:

```wf
type Row { id: Number, label: String, score: Number? }

page Infer(path: "/", title: "Infer", description: "Types the checker works out.") {
    state rows: [Row] = [Row(id: 1, label: "a"), Row(id: 2, label: "b", score: 9)]
    derived labels = rows.map(r => r.label)                 // [String]
    derived best = rows.find(r => r.score != null)          // Row?
    derived total = rows.reduce((n, r) => n + (r.score ?? 0), 0)   // Number
    derived kind = if total > 5 { "high" } else { "low" }   // String
    derived firstScore = best?.score ?? 0                   // Number
    derived joined = labels.join(", ")                      // String
    Heading("Infer").h1
    Text("{joined} {kind} {firstScore}")
}
```

The rules for operators and forms:

- `a ?? b` is `a` without its `null`, joined with `b`.
- `a?.b` is `b`'s type made optional, and the rest of the chain with it.
- `if` and `match` used as values have the type both arms fit: the same
  type, `T?` when one arm is `null`, and `Any` otherwise.
- `-`, `*`, `/` and `%` give a `Number`; `+` gives a `String` when either
  side is one; comparisons and `&&`, `||`, `!` give a `Bool`.
- `await e` on a `fetch` is `Any` unless you annotate it:
  `let r: [Row] = await fetch(…)`.
- `let { a, b } = m` and `let [x, y] = l` bind the fields and the items.

## Narrowing optionals

A value of type `T?` may be `null`, so you must *narrow* it — prove it is
not `null` — before you read a field or method off it. Reading one without
narrowing is `T04`. Each of these forms narrows a name within its branch:

```wf
type Todo { id: String, title: String, note: String? }

page Narrow(path: "/", title: "Narrow", description: "Values that may be null, narrowed.") {
    state sel: Todo? = null
    state todo: Todo = Todo(id: "1", title: "x")
    Heading("Narrow").h1
    if let n = todo.note { Text("{n.length} chars") }
    if sel != null { Text(sel.title) }
    if sel { Text(sel.title) }
    derived label = if sel != null { sel.title } else { "none" }
    Text(todo.note ?? "no note")
    Text(sel?.title ?? "nothing selected")
    Button("Pick") { on click { sel = todo } }
}
```

Narrowing follows the flow of a block: it holds in the branch the condition
guards, not after it. A check for `null` also narrows the `else` branch,
and the code after `if x == null { return }`. An item at a fixed index,
such as `todos[0]`, may be missing, so it counts as `T?` unless a condition
like `todos.length > 0` encloses it.

A list narrows too: `xs.filter(x => x != null)` is a list of the items that
are there, so a `[Todo?]` filtered that way is a `[Todo]` whose items need
no `?.`.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** `{user && <Profile user={user} />}` becomes
> `if let u = user { Profile(u) }`, and inside the branch `u` is a `User`, not
> a `User?`. `undefined` is not a separate value to check for: a value that
> may be missing is `T?`, and missing is `null`. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

> [!WARNING]
> Splicing a value that may be `null` into text shows the word `null` on
> the page. The checker warns (`T19`); say what to show instead with `??`,
> as in `Text(todo.note ?? "no note")`.

## Typing data from the network

`fetch` returns `Any`, because the checker cannot see what a URL will
return. Annotate the resource or the local variable to type its value:

```wf
type Deploy { id: String, status: String, startedAt: String }

page Deploys(path: "/", title: "Deploys", description: "A typed resource.") {
    resource deploys: [Deploy] = fetch("/api/deploys")
    Heading("Deploys").h1
    match deploys {
        loading { Spinner }
        error(e) { Alert("Failed: {e.message}").danger }
        ready(rows) {
            for d in rows by d.id { Text("{d.id} {d.status} {ago(d.startedAt)}") }
        }
    }
}
```

The checker trusts the annotation. A development build (`wf serve`) also
holds each response to its declared type, and a mismatch is a `.parse`
error that names the place, such as `$[1].status is missing`.

When the server publishes an OpenAPI specification, let the compiler read
it instead: `api Backend from "openapi.json"` types every endpoint,
parameter, response and error from the file, and turns each named schema
into a `type`, or an `enum` for a string with cases (see
[Data and APIs](/learn/15-data#read-the-service-from-an-openapi-file)). An `api` you write by
hand types its calls the same way: `get users() -> [User]`.

## The checks

The type checker reports these codes. All are errors except `T19`, `T20`
and `T21`, which are warnings.

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| `T01` | A value of the wrong type given to a prop, a state, a field, a parameter, an assignment, an argument, or a `bind:` |
| `T02` | A case the enum does not have |
| `T04` | A field or method read off a value that may be `null` |
| `T05` | A field or method a record or shape does not have |
| `T06` | A member or action a store does not have, or an endpoint a service does not have |
| `T07` | A list, a record or an action used as a condition, which is always true |
| `T08` | A `for` over something that is not a list |
| `T09` | An `emit` whose arguments do not match the event's |
| `T10` | A call with the wrong arguments: too many or too few, a name the callee does not take, or one of the wrong kind |
| `T11` | A `match` on something that is neither a resource nor an enum, or an arm the value cannot take |
| `T12` | A `Secret` where it would escape — shown, spliced into text, joined with `+`, handed to a browser global, logged, or kept with `persist` |
