| `T13` | A name, or a function called, that nothing declares — which the browser would throw on |
| `T14` | A comparison that is always the same: `"1" == 1`, a record against a string, an enum against a case it does not have |
| `T15` | A `match` with no `else` that misses a case of the enum, or has a case twice |
| `T16` | A method a number, a string or a list does not have, with the nearest one it does |
| `T17` | An async action's result used before it is awaited, or `await` where it cannot run |
| `T18` | Arithmetic on something that is not a number |
| `T19` | A value that may be `null` spliced into text (warning) |
| `T20` | A list or a record shown as text (warning) |
| `T21` | A resource `match` with no `error` arm and no `else` (warning) |
| `T22` | A handler that names more values than its event sends |

Most findings come with a hint: a conversion (`Number(value)`,
`"{value}"`), the cases an enum takes, the fields a record has, or one of
the narrowing forms above. `wf explain T05` prints a code's full entry, and
[Diagnostics](/errors) has every code with an example.

## What the checker does not check

- It does not check a lambda's body against a return type.
- It does not know what a plain `fetch` returns. Annotate it, or describe
  the service with an `api`.

## In the editor

Hover shows a name's inferred type: `state draft: String`, `derived
remaining: Number`, `Todos.add: action(String)`. Completion after `.`
offers a record's fields, an enum's cases where one is wanted, and the
methods of a `String`, a `Number` or a list. A type error appears as a
diagnostic on the argument it belongs to. To set up the editor, see
[Editors](/reference/cli#editors).

## Quick reference

| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `state x: T = v` | Annotate a state; props, parameters, fields and `let` take `: T` the same way |
| `[T]` · `T?` · `Map` · `Any` | A list, a value that may be `null`, an object with unknown keys, anything |
| `type Name { field: T = default }` | Declare a record |
| `type B = A { extra: T }` | Extend a record |
| `Name(field: v)` · `Name()` | Build a record |
| `enum Name { a, b(x: T) }` | Declare an enum, with an optional payload per case |
| `.case` · `.case(v)` | Write a case |
| `Number(1..=30)` · `String(minLength: 8)` | A type with a condition |
| `if let x = v { … }` · `v ?? d` · `v?.f` | Narrow or read through `null` |
| `resource r: [T] = fetch(…)` | Type data from the network |

## Common mistakes

**A field read off a value that may be `null`.** `email` is a `String?`, so
`.length` would throw when it is missing:

```wf expect=T04
type User { name: String, email: String? }

page P(path: "/", title: "T", description: "D") {
    state user: User = User(name: "Ada", email: null)
    Heading(user.name).h1
    Text("{user.email.length} characters")
}
```

Narrow it first, `if let mail = user.email { Text("{mail.length} characters") }`,
or read through it with a fallback, `user.email?.length ?? 0`. See
[T04](/errors/T04).

**A misspelled field on a map literal.** A map literal has the fields it was
written with, so a typo is caught where it is read:

```wf expect=T05
page P(path: "/", title: "T", description: "D") {
    state form = { name: "", age: 0 }
    Heading("Profile").h1
    Input(bind: form.name, label: "Name")
    Text("Hello, {form.nmae}")
}
```

Use one of the fields the hint lists, `form.name`. See [T05](/errors/T05).

**A value that may be `null` spliced into text.** The page would show the
word `null` when there is no note:

```wf expect=T19
type Todo { id: String, title: String, note: String? }

page P(path: "/", title: "T", description: "D") {
    state todo: Todo = Todo(id: "1", title: "Ship")
    Heading(todo.title).h1
    Text("Note: {todo.note}")
}
```

Say what to show instead, `Text("Note: {todo.note ?? "none"}")`, or draw the
line only when there is a note with `if let`. See [T19](/errors/T19).

Going further: [Expressions](/reference/expressions) lists every
operator and helper a typed value can be used with.

## Next

[Styling](/learn/13-styling).



---

# Styling

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/13-styling

This chapter covers styling in WebFluent: a theme for the whole site, a
`style { }` block for one element, and your own stylesheets for what sits
between. Every built-in element already ships styled, so you write styles
only for what you want to change.

This page sets the brand colour for the whole site, then gives one card a
border of that colour and a deeper shadow on hover:

```wf
theme Brand {
    color-primary: #0F766E
    radius-md: 14px
}

page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "A themed page.") {
    Heading("Welcome").h1
    Card {
        style {
            border-left: 4px solid $color-primary
            &:hover { box-shadow: $shadow-lg }
        }
        Text("Every primary button on the site is teal now.")
        Button("Start").primary
    }
}
```

The `theme` changes every element that reads `color-primary`; the
`style { }` block changes only the card it is written in.

You will be able to:

- change colours, fonts and spacing across the site with a `theme`;
- style one element with a `style { }` block, including live values, hover
  states and media queries;
- share rules between elements with classes and your own `.css` files;
- add dark mode;
- make a layout change with the width of the screen.

## Before you start

You need a project that builds (see [Getting started](/learn/01-getting-started))
and you should know how to place elements and pass them props
([Elements](/learn/06-elements)). Styles that follow state use `state` values
([State and reactivity](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity)).

Three tools cover almost everything. Pick the narrowest one that does the
job:

| To change… | Use | Section |
|---|---|---|
| The whole site: every button, card and link | a `theme` | [Change the whole site with a theme](#change-the-whole-site-with-a-theme) |
| One element | a `style { }` block on it | [Style one element](#style-one-element) |
| A group of elements, or something a block cannot say | a class and a `.css` file | [Classes and your own stylesheet](#classes-and-your-own-stylesheet) |

## Change the whole site with a theme

To change the colours, fonts, spacing or corner radius of everything at
once, declare a `theme`. A theme sets *design tokens* — named values such as
`color-primary` or `radius-md` that every built-in reads.

This theme gives the site a teal brand colour, the Inter font and rounder
corners:

```wf
theme Brand {
    color-primary: #0F766E
    color-secondary: #134E4A
    color-background: #FFFFFF
    color-surface: #F8FAFC
    color-text: #0F172A
    color-text-muted: #64748B
    color-border: #E2E8F0
    font-family: 'Inter', system-ui, sans-serif
    font-family-mono: 'JetBrains Mono', monospace
    radius-md: 14px
    spacing-lg: 2.5rem
    shadow-md: 0 4px 12px rgba(0,0,0,0.08)
}
```

Every primary button, link and focus ring now uses `#0F766E`, because the
built-ins read `color-primary` rather than a fixed colour.

How a theme works:

- Each value is raw CSS, to the end of its line. Do not quote it.
- You list only the tokens you change. Every token you leave out keeps its
  *baseline* value — the default the compiler ships.
- The baseline has 71 tokens, in groups: colour, font, spacing, radius,
  shadow, motion, easing, breakpoints, code and layout.
  [Design tokens](/reference/tokens) lists each one with its baseline
  value.
- Every token becomes a CSS custom property on `:root` (`--color-primary`).
  You read it from a style block as `$color-primary` and from a stylesheet
  as `var(--color-primary)`.
- A theme may add tokens of its own, such as `surface-raised: #131519`. They
  become custom properties like the rest.
- The breakpoints are tokens too, so moving one moves every media query the
  build writes (see [Responsive values](#responsive-values)).

If the project declares one theme, the build uses it. If it declares
several, choose one in `webfluent.app.json`:

```json
{ "theme": { "name": "Brand" } }
```

The contrast lint, `A13`, checks the text and background pairs of your theme
and warns when one falls below the WCAG AA contrast ratio. Run `wf theme` to
see every token, where it comes from and which pairs it checked.

To keep the built-ins' layout and mechanics but drop their look — for a site
that brings its whole design — set `theme.builtin` in `webfluent.app.json`:

| `theme.builtin` | What the build ships for each built-in you use |
|---|---|
| `"full"` (default) | Its layout, its mechanics and its baseline look |
| `"structural"` | Only its layout and mechanics: focus rings, overlays, the grid |

## Style one element

To change one element, give it a `style { }` block. The block holds CSS
declarations, and they apply to that element only.

This card uses tokens for its spacing and colours, a live value for its
accent border and width, a hover rule, a rule for its paragraphs and a media
query:

```wf
page Styled(path: "/styled", title: "Styled card", description: "A card with its own style.") {
    state accent = "#D97706"
    state wide = false

    Heading("Styled card").h1
    Card {
        style {
            padding: $lg                       // spacing-lg, from the property
            background: $surface              // color-surface
            border: 1px solid $border
            border-radius: $radius-lg
            box-shadow: $shadow-md
            border-left: 4px solid {accent}    // repaints when `accent` changes
            max-width: {if wide { "100%" } else { "40rem" }}
            &:hover { box-shadow: $shadow-lg }
            & > p { margin: 0 }
            @media (max-width: 640px) { padding: $sm }
        }
        Text("Hover me, or widen me.")
        Button("Widen") { on click { wide = !wide } }
        Button("Make it blue") { on click { accent = "#2563EB" } }
    }
}
```

The card gets a deeper shadow on hover. **Widen** lets it fill the page, and
**Make it blue** recolours its left border at once.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from HTML and CSS?** There is no `style="…"` attribute:
> `style:` as an argument is `E106`. The declarations go in the element's
> `style { }` block, and the build turns the parts that never change into a
> stylesheet rule, so a strict content security policy still holds. See
> [Coming from HTML and CSS](/coming-from/html-css).

### Write declarations

- Write one declaration per line, or several on one line separated by `;`.
- Write values as CSS, with no quotes: `padding: 2rem`, not `"2rem"`.
- Never separate two declarations with a comma. `width: 2rem, flex: none` is
  `E002`, because a style block is CSS, not a map.

### Use a token

`$name` reads a design token. A full name, such as `$color-primary` or
`$surface-raised`, works on any property. A short name is resolved by the
property it is written on:

| You write | It means |
|---|---|
| `padding: $lg` (and `margin`, `gap`, `width`, `height`, `top` …) | `spacing-lg` |
| `color: $primary`, `background: $surface`, `border: 1px solid $border` | `color-primary`, `color-surface`, `color-border` |
| `border-radius: $lg` | `radius-lg` |
| `box-shadow: $md` | `shadow-md` |
| `font-size: $xl` | `font-size-xl` |
| `transition: $fast` | `transition-fast` |

A token that the theme does not declare is `V06`, an error, because the
browser would drop the declaration. A property name that CSS does not have,
such as `colr:`, is `V05`, a warning that suggests the nearest property.

### Splice a live value

`{expr}` puts a value into a declaration. When the value reads state, the
declaration updates whenever that state changes. A splice may be the whole
value (`{accent}`) or part of one (`{pct}%`).

A splice that is a bare number for a length, such as `width: {pct}`, is
`V07`: the browser drops a length with no unit. Write `width: {pct}%` or
`width: {pct}px`.

### Style a state with a nested rule

A nested rule styles the element while it is in some state. `&` is the
element itself, as in CSS nesting:

- `&:hover`, `&:focus-visible` (the keyboard focus ring), `&:active`,
  `&:disabled`, `&::placeholder`, `&:focus-within`;
- `&.active`, `& > p`;
- the ARIA states a control keeps in its attributes:
  `&[aria-current="page"]`, which the router sets on the current `Link`,
  and `&[aria-pressed="true"]`, `&[aria-selected="true"]`,
  `&[aria-checked="true"]`, `&[aria-expanded="true"]`,
  `&[aria-invalid="true"]`.

`@media (…) { }` and `@container (…) { }` nest the same way.

A nested rule is compiled into the stylesheet, so its values must be known
at build time: literals and tokens, not state. To make a hover colour follow
state, set a custom property on the element and read it in the rule:

```wf
page Swatch(path: "/swatch", title: "Swatch", description: "A hover colour that follows state.") {
    state hoverColor = "#0F766E"

    Heading("Swatch").h1
    Button("Hover me") {
        style {
            --hover-bg: {hoverColor}
            &:hover { background: var(--hover-bg) }
        }
    }
    Button("Use amber") { on click { hoverColor = "#D97706" } }
}
```

Read your own custom property with `var(--name)`. `$name` is only for design
tokens.

### How the build compiles a style block

- The parts of a block that do not read state become a stylesheet rule,
  under a class named by the block's content. The element carries the
  class, so a hundred identical cards share one rule and the pre-rendered
  page has it before any script runs.
- A declaration that reads state is set on the element by the runtime and
  updated when the state changes.
- Nested state rules and media rules are marked `!important`, so they win
  over the element's base declarations while they apply. When a state rule
  and a media rule set the same property, the media rule wins.

## Animate a style change

To make a property change smoothly instead of jumping, add a
`transition { }` block. Each line names a property, a duration and an
optional easing.

This card fades and grows when you press **Toggle**:

```wf
page Fade(path: "/fade", title: "Fade", description: "A card that fades in and out.") {
    state active = false

    Heading("Fade").h1
    Card {
        style { opacity: {if active { 1 } else { 0.4 }}; transform: {if active { "none" } else { "scale(0.98)" }} }
        transition { opacity: $fast; transform: 200ms ease-out }
        Text("Fades")
    }
    Button("Toggle") { on click { active = !active } }
}
```

A duration may be a token — `$fast`, `$normal` or `$slow` — or a raw value
such as `200ms ease-out`. A reader who asked their system for less motion
gets no transition. Enter and exit animations, and other motion, are in
[Animate an element in and out](/recipes/animate-in-and-out).

## Classes and your own stylesheet

To share a rule between many elements, or to write what a `style { }` block
cannot say, put it in a `.css` file and add its class with `class:`.

Use a stylesheet for:

- a selector over several elements;
- a `@keyframes` or a `@font-face`;
- a class that a dozen elements share by name;
- a rule on `html`, `body` or `::selection`.

### Add a stylesheet

Every `.css` file anywhere under `src/` is part of the build. You can keep
one global file, or put a file beside the component it styles:

```text
src/
├── styles.css            # global rules
└── components/
    ├── Card.wf
    └── card.css          # beside the component it styles
```

```css
/* src/components/card.css */
.feature {
  container-type: inline-size;
}
.feature--first::before {
  content: counter(feature, upper-roman);
  color: var(--color-text-muted);
}
```

The build reads the files in path order, minifies them and bundles them
into `styles.css`. `var(--token)` reaches every design token. There is no
scoping: a class is global, so name it on purpose.

To link a sheet the build does not compile — a file in `public/` or a URL —
list it in `meta.stylesheets` in `webfluent.app.json`. It is linked ahead of
`styles.css`.

### Add a class

`class: "name"` adds a class to the element. It does not replace the
element's own classes: `Container(class: "hero")` renders
`class="wf-container hero"`.

The value may be an expression, so a class can follow state:

```wf
page Welcome(path: "/welcome", title: "Welcome", description: "A heading whose class follows state.") {
    state active = true

    Container(class: "hero") {
        Heading("Welcome", class: if active { "title is-on" } else { "title" }).h1
        Button("Switch") { on click { active = !active } }
    }
}
```

When several classes each have their own condition, pass a map or a list:

- In a **map**, each key is a class, and it is on while its value is true.
- A **list** joins strings and maps, and skips anything that is `null`.

```wf
page Chores(path: "/chores", title: "Chores", description: "Classes that follow state.") {
    state done = false
    state urgent = true
    state tone = "calm"

    Heading("Chores").h1
    Text("Water the plants", class: { "is-done": done, "is-urgent": urgent })
    Container(class: ["panel", tone, if urgent { "is-loud" }]) { Text("Due today") }
    Button("Done") { on click { done = !done } }
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** `className` is a string you assemble, often with
> `clsx`. `class:` *adds* to the element's own classes, and takes the map
> `clsx` would build: `class: { "is-done": done }`. For one element's look,
> reach for a flag or a `style { }` block before a class. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

The rules for a class value:

- A map's values must be conditions (`Bool`).
- A bare condition is not a class: `class: active` is `T01`. Write
  `{ "is-active": active }`, which says what `active` turns on.
- When the value changes, only the classes that `class:` itself named come
  off. A class a script added with `classList.add` stays.

### Target the built-ins

Each built-in wears `wf-*` classes, such as `wf-btn`, `wf-btn--primary` and
`wf-card`. They are stable across releases, so a stylesheet may target them.

Do not add another built-in's class to an element with `class:`. It brings
that built-in's rules with it, and draws `V04`.

## Override a built-in's look

To decide which rule wins, know the three layers of CSS on a page. From
weakest to strongest:

1. **The built-ins' own rules** (`.wf-btn`, `.wf-card`), shipped in
   `styles.css`.
2. **Your stylesheets** (`src/**/*.css`), bundled after them. On equal
   specificity, yours win.
3. **`style { }` blocks**, compiled to rules with tripled specificity, with
   nested state and media rules marked `!important`. An element's own block
   beats any stylesheet, as the inline style it replaces would.

So choose the tool by how far the change reaches:

- To restyle **one element**, use its `style { }` block.
- To restyle **every button**, write `.wf-btn { … }` in a stylesheet, or
  change the tokens in a theme. Because the built-ins read tokens,
  `color-primary` recolours every primary button, link and focus ring at
  once.
- To drop the built-ins' look entirely, set `theme.builtin: "structural"`
  (see [Change the whole site with a theme](#change-the-whole-site-with-a-theme)).

## Style a component's variants

To style each variant of your own component from a stylesheet, use its enum
props. A component writes each enum prop to its root element as a
`data-<prop>` attribute, such as `data-tone="loud"`, so one rule styles one
variant. The `Note` component of
[Components](/learn/10-components#enum-props) gives its root `class: "note"`,
so this rule styles its loud notes and nothing else:

```css
.note[data-tone="loud"] { font-weight: 700; color: var(--color-danger) }
```

## Dark mode

To add dark mode, declare a second theme with the tokens that change, and
name both themes in `webfluent.app.json`:

```json
{ "theme": { "name": "Light", "dark": "Night" } }
```

The dark theme's tokens replace the light theme's in two cases:

- when the reader's system prefers dark (`prefers-color-scheme: dark`) and
  the reader has not chosen light;
- whenever the reader chose dark with `setTheme("dark")`.

This page declares both themes and lets the reader choose:

```wf
theme Light {
    color-background: #FFFFFF
    color-text: #0F172A
}

theme Night {
    color-background: #0B1220
    color-surface: #111827
    color-text: #E5E7EB
    color-text-muted: #9CA3AF
    color-border: #1F2937
}

page Prefs(path: "/prefs", title: "Appearance", description: "Choose light or dark.") {
    Heading("Appearance").h1
    Text("You are on the {theme} theme")
    Row(gap: .sm) {
        Button("Light") { on click { setTheme("light") } }
        Button("Dark") { on click { setTheme("dark") } }
        Button("System") { on click { setTheme("system") } }
    }
}
```

The text under the heading reads `You are on the dark theme` after you press
**Dark**.

- `setTheme("light")` forces light, `setTheme("dark")` forces dark, and
  `setTheme("system")` follows the system again.
- `theme` reads the reader's choice: `"light"`, `"dark"` or `"system"`.
- The choice is kept in the browser's storage across visits. The page's
  script applies it before it draws the page. The system preference needs
  no script: it is a media query in the stylesheet, so it applies from the
  first paint.

> [!WARNING]
> Only what reads tokens switches with the theme. A colour written raw, such
> as `background: #FFFFFF`, stays the same in dark mode. Use tokens such as
> `$surface` and `$text` for anything that should change.

## Lay out a page without CSS

Most layout needs no `style` at all. `Stack`, `Row`, `Grid`, `Container`,
`Spacer` and `Divider` take `gap:`, `align:`, `justify:` and `columns:`
props ([Elements](/learn/06-elements#layout-elements)).

This page puts a title and a button on one line, with a grid of cards below
that has one, two or three columns depending on the screen:

```wf
page Layout(path: "/projects", title: "Projects", description: "A grid of projects.") {
    Container {
        Stack(gap: .lg) {
            Row(justify: .between, align: .center) {
                Heading("Projects").h1
                Button("New").primary.sm
            }
            Grid(columns: { base: 1, md: 2, lg: 3 }, gap: .md) {
                for n in 1..=6 { Card { Text("Project {n}") } }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

## Responsive values

To make a layout prop change with the screen width, give it one value per
breakpoint instead of one value:

```wf
Grid(columns: { base: 1, md: 2, lg: 3 }, gap: { base: .sm, lg: .lg }) { … }
Row(direction: { base: .column, md: .row }) { … }
Column(span: { base: 12, md: 6 }) { … }
```

The build compiles each step to a class and a media query. No JavaScript
runs and no resize listener is added, so the first paint already has the
right layout. A `viewport` test, by contrast, paints one branch and swaps
it after the page's script starts.

- The steps are `base`, `sm`, `md`, `lg` and `xl`.
- A step you leave out keeps the value of the step below it, so
  `{ base: 1, lg: 3 }` is one column until `lg`.
- Each step is a design token, `screen-sm` to `screen-xl`. Move one in your
  theme and every media query moves with it, `viewport.md` included:

```wf
theme Brand { screen-md: 900px }
```

The same names work inside a `style { }` block: `@md { … }` means
`@media (min-width: $screen-md)`.

```wf
Heading("Title").h1 {
    style {
        font-size: 24px
        @md { font-size: 34px }
    }
}
```

### Make a layout reflow on a narrow screen

A `Row`, `Grid` or `Column` stays as you write it at every width. To make
one reflow on a narrow screen, add the `.stacks` flag, or say what it does
at each width with a responsive value:

```wf
Row.stacks { … }                          // a column on a narrow screen
Grid.stacks { … }                         // one column on a narrow screen
Grid(columns: { base: 1, md: 3 }) { … }   // or say what it does at each width
```

What `.stacks` does:

| Element | Below 1024px | Below 768px |
|---|---|---|
| `Row.stacks` | unchanged | a column |
| `Grid.stacks` | two columns | one column |
| `Column.stacks` | half width, when its span is 3 or 4 | full width |

Older versions of the engine reflowed every `Row` and `Grid` this way below
768px, with `!important`, whether you asked or not. They no longer do.
`wf migrate` adds `.stacks` to every `Row`, `Grid` and `Column` of a
WebFluent 2 project, so the old behaviour carries over, written where you
can see and change it.

Keep `viewport` ([State and reactivity](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity#the-browser-as-values))
for what changes behaviour, such as a drawer instead of a sidebar. It
follows `matchMedia`, which fires once when the answer changes, not on every
pixel of a drag.

## Find your styles in the build output

The build writes your styles to two places:

- `styles.css` holds the tokens something in the output uses
  (`:root { --color-primary: … }`), the dark theme's overrides, the rules of
  the built-ins you used (and only those), your bundled stylesheets, and the
  compiled `style { }` rules that more than one page reaches.
- `pages/<Name>.css` holds the `style { }` rules that only one page can
  reach. The page loads it after `styles.css`.

[Performance](/about/what-a-build-ships) shows how to see what each file weighs.

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | Why, and what to do |
|---|---|
| `E002`: a `,` after the value of a property | Declarations are separated by a new line or `;`, never `,`. |
| `V06`: a token the theme does not declare | Check the token's spelling against `wf theme`, or declare it in your theme. |
| `V05`: a property CSS does not have | Fix the property name; the warning names the nearest one. |
| `V07`: a bare number spliced as a length | Add the unit: `width: {pct}%`. |
| A hover rule ignores a state value | Nested rules are compiled at build time. Set a custom property from state and read it with `var(--…)` in the rule. |
| Your stylesheet rule loses to an element | The element's `style { }` block is stronger than any stylesheet. Move the rule into the block, or remove the declaration from the block. |
| Part of the page stays light in dark mode | That part uses a raw colour. Replace it with a token. |
| `V04`: a `wf-*` class in `class:` | Give your element its own class instead of a built-in's. |
| A `Row` or `Grid` does not reflow on a phone | Add `.stacks`, or give the prop a responsive value. |

## Common mistakes

**A comma between two declarations.** A `style { }` block is CSS, not a map,
so a comma after a value does not build:

```wf expect=E002
page P(path: "/", title: "Card", description: "A styled card.") {
    Heading("Card").h1
    Card {
        style { padding: $lg, border-radius: $radius-md }
        Text("Hello")
    }
}
```

Put each declaration on its own line, or separate them with `;`
([E002](/errors/E002)).

**A number spliced as a length.** A splice puts in the value as it is, and a
length with no unit is one the browser drops:

```wf expect=V07
page P(path: "/", title: "Progress", description: "A bar that fills.") {
    state pct = 40
    Heading("Progress").h1
    Stack {
        style { width: {pct}; background: $primary; height: 8px }
    }
    Button("More") { on click { pct = pct + 10 } }
}
```

Write the unit after the splice: `width: {pct}%` ([V07](/errors/V07)).

**A condition as a class.** `class:` wants class names, and a `Bool` says
nothing about which class it turns on:

```wf expect=T01
page P(path: "/", title: "Chores", description: "A class that follows state.") {
    state done = false
    Heading("Chores").h1
    Text("Water the plants", class: done)
    Button("Done") { on click { done = !done } }
}
```

Name the class and its condition in a map: `class: { "is-done": done }`
([T01](/errors/T01)).

Going further: [Animate an element in and out](/recipes/animate-in-and-out)
declares how an element enters and leaves; the runtime plays it, or skips
it for readers who asked for less.

## Next

[Forms and validation](/learn/14-forms).



---

# Forms and validation

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/14-forms

This chapter is about forms in WebFluent: controls that read and write
state, rules that say what each value must be, and a submit that sends the
form to a server and shows what came back.

You will be able to:

- bind any control to a state, in both directions;
- validate a field with a `validate` block, without writing the error
  messages' markup;
- know whether the whole form is valid, and submit it;
- upload a file and show its progress;
- show the errors a server sends back, and a busy state while a request runs.

WebFluent writes the accessible parts for you: a real `<label>` for every
label, `aria-describedby` for hints and errors, `aria-invalid`, errors
announced as they appear, and focus moved to the first problem.

## Before you start

You should know how to declare `state` and an `action`
([State and reactivity](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity)) and how to handle an
event ([Events](/learn/08-events)). Sending a form to a server uses an `api`,
which [Data and APIs](/learn/15-data) covers in full.

## Bind a control to state

To keep a control and a state in step, give the control `bind:` and the
state's name. Typing in the control writes the state, and changing the
state updates the control.

This sign-up page binds one of each kind of control:

```wf
page Signup(path: "/signup", title: "Sign up", description: "Every control, bound to state.") {
    state name = ""
    state email = ""
    state plan = "free"
    state agree = false
    state seats = 1
    state when: Date? = null

    Heading("Sign up").h1
    Input(bind: name, label: "Name", placeholder: "Ada Lovelace").required
    Input(bind: email, label: "Email").email.required
    Select(bind: plan, label: "Plan") {
        Select.Option("Free", value: "free")
        Select.Option("Team", value: "team")
    }
    Radio(bind: plan, value: "free", label: "Free")
    Radio(bind: plan, value: "team", label: "Team")
    Checkbox(bind: agree, label: "I agree to the terms")
    Switch(bind: agree, label: "Same thing, as a switch")
    Slider(bind: seats, min: 1, max: 50, label: "Seats")
    DatePicker(bind: when, label: "Start date")
    Text("{name} <{email}> wants {seats} {plan} seats")
    if let start = when { Text("Starting {start}") }
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** A controlled input needs `value={q}` and an
> `onChange` that calls the setter. `bind: q` is both directions at once, and
> the control holds the state's type, so a `Slider` writes a `Number`, not
> the string `e.target.value` would give you. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

The last lines repeat what you type and pick. The `Select` and the two
`Radio`s share `plan`, so choosing in one moves the others.

For several lines of text, use a `Textarea`. With `maxLength:` it shows how
many characters are left, and tells a screen reader politely (without
interrupting):

```wf
Textarea(bind: note, label: "Notes", rows: 4, maxLength: 200)
```

### What each control holds

The checker knows the type each control writes, and refuses a `bind:` to a
state of another type (`F02`):

| Control | Holds |
|---|---|
| `Checkbox`, `Switch` | `Bool` |
| `Slider` | `Number` |
| `Input.number` | `Number`, and `null` when the reader empties it |
| `DatePicker` | [`Date?`](/learn/12-types#the-types-the-language-brings-with-it) — `null` until a date is picked |
| `Select` | the option's `value:`, as written |
| `Input`, `Textarea`, `Radio` | `String` |

A value comes back as the type it went in as. `Select.Option("Two",
value: 2)` binds the number `2`, not the string `"2"`.

Every control needs an accessible name: a `label:`, a `placeholder:` (on an
`Input`), or an `aria-label:`. The accessibility lints (`A03`, `A04`) warn
when one has none.

### Bind to a store or a list item

`bind:` takes anything that can be written:

- a state;
- a store's member, such as `bind: Cart.note`;
- a field of a loop's item.

This list lets the reader rename and tick off each todo in place:

```wf
type Todo { id: String, title: String, done: Bool = false }

page Todos(path: "/todos", title: "Todos", description: "Edit each todo in place.") {
    state todos: [Todo] = [Todo(id: "1", title: "Water the plants"), Todo(id: "2", title: "Post the letter")]

    Heading("Todos").h1
    for todo in todos by todo.id {
        Input(bind: todo.title, label: "Title")
        Checkbox(bind: todo.done, label: "Done")
    }
    Text("{todos.filter(todo => !todo.done).length} left")
}
```

The count at the bottom drops as you tick items. The item is written and
the list is told it changed, so everything that reads `todos` follows:

- In a keyed loop (`for … by`), the list hears of the change as the reader
  types.
- In a loop with no `by`, which redraws every item when its list changes,
  the list hears of it when the reader leaves the field, so the row is not
  redrawn under the cursor.

You cannot bind to a constant, a derived value, a prop or a literal: that is
`F01`.

## Add a label, a hint or your own error

Every control takes `label:`, `hint:` and `error:`. With any of them, the
control is wrapped in a field:

- the label is a real `<label for>`;
- the hint and the error are linked to the control with `aria-describedby`;
- the error is a string, empty when there is none. When it appears, it is
  announced, and it sets `aria-invalid` on the control.

This page shows an error while the handle is too short:

```wf
page Handle(path: "/handle", title: "Handle", description: "Pick a handle.") {
    state handle = ""
    derived problem = if handle.length > 0 && handle.length < 3 { "At least three characters" } else { "" }

    Heading("Pick a handle").h1
    Input(bind: handle, label: "Handle", hint: "Letters, numbers and dashes", error: problem)
}
```

For a rule about the value itself, a `validate` block is usually better: it
works out the error for you ([Validate a field](#validate-a-field)). Use
`error:` for a message that comes from somewhere else.

## Group controls in a form

To submit several controls together, put them in a `Form`. Its `on submit`
handler runs when the form is submitted, and the page never navigates away.
`Form(bind: form)` gives you a handle, named `form` here, that knows the
state of the whole form.

This contact form sends its fields, disables **Send** until every field is
valid, and thanks the reader:

```wf
page Contact(path: "/contact", title: "Contact", description: "Send us a message.") {
    state name = ""
    state email = ""
    state message = ""
    state sent = false

    action send() {
        let r = await fetch("/api/contact", { method: "POST", body: { name: name, email: email, message: message } })
        sent = true
        form.reset()
    }

    Heading("Contact us").h1
    Form(bind: form) {
        on submit { send() }
        Input(bind: name, name: "name", label: "Name").required
        Input(bind: email, name: "email", label: "Email").email.required
        Input(bind: message, name: "message", label: "Message").required
        Button("Send", type: .submit, disabled: !form.valid || send.pending).primary
        Text("Fields: {form.values.name} {form.values.email}").muted.sm
    }
    if sent { Alert("Thanks — we will be in touch.").success }
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** A submit handler there starts with
> `event.preventDefault()`. A `Form`'s `on submit` never reloads or leaves
> the page, so the handler holds only what the submit does. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

### The form handle

| Member | What it is |
|---|---|
| `form.valid` | `true` when every control passes its own checks and every `validate` rule holds. It stays current as the reader types. |
| `form.errors` | The message of every field that has one, by name |
| `form.touched` | Which fields the reader has left |
| `form.pending` | Whether an `async` rule is still waiting for its answer |
| `form.values` | A map of the controls' values, by their `name:` attribute |
| `form.reset()` | Clears the form, and every message it was showing |
| `form.submit()` | Submits the form from code |
| `form.apply(errors)` | Shows what the server said, on the fields it named ([Show what the server said](#show-what-the-server-said)) |
| `form.element` | The `<form>` element itself |

### Choose which buttons submit

A `Button` with `type: .submit` (or the `.submit` flag) submits the form,
and so does Enter in a field. The browser's own constraint checks run first
(`.required`, `.email` and the rest), so an invalid form never reaches
`on submit`.

Every other button in a form — **Add a row**, **Show password** — is
`type="button"`, and does only what its `on click` says.

## Validate a field

To say what a value must be, put a `validate` block beside the state it
guards. Each rule is one line. The control bound to that state shows the
rules' messages itself: you write no `error:` and no `derived` value.

This page requires an email, a password of at least eight characters with a
number in it, and a matching confirmation:

```wf
page Join(path: "/join", title: "Join", description: "Make an account.") {
    state email = ""
    state password = ""
    state confirm = ""

    validate email {
        required
        email
    }
    validate password {
        required
        minLength(8) "Use at least 8 characters"
        pattern(/[0-9]/) "Include a number"
    }
    validate confirm {
        matches(password) "The two passwords differ"
    }

    Heading("Join").h1
    Form(bind: form) {
        on submit { log("signing up") }
        Input(bind: email, label: "Email").email
        Input(bind: password, label: "Password").password
        Input(bind: confirm, label: "Confirm").password
        Button("Join", type: .submit, disabled: !form.valid).primary
    }
}
```

Leave the password field after typing `abc`, and it shows
`Use at least 8 characters`. **Join** stays disabled until every rule holds.

A `validate` block must guard a state that a control binds. A block for a
state no control binds, or for a derived value, can never pass: that is
`F03`.

### Validation rules

| Rule | Holds when |
|---|---|
| `required` | Something was given: a non-blank string, a non-empty list, a ticked checkbox |
| `email`, `url` | The value looks like an email address, or a URL |
| `minLength(n)`, `maxLength(n)` | The text is at least, or at most, that long |
| `min(v)`, `max(v)` | The number, date or time is within the limit |
| `pattern(/…/)` | The text matches the regular expression |
| `matches(other)` | The value equals another value, and follows it as it changes |
| `oneOf([…])` | The value is one of those listed |
| `custom "…" { expr }` | The expression is true |
| `async "…" { await … }` | The answer is true, once it arrives |

How the rules behave:

- **Messages.** Each rule takes an optional message after it: a string, or
  `t("key")`, which is read in the reader's language. Without one, the rule
  uses its own message. A project with translations replaces those by
  naming the keys `form.required`, `form.email`, `form.minLength` and so on
  ([Translate a site](/recipes/translate-a-site),
  [Show validation messages](/recipes/validation-messages)).
- **Arguments that read state.** An argument such as `max(Ledger.today)` is
  read again each time the rule is checked.
- **Types.** A rule is checked against the type of what it guards:
  `minLength` on a `Number` is `T01`.
- **Empty values.** Every rule but `required` passes an empty value, so a
  blank optional field shows one message rather than two.
- **Async rules.** An `async` rule is asked only once the other rules pass,
  and once per value. A server is not asked about every keystroke of an
  address that is not valid yet. While it waits, `form.pending` is `true`.

This rule asks the server whether an address is free. The rule passes when the check's answer is `true`, so ask the question whose answer you want to be yes:

```wf
api Backend(base: "/api") {
    get emailFree(email: String) -> Bool
}

page Register(path: "/register", title: "Register", description: "Check an address is free.") {
    state email = ""

    validate email {
        required
        email
        async "That address is taken" { await Backend.emailFree(email: email) }
    }

    Heading("Register").h1
    Form(bind: form) {
        on submit { log("registering") }
        Input(bind: email, label: "Email").email
        Button("Register", type: .submit, disabled: !form.valid || form.pending).primary
    }
}
```

### Choose when a message shows

`Form(show:)` sets when the messages appear:

| `show:` | A field's message appears |
|---|---|
| `.onBlur` (default) | after the reader leaves the field |
| `.onSubmit` | only after a submit |
| `.live` | as the reader types |

The rules run either way, so `form.valid` is always true to the values,
whatever the reader has seen.

A submit that fails shows every message, moves focus to the first field
that has one, announces it, and does not run `on submit`.

### Preview every message at once

To see a form as a failed submit would leave it, without filling it in, set
`data-wf-validation="shown"` on the page's root element:

```js
document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-wf-validation", "shown")
```

Every field then shows what its rules say about its value now. Remove the
attribute and the messages go again. An editor's preview sets this
attribute to show a form as *Invalid*.

### Let a refined type do the checking

A *refined type* is a type with a condition, such as `Number(1..=30)`. The
condition is already a rule, so you only write the rules the type does not
say:

```wf
state nights: Number(1..=30) = 2
validate nights { required }
```

- A range's open end is excluded: `Number(0..10)` does not take `10`.
- A date's `after:` and `before:` are checked as the reader types, like
  `min` and `max`.

See [Types](/learn/12-types#a-condition-on-a-type) for every condition a type
can carry.

### Read the rules as data

`wf rules --json` lists, for a tool to read:

- every rule, what it takes, its own message and the translation key that
  replaces it;
- the patterns people write, by name: `a number`, `a letter` (in any
  script), `no spaces` …;
- the `show:` choices;
- every state the project holds to a rule, in order, including the rules its
  type implies.

The Rust library has the same data as `webfluent::validation` (with the `internals` feature, outside semver), which can
also write a state's `validate` block back one rule at a time.

### Show what the server said

When the server rejects a value — an address already taken, a code that
expired — pass its messages, by field name, to `form.apply`:

```wf
api Backend(base: "/api") {
    post signUp(body: Map) -> Map
        errors { 422 -> Map }
}

action join() {
    try {
        await Backend.signUp(body: { email: email, password: password })
    } catch e {
        form.apply(e.body.errors)     // { email: "That address is taken" }
    }
}
```

Each message is shown on the field whose `name:` it matches, and moves focus
to the first one. A message stays until the reader changes that field's
value. A field may also be given a list of messages; the first is shown.
[Send a form to a server](#send-a-form-to-a-server) shows the whole page.

## Upload a file

To let the reader pick a file, place a `FileUpload`. The files arrive in its
`change` event. Each is a `File`, with:

- `.name`, `.size` (in bytes) and `.type`;
- `.preview()`, an object URL that shows an image before it is uploaded. It
  is revoked when the page leaves.

This page shows the picture the reader picks, then uploads it with a
progress bar:

```wf
api Backend(base: "/api") {
    post avatar(id: String, file: File) at "users/:id/avatar"
}

page Avatar(path: "/avatar", title: "Your picture", description: "Change your picture.") {
    state picked: File? = null
    state done = false

    action upload() {
        if let f = picked {
            await Backend.avatar(id: "me", file: f)
            done = true
        }
    }

    Heading("Your picture").h1
    FileUpload(accept: "image/*", label: "Choose a picture") {
        on change(e) { picked = e.target.files[0] }
    }
    if let f = picked {
        Image(src: f.preview(), alt: "The picture you chose")
        Text("{f.name}, {format(f.size / 1024, .integer)} kB").muted.sm
        Button("Upload", disabled: upload.pending).primary { on click { upload() } }
        if upload.pending { Progress(value: Backend.avatar.progress * 100, max: 100) }
    }
    if done { Alert("Uploaded.").success }
}
```

- An endpoint with a `File` parameter sends a multipart form.
- `Backend.avatar.progress` follows the upload from 0 to 1.
- `FileUpload(…).multiple` lets the reader pick several files.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> `accept:` and any size limit you show are for the reader's convenience,
> not checks. The server decides what it accepts
> ([Security](/about/security#uploads-are-checked-on-the-server)).

## Send a form to a server

To send a form, describe the service once with `api`, call it from the
submit handler, and hand what a `422` said back to the form.

```wf
api Backend(base: "/api") {
    post signUp(body: Map) -> Map
        errors { 422 -> Map }
}

page Welcome(path: "/welcome", title: "Join", description: "Make an account.") {
    state email = ""
    state password = ""
    state joined = false

    validate email { required  email }
    validate password { required  minLength(8) }

    action join() {
        try {
            await Backend.signUp(body: { email: email, password: password })
            joined = true
        } catch e {
            form.apply(e.body.errors)
        }
    }

    Heading("Join").h1
    if joined { Alert("Welcome aboard.").success }
    Form(bind: form) {
        on submit { join() }
        Input(bind: email, name: "email", label: "Email").email
        Input(bind: password, name: "password", label: "Password").password
        Button("Join", type: .submit, disabled: !form.valid || join.pending).primary
    }
}
```

`errors { 422 -> Map }` types the body of a `422` response, so
`e.body.errors` is what the server sent. If the server answers
`{ "errors": { "email": "That address is taken" } }`, the message appears
under **Email**.

[Data and APIs](/learn/15-data) covers the service in full: retries, timeouts
and typed errors.

## Show that a request is running

An action that `await`s has a `.pending` value, `true` while a call of it
runs. Use it to show a spinner, or to keep a button busy with `loading:`.
On a store's action, read it as `Store.action.pending`:

```wf
store Api {
    state saved = 0
    action save(payload: Map) {
        let r = await fetch("/api/save", { method: "POST", body: payload })
        saved = saved + 1
    }
}

page Notes(path: "/notes", title: "Notes", description: "Save a note.") {
    use Api
    state text = ""

    Heading("Notes").h1
    Input(bind: text, label: "Note")
    Button("Save").primary { on click { Api.save({ text: text }) } }
    Button("Save a copy", loading: Api.save.pending) { on click { Api.save({ text: text, copy: true }) } }
    Text("Saved {Api.saved} times")
}
```

- **A button or a form waits for its work.** A `Button`'s `on click` or a
  `Form`'s `on submit` that calls an action that awaits is busy until that
  call ends: `aria-busy`, a press that does nothing, and, past a moment, a
  spinner in place of its label at the same width. The focus stays on it.
  Nothing has to be written for it.
- **A double click submits once.** A call of an action with the same
  arguments as one still running *is* that call: the work is not done
  twice, and both get the same answer. A call with other arguments — the
  next row's save — runs beside it. An action whose every call should run,
  a poll, says so: `action poll() concurrent { … }`.
- **`loading:`** keeps any button busy while a value holds — another
  button's work, a store's state.

Reading `.pending` on an action that awaits nothing is `T17`.

## Choosing: toggles, groups, steps and days

Some choices are not a text field. These built-ins draw them, each with the
keyboard a reader expects:

```wf
page Order(path: "/", title: "Order", description: "Choose how it is sent.") {
    state view = "grid"
    state plan = "free"
    state qty = 1
    state step = 0
    state day: Date? = null
    Heading("Order").h1
    ToggleGroup(bind: view, label: "View") {
        ToggleGroup.Item("Grid", value: "grid", icon: "grid")
        ToggleGroup.Item("List", value: "list", icon: "list")
    }
    RadioGroup(bind: plan, label: "Plan").cards {
        RadioGroup.Option("Free", value: "free", hint: "For trying it out")
        RadioGroup.Option("Team", value: "team", hint: "€8 a seat")
    }
    NumberInput(bind: qty, min: 1, max: 9, label: "Quantity")
    Stepper(bind: step) {
        Stepper.Step("Address") { Text("Where it goes.") }
        Stepper.Step("Delivery") {
            Calendar(bind: day, disabled: d => d.weekday() >= 6, label: "Delivery day")
        }
    }
}
```

- **`Toggle`** is one button that stays pressed; **`ToggleGroup`** is a row
  of them, one chosen (or several, `.multiple`). Tab stops once on the
  group, and the arrow keys move inside it.
- **`RadioGroup`** is native radio buttons under a legend; `.cards` draws
  each as a card with its hint.
- **`NumberInput`** steps with − and +, the arrow keys, and PageUp and
  PageDown, and stays between `min:` and `max:`.
- **`Pagination(bind: page, pages: n)`** draws the pages of a list, with
  gaps for the ones it leaves out.
- **`Stepper`** shows one step at a time and each step's state.
- **`Calendar`** is a month a keyboard can work: the arrows by day and
  week (the other way round right to left), PageUp and PageDown by month.
  `.range` holds `{ start, end }`, `.multiple` a list.

## Checklist for a good form

- Every control has a `label:`. A placeholder is not a label.
- Rules live in `validate` blocks, not in hand-written `derived` errors.
- The submit button is `type: .submit`, so Enter submits.
- The submit button is disabled while the request runs:
  `disabled: save.pending`.
- The page says what happened afterwards, in an `Alert` or a `Toast`.
- Server errors go back to their fields with `form.apply`.
- The server checks everything again. The page's rules are for the reader.

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | Why, and what to do |
|---|---|
| `F01` on a `bind:` | The target cannot be written: a constant, a derived value, a prop or a literal. Bind a `state` instead. |
| `F02` on a `bind:` | The control cannot hold the state's type, such as a text `Input` on a `Number`. Use `.number`, or change the state's type. |
| `F03` on a `validate` | No control binds that state, or it is a derived value, so its rules can never pass. |
| `T01` on a rule | The rule does not fit the type, such as `minLength` on a `Number`. Use `min`/`max`. |
| `on submit` never runs | The form is invalid, so the submit stopped. Check `form.errors`, or set `data-wf-validation="shown"` to see every message. |
| A button submits the form by accident | Only `type: .submit` submits. Check that the button is not the submit button. |
| A server message never shows | `form.apply` matches each key to a field's `name:`. Give the control a `name:` equal to the key. |
| A message shows before the reader has typed | The form uses `show: .live`. Use `.onBlur` or `.onSubmit`. |

## Common mistakes

**A text field bound to a number.** An `Input` with no type flag holds a
`String`, so it cannot write a `Number` state:

```wf expect=F02
page P(path: "/", title: "Seats", description: "Pick a number of seats.") {
    state seats = 1
    Heading("Seats").h1
    Input(bind: seats, label: "Seats")
    Text("{seats} seats")
}
```

Add `.number`, which holds a `Number`, or use a `Slider`
([F02](/errors/F02)).

**A `validate` block for a state no control binds.** The rules check the
state, and nothing the reader types reaches it:

```wf expect=F03
page P(path: "/", title: "Join", description: "Make an account.") {
    state email = ""
    validate email { required  email }
    Heading("Join").h1
    Input(label: "Email").email
    Text("You typed {email}")
}
```

Bind the control to the state the rules guard: `Input(bind: email,
label: "Email")` ([F03](/errors/F03)).

**A `bind:` to a derived value.** A control writes back to what it binds,
and a `derived` value is worked out, never assigned:

```wf expect=F01
page P(path: "/", title: "Handle", description: "Pick a handle.") {
    state first = ""
    derived handle = first.toLowerCase()
    Heading("Handle").h1
    Input(bind: first, label: "First name")
    Input(bind: handle, label: "Handle")
}
```

Bind a `state` instead, and show the derived value with `Text(handle)`
([F01](/errors/F01)).

## Next

[Fetching data](/learn/15-data).



---

# Fetching data

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/15-data

This chapter is about getting data onto a WebFluent page and sending data
back: from a request the page makes when it shows, from a request an action
makes on demand, and from a file the build reads.

You will be able to:

- show a request's loading, error and ready states with `resource` and
  `match`;
- refresh data without the page going blank;
- describe a service once with `api`, so every call is typed, retried,
  cached and cancelled for you;
- read a service's surface from an OpenAPI file;
- fetch on demand from an action, and show a change before the server
  agrees;
- read a JSON file at build time and render one page per item in it.

## Before you start

You should know `state` and `action`
([State and reactivity](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity)), `match`
([Control flow](/learn/09-control-flow)) and how to declare a `type`
([Types](/learn/12-types)).

This chapter does not cover:

- a connection the page holds open — a socket, a stream, a channel or a
  peer — which is [Open a socket](/recipes/open-a-socket);
- working without a network, which is [Make a site work offline](/recipes/work-offline);
- values fixed for each build, which are
  [Environments and secrets](/recipes/environments-and-secrets).

## Choose how to get data

| You want… | Use | Section |
|---|---|---|
| Data the page shows as soon as it opens | `resource` | [Show a request with resource](#show-a-request-with-resource) |
| One place that describes a service and its endpoints | `api` | [Describe a service with api](#describe-a-service-with-api) |
| A request made when something happens: a save, a delete, a step in a flow | `await fetch` in an action | [Fetch on demand with await fetch](#fetch-on-demand-with-await-fetch) |
| Content that is known at build time | `data` | [Read a file at build time with data](#read-a-file-at-build-time-with-data) |

## Show a request with `resource`

To fetch data while a page shows, declare a `resource` and show its states
with `match`. A *resource* is a request the page makes, and a value that
says where the request is: loading, failed or ready.

This page lists recent deploys, with a spinner while they load and an alert
if the request fails:

```wf
type Deploy { id: String, status: String, startedAt: String }

page Deploys(path: "/deploys", title: "Deploys", description: "Recent deploys.") {
    resource deploys: [Deploy] = fetch("/api/deploys")

    Heading("Deploys").h1
    match deploys {
        loading { Spinner }
        error(e) { Alert("Could not load: {e.message}").danger }
        ready(rows) {
            if rows.length == 0 { Text("No deploys yet.").muted }
            for d in rows by d.id {
                Row(justify: .between) {
                    Text(d.id).bold
                    Badge(d.status, tone: if d.status == "ok" { .success } else { .danger })
                    Text(ago(d.startedAt)).muted.sm
                }
            }
        }
    }
    Button("Refresh") { on click { deploys.reload() } }
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from React?** There, a fetch is a `useEffect` that sets
> `loading`, `error` and `data` states by hand, or a `useQuery`. A
> `resource` is the request and its state together: no effect, no flags to
> keep in step, and a `match` with one arm per state. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

How it works:

- `resource name = fetch(url)` starts the request when the page renders.
- The annotation (`: [Deploy]`) types the value. Without one, the value is
  `Any`.
- A `match` over a resource has three arms — `loading`, `error(e)` and
  `ready(v)` — and may have an `else`. A resource `match` with no `error`
  arm and no `else` is `T21`.
- The pre-rendered page — the HTML the build writes for a static site —
  shows the `loading` arm. The live page fetches and replaces it.
- A failed response (one that is not `ok`) is an error whose `e.message` is
  `HTTP 500`, or whatever the status was.

### Read a resource's state anywhere

A resource has these values. Each is live wherever you read it — a label, a
splice, an attribute — with no `derived` in between:

| Value | What it is |
|---|---|
| `name.state` | `"loading"`, `"ready"` or `"error"` |
| `name.data` | The last value, or `null` before the first (`T?`) |
| `name.error` | The last error |
| `name.refreshing` | `true` while a refresh runs ([Refresh without clearing the page](#refresh-without-clearing-the-page)) |
| `name.pending` | `true` while any request of it runs, the first load included |
| `name.reload()` | Makes the request again |
| `name.invalidate()` | Drops what the cache holds for it, and asks again |
| `name.cancel()` | Aborts the request that is running |

So `Button(if plan.data != null { "Request approval" } else { "Deploy" })`
changes its label when the plan arrives.

### Refresh without clearing the page

These ask for a resource again:

- the `on:` option of `fetch(…)` or of an endpoint's call: `.focus` (when
  the reader comes back to the tab), `.reconnect` (when the network
  returns), or `.interval(30.seconds)`;
- `name.reload()` and `name.invalidate()`.

Asking again for the request already shown is a *refresh*. The page stays
as it is while a refresh runs: `name.state` stays `"ready"`, the data stays,
and the answer is drawn in place.

This page polls a list of servers every 30 seconds, and shows a small
spinner during each refresh:

```wf
type Server { id: String, name: String, status: String }

page Servers(path: "/servers", title: "Servers", description: "Every server, kept current.") {
    state stage = "test"
    resource servers: [Server] = fetch("/api/servers?env={stage}", on: .interval(30.seconds))

    Heading("Servers").h1
    Button("Production") { on click { stage = "prod" } }
    match servers {
        loading { Skeleton(height: "20px") }
        error(e) { Alert(e.message).danger }
        ready(list) {
            if servers.error != null { Alert("Could not refresh; this is what was there.").warning }
            if servers.refreshing { Spinner.sm }
            for s in list by s.id { Text("{s.name}: {s.status}") }
        }
    }
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from TanStack Query?** `isLoading` is `name.state == "loading"`,
> true only while there is nothing to show; `isFetching` is `name.pending`;
> and `name.refreshing` is a fetch while data is on screen. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

What a refresh keeps:

- **The arm.** The `ready` arm's binding is live. Text, attributes, `if`,
  `if let`, a keyed `for … by` and component props inside the arm follow the
  new data. The arm is drawn again only when the arm changes — loading,
  ready, error.
- **The rows.** A row whose key is still in the list keeps its nodes, its
  focus and its components' state. An input keeps what was typed.
- **Unchanged data.** The parts of an answer equal to what was shown are
  kept as the same objects. An item is matched by its `id`, by its value, or
  by its place. An answer that changed nothing redraws nothing.

What happens when a request fails, or changes:

- A refresh that fails keeps the data and `"ready"`, and sets `name.error`
  until the next answer, so the arm can say the data is stale.
- A first load that fails is `"error"`, and its `reload()` is a first load
  again.
- A request that changed is a first load again, shown as `loading`. A
  request changes when an address or an argument that reads state now names
  something else — another environment, another page — because the data on
  screen would be the wrong data. What the last request brought goes with
  it: `name.data` is `null` (and a paged resource's `name.items` empty)
  until the answer arrives, and stays so if it fails, so a `derived` value
  over it never reads the other request's answer. With `paginate:`, the
  next page is a refresh instead.

Pressing **Production** above changes `stage`, so the list shows its
`loading` arm and then the production servers.

### Send options with a request

Options follow the URL, by name:

- `method:` — `"GET"` unless you say otherwise;
- `headers:` — a map;
- `body:` — a map, sent as JSON with the content type set.

The response body is parsed as JSON.

This page searches with a `POST` and an authorization header:

```wf
page Search(path: "/search", title: "Search", description: "Search the catalogue.") {
    state q = ""
    state token = "demo-token"
    resource hits = fetch("/api/search", method: "POST",
        headers: { Authorization: "Bearer {token}" },
        body: { query: q, limit: 20 })

    Heading("Search").h1
    Input(bind: q, label: "Search")
    match hits {
        loading { Spinner.sm }
        error(e) { Text(e.message).danger }
        ready(list) { Text("{list.length} hits") }
    }
}
```

### Fetch again when state changes

A URL that reads state is fetched again whenever that state changes. Use it
for a search box that fetches as the reader types, or a detail page that
follows its route parameter:

```wf
type Post { slug: String, title: String, body: String }

page PostPage(path: "/posts/:slug", title: "Post", description: "One post.", slug: String) {
    resource post: Post = fetch("/api/posts/{slug}")
    match post {
        loading { Skeleton }
        error(e) { Alert("Not found").warning }
        ready(p) {
            Heading(p.title).h1
            Markdown(p.body)
        }
    }
}
```

A value spliced into the address is URL-encoded for you where it stands for
a value.

To fetch less often than the reader types, derive the URL from a slower
value. This page keeps what the reader types in `draft`, and searches only
when they press Enter:

```wf
page Lookup(path: "/lookup", title: "Lookup", description: "Search when you press Enter.") {
    state draft = ""
    state submitted = ""
    resource hits = fetch("/api/search?q={submitted}")

    Heading("Lookup").h1
    Input(bind: draft, label: "Search") { on key("Enter") { submitted = draft } }
    match hits {
        loading { Spinner.sm }
        error(e) { Text(e.message).danger }
        ready(list) { Text("{list.length} results for {submitted}") }
    }
}
```

## Describe a service with `api`

To call a service from many places, describe it once with `api`: its
address, how it is reached and what endpoints it has. Every call site is
then typed, cached and cancellable.

This service has four endpoints, and the page shows a list of users with a
different alert for each kind of failure:

```wf
type User { id: String, name: String }

api Backend(base: "/api/v1") {
    credentials: .sameOrigin      // the session cookie goes with every call
    timeout: 10.seconds
    retry: .backoff(times: 3, on: [.network, .timeout, .status5xx])

    get    users(page: Number = 1, q: String?) -> [User]
    get    user(id: String) at "users/:id"     -> User
    post   createUser(body: Map)               -> User
        errors { 422 -> Map }
    delete removeUser(id: String) at "users/:id"
}

page Users(path: "/users", title: "Users", description: "Everyone.") {
    state page: Number = 1
    resource rows = Backend.users(page: page, cache: .swr(60.seconds), on: .focus)

    Heading("Users").h1
    match rows {
        loading { Skeleton(height: "20px") }
        error(e) {
            match e {
                .offline { Alert("You are offline.").warning }
                .timeout { Alert("The server took too long.").warning }
                else     { Alert(e.message).danger }
            }
            Button("Try again") { on click { rows.reload() } }
        }
        ready(list) { for u in list by u.id { Text(u.name) } }
    }
}
```

- A parameter the path names goes in the path. Every other parameter goes in
  the query string.
- `->` says what a success returns. A `resource` over the endpoint is typed
  by it, so `u.nam` is `T05` before the page ever runs.
- An endpoint the service does not have is `T06`, and an argument it does
  not take is `T10`.

### Add headers and hooks to every call

To send the same headers with every call, add a `headers { }` block. Each
value is read at the moment of the request, not when the service is
declared, so a token refreshed a moment ago is the one that is sent.

This service sends a bearer token and the reader's language, tags each
request with an ID, logs each response, and refreshes the token on a `401`:

```wf
type User { id: String, name: String }

store Session {
    state token = ""
    state language = "en"
    action refresh() { token = await fetch("/api/token") }
}

api Backend(base: env.PUBLIC_API ?? "/api/v1") {
    headers {
        Authorization: "Bearer {Session.token}"
        Accept-Language: Session.language
    }

    on request(r)  { r.headers["X-Request-Id"] = uuid() }
    on response(r) { log("{r.status} {r.url}") }
    on error(e)    { if e.status == 401 { await Session.refresh()  return "retry" } }

    get me() -> User
}
```

The three hooks run around every call the service makes:

| Hook | When it runs | What it gets | What returning does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `on request(r)` | Before the request is sent, after `headers { }` | `r.url`, `r.method`, `r.headers`, `r.body` — change them in place | The changed request is what goes out |
| `on response(r)` | After a reply arrives, before it is decoded | `r.status`, `r.headers`, `r.url` | Nothing; it is for recording |
| `on error(e)` | After every retry the policy allows has failed | The error, as [What every call does for you](#what-every-call-does-for-you) describes it | `return "retry"` runs the call once more, which is how a `401` refreshes a token and carries on. Anything else lets the error through. |

A hook may `await`. A hook that throws fails the call it was watching.

### What every call does for you

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| Abort | A call is aborted when its scope leaves, when an argument that reads state changes, on `.cancel()`, and on timeout |
| Errors | `.offline`, `.timeout`, `.aborted`, `.parse`, `.network`, `.status(code, body)` — each with `.message`, `.status`, `.body` and `.headers` to read |
| Retry | Exponential backoff with jitter, per error kind, honouring `Retry-After` |
| Cache | `cache: .swr(60.seconds)`, `.none`, `.forever` — keyed by method, address, body and credentials, revalidated with `ETag`, and holding the 256 answers read most recently |
| Dedupe | Two readers of one address make one request |
| Refetch | `on: .focus`, `.reconnect`, `.interval(30.seconds)` |
| Pagination | `paginate: .page` gives `.items`, `.loadMore()` and `.hasMore` |
| Progress | A `File` parameter makes `Backend.avatar.progress` a number from 0 to 1 |

Beside each endpoint you also get `Backend.users.invalidate()`,
`.prefetch(args)`, `.url(args)` and `.key(args)`.

### Read the service from an OpenAPI file

To take every endpoint from a specification instead of writing them,
name the file with `from`:

```wf
api Backend from "openapi.json" (base: env.PUBLIC_API)
```

The build reads every endpoint, parameter, response type and error shape
from the file, and each named schema becomes something the program can
name. The day the server changes its contract, the build says so. A missing
`openapi.json` is `E111`.

How each schema becomes a type:

| The schema | What the program gets |
|---|---|
| An object: `{ "type": "object", "properties": … }` | A `type` with those fields; a field the schema does not `require` is `T?` |
| An `allOf`: `[{ "$ref": "…/EnvSummary" }, { "properties": … }]` | `type ServerDetail = EnvSummary { … }`: it extends the first record it names, and every other part adds fields of its own |
| A string with cases: `{ "type": "string", "enum": ["prod", "test"] }` | `enum Env { prod, test }`, whose cases are the strings the server sends |
| A string with a case no name can spell: `"operate.flags"` | `String`, wherever the schema is named |
| Anything else: a string, a number, a list, another schema's `$ref`, a `oneOf` of one type and `null` | That type, wherever the schema is named; a `oneOf` of several types is `Any` |

A value that may be null becomes its type made optional, however the
document says so:

- OpenAPI 3.1's `"type": ["string", "null"]` is `String?`;
- a `oneOf` of `{ "type": "null" }` and a `$ref` is that type's `?`;
- 3.0's `"nullable": true` is the same, beside a `type`, an `allOf` or a
  `$ref`;
- a record or an enum whose own schema allows null is `T?` wherever it is
  named.

A string's `format` gives the language's type for what the server sends:

| `format` | In a response, and in every record only responses reach |
|---|---|
| `date-time` | `DateTime` |
| `date` | `Date` |
| `uuid` | `Uuid` |
| `email` | `Email` |
| `uri` | `Url` |
| `time` | `String`, everywhere: JSON Schema's carries an offset (`09:30:00Z`) that `Time` does not read |

What the program sends — a parameter, a request body, and every record one
of them reaches, except for the fields marked `readOnly` — keeps `String`.
So a value the program holds as a `String`, such as a route parameter or
what an input holds, can still be sent.

Also:

- A parameter or a request body may be a `$ref` into `components`, as a
  shared `limit` often is.
- A body is required when the document says so.
- A `type` or an `enum` the program declares itself wins over the
  specification's of the same name.

### Service settings

These go in the service's parentheses or at the top of its block, before
the endpoints:

| Setting | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `base:` | The address every path is relative to: `"/api/v1"`, `env.PUBLIC_API` | — |
| `timeout:` | A duration after which a call gives up with `.timeout`: `10.seconds` | none |
| `retry:` | A count (`3`), `.never`, or `.backoff(times: 3, on: [.network, .timeout, .status5xx], delay: 300, max: 30000, jitter: true)` | no retries |
| `cache:` | `.swr(60.seconds)` (serve what is held, revalidate behind it), `.cache(5.minutes)`, `.forever`, `.none` | `.none` |
| `credentials:` | `.omit`, `.sameOrigin`, `.include` — whether cookies go with a call | the browser's (`.sameOrigin`) |
| `mode:` | `.cors`, `.noCors`, `.sameOrigin` | `.cors` |
| `redirect:` | `.follow`, `.error`, `.manual` | `.follow` |
| `referrer:` | A referrer policy: `.noReferrer`, `.origin`, … | the page's |
| `headers { }` | Headers every call carries, each read at the moment of the call | — |

How `retry` works:

- Its `on:` takes `.network`, `.timeout`, `.status5xx`, `.status4xx`, and
  single codes in the form `.status429` or `.status503`.
- Without `on:`, it retries network failures, timeouts, 5xx responses and
  429.
- The wait doubles from `delay` (in milliseconds) up to `max`, with jitter.
  A `Retry-After` from the server wins.
- An aborted call is never retried.

### Declare endpoints

Each line of a service, after its settings, is an endpoint:

```text
get users(page: Number = 1, q: String?) -> [User]
get user(id: String) at "users/:id" -> User
post createUser(body: Map) -> User
    errors { 422 -> Map }
put rename(id: String, body: Map) at "users/:id" -> User
patch settings(body: Map) -> Map
delete removeUser(id: String) at "users/:id"
get report(id: String) at "reports/:id" as: .blob
```

- **The verb** is `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`, `head` or
  `options`.
- **Path parameters.** A parameter the path names (`:id`) goes in the path.
  One that is empty (`null` or `""`) is not sent at all, since `users/`
  would be the whole collection, not the user; nor is one that is `.` or
  `..`, which the browser reads as this folder or the one above. The call
  ends as `.aborted`, and a resource over it stays `loading` until the value
  arrives.
- **The body.** A parameter called `body` is the request body; a map is
  sent as JSON. A `File` parameter makes the call a multipart upload.
- **Query parameters.** Every other parameter goes in the query string, and
  one that is `null` is left out.
- **What comes back.** `-> T` is what a success returns. Without it the call
  returns `Any`, and `204 No Content` returns nothing.
- **Typed failures.** `errors { 422 -> T }` types the body of a failure with
  that status: the `.status(code, body)` error carries it decoded.
- **Other responses.** `as:` says how to read a response that is not JSON:
  `.text`, `.blob`, `.arrayBuffer` or `.none`. `errorAs:` does the same for
  a failure's body. `cache:` sets a cache policy for that endpoint alone.

A call passes the endpoint's parameters by name. It may add `cache:` and
`retry:`, and in a `resource` also `on:` (`.focus`, `.reconnect`,
`.interval(30.seconds)`) and `paginate:`.

### Load results a page at a time

To show a long list in pages, call the endpoint with `paginate: .page`.
This page shows items and a **Load more** button while there are more:

```wf
type Item { id: String, name: String }

api Catalog(base: "/api") {
    get items(page: Number = 1) -> [Item]
}

page Items(path: "/items", title: "Items", description: "Everything, a page at a time.") {
    state page = 1
    resource list = Catalog.items(page: page, paginate: .page)

    Heading("Items").h1
    for item in list.items by item.id { Text(item.name) }
    if list.hasMore {
        Button("Load more") { on click { list.loadMore() } }
    }
}
```

- `.items` gathers every page loaded so far. It is a list of what a page
  holds — the answer, when the endpoint returns a list, or its `items`
  field — so `item.name` is checked against `Item`.
- `.loadMore()` moves `page` on by one and fetches the next page, as a
  refresh.
- `.hasMore` turns false when a page comes back empty.

### Call an API on another origin

A page on `https://example.com` that calls `https://api.example.com` makes a
*cross-origin request*. The API must answer with CORS headers —
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` if
cookies go with the call — or the browser refuses the response.

The same applies while you develop. `wf serve` answers on `localhost:3000`
and has no proxy, so an API on `localhost:8080` must allow that origin.

The alternative is to serve the API and the site from one origin behind a
reverse proxy, where `base: "/api"` needs no CORS at all
([Deploying](/recipes/api-on-the-same-origin)).

If the page's build ships a content security policy, list the API's origin
in `meta.connect` too ([Security](/about/security)).

### Show a change before the server agrees

To make an edit appear at once instead of after the round trip, call
`optimistic(holder, change)` before the request. If anything later in the
action throws, the change is taken back: the action rolls itself back.

```wf
action rename(id: String, name: String) {
    optimistic(Todos.items, items => items.map(i => if i.id == id { { ...i, title: name } } else { i }))
    await Backend.updateUser(id: id, body: { name: name })
    Backend.users.invalidate()
}
```

The new title shows at once. If `updateUser` fails, the old title comes
back.

## Fetch on demand with `await fetch`

For a request made when something happens — a save, a delete, a step in a
flow — call `await fetch` in an action. It returns the parsed body, and
throws on a failed response, so you catch the failure with `try`.

This page loads a list of todos, adds one, and toggles one, each with a
request:

```wf
type Todo { id: String, title: String, done: Bool = false }

page Todos(path: "/todos", title: "Todos", description: "Todos saved to a server.") {
    state todos: [Todo] = []
    state draft = ""
    state error = ""

    action load() {
        let r: [Todo] = await fetch("/api/todos")
        todos = r
    }

    action add() {
        if draft.trim() == "" { return }
        try {
            let created: Todo = await fetch("/api/todos", { method: "POST", body: { title: draft } })
            todos.push(created)
            draft = ""
        } catch e {
            error = "Could not save: {e.message}"
        }
    }

    action toggle(id: String) {
        let found = todos.find(x => x.id == id)
        if let todo = found {
            let updated: Todo = await fetch("/api/todos/{id}", { method: "PATCH", body: { done: !todo.done } })
            todos = todos.map(x => if x.id == id { updated } else { x })
        }
    }

    load()
    Heading("Todos").h1
    Input(bind: draft, label: "New todo") { on key("Enter") { add() } }
    Button("Add", disabled: add.pending).primary { on click { add() } }
    if error != "" { Alert(error).danger }
    for todo in todos by todo.id {
        Checkbox(checked: todo.done, label: todo.title) { on change { toggle(todo.id) } }
    }
}
```

- The second argument is a map of `method`, `headers` and `body`.
- `load()` at the top of the page is set-up code: it runs once, when the
  page renders.
- `todos.push(created)` changes the state in place. The compiler turns it
  into a new list, so everything that reads `todos` repaints.
- `name.pending` is `true` while the action runs, so **Add** is disabled
  during a save.
- `await fetch` goes through the same engine as an `api` call. For the
  browser's own `fetch`, with the raw response, call `window.fetch`.

## Read a file at build time with `data`

To use content that is known before the site is built — posts, a price
list, a team page — read it with `data`. `data name = "file.json"` reads a
JSON file from the project directory or `src/` at build time, and makes its
value a constant.

A `data` constant:

- is in scope in every page and component;
- costs nothing at run time, because its value is in the bundle;
- is written into the pre-rendered page.

This blog lists every post in `posts.json`, newest first:

```wf
type Post { slug: String, title: String, date: String, body: String }

data posts: [Post] = "posts.json"

page Blog(path: "/", title: "Blog", description: "Every post.") {
    derived sorted = posts.sortBy(p => p.date).reverse()

    Heading("Blog").h1
    for p in sorted by p.slug {
        Card {
            Link(p.title, to: "/posts/{p.slug}")
            Text(format(p.date, .date)).muted.sm
        }
    }
}
```

```json
[
  { "slug": "hello", "title": "Hello", "date": "2026-01-10", "body": "# Hi\nFirst post." },
  { "slug": "second", "title": "Second", "date": "2026-02-02", "body": "More." }
]
```

Annotate it (`data posts: [Post]`) and the checker knows every field.

### Render a page for each item

To give each post its own HTML file in a static build, list the values of
the route parameter in `paths:`. The build renders the page once per value,
each with its own title and description, and lists each in the sitemap:

```wf
type Post { slug: String, title: String, date: String, body: String }

data posts: [Post] = "posts.json"

page PostPage(path: "/posts/:slug", slug: String, title: "Post", description: "A post.", paths: posts.map(p => p.slug)) {
    derived post = posts.find(p => p.slug == slug)
    head { meta(property: "og:title", content: post?.title ?? "Post") }
    if let p = post {
        Heading(p.title).h1
        Markdown(p.body)
    } else {
```
