```wf
        Alert("No such post").warning
    }
}
```

The build writes `posts/hello/index.html` and `posts/second/index.html`.

- `paths:` must be known at build time: a `data` file, a `const` or a
  literal.
- For a route with several parameters, each value is a map naming them:
  `paths: pairs.map(x => { year: x.y, slug: x.s })`.
- A route not in `paths:` still works in a single-page app. Only the static
  build needs the list.

## Where data lands in the pre-rendered page

A static build writes each page's HTML before any script runs. What each
source of data puts in that HTML:

| Source | In the pre-rendered HTML |
|---|---|
| `data`, `const`, `env` | Fully painted |
| `state` initial values, and `derived` values over them | Painted |
| `resource` | The `loading` arm; the live page fetches and replaces it |
| `await fetch` | Nothing until the action runs |

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | Why, and what to do |
|---|---|
| The browser console says a response was blocked by CORS | The API is on another origin and does not allow yours. Add CORS headers to the API, or serve both from one origin ([Call an API on another origin](#call-an-api-on-another-origin)). |
| A `fetch` gets a `404` under `wf serve`, with a line in the terminal | `wf serve` has no file or page for that address, and no proxy. Point `base:` at the real API. |
| A `.parse` error naming a place, such as `$[1].name is missing` | Under `wf serve`, a response is checked against its declared type. The server sent another shape: fix the server or the `type`. |
| A resource stays `loading` | A path parameter is `null` or `""`, so the call is not sent. It goes out when the value arrives. |
| The page goes back to `loading` when state changes | The address now names something else, so it is a first load. A refresh of the same address keeps the data. |
| `T05` on a field of the data | The declared type has no such field. Fix the name, or add the field to the `type`. |
| `T06` or `T10` on an endpoint call | The service has no such endpoint, or the endpoint takes no such argument. |
| A post's page is missing from a static build | Its value is not in `paths:`. |

## Quiz

```quiz
A resource's `match` has a `loading` arm and a `ready` arm, and no other. What does the reader see when the request fails?
- An error message the runtime draws for you -- The runtime draws only the arms you write; the build warns about the missing one with T21.
+ Nothing where the `match` is, and the build warns with T21 -- No arm matches `"error"`, so the place stays empty. Add `error(e) { … }` or an `else`.
- The `loading` arm, until a retry succeeds -- A first load that fails is `"error"`, not `"loading"`.
```

```quiz
A resource is making its very first request. Which is true?
+ `pending` is true and `refreshing` is false -- `pending` covers every request of it, the first load included; `refreshing` only a request made again while data is shown.
- `refreshing` is true and `pending` is false -- It is the other way round: there is no data yet to refresh.
- Both are true -- `refreshing` is true only while data is on screen, and on a first load there is none.
```

```quiz
A resource with `on: .interval(30.seconds)` asks again while its list is on screen. What does its `match` show while that refresh runs?
- The `loading` arm, then the new list -- Only a first load, or a request whose address changed, shows `loading`.
- An empty list until the answer arrives -- The data stays while a refresh runs; `name.data` is never cleared by one.
+ The `ready` arm with the old list, then the answer drawn in place -- A refresh keeps `"ready"` and the data; rows whose key is still there keep their nodes.
```

```quiz
The address is `fetch("/api/servers?env={stage}")`, and a button sets `stage` from `"test"` to `"prod"`. What shows next?
+ The `loading` arm, then the production servers -- The request now names something else, so it is a first load; the test servers would be the wrong data.
- The test servers, with `refreshing` true, until the production servers arrive -- That is a refresh, which asks again for the same request; this one changed.
- Nothing changes until the reader reloads the page -- An address that reads state is fetched again whenever that state changes.
```

## Common mistakes

**A `match` with no `error` arm.** When the request fails, no arm draws, and
the reader is not told:

```wf expect=T21
page P(path: "/", title: "Users", description: "Everyone.") {
    resource users = fetch("/api/users")
    Heading("Users").h1
    match users {
        loading { Spinner }
        ready(list) { Text("{list.length} users") }
    }
}
```

Add `error(e) { Alert(e.message).danger }`, or an `else`
([T21](/errors/T21)).

**A field the declared type does not have.** Once a resource is typed, every
field read from it is checked against the `type`:

```wf expect=T05
type User { id: String, name: String }

page P(path: "/", title: "Users", description: "Everyone.") {
    resource users: [User] = fetch("/api/users")
    Heading("Users").h1
    match users {
        loading { Spinner }
        error(e) { Alert(e.message).danger }
        ready(list) { for u in list by u.id { Text(u.fullName) } }
    }
}
```

Use the field the type declares, `u.name`, or add `fullName` to the `type`
if the server sends it ([T05](/errors/T05)).

**Reading `.data` as if it had arrived.** Before the first answer,
`name.data` is `null`:

```wf expect=T04
type User { id: String, name: String }

page P(path: "/", title: "Users", description: "Everyone.") {
    resource users: [User] = fetch("/api/users")
    Heading("Users").h1
    Text("{users.data.length} users")
}
```

Read it through `?.` with a fallback, `{users.data?.length ?? 0}`, or show
it inside the `ready` arm, where the binding is never null
([T04](/errors/T04)).

Going further: [Open a socket](/recipes/open-a-socket) keeps a
connection open for data the server pushes.

## Next

[Testing](/learn/16-testing).

# Testing

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/16-testing

This chapter is about testing a WebFluent project: render a component and
check what it shows, click and type through a page in a real browser, and
load every page of the built site to catch errors before a reader does.

You write tests in WebFluent itself, as `test "name" { … }` declarations. A
test renders something — a component, a fragment of a page, a whole page —
and holds it to what it must and must not show. A test that clicks or types
runs in a headless browser. `wf verify` then loads every page of the built
site in one.

## Before you start

- A project with at least one component or page to test.
- For a test that clicks, types or presses a key, and for `wf verify`:
  Chrome or Chromium on the machine, or the `WF_CHROME` environment
  variable pointing at one. A test that only looks needs neither.

## Write a test that looks

To check what a component shows, place it in a test and say what the text
must and must not contain. Put tests in `tests/*.wf`, or beside the code in
`src/`. A test has the project's components, stores, types and constants at
hand.

This file declares a price tag and three tests of it:

```wf
component PriceTag(_ amount: Number, sale: Bool = false) {
    Row(gap: .sm, align: .center) {
        Text(format(amount, .currency)).bold
        if sale { Badge("Sale").danger }
    }
}

test "a price tag shows the amount as currency" {
    PriceTag(1234.5)
    expect "$1,234.50"
    expect not "Sale"
}

test "a sale tag carries the badge" {
    PriceTag(10, sale: true)
    expect "Sale"
}

test "a list renders each row"(data: { rows: [{ name: "Ada" }, { name: "Grace" }] }) {
    for r in rows { Text(r.name) }
    expect "Ada"
    expect "Grace"
}
```

Run `wf test`, and each test prints a line; all three pass. The parts of a
test that looks:

- `expect "text"` — the text must appear in what the page shows.
  `expect not "text"` — it must not.
- `data: { … }` — values the body reads, by name. A `state` in the body
  starts with its initial value.
- `t("key")` — reads the project's translations, in its default locale.

### How `expect` reads the page

`expect` reads the text a reader sees, never the markup: a class name in
the HTML does not count. It reads the text laid out as a browser lays it
out:

- runs of white space are one space;
- a block, or anything a `Row`, `Stack` or `Grid` lays out, is set apart
  from what is beside it;
- inline elements that touch read as touching, so
  `Text { Code("live") Code(": ") Code("[Deploy]") }` reads
  `live: [Deploy]`.

The line breaks and indentation of the snapshot are not text. A render and
a browser read the same page the same way.

In a browser, a page may still be moving — a row on its way out, a fetch on
its way in. `expect` reads the page again until it holds, for up to a
second and a half.

### Snapshots

Each render is also compared to a *snapshot*, the HTML saved in
`tests/__snapshots__/<file>/<test>.html`. `wf test` writes a snapshot when
it is missing and fails, with a diff, when a render no longer matches it.
After a change you meant, run `wf test --update` to rewrite them.

## Write a test that acts

To check what a click, a keystroke or typed text does, add steps that act.
A click cannot be rendered — it runs a handler, which runs an action, which
changes a store, which repaints — so a test with an action in it is
compiled into a real page, served, and run in a headless browser. It uses
the same compiler, the same runtime and the same output a reader gets.

This test types an incident, reports it, and checks the count goes up:

```wf
store IncidentStore {
    state titles: [String] = ["Disk full", "Login slow"]
    derived open = titles.length
    action report(title: String) { titles = titles.concat([title]) }
}

test "reporting an incident opens one more" {
    use IncidentStore
    state draft = ""
    Text("{IncidentStore.open} open")
    Input(bind: draft, label: "What happened")
    Button("Report") { on click { IncidentStore.report(draft) } }

    expect "2 open"
    type "Queue backing up" into "What happened"
    click "Report"
    expect "3 open"
}
```

The steps run **in the order you write them**. That order is the test:
what a click did is visible only in the `expect` that follows it.

| Step | What it does |
|---|---|
| `expect "text"` · `expect not "text"` | What the page must, or must not, show |
| `expect focus "Beta"` | What has the focus is called that: its `aria-label`, its label, its placeholder or its text |
| `click "Save"` | Clicks whatever carries that name: a button or a link, a control, a tab, a menu's item, an option, a row of a tree. The focus goes to it, as a real click puts it there |
| `type "Ada" into "Name"` | Types into the control that label names |
| `press "Enter"` · `press "Escape" in "Search"` · `press "mod+k"` | A key, on the focused element or a named one, with the modifiers a combination names (`mod` is ⌘ on a Mac, Ctrl elsewhere); `Escape` closes an open `Modal` or `Dialog` as a real one would |

A step finds what it acts on the way a reader does: by the name on it. A
button's name is its text; a control's is its label, its placeholder or its
`aria-label`. The accessibility checks hold a page to the same names
([Accessibility](/about/accessibility)), so a test that passes here is a
page somebody can use.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from Testing Library?** There is no `getByTestId` and no
> `waitFor`. A step finds an element only by the name a reader sees, so a
> control with no label cannot be clicked or typed into, and `expect` waits
> on its own, for up to a second and a half. See
> [Coming from React](/coming-from/react).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **A handler that throws fails the test**, even when every `expect` would
> have passed. A click that quietly did nothing is the bug, not a pass.

A test that acts takes no snapshot: its expects are the test.

### The page a test that acts runs on

The page is drawn as the built site is:

- it links the project's scripts under `src/`, so a click that calls one
  runs it;
- it bundles the project's stylesheets under `src/` after the theme's rules
  and before the rules `style { }` blocks compile to;
- it links the stylesheets `meta.stylesheets` names;
- it serves `public/` beside it.

So a rule that hides a word, or one that names a font or an image under
`public/`, behaves the same in a test as on the site. A test that only
looks renders without any of them.

### Test a portal

A `Portal` draws its block into a node that `into:` names, and only the
running page draws it. So a test whose body holds a portal — or places a
component that holds one — is compiled into a page and run in the browser
too, with no snapshot:

```wf
test "a portal draws into the element a handle names" {
    Stack(ref: spot)
    Portal(into: spot) { Text("in") }
    expect "in"
}
```

## Seed data and stores

To start a test from a known state, name it in `data:`. A key that is a
value's name supplies that value; a key that is a store's name seeds that
store's state. Seeding works the same in a test that only looks and in one
that clicks.

This test fills the cart with two of one item and checks the summary:

```wf
type CartItem { id: String, qty: Number }

store Cart {
    state items: [CartItem] = []
    derived count = items.map(i => i.qty).sum()
}

component CartSummary {
    use Cart
    Text("{Cart.count} items")
}

test "the cart shows what is in it"(data: { Cart: { items: [{ id: "a", qty: 2 }] } }) {
    CartSummary
    expect "2 items"
}
```

## Test a whole page

To click through a page as a reader does, place the page in a test by its
name, as you would a component. This works for a page whose route takes no
parameter. Its state, its stores and its handlers all run:

```wf
test "a task is added with Enter" {
    Tasks
    type "Walk the dog" into "New task"
    press "Enter" in "New task"
    expect "Walk the dog"
}
```

`press "Enter"` in a form's text field submits the form, as a real key
does. The `spa` and `static` projects that `wf init` writes carry tests
like this under `tests/`; run `wf test` in a new project to see them pass.

## Run the tests

To run every test under `tests/`, and any declared in `src/`:

```bash
wf test
```

To run one file's tests, in the project it belongs to:

```bash
wf test tests/cart.wf
```

To rewrite the snapshots after a change you meant:

```bash
wf test --update
```

`wf test` prints a line per test and exits non-zero when one fails, so it
works as a CI step as it is. A build never includes tests.

## Check every page with `wf verify`

To catch what only a running page shows, build the site and load every
page of it:

```bash
wf build && wf verify
```

`wf verify` serves the build and opens every route in headless Chrome. It
fails on:

- an uncaught exception or a `console.error`;
- a request that failed, or an image that did not load;
- a page that rendered no text.

For each route it prints the first contentful paint, the size and the
requests. It also lists the built-ins no page drew — a fact about
coverage, not a failure. Its options:

- `--budget 400` fails a route that takes more than 400 ms to paint;
- `--json` prints the report for a pipeline;
- `--returning-visitor` visits every route again with storage holding what
  the previous build's pages kept.

[CLI](/reference/cli#wf-verify) has the details.

## Run the checks in CI

To run the formatter, the build, the tests and `wf verify` on every push,
add a workflow such as this one to `.github/workflows/check.yml`:

```yaml
name: Check
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/master/install.sh | bash
      - run: echo "$HOME/.webfluent/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
      - run: wf fmt --check
      - run: wf build
      - run: wf test
      - run: wf verify --budget 1000
```

GitHub's Ubuntu runners come with Chrome, so the tests that act and
`wf verify` run there as they do on your machine.

## Choose what to test

The type checker and the accessibility lints already catch a large class
of mistakes. Tests are for the behaviour they cannot see:

- **Components** with more than one state: each branch a prop can take.
- **Stores**, through what a component shows of them, seeded with `data:`.
- **Flows** a reader depends on — signing in, adding to a cart, submitting
  a form — as tests that act.
- **Every page**, with `wf verify`, on every build.

## Troubleshooting

**A step cannot find what it names.** The test fails and prints what the
page showed instead:

```text
  FAIL  tests/cart.wf — the count follows what is added
        nothing to click called "Publish"
        the page showed:
        Nothing here
```

Check that the name matches the button's text or the control's label,
placeholder or `aria-label` exactly, and that an earlier step has drawn it.

**A test that acts says there is no browser.** Install Chrome or Chromium,
or set `WF_CHROME` to the path of one.

**A snapshot test fails after a change you meant.** Run `wf test --update`
and commit the new snapshots.

## Common mistakes

A step finds what it acts on by its accessible name, so the mistakes that
break a test are the ones the accessibility lints already report.

**A field with no label.** `type "…" into "…"` names a control by its label,
placeholder or `aria-label`, and this one has none:

```wf expect=A03
page Tasks(path: "/", title: "Tasks", description: "What to do.") {
    state draft = ""
    Heading("Tasks").h1
    Input(bind: draft)
    Text("Next: {draft}")
}
```

Give it `label: "New task"`, and the test types `into "New task"`
([A03](/errors/A03)).

**A button with no text.** `click "…"` finds a button by its text, and an
empty one has nothing to find:

```wf expect=A05
page Tasks(path: "/", title: "Tasks", description: "What to do.") {
    state count = 0
    Heading("Tasks").h1
    Text("{count} done")
    Button { on click { count = count + 1 } }
}
```

Write its text, `Button("Mark done")`, or give it an `aria-label:`
([A05](/errors/A05)).

**An icon button with no label.** An `IconButton` shows no text, so its
`label:` is the only name a step can use:

```wf expect=A02
page Tasks(path: "/", title: "Tasks", description: "What to do.") {
    state count = 0
    Heading("Tasks").h1
    Text("{count} done")
    IconButton(icon: "plus") { on click { count = count + 1 } }
}
```

Add `label: "Add one"`, and click it with `click "Add one"`
([A02](/errors/A02)).

Going further: [Security](/about/security) covers what the compiler
guarantees, what it cannot, and the decisions left to you: markup,
secrets, storage, headers and a deployment checklist.

## Next

[PDF and slides](/learn/17-pdf-and-slides).



---

# PDF and slides

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/learn/17-pdf-and-slides

This chapter is about compiling a WebFluent project to paper: a paginated
PDF document, such as an invoice or a report, or a slide deck for a talk. You write the pages with the same elements and the same CSS as a
website, and `wf build` lays them out on pages.

In this chapter:

- choosing what the build writes;
- how the paged engine lays out a page;
- making a PDF document: paper, headers, page breaks, contents, charts,
  fonts and right-to-left text;
- making a slide deck.

## Before you start

You need a WebFluent project. To start one already set up for paper, run
one of these commands:

```bash
wf init my-report --template pdf
wf init my-deck --template slides
```

Then run `wf build` in the project's folder. The build prints the page
count and writes one file, `build/<name>.pdf`, named after the project
unless `output_filename` says otherwise:

```text
  PDF: 45586 bytes, 3 page(s)
  Output: ./build/my-report.pdf
Build complete.
```

To produce one PDF per invoice from data, use the same templates with
[server rendering](/recipes/render-a-template) instead.

## Choose what the build writes

`build.output_type` in `webfluent.app.json` chooses what `wf build` writes:

| Output | `output_type` | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| A website | `spa` (default), with `build.ssg` for pre-rendered pages; or `static`, which is the same as `ssg` | HTML, CSS and JavaScript ([Static sites and SPAs](/about/static-or-single-page)) |
| PDF document | `pdf` | One `.pdf`, paginated |
| Slide deck | `slides` | One `.pdf`, one slide per page |
| Custom elements | `elements` | `elements.js` for other frameworks ([JavaScript interop](/recipes/publish-custom-elements)) |

## The paged engine

A PDF is the page, printed. The compiler renders the program to the same
static HTML and CSS a template renders, then lays that HTML out on paper
itself, with no browser and no external tool. The engine covers five
areas:

- **The page's own stylesheet.** The engine's rules for every built-in, the
  theme's tokens, every `.css` file under `src/` and every `style { }`
  block go through a real CSS cascade. It supports selectors with
  descendant, child and sibling combinators, attribute selectors,
  `:first-child`/`:nth-child`, `:not()`, `:is()` and `:where()`;
  specificity; inheritance; `var()`; and `em`, `rem` and `%`. A `Card` in a
  PDF looks like the `Card` on the page, and a class of your own
  (`class: "callout"`) brings its rules with it. `@media print` applies;
  rules only a screen has (`:hover`, a media query on width) do not.
- **Layout.** Block, flex and grid work as CSS defines them — `Row`,
  `Stack`, `Grid` and `Column` sit side by side exactly as on the web —
  with absolute positioning, `gap`, `min-`/`max-` sizes, `aspect-ratio`,
  inline-blocks on a line of text (a badge in a sentence), tables sized by
  their content, and list markers.
- **Text.** Every run is shaped (ligatures, kerning, Arabic joining,
  combining marks), set right to left where the language is, broken at
  Unicode's line-break opportunities, and aligned or justified. A word too
  long for its line is cut rather than overflowing.
- **Paint.** Backgrounds (colours, linear and radial gradients with any
  number of stops, pictures), borders per side (solid, dashed, dotted) with
  rounded corners, shadows, opacity, `overflow: hidden`, `transform:
  rotate()`, and pictures with their transparency — PNG, JPEG (embedded
  as it is), WebP, GIF, and SVG, which stays vector.
- **The file.** Fonts are embedded as subsets with the text attached, so a
  reader can copy and search it. The file is compressed, carries its title
  and author, has an outline of its headings in the reader's sidebar, and
  its links work.

## Make a PDF document

To build a PDF, set `output_type` to `pdf`. The `pdf` key sets the paper,
margins (in points) and default font for every document in the project:

```json
{
  "build": {
    "output_type": "pdf",
    "pdf": {
      "page_size": "A4",
      "margins": { "top": 72, "bottom": 72, "left": 72, "right": 72 },
      "default_font": "Helvetica",
      "default_font_size": 12,
      "output_filename": "report.pdf"
    }
  }
}
```

A PDF page holds a `Document`, and everything inside it flows from page to
page. This invoice has a header on every page but the first, a page number
in the footer, a watermark, a table, and a totals card that is never split:

```wf
type Line { item: String, qty: Number, price: Number }

const LINES: [Line] = [
    Line(item: "Design", qty: 12, price: 90),
    Line(item: "Build", qty: 40, price: 110),
]

page Invoice(path: "/", title: "Invoice", description: "An invoice.") {
    derived total = LINES.map(l => l.qty * l.price).sum()
    Document(size: "A4", title: "Invoice 2026-014", author: "Acme Studio") {
        Header(on: .rest) { Text("Acme Studio · invoice 2026-014").muted.sm.right }
        Footer { Text("Page {page} of {pages}").muted.sm.center }
        Watermark("PAID")

        Row(justify: .between, align: .start) {
            Heading("Invoice").h1
            Stack(gap: .xs) {
                Text("No. 2026-014").bold
                Text("Issued {format("2026-09-01", .date, "long")}").muted
            }
        }
        Table {
            Table.Head {
                Table.Row { Table.Cell("Item")  Table.Cell("Qty")  Table.Cell("Price")  Table.Cell("Amount") }
            }
            Table.Body {
                for l in LINES {
                    Table.Row {
                        Table.Cell(l.item)
                        Table.Cell("{l.qty}")
                        Table.Cell(format(l.price, .currency))
                        Table.Cell(format(l.qty * l.price, .currency))
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        Card {
            style { break-inside: avoid; margin-top: 12pt }
            Text("Total: {format(total, .currency)}").bold.lg
        }
        PageBreak
        Heading("Terms").h2
        Paragraph { Text("Payment within 30 days.") }
    }
}
```

The result is a two-page PDF: the invoice on the first page, ending with
`Total: $5,480.00`, and the terms on the second, under the header.

> [!NOTE]
> **Coming from LaTeX or Typst?** There is no document class and there are
> no TeX boxes: a document is laid out by CSS. `\newpage` is `PageBreak`,
> a `minipage` that must not split is `style { break-inside: avoid }`, and
> `fancyhdr` is a `Header` and a `Footer`. See
> [Coming from LaTeX and Typst](/coming-from/latex).

### Set the paper, headers and footers

These elements shape every page of a document:

| Element | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Document(size:, landscape, margin:, title:, author:, subject:, keywords:, lang:)` | The paper (`A4`, `A3`, `A5`, `Letter`, `Legal`, `Tabloid`, or two lengths: `"210mm 297mm"`), its margins (one length or four, `"20mm 25mm"`), and what the file says about itself. What it leaves out, `build.pdf` decides |
| `Header`, `Footer` | Drawn in the top and bottom margins of every page, or of the pages `on:` names: `.all` (the default), `.first`, `.rest`, `.odd`, `.even` |
| `Background` | Drawn behind each page's content, the size of the whole page, margins and all: a cover's full-bleed gradient, a coloured band, a sidebar strip that runs down every page. It takes `on:` too |
| `Watermark("DRAFT")` | Large, faint, rotated text behind each page. Its look is the rule `.wf-watermark`, which a stylesheet may change |
| `PageBreak` | Starts a new page; so do `break-before: page` and `break-after: page` in a style |

`Header` and `Footer` are the same built-ins that draw the `<header>` and
`<footer>` landmarks on a web page ([Elements](/learn/06-elements#layout-elements)).
Inside a `Document` they become the margins of every page.

Inside a `Header`, `Footer` or `Background`, `page` and `pages` are the
page's number and the page count: `Text("Page {page} of {pages}")`.

The page's background — the `html` or `body` rule's — fills every page,
edge to edge, so a dark theme prints dark.

### Control where pages break

Content flows onto as many pages as it needs, and never breaks through the
middle of a line of text. The engine follows these rules:

- Paragraphs break between lines, keeping at least two on each side
  (`orphans`, `widows`).
- Tables break between rows, and **the header row is drawn again** at the
  top of every page the table continues on.
- A grid breaks between its rows; a row of cards moves to the next page
  together.
- Side-by-side columns taller than a page break each on its own, and what
  follows waits for the longer column.
- A heading never ends a page: it moves with what follows.
- A box that runs onto the next page is painted on both, its border open
  at the break.

To keep a box whole — a totals block, a signature — give it
`break-inside: avoid`, as the invoice's totals card does. To start a new
page, place `PageBreak`.

### Add a table of contents, links and an outline

`TableOfContents(levels: 2)` lists the document's headings with the page
each one lands on, dotted leaders between them, and each entry a link to
its heading. The engine lays the document out, learns where every heading
landed, and fills in the numbers. `title:` puts a heading above the list.

A `Link` is a link in the PDF too: to a URL, or `to: "#terms"` to the
element whose `id:` is `terms`. Every heading appears in the reader's
outline, nested by level.

### Draw charts and QR codes

This report draws a grouped bar chart, a donut chart and a QR code from a
constant list of records:

```wf
const SALES = [
    { month: "Jan", web: 41, store: 22 },
    { month: "Feb", web: 48, store: 25 },
    { month: "Mar", web: 55, store: 21 },
]

page Report(path: "/", title: "Sales", description: "The quarter.") {
    Document {
        Heading("Sales by channel").h1
        Chart(kind: .bar, data: SALES, x: "month", y: ["web", "store"], unit: "k")
        Chart(kind: .donut, data: SALES, x: "month", y: "web", labels: true)
        QrCode("https://example.com/report/q1")
    }
}
```

`Chart` draws a list of records as vector graphics. It takes these props:

| Prop | What it sets |
|---|---|
| `kind` | `.bar` (grouped, or `stacked`), `.line`, `.area`, `.pie` or `.donut` |
| `x` | The field that names each row's label |
| `y` | The field that holds each row's value, or a list of fields (one series each) |
| `colors`, `ink` | The series' colours, and the colour of the labels |
| `grid`, `legend` | Whether to draw grid lines and a legend |
| `labels` | Values written on bars and slices |
| `unit` | A unit after each value |
| `width`, `height` | The size in user units. The chart scales to its box, so draw a narrow chart narrower for larger text |

`QrCode(value, color:, background:)` encodes a URL or any text.

Both work on a web page too, as an SVG drawn when the page is built. There,
what they read must be known at build time — a literal, a `const` or a
`data` file — or the build reports `E109`.

### Use your own fonts

The default faces are Liberation Sans, Serif and Mono — the metric twins of
Helvetica, Times and Courier — built into `wf`. So `Helvetica`, `Arial`,
`system-ui`, `sans-serif`, `Times`, `serif`, `Courier` and `monospace` all
resolve with nothing installed, and cover Latin, Greek and Cyrillic.

To use any other family, add its file:

1. Put `.ttf` or `.otf` files under the project's `fonts/` folder (or
   `src/fonts/`, or name them in `pdf.fonts`).
2. Name the family as the file names it, for example in the theme:
   `font-family: Manrope, sans-serif`.

Variable fonts are drawn at the weight a style asks for. A weight or an
italic a family does not have is synthesised. A font a stylesheet's
`@font-face` names, from a local file, is used too.

A character no named face has is drawn from a face that has it — the
project's fonts first, then the machine's. The build names, in a `note:`
line, each family it took from the machine, so you can make the document
the same everywhere by copying those fonts into `fonts/`. To forbid the
machine's fonts, set `"system_fonts": false`. A character no font has is
reported, never drawn as `?`.

### Lay out a right-to-left document

A document whose `lang` is right to left (`ar`, `he`, `fa`, `ur`) is laid
out right to left — text, flex rows, grids, table columns, list markers.
A run of the other direction inside it is ordered by the Unicode
bidirectional algorithm.

A code or a figure written in Latin characters inside Arabic text — an
invoice number like `2026-0417`, a product code — can come out with its
parts in the wrong order. The bidirectional algorithm reads the hyphen as
part of the right-to-left text around it. To fix it, give the code a run of
its own that says it is left to right: `Text("2026-0417", class: "ltr")`,
with `.ltr { direction: ltr; unicode-bidi: isolate; }` in the project's
CSS. The fix works on a web page and in a PDF alike.

### What a PDF does not draw

Everything static draws. What only means something in a browser is refused
where it is written, with `E109`:

- controls (`Button`, `Input`, `Form`, …);
- navigation (`Router`, `Navbar`, `Tabs`, `Menu`);
- overlays (`Modal`, `Dialog`, `Toast`, `Tooltip`);
- media that plays (`Video`, `Audio`, `Carousel`);
- elements a script draws (`Host`, `Element`, `Portal`);
- handlers, `resource` and motion.

## Make a slide deck

To build a deck, set `output_type` to `slides`. The `slides` key sets the
deck's size and its chrome:

```json
{
  "build": {
    "output_type": "slides",
    "slides": {
      "size": "16:9",
      "show_slide_numbers": true,
      "footer_text": "Acme — Q4 review",
      "background_color": "#FFFFFF"
    }
  }
}
```

A deck is a `Presentation` inside a page. This deck uses every kind of
slide, and restyles the last one with a gradient:

```wf
page Deck(path: "/", title: "Q4 review", description: "The quarter in slides.") {
    Presentation {
        TitleSlide("Q4 review", subtitle: "Acme Studio, October 2026")
        SectionSlide("Numbers").primary
        Slide {
            Heading("Revenue").h2
            List {
                List.Item { Text("Up 18% on Q3") }
                List.Item { Text("Three new enterprise accounts") }
                List.Item { Text("Churn at 1.2%") }
            }
        }
        TwoColumn {
            Container {
                Heading("What worked").h3
                Text("Self-serve onboarding.")
            }
            Container {
                Heading("What did not").h3
                Text("The March pricing test.")
            }
        }
        ImageSlide(src: "/chart.png", caption: "Monthly recurring revenue")
        Slide {
            style { background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1E3A8A, #0F172A); color: #fff }
            Heading("Thank you").h1
        }
    }
}
```

The `ImageSlide` reads `public/chart.png`: put a picture of your own there
first. The build warns (`D01`) when the file is missing. The result is a
six-page PDF, one slide per page.

### Write the slides

A deck is laid out by the same engine, one slide to a page. A slide is a
box the size of the page, with `slides.margin` as its padding (a rule of
the deck's own overrides it). What runs past a slide's edge is clipped,
with a note naming the slide.

The slide kinds:

| Element | What it draws |
|---|---|
| `Slide { … }` | A freeform slide, laid out as a column from the top |
| `TitleSlide(title, subtitle:)` | A cover, centred |
| `SectionSlide(label)` | A full-bleed band; `.primary`, `.success`, `.danger`, `.warning` or `.info` |
| `TwoColumn { … }` | Two equal columns |
| `ImageSlide(src:, caption:)` | A picture with an optional caption |

Each kind is styled by the engine's sheet, and a project's rules or a
`style { }` block change it as anywhere. Everything a document draws, a
slide draws: layout, charts, pictures, tables, Arabic.

A `Presentation` holds slides, a `for` or an `if` over them, and components
whose body is a slide. So a deck writes its section openers, headings and
footers once, and makes a slide per item of its data. A page's `derived`
values are worked out before the deck is drawn, so a slide can show a
figure computed from a `data` file.

### Size and frame the deck

These keys under `build.slides` set the deck's size and chrome:

| Key | What it sets |
|---|---|
| `size` | `16:9` (default, 960×540pt), `4:3` (720×540), `A4-landscape` (841.89×595.28), or `WIDTHxHEIGHT` in points |
| `width`, `height` | Override `size` outright |
| `show_slide_numbers` | Draws `n / total` in the bottom right |
| `footer_text` | Text in the bottom left |
| `chrome_color` | The colour of the numbers and footer; when unset, it flips between dark and light on each slide's background |
| `background_color` | Paints every slide |
| `default_font`, `default_font_size` | The deck's font, and its size (24pt). Every size in the engine's slide rules is relative to it |
| `output_filename` | The file the build writes |

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| `E109` on a `Button`, a handler or a `resource` | Remove it from the document or deck: a PDF has nothing to run it |
| `E109` on a `Chart` or `QrCode` in a web page | Give it data known at build time: a literal, a `const` or a `data` file |
| A `note:` names a family taken from the machine | Copy that font into `fonts/` so the document is the same on every machine |
| A note says a slide was clipped | Shorten the slide, or split it in two |
| A totals block or signature is split across two pages | Add `break-inside: avoid` to its `style { }` |
| A Latin code in Arabic text shows its parts out of order | Give it a left-to-right run (see [Lay out a right-to-left document](#lay-out-a-right-to-left-document)) |

## Common mistakes

**A page number outside a header or footer.** `page` and `pages` exist only
inside a `Header`, a `Footer` or a `Background`, which are drawn once per
page:

```wf expect=T13
page Report(path: "/", title: "Report", description: "The quarter.") {
    Document(size: "A4", title: "Q1 report") {
        Heading("Q1 report").h1
        Text("Revenue grew 15% this quarter.")
        Text("Page {page} of {pages}").muted.sm.center
    }
}
```

Move the line into `Footer { Text("Page {page} of {pages}") }`
([T13](/errors/T13)).

**A component named like a built-in.** `Footer` is already a built-in: the
document's footer, drawn at the bottom of every page. A component you name
`Footer` takes its place, so it is drawn once, where it is called, and no
page gets a footer:

```wf expect=V11
component Footer(_ note: String) {
    Text(note).muted.sm.center
}

page Invoice(path: "/", title: "Invoice", description: "An invoice.") {
    Document(size: "A4", title: "Invoice 2026-014") {
        Heading("Invoice").h1
        Text("Total: $5,480.00").bold
        Footer("Acme Studio · invoice 2026-014")
    }
}
```

For a line on every page, use the built-in:
`Footer { Text("Acme Studio · invoice 2026-014") }`, and name your own
component for what it is, such as `component InvoiceNote`
([V11](/errors/V11)).

**A table with no header row.** Without `Table.Head`, a reader of the file
has no column names, and a table that runs onto a second page has no header
to draw again there:

```wf expect=A10
page Invoice(path: "/", title: "Invoice", description: "An invoice.") {
    Document(size: "A4", title: "Invoice 2026-014") {
        Heading("Invoice").h1
        Table {
            Table.Body {
                Table.Row { Table.Cell("Design")  Table.Cell("$1,080.00") }
                Table.Row { Table.Cell("Build")  Table.Cell("$4,400.00") }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Add `Table.Head { Table.Row { Table.Cell("Item")  Table.Cell("Amount") } }`
([A10](/errors/A10)).
