# Keep the active tab in the address

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/active-tab-in-the-address

A tab held in a `state` goes back to the first one on every reload. To
make the tab survive a reload, and a shared link open on the same tab,
read it from the address's `#fragment`:

```wf
page Account(path: "/account", title: "Account", description: "Your profile and billing.") {
    derived tab = if hash != "" { hash } else { "profile" }
    Heading("Account").h1
    Tabs(value: tab, label: "Account") {
        on change(v) { navigate("/account#{v}") }
        Tabs.Page("Profile", value: "profile") { Text("Profile settings") }
        Tabs.Page("Billing", value: "billing") { Text("Billing settings") }
    }
}
```

Open `/account#billing` and the Billing tab is selected; click Profile and
the address becomes `/account#profile`.

## How it works

- [`hash`](/learn/05-pages-and-routing#query-strings-and-fragments) is
  the address's fragment without the `#`, kept current by the runtime.
- `tab` is a [`derived`](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity#derived) value:
  the fragment when there is one, `"profile"` when there is none.
- `Tabs(value: tab)` opens the page whose `value:` is `tab`. It only reads
  it: picking a tab fires `on change(v)` with that page's value, which
  navigates to the same page with another fragment. `hash` changes, `tab`
  follows, and the tab opens. Each pick is a step in the history, so the
  back button steps through the tabs the reader opened.
- The tabs are a tab list to a screen reader, each linked to its panel.
  Only the open tab is in the Tab order; the arrow keys move between tabs
  (the other way round in a right-to-left page), and Home and End go to
  the ends.

For a tab that need not survive a reload, `Tabs(bind: tab)` reads and
writes a `state` instead.

Why not a `Link` per tab? The router marks a link current by its path, not
its fragment: on `/account#billing`, both `/account#profile` and
`/account#billing` are links to the current page, so both get the `active`
class and `aria-current="page"`, and neither the look nor a screen reader
says which tab is open.

To keep several settings in the address, such as a sort and a filter, use
the query string instead: see
[Keep filters in the address](/recipes/filters-in-the-address).



---

# Add a picture, sized for every screen

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/add-a-picture

Put a picture in `public/` and show it with `Image`, and the build writes it
again at every width a screen may ask for, sets its size so nothing on the
page shifts, and fills its box while it loads. Use this for a photograph, a
hero picture or a decorative image.

This page declares a hero picture with `image` and shows it with a blurred
placeholder, prints its real size and colour, and shows a second picture
and a decorative one straight from `public/`:

**Needs:** `hero.jpg`, `office.jpg` and `deco.png` in `public/` (any
pictures will do); without them the build stops at `image hero`. It claims
`/`: paste it into a new project, or replace the starter's
`src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
image hero = "hero.jpg"

page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "The front page.") {
    Heading("Home").h1
    Image(hero, alt: "The team at the launch",
          sizes: "(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 1200px",
          placeholder: .blur)
    Text("It is {hero.width} by {hero.height}, and mostly {hero.color}.")
    Image(src: "/office.jpg", alt: "The office on a quiet morning")
    Image(src: "/deco.png", alt: "")
}
```

## How it works

### A picture from `public/`

Files in `public/` are served from the site's root, so `public/office.jpg`
is `/office.jpg`. Name it in `Image(src:)` with that site-relative path.

Give every `Image` an `alt:` that says what the picture shows. A decorative
picture takes `alt: ""`, so a screen reader skips it.

When `src:` is a literal path into `public/` that names a PNG, JPEG, GIF or
WebP file, the build processes the file the same way it processes an
[`image` declaration](#a-picture-declared-with-image):

- It writes the picture again at each width the page may ask for.
- It sets `width` and `height` from the file, so nothing on the page shifts
  when the picture arrives.
- It serves the picture as a `<picture>` element. `sizes:` and
  `placeholder:` work here too.

The build uses an SVG file, a URL, or a path built at run time as it is
written. Give those a `width:` and `height:` when you know them, as in
`Image(src: "/hero.jpg", alt: "The team at the launch", width: 1200, height: 630)`.
To turn processing off, set `build.media.pipeline` to `false`.

The first image on a page loads eagerly at high priority, because it is
usually the largest thing the reader sees first. Every later image loads
lazily. Set `loading:` on an `Image` to choose for yourself.

### A picture declared with `image`

To use a picture's real size and colour in your page, declare it with
`image`, as `hero` is above. The declaration hands the build the file
itself. The build looks for the path in the project's folder, then in
`src/`, then in `public/`.

The build reads the picture's real size and average colour, writes it again
at every width in `media.widths` that is smaller than the original, and
gives the page a `<picture>` with:

- a `<source>` per format, each with a `srcset` of the widths, so the
  browser picks the file it needs for the space `sizes:` describes;
- `width` and `height` from the file, so the box has the right shape before
  any of the picture arrives and **nothing on the page moves**;
- a placeholder while the picture loads: `.blur` inlines a copy sixteen
  pixels wide as a data URI, `.color` fills the box with the average colour,
  and `.none` does neither;
- a content hash in every file's name, so a host can cache each file forever.

The name `hero` is also a value. You can read `hero.src`, `hero.width`,
`hero.height`, `hero.color`, `hero.placeholder` and `hero.srcset`.

The attributes any element takes (`id:`, `aria-*`, `data-*`, `ref:`, an
`on load` handler) go on the `<img>` inside the `<picture>`. That is where
its `alt:` is and where `load` fires. The width, the height and the sources
stay the build's.

A PDF or a slide deck embeds the real picture rather than drawing an empty
box.

## Tune the image pipeline

To change which formats and widths the build writes, set `build.media` in
`webfluent.app.json`. These are the defaults:

```json
{ "build": { "media": {
    "formats": ["webp"],
    "widths": [480, 960, 1440, 1920],
    "quality": 78,
    "pipeline": true
} } }
```

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| `formats` | The formats each picture is written in, best first: `webp`, `png`, `jpeg` |
| `widths` | The widths written. A width larger than the original is skipped; the build never scales a picture up |
| `quality` | The quality of a lossy file. WebP and JPEG are written lossily at this quality; PNG is written losslessly |
| `pipeline` | `false` copies each file as it is, as `public/` files always were |

The build writes a file only when it saves something. A file that would be
no smaller than the original is not written: the original, which the
`<img>` falls back to, serves at that width instead. A format that has no
width left gets no `<source>`. A JPEG that was already saved small often
ends up this way.

The build caches its work in `.wf-cache/media/`, so a build that changes no
image does no image work.

To see what the pipeline will make of a picture before it does it, run
`wf assets --plan`:

```bash
wf assets --plan /hero.jpg
```

It prints each width and format, what each file comes to, and the widths it
will not write because they save nothing. `wf assets` with no option lists
every file in `public/` with where it is used, and counts the files nothing
uses.

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | Why, and what to do |
|---|---|
| The page jumps when a picture arrives | The picture is an SVG, a URL or a path built at run time, which the build cannot measure. Give it `width:` and `height:` |
| `A01` on an `Image` | Add an `alt:` that says what it shows, or `alt: ""` for a decorative picture |
| `wf assets --plan` lists widths it will not write | Those files would save nothing; the original serves at those widths |



---

# Allow other origins in the security policy

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/allow-other-origins

With `"build": { "csp": true }` (on for a project `wf init` creates), every
page carries a Content-Security-Policy that is `'self'` throughout. A page
that talks to an API on another domain, loads images from a CDN or embeds
a video names those origins in `webfluent.app.json`, and the build widens
the policy by exactly them. This config loads Google's tag manager after the
page and allows what it sends and draws:

```json
{
  "meta": {
    "scripts": [{ "src": "https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtag/js?id=G-XXXXXXX", "load": "after" }],
    "connect": ["https://*.google-analytics.com", "https://*.analytics.google.com",
                "https://www.googletagmanager.com"],
    "img": ["https://*.google-analytics.com", "https://www.googletagmanager.com"]
  }
}
```

## How it works

- **Requests.** A page may send requests only to its own origin. Each
  entry of `meta.connect` — an origin such as `https://api.example.com`, or
  `https://*.example.com` for its subdomains — joins `connect-src`.
- **Images.** A page may load images from its own origin and `data:`,
  unless `meta.img` names others, which join `img-src`. Name a CDN there,
  or the pixels a tag requests (`https://www.googletagmanager.com/a`,
  `/td`), which a tag assistant otherwise reports as blocked.
- **Frames.** `meta.frame` names the origins a page may embed — a video
  player (`https://www.youtube-nocookie.com`), a map — and they join
  `frame-src`.
- **Fonts, stylesheets and scripts** need nothing here: the origins
  `meta.fonts`, `meta.stylesheets` and `meta.scripts` declare are added to
  the policy already, and your own scripts under `src/` are same-origin.
- An entry with a path, or a keyword such as `'self'`, is `E111`.

A tag manager's own set-up — the `dataLayer` and the `gtag('config', …)`
call a vendor gives you as an inline `<script>` — goes in a plain script
under `src/`, which the policy already allows: the build refuses an inline
script ([Call your own JavaScript](/recipes/call-your-own-script)).

## Variations

- **An app's own scheme.** An app that serves its pages itself — a desktop
  shell — has schemes of its own. `meta.connect` and `meta.frame` take one
  as a scheme alone: `"ipc:"` for the channel a shell's pages call it on,
  `"wfpreview:"` for a frame the app fills from its own protocol. A scheme
  named in `meta.frame` is also one a frame's `src` may use: the address is
  kept, where any other unknown scheme is emptied. The web's schemes are
  refused: `https:` alone would allow every origin, and `data:`, `blob:`
  and `javascript:` run whatever a page writes
  ([Make a desktop or phone app with Tauri](/recipes/tauri-app)).
- **WebAssembly.** A page that compiles WebAssembly — a parser, an image
  codec — sets `meta.wasm: true`, and `script-src` gains
  `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`. WebAssembly compiles; `eval` is still refused.
- **Style elements.** A page whose scripts write `<style>` elements — an
  editor such as CodeMirror, a chart library — sets
  `meta.style_elements: true`, and `style-src` gains `'unsafe-inline'`, for
  styles only.
- **Pin another origin's files.** A stylesheet or a font from another
  origin is code that origin can change after you read it. Declare its hash
  in `meta.integrity`, keyed by its URL:

  ```json
  {
    "meta": {
      "stylesheets": ["https://cdn.example.com/brand.css"],
      "integrity": { "https://cdn.example.com/brand.css": "sha384-…" }
    }
  }
  ```

  The build emits `integrity` and `crossorigin="anonymous"` on the tag, and
  warns (`D05`) about a declared external asset that has no hash. It never
  fetches the file to work the hash out, so a build does not depend on the
  network. A Google Fonts stylesheet is exempt: Google writes it per
  browser, so its bytes differ between readers and no hash can match. A
  library is pinned the same way
  ([Load a library from a CDN](/recipes/library-from-a-cdn)).

[Security](/about/security#the-content-security-policy) explains the
policy itself, and how the build holds every page to it.



---

# Animate a list

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/animate-a-list

Make a list fill in one item after another, slide its items to their new
places when it is reordered, and fade an item out as it is removed. The
list is a keyed `for … by`, and each item's element carries `animate:`,
`exit:` and `stagger:`:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/` and the name `Tasks`,
as two of the starter's pages do: paste it into a new project, or replace
`src/pages/Home.wf` and remove `src/pages/Tasks.wf`.

```wf
type Item { id: Number, text: String }

page Tasks(path: "/", title: "Tasks", description: "A list that animates.") {
    state items: [Item] = [Item(id: 1, text: "First"), Item(id: 2, text: "Second")]
    state next = 3
    action add() { items.push(Item(id: next, text: "Item {next}"))  next = next + 1 }
    action shuffle() { items = items.reverse() }
    Heading("Tasks").h1
    Row(gap: .sm) {
        Button("Add") { on click { add() } }
        Button("Reverse") { on click { shuffle() } }
    }
    for item in items by item.id {
        Card(animate: .fadeIn, exit: .fadeOut, stagger: "40ms") {
            Row(justify: .between) {
                Text(item.text)
                Button("Remove").sm { on click { items = items.filter(i => i.id != item.id) } }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

## How it works

Each change to `items` plays a different motion:

- **An item arrives.** It plays its `animate:`. `stagger: "40ms"` delays
  each item's enter by its index × 40ms, so a list fills in one item after
  another.
- **An item moves** — a sort, a reverse, an insert above it. It slides to
  its new place. This is a *FLIP* transform: the runtime measures where the
  node was and where it is, and animates between them. It works because
  `by item.id` keeps the item's node alive
  ([Control flow](/learn/09-control-flow)).
- **An item leaves.** It plays its `exit:` first, and the runtime removes
  the node when it ends.

A `for` with no `by`, or a key that changes, makes a new node for the item,
so it fades out and in again instead of moving. Key the list by what
identifies the item.

A reader who asked for reduced motion sees items appear, move and go at
once: no animation, no FLIP and no wait before removal
([Respect reduced motion](/recipes/motion-defaults#respect-reduced-motion)).



---

# Animate an element in and out

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/animate-in-and-out

Give an element an enter animation to play when it appears, and an `exit:`
to play before it is removed. Motion attaches to the `if`, `for`, `show`
and `match` that draw and remove elements, so read
[Control flow](/learn/09-control-flow) first if those, or how a keyed
`for … by` keeps an item's nodes, are new to you. This page opens four cards
that each enter a different way, and an alert that fades out when you
dismiss it:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Notices(path: "/", title: "Notices", description: "Cards and an alert that animate in and out.") {
    state open = false
    state toast: String? = "Saved"
    Heading("Notices").h1
    Button("Toggle the cards") { on click { open = !open } }
    if open {
        Card.fadeIn { Text("Faded in") }
        Card(animate: .slideUp, speed: .fast) { Text("Slid up, quickly") }
        Card.scaleIn.slow { Text("Grew, slowly") }
        Card(animate: .fadeIn, duration: "600ms", delay: "200ms", easing: "ease-out") { Text("Tuned") }
    }
    if let message = toast {
        Alert(message, animate: .slideDown, exit: .fadeOut).success {
            Button("Dismiss").sm { on click { toast = null } }
        }
    }
    Button("Show the alert") { on click { toast = "Saved again" } }
}
```

## How it works

### Animate an element in

An element plays its enter animation when it appears: on the first paint,
and each time the `if`, `for`, `match` or `show` around it brings it back.
Name the animation with `animate:`, or write it as a flag (`Card.fadeIn`).

The built-in animations are `fadeIn`, `fadeOut`, `slideUp`, `slideDown`,
`slideLeft`, `slideRight`, `scaleIn`, `scaleOut`, `bounce`, `shake`,
`pulse`, `spin`, and `expand` and `collapse`, which open and close a box to
the height of what is inside it ([Open a box to the height of its
content](/recipes/expand-to-content)).

Four props set how long it takes and how it is paced:

| Prop | What it sets | Values |
|---|---|---|
| `speed:` | A preset length | `.fast` (150ms), `.normal`, `.slow` (500ms); `.fast` and `.slow` are also flags |
| `duration:` | An exact length | a length of time: `"600ms"` |
| `delay:` | A wait before it starts | a length of time: `"200ms"` |
| `easing:` | How it is paced | a named easing, or any CSS timing function as a string |

The named easings are `.standard`, `.spring`, `.ease`, `.easeIn`,
`.easeOut`, `.easeInOut`, `.linear`, `.bouncy` and `.smooth`. Each is a
design token (`$ease-standard`, `$ease-spring`, …), so a theme retunes every
animation at once. A spring is not a curve CSS can name, so the engine
samples the spring into a `linear()` easing: it overshoots and settles the
way a spring does.

An element that stands still plays its enter animation as a stylesheet
rule, with no JavaScript, so a pre-rendered page animates before its script
has loaded. Everything the runtime plays — a branch arriving or leaving, a
list reordering, a route changing — goes through the Web Animations API,
where an animation that is interrupted gives way to the one that replaced
it instead of jumping.

### Animate an element out

`exit:` names the animation to play when the element leaves. The runtime
waits for it to finish before it removes the node: here the alert fades
out after **Dismiss** sets `toast` to `null`.

Any element may carry `exit:`, not only the root of a branch. All the
elements that are leaving animate out together, and the removal waits for
the longest.

A reader who asked for reduced motion sees the cards and the alert appear
and go at once, with no wait before removal
([Respect reduced motion](/recipes/motion-defaults#respect-reduced-motion)).

## Variations

### Play an animation when it is scrolled to

To hold an animation until the reader has scrolled to the element, add
`on: .enterView`. It plays once. `on: .mount`, the default, plays it when
the element appears.

```wf
page Story(path: "/", title: "Story", description: "Sections that arrive as you read.") {
    Heading("Our story").h1
    Text("Scroll down.")
    Section(animate: .fadeIn, on: .enterView) { Heading("Further down").h2 }
}
```

### Animate `show` and `match` branches

`show` toggles whether its content is visible, so that content animates
with `animate:` and `exit:` as an `if` branch does. A `match` arm's elements
animate as one arm replaces another. This wizard slides each step in:

```wf
enum Step { one, two, three }

page Wizard(path: "/", title: "Wizard", description: "Three steps, animated.") {
    state step: Step = .one
    Heading("Set up").h1
    match step {
        .one { Card(animate: .slideLeft, exit: .fadeOut) { Text("Step one")  Button("Next") { on click { step = .two } } } }
        .two { Card(animate: .slideLeft, exit: .fadeOut) { Text("Step two")  Button("Next") { on click { step = .three } } } }
        .three { Card(animate: .scaleIn) { Text("Done") } }
    }
}
```

## Troubleshooting

- **An enter animation does not play.** It plays only when the element
  appears. An element that is already on the page and changes does not
  re-enter: use `replayAnimation`, `animate(…)`
  ([Drive an animation yourself](/recipes/drive-an-animation)) or a
  `transition { }` ([Tween a property when state changes](/recipes/tween-on-change)).
- **A list item fades out and in again instead of moving.** The `for` has no
  `by`, or its key changes, so the runtime makes a new node. Key the list by
  what identifies the item ([Animate a list](/recipes/animate-a-list)).
- **A leaving element disappears at once.** Give it `exit:`. Without one,
  nothing delays the removal.
- **A `shared:` element crossfades instead of moving.** The two pages give
  it different names, or two elements on one page carry the same name
  ([Carry an element across a route change](/recipes/shared-element)).
- **Nothing animates at all.** Your system, or the page's root
  (`data-wf-motion="reduce"`), asks for reduced motion.
- **`` E103: Badge has no flag or enum case `Drop` ``, or `` `Card.Drop` is
  not a part of `Card` `` with a `C03`.** Your own keyframes were written
  as a flag. Write `animate: .Drop`; only the built-in animations are flags
  ([Declare your own keyframes](/recipes/keyframes)).



---

# Run a sequence of animations

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/animation-sequence

Bring a page's opening elements in one after another — a heading, then a
line of text, then a button — by wrapping them in `sequence` and putting
each in a `step`:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Landing(path: "/", title: "Welcome", description: "A page that introduces itself.") {
    sequence {
        step { Heading("Welcome").h1.fadeIn }
        step(after: "120ms") { Text("What we do.").slideUp }
        step(after: "120ms") { Button("Start").primary.slideUp }
    }
}
```

The heading fades in as the page opens, the line beneath it slides up a
moment later, and the button slides up last, so the page arrives in order
rather than all at once.

## How it works

- `after:` is measured from the step before it, so the three start at 0ms,
  120ms and 240ms.
- A step with no `after:` starts when the step before it does, which is how
  several elements move together.
- A `sequence` does nothing but timing: it writes the clock onto its
  elements as `delay:` and leaves nothing of itself behind. What the rest
  of the build sees is the program you would have written by hand, with
  `delay: "120ms"` and `delay: "240ms"` on the second and third elements.



---

# Serve an API on the same origin

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/api-on-the-same-origin

To call a backend without CORS, serve the site and the backend from one
origin: the site at `/`, the backend at `/api`. A session cookie then works
with no extra setting.

You need a server that serves the site, as in
[Serve a site with nginx](/recipes/serve-with-nginx), and a backend it can reach.
In nginx, add this `location` to the site's `server` block:

```nginx
location /api/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080/;
}
```

## How it works

1. nginx sends every request under `/api/` to the backend on port 8080,
   with the `/api` prefix taken off (the trailing `/` of `proxy_pass` does
   that), and serves everything else from the build.
2. To the browser, the pages and the backend share one origin, so a
   request needs no CORS headers and carries the site's cookies.
3. A page then declares the service with `api Backend(base: "/api")`, and
   it needs nothing else.

## Variations

Netlify, Vercel and Cloudflare Pages do the same with a rewrite to an
external URL.

After the deploy, [check it](/recipes/check-a-deploy).



---

# Build a budget app that works offline

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/build-a-budget-app

**What you will build.** A personal budget tracker that lives entirely in
the reader's browser: money in and money out, a budget per category, what
is left of it this month, six months of bars, two languages, a CSV export
and import, and a page that keeps working offline. There is no server and
no account. The finished project is
[`examples/tutorials/hard-pocket`](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/tree/master/examples/tutorials/hard-pocket).

**Time:** a couple of hours.

## Before you start

You need `wf`, Chrome and a copy of the repository
(see [Before you start](/learn/03-tutorial-todos#before-you-start) in the Todos tutorial). This tutorial assumes
the Todos tutorial, and each step links the chapter that goes deeper.

**This tutorial is read along, not typed along.** Like [Field Notes](/recipes/build-a-notebook-site), each
step shows the part of a file that teaches something new, not every line
of it, so the snippets alone do not make a working project. Open the
finished project, run it, and read each file as its step comes up:

```bash
cd WebFluent/examples/tutorials/hard-pocket
wf serve
```

To build it yourself instead, start a project with
`wf init pocket -t spa --locales en,ar`, then copy each file from
`examples/tutorials/hard-pocket` into it as its step names it, and run
`wf check` after each step.

## Step 1: Configure the project

The project's `webfluent.app.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "pocket",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": "WebFluent tutorials",
  "theme": { "name": "Pocket", "dark": "PocketNight" },
  "build": {
    "output": "./build",
    "output_type": "spa",
    "csp": true
  },
  "meta": {
    "title": "Pocket",
    "description": "A budget that lives in your browser: income, spending and what is left, month by month.",
    "lang": "en"
  },
  "i18n": {
    "default_locale": "en",
    "locales": ["en", "ar"],
    "dir": "src/translations"
  },
  "offline": {
    "precache": ["/", "/entries", "/categories", "/settings"],
    "fallback": "/"
  }
}
```

It adds three things to the Todos config:

- `i18n` names the languages and the folder their messages live in
  ([Translate a site](/recipes/translate-a-site)).
- `offline` makes `wf build` write a service worker that stores the four
  pages, so a second visit opens with no network ([Make a site work offline](/recipes/work-offline)).
- `theme` names two themes, light and dark, and the build ships both.

**Check it:** `wf build` prints a line that starts `Offline: sw.js`, then
`2 locales` in its summary.

## Step 2: Describe money

The ledger's types use four of the types the language brings:

```wf
// src/types.wf
/// Which way the money went.
enum Kind { income, expense }

/// Something money is spent on, with what the reader means to spend on it
/// in a month.
type Category {
    id: String
    name: String
    color: Color
    budget: Money
}

/// One line of the ledger: money in, or money out.
type Entry {
    id: Uuid
    date: Date
    amount: Money
    kind: Kind
    category: String
    note: String = ""
}
```

`Money`, `Date`, `Color` and `Uuid` are each a plain JSON value at run time
([Types](/learn/12-types)). Money is kept in minor units, `{ amount: 1299,
currency: "USD" }`, so a sum never drifts by a fraction of a cent. You
write it `$12.99` and show it with `format(m)`. What the language works out
is a call — `a.plus(b)`, `a.minus(b)`, `ONE.times(12.5)` — and what the
value carries is a field: `m.amount`. Two constants give every sum a
starting point:

```wf
// src/types.wf
/// Nothing yet: the starting point every sum adds to.
const ZERO: Money = $0.00

/// One dollar — `ONE.times(12.5)` is $12.50, rounded to the cent.
const ONE: Money = $1.00
```

**Check it:** `wf check` prints `No problems in pocket.` Change `$0.00` to
`$0.001`, and the check refuses it: money has two decimals in dollars.
Change it back.

## Step 3: Add up the ledger

Every figure on every page is a `derived` value of the `Ledger` store:

```wf
// src/stores/Ledger.wf
    derived today = now.date()
    derived newestFirst = entries.sortBy(e => e.date).reverse()

    derived income = sum(entries.filter(e => e.kind == .income))
    derived spent = sum(entries.filter(e => e.kind == .expense))
    derived balance = income.minus(spent)

    derived thisMonth = entries.filter(e => e.date.startOfMonth().isSame(today.startOfMonth()))
    derived monthIncome = sum(thisMonth.filter(e => e.kind == .income))
    derived monthSpent = sum(thisMonth.filter(e => e.kind == .expense))
    derived monthBudget = categories.reduce((s, c) => s.plus(c.budget), ZERO)
    derived budgetLeft = monthBudget.minus(monthSpent)
```

Add an entry, and the balance, this month's spending, each budget bar and
the chart all follow, with no code written to keep them in step
([Stores](/learn/11-stores)). `now` is the browser's clock as a value, so
`today` turns over at midnight. `sum` is an action that only returns a
value, which a derived value may call:

```wf
// src/stores/Ledger.wf
    // The money in a list of entries, added up.
    action sum(list: [Entry]) {
        return list.reduce((total, e) => total.plus(e.amount), ZERO)
    }
```

**Check it:** the dashboard shows a balance, this month's income and
spending, and what is left of the budget. Each is a sum of the sample
ledger.

## Step 4: Change the stored shape without losing data

What a `persist` keeps outlives the build that wrote it: a reader who
visited last month has last month's shape in their browser. The entries
declare which version of the shape this build writes, and how to bring an
older one forward:

```wf
// src/stores/Ledger.wf
    // Version 1 of Pocket kept an amount as a plain, signed number of
    // dollars (`-52.4` was money out). Version 2 keeps a `Money` and a
    // `Kind`, so `migrate 1 -> 2` turns what a returning reader's browser
    // holds into the new shape instead of throwing it away.
    persist entries: [Entry] = SAMPLE_ENTRIES.map(s => Entry(
            id: s.id,
            date: now.date().minus(days: s.ago),
            amount: s.amount,
            kind: s.kind,
            category: s.category,
            note: s.note,
        )) {
        version: 2
        migrate 1 -> 2 {
            old.map(e => Entry(
                    id: e.id,
                    date: e.date,
                    amount: ONE.times(Math.abs(e.amount)),
                    kind: if e.amount < 0 { .expense } else { .income },
                    category: e.category,
                    note: e.note ?? "",
                ))
        }
    }
```

- `version: 2` says which shape this build writes.
- `migrate 1 -> 2` brings an older value forward. Its body receives the
  stored value as `old`.
- If you raise the version with no migration, the build warns (`P01`). If
  you change the shape without raising the version, it warns too (`D04`),
  from the shapes it keeps in `.wf-cache/` ([Stores](/learn/11-stores)).
- A first visit opens on a sample ledger dated from today, so the
  dashboard is never empty.

**Check it:** `wf check --deny-warnings` passes. Delete the `migrate`
block and check again: the check reports `P01`. Put the block back.

## Step 5: Fit the shell to the screen

The shell draws a `Sidebar` when `viewport.lg` holds, and a top bar with a
drawer when it does not. This is the drawer:

```wf
// src/App.wf
            if Ui.menuOpen {
                Host(tag: "div", class: "scrim") { on click { Ui.closeAll() } }
                Stack(gap: .md, class: "drawer", animate: .slideRight, exit: .fadeOut) {
                    on click { Ui.menuOpen = false }
                    Brand
                    NavLinks
                }
            }
```

- `viewport` is the window's size as a value. It follows `matchMedia`, so
  the switch happens once, as the window crosses the breakpoint
  ([Styling](/learn/13-styling)).
- The layout itself — grids that are one column on a phone — uses
  responsive values, `Grid(columns: { base: 1, lg: 2 })`, which need no
  script.
- A second store, `Ui`, holds what the interface is doing — the dialog,
  the menu, the notices — apart from what the ledger holds.

**Check it:** on a wide window, the sidebar shows. Narrow the window: a top
bar replaces it, and its menu button opens the drawer, which a click on the
dimmed page behind it closes.

## Step 6: Draw a dashboard from elements

The built-in `Chart` draws at build time, from data the build can see. This
ledger exists only in the reader's browser, so the chart is made of plain
elements whose heights follow the store:

```wf
// src/components/MonthChart.wf
/// Six months of money in and money out, as pairs of bars.
///
/// The built-in `Chart` draws at build time, from data the build can see.
/// This ledger only exists in the reader's browser, so the chart is made of
/// plain elements whose heights follow the store: `height: {share}%` is a
/// style value that reads state, and repaints when it changes.
component MonthChart(months: [MonthTotal], top: Number) {
    Stack(gap: .sm) {
        Row(class: "chart", align: .end, role: "img", aria-label: t("chart.label")) {
            for m in months by m.month {
                Stack(gap: .xs, align: .center, class: "chart__month") {
                    Row(gap: .xs, align: .end, class: "chart__bars") {
                        Host(tag: "span", class: "chart__bar chart__bar--in") {
                            style { height: {m.income.amount / top * 100}% }
                        }
                        Host(tag: "span", class: "chart__bar chart__bar--out") {
                            style { height: {m.spent.amount / top * 100}% }
                        }
                    }
```

- A `{…}` in a style value reads state, and the property follows it
  ([Styling](/learn/13-styling)).
- The chart is one `role="img"` with a label, so a screen reader hears what
  it shows rather than twelve unnamed boxes
  ([Accessibility](/about/accessibility)).

The figures above the chart are one component, placed four times:

```wf
// src/pages/Dashboard.wf
    Grid(columns: { base: 2, xl: 4 }, gap: .md) {
        KpiCard(t("kpi.balance"), value: Ledger.balance, note: t("kpi.balanceNote"))
        KpiCard(t("kpi.income"), value: Ledger.monthIncome, note: t("kpi.thisMonth"), lean: .good)
        KpiCard(t("kpi.spent"), value: Ledger.monthSpent, note: t("kpi.thisMonth"), lean: .bad)
        KpiCard(t("kpi.left"), value: Ledger.budgetLeft, note: t("kpi.leftNote", { budget: format(Ledger.monthBudget) }),
            lean: if Ledger.budgetLeft.amount < 0 { .bad } else { .good })
    }
```

`lean` is an enum prop. A component writes its enum props to its root
element, here as `data-lean="good"`, and `pocket.css` colours the card by
that attribute ([Components](/learn/10-components)).

**Check it:** the dashboard shows four cards and six pairs of bars. Add an
expense in step 9's dialog, and this month's bar and the **Spent** card
grow at once.

## Step 7: Keep the filters in the address

The Entries page reads its filters from the address:

```wf
// src/pages/Entries.wf
    // The filters live in the address — `/entries?month=2026-09&category=dining` —
    // so they survive a reload, a shared link and the back button.
    derived month = query.month ?? ""
    derived category = query.category ?? ""
    derived shown = Ledger.newestFirst.filter(e => (month == "" || e.date.slice(0, 7) == month) && (category == "" || e.category == category))
```

Choosing a month calls `navigate("/entries?month=…")`. The address
changes, `query` follows it, and so does the list.

An entry also has a page of its own at `/entries/:id`, where `id` is a
typed parameter. The page looks the entry up with
`Ledger.entries.find(…)` and draws it inside `if let e = entry`. `if let`
binds the value only when it is there, which the checker requires before
the page reads its fields ([Pages and routing](/learn/05-pages-and-routing)).

**Check it:** on `/entries`, pick a month. The address gains `?month=…`
and the list narrows. Press the browser's back button: the filter goes.

## Step 8: Use one form for new and for edit

`EntryForm` adds an entry or, given one, changes it:

```wf
// src/components/EntryForm.wf
/// The form for a new entry — or, given one, for changing it. It checks what
/// the reader typed, writes it to the ledger, and says so with `saved`.
component EntryForm(entry: Entry? = null) {
    use Ledger
    event saved()

    state kind: Kind = entry?.kind ?? .expense
    state amount: Number? = if let e = entry { e.amount.amount / 100 } else { null }
    state date: Date? = entry?.date ?? Ledger.today
    state category = entry?.category ?? "groceries"
    state note = entry?.note ?? ""

    validate amount {
        required
        min(0.01)
    }
    // Not in the future. With no message of its own, the rule shows the
    // translation of `form.max`; `Ledger.today` is read each time it checks.
    validate date {
        required
        max(Ledger.today)
    }
    validate note { maxLength(60) }
```

- A `validate` block sits beside the state it guards. The control bound to
  that state shows what the rules say — the message, `aria-invalid` and the
  link between them — with nothing more written ([Forms](/learn/14-forms)).
- A rule with no message of its own shows the translation of
  `form.<rule>`, so `en.json` and `ar.json` each say "that date has not
  happened yet" once.
- The form says it is done with an event, `saved`. The caller decides what
  that means: close the dialog, or go back to the entry.

The submit button follows the form:

```wf
// src/components/EntryForm.wf
        Row(justify: .end, gap: .sm) {
            Button(if entry != null { t("action.save") } else { t("action.add") }, type: .submit, disabled: !form.valid).primary
        }
```

`Form(bind: form)` hands the component a handle on the form. `form.valid`
is whether every rule holds, and the button follows it as the reader
types.

**Check it:** in the new-entry dialog, type `0` as the amount and leave the
field: it says *Enter an amount above zero*, and **Add entry** stays
disabled. Type `12.50`, and the button turns on.

## Step 9: Add a dialog and a shortcut

The app listens for two keys at the top of `src/App.wf`:

```wf
// src/App.wf
    // `n` opens a new entry from anywhere. A key with no modifier is left to
    // the field the reader is typing in, so an `n` in a note is just a letter.
    on key("n") { Ui.compose() }
    on key("Escape") { Ui.closeAll() }
```

`on key` at the top of the app listens on the document for as long as the
page shows ([Events](/learn/08-events)). The dialog is a `Modal` whose `title:`
is its accessible name. It keeps focus inside while it is open, and Escape
closes it:

```wf
// src/App.wf
    Modal(visible: Ui.composing, title: t("compose.title")) {
        if Ui.composing {
            EntryForm {
                on saved {
                    Ui.composing = false
                    Ui.notify(t("toast.added"))
                }
            }
        }
    }
```

**Check it:** press `n` anywhere outside a field, and the new-entry dialog
opens with focus inside it. Press Escape, and it closes. Add an entry, and
the dialog closes and a notice says it was added.

## Step 10: Speak two languages

Every word on screen is `t("key")`, read from `src/translations/en.json`
or `ar.json`. A message with plural forms is several keys:

```json
{
  "entries.zero": "No entries",
  "entries.one": "{count} entry",
  "entries.other": "{count} entries"
}
```

- `t("entries", { count: n })` picks the form the language's rules call
  for. English needs two forms and a zero; Arabic has six
  ([Translate a site](/recipes/translate-a-site)).
- Switching to Arabic sets `dir="rtl"` on the page, and the sidebar, the
  rows and the grids mirror themselves.
- `format(m)` and dates follow the language too.
- The reader's choice is a `persist` in a small `Prefs` store, and an
  `effect` in the app shell applies it on every visit.

**Check it:** on **Settings**, choose Arabic. The page reads right to
left, and every label is in Arabic. Reload: it stays in Arabic.

If a key shows on screen instead of its words, it is missing from a
translation file; `wf check` reports it as `I01`, and `wf translations`
lists what each locale lacks.

## Step 11: Export and import the data

The Settings page writes the ledger out as a CSV file:

```wf
// src/pages/Settings.wf
    action exportCsv() {
        let lines = Ledger.newestFirst.map(e => csvLine(e))
        saveTextFile("pocket-{Ledger.today}.csv", [CSV_HEADER, ...lines].join("\n"), "text/csv")
    }
```

`saveTextFile` is not WebFluent. It is a function in `src/files.js`, a
plain browser script that the build links on every page. Its JSDoc types
the call, so `saveTextFile(1)` is an error where it is written
([Call your own JavaScript](/recipes/call-your-own-script)).

Importing reads a file from a `FileUpload` with `await f.text()`, parses
each line and merges what is new. Then it tells every other open tab:

```wf
// src/pages/Settings.wf
        let added = Ledger.merge(parsed)
        news.post({ count: added })
```

`news` is `channel news = broadcast("pocket")`, a channel every tab of the
site hears. The app shell listens on it and shows a notice
([Talk to the site's other tabs](/recipes/talk-between-tabs)). The ledger itself needs no channel: `persist`
already keeps every tab in step.

**Check it:** on **Settings**, export the ledger, and the browser saves
`pocket-<today's date>.csv`. Open a second tab, import the file in the
first: the second tab shows a notice of how many entries were added.

## Step 12: Test it, and run the checks

A test drives the real form by the labels a reader sees — the English
ones, since a test reads the project's default locale
([Testing](/learn/16-testing)):

```wf
// tests/pocket.wf
test "an entry added through the form moves the balance" {
    use Ledger
    Text("Balance {format(Ledger.balance)}")
    EntryForm

    expect "Balance $16,533.56"
    click "Money in"
    type "250" into "Amount"
    click "Add entry"
    expect "Balance $16,783.56"
```

Pocket has eight tests: the cards and rows draw what they should, a blank
amount is refused, `n` opens the dialog and Escape closes it, and removing
an entry takes it out of every total. Run them and the checks:

```bash
wf test
wf check --deny-warnings
wf build
wf verify
```

**Check it:** `wf test` reports `8 passed`, and `wf verify` ends with `0
problem(s)`. `build/` is a single-page app with a service worker, `sw.js`,
beside it. Put it on a host that answers every path with `index.html`
([Install wf on a build machine](/recipes/install-wf-in-ci)), and the second visit works with no network.

## What you built

- A ledger typed with `Money`, `Date`, `Color` and `Uuid`
  ([Types](/learn/12-types)).
- Totals that are all `derived` values of one store, and a `persist`
  migration that keeps returning readers' data ([Stores](/learn/11-stores)).
- A shell that changes with the window, and responsive grids
  ([Styling](/learn/13-styling)).
- A form that validates itself, a dialog and keyboard shortcuts
  ([Forms](/learn/14-forms), [Events](/learn/08-events)).
- Two languages, plural forms and right-to-left layout
  ([Translate a site](/recipes/translate-a-site)).
- A script of your own, and a channel between tabs
  ([Call your own JavaScript](/recipes/call-your-own-script),
  [Talk to the site's other tabs](/recipes/talk-between-tabs)).
- A site that works offline ([Make a site work offline](/recipes/work-offline)).

# Build a statically generated notebook

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/build-a-notebook-site

**What you will build.** A notebook kept in public — notes from a garden, a
kitchen and a few trips — built as a static site. The notes are a JSON file
the build reads. Every page, including one page per note, is written out
as HTML that a search engine can read. The one thing a reader changes, the
notes they save for later, stays in their browser. The finished project is
[`examples/tutorials/medium-field-notes`](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/tree/master/examples/tutorials/medium-field-notes).

**Time:** about an hour.

## Before you start

You need `wf`, Chrome and a copy of the repository
(see [Before you start](/learn/03-tutorial-todos#before-you-start) in the Todos tutorial).

**This tutorial is read along, not typed along.** Each step shows the part
of a file that teaches something new, not every line of it, so the
snippets alone do not make a working project. Open the finished project,
run it, and read each file as its step comes up:

```bash
cd WebFluent/examples/tutorials/medium-field-notes
wf serve
```

To build it yourself instead, run the `wf init` in Step 1, then copy each
file from `examples/tutorials/medium-field-notes` into your project as its
step names it, and run `wf check` after each step.

The Todos tutorial explains state, stores and components; this one
assumes them.

## Step 1: Create a static project and its look

The project started from the `static` template (if you are building it
yourself, this is where you start):

```bash
wf init field-notes -t static
cd field-notes
```

The project's `webfluent.app.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "field-notes",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": "Field Notes",
  "theme": { "name": "Meadow", "dark": "Dusk" },
  "build": {
    "output": "./build",
    "ssg": true,
    "csp": true
  },
  "meta": {
    "title": "Field Notes",
    "description": "Notes from a small garden, a busy kitchen and the roads between them.",
    "lang": "en",
    "site_url": "https://field-notes.example.com",
    "site_name": "Field Notes",
    "favicon": "/favicon.svg",
    "image": "/card.png",
    "sitemap": true
  }
}
```

- `"ssg": true` pre-renders every page to its own `index.html`. When the
  page loads, the script takes it over in place — *hydration*
  ([Static sites and SPAs](/about/static-or-single-page)).
- `site_url` lets the build write what search engines and link previews
  read: a canonical address, Open Graph tags, JSON-LD, `sitemap.xml` and
  `robots.txt` ([Describe pages to search engines and link previews](/recipes/search-and-link-previews)).

The dark theme names only the tokens that change:

```wf
// src/theme.wf
/// The dark theme: only the tokens that change.
theme Dusk {
    color-primary: #86C9A6
    color-secondary: #E8A086
    color-background: #121614
    color-surface: #1A201D
    color-text: #E9E5DA
    color-text-muted: #A6AFA9
    color-border: #2B3430
    paper-raised: #171C19
    tag-bg: #213129
    tag-text: #A9DCC1
}
```

The light theme, `Meadow`, sets the same names. A theme may declare tokens
of its own, such as `paper-raised` and `tag-bg`. The project's stylesheet,
`src/styles.css`, reads every colour as a token (`var(--tag-bg)`), so the
dark theme needs no rule of its own ([Design tokens](/reference/tokens)).

**Check it:** with `wf serve` running, set your system to dark mode. The
page turns dark green and cream without a reload.

## Step 2: Type the data

The notes are data, and a `type` says what each one holds:

```wf
// src/types.wf
/// One note in the notebook.
type Note {
    slug: String
    title: String
    date: Date
    tags: [String]
    summary: String
    minutes: Number
    body: String
}

/// Every note, read from `notes.json` when the site is built.
data notes: [Note] = "notes.json"
```

- `data` reads a JSON file at build time. The result is a constant, typed
  by the annotation, inlined into the bundle and seeded into every
  pre-rendered page ([Fetching data](/learn/15-data)).
- The checker holds the program to `Note`: a page that reads `note.titel`
  is an error where it is written.
- `date` is a `Date`: a plain `"2026-03-08"` string the language knows how
  to format. `{note.date:.date(long)}` shows `March 8, 2026`.

`src/notes.json` holds seven notes, each with a Markdown `body`.

**Check it:** `wf check` prints `No problems in field-notes.` If one note
in `notes.json` has a field that `Note` does not declare, the check reports
`T05` at the `data` line and names the field; if a note leaves out a field
`Note` requires, it reports `C01`.

## Step 3: Write the shell and a layout

The `app` declaration wraps every page. The current page is drawn where
`Router` stands, inside `<main>`, so the skip link each page carries jumps
past the navigation ([Pages and routing](/learn/05-pages-and-routing)). The
start of `src/App.wf`:

```wf
// src/App.wf
app {
    use Saved

    Navbar(class: "site-nav") {
        Navbar.Brand {
            Link("Field Notes", to: "/", class: "brand")
        }
        Navbar.Links {
            Link("Notes", to: "/")
            Link("Tags", to: "/tags")
            Link(to: "/saved", class: "saved-link") {
                Text("Saved")
                if Saved.count > 0 {
                    Badge("{Saved.count}").pill
                }
            }
            Link("About", to: "/about")
        }
        Navbar.Actions {
            ThemeToggle
        }
    }

    Router(transition: .fade, duration: "160ms")
```

- The link whose `to:` is the page shown is marked `aria-current="page"`.
- `ThemeToggle` is two icon buttons that call `setTheme("dark")` and
  `setTheme("light")`. The reader's choice is kept across visits.
- `Router(transition: .fade, duration: "160ms")` fades one page out and
  the next in.

Each page names the column it is set in with `layout:` — a component whose
default slot is the page:

```wf
// src/components/Sheet.wf
/// The column a page is set in, and the frame every page names with
/// `layout: Sheet`. A narrow sheet is for reading; a wide one holds a grid.
component Sheet(wide: Bool = false) {
    slot
    Container(class: ["sheet", if wide { "sheet--wide" }]) {
        children
    }
}
```

**Check it:** the navbar shows **Notes**, **Tags**, **Saved** and
**About**. Click **Tags**: the page fades over, and the **Tags** link is
marked as the current page.

## Step 4: Build a card

A card shows a note at a glance:

```wf
// src/components/NoteCard.wf
/// A note at a glance: when it was written, its title, a summary, its tags
/// and the button that saves it.
component NoteCard(
    _ note: Note,
    /// Keeps the card in the page but out of sight — what a filter does.
    hidden: Bool = false
) {
    Card(class: "note-card", hidden: hidden) {
        Stack(gap: .sm) {
            Row(justify: .between, align: .center, gap: .sm) {
                Text("{note.date:.date(long)} · {note.minutes} min read", class: "note-meta").sm
                SaveButton(note.slug, title: note.title)
            }
            Link(to: "/notes/{note.slug}", class: "note-card__link") {
                Heading(note.title).h2
            }
            Text(note.summary, class: "note-card__summary")
            TagList(note.tags)
        }
    }
}
```

- A `///` comment above a component or a prop is its documentation. Your
  editor shows it when you hover a call ([Components](/learn/10-components)).
- A splice may say how to show its value: `{note.date:.date(long)}` is
  `format(note.date, .date, "long")`, written where it is read
  ([Expressions](/reference/expressions)).
- `TagList` is a row of `#tag` links to `/?tag=…`.

**Check it:** the front page shows a card per note, each with a line such
as `March 8, 2026 · 4 min read`, a title, a summary and its tags.

## Step 5: Search and filter the front page

The front page lists every note, narrowed by a search box and by the tag in
the address. `NoteFinder` works the list out:

```wf
// src/components/NoteFinder.wf
    state q = ""

    derived needle = q.trim().toLowerCase()
    derived newest = all.sortBy(n => n.date).reverse()
    derived shown = newest.filter(n =>
        (tag == "" || n.tags.includes(tag))
        && (needle == ""
            || n.title.toLowerCase().includes(needle)
            || n.summary.toLowerCase().includes(needle)))
    derived visible = shown.map(n => n.slug)
    derived allTags = all.flatMap(n => n.tags).unique().sort()
```

`q` is bound to the search box, and everything else follows it. `sortBy`,
`flatMap` and `unique` are list helpers the language brings. Each also runs
at build time, so the pre-rendered page shows the sorted list
([State and reactivity](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity)).

A static site adds one idea here. Its HTML is written once, before any
reader arrives, so the HTML cannot depend on what only the browser knows,
such as the address's query or what is in storage. So the finder draws
every note and hides the ones that do not match:

```wf
// src/components/NoteFinder.wf
            // Every note is drawn, and the ones that do not match are hidden.
            // A pre-rendered page cannot know the URL's query, so a list
            // filtered by it would be missing from the HTML; this way the
            // page carries every note, and the filter applies once it is live.
            for note in newest by note.slug {
                NoteCard(note, hidden: !visible.includes(note.slug))
            }
```

The HTML then holds every note, for a reader without script and for a
search engine, and the filter applies the moment the page is live. The
front page hands the finder the address's tag:

```wf
// src/pages/Home.wf
        // `query.tag` is the URL's `?tag=…`; it is missing when the URL has
        // none, and `?? ""` turns that into the finder's "every note".
        NoteFinder(notes, tag: query.tag ?? "")
```

**Check it:** the front page reads `7 of 7 notes`. Type `tomato` in the
search box, and the count and the cards narrow as you type. Open
`/?tag=garden`, and only the notes tagged `garden` show. Run `wf build` and
open `build/index.html` in a text editor: all seven notes are in it.

If a filtered list is empty in the built HTML, you probably filtered the
`for` itself by `query`; hide the cards instead, as above.

## Step 6: Give each note a page

Each note gets a page at `/notes/<slug>`:

```wf
// src/pages/NotePage.wf
page NotePage(path: "/notes/:slug", slug: String,
    title: "{notes.find(n => n.slug == slug)?.title ?? slug} — Field Notes",
    description: "{notes.find(n => n.slug == slug)?.summary ?? slug}",
    type: "article",
    layout: Sheet,
    paths: notes.map(n => n.slug)) {

    derived note = notes.find(n => n.slug == slug)
```

- `:slug` in the path is a typed parameter of the page.
- `paths:` names the values a static build renders the page for: one
  `notes/<slug>/index.html` per note, each listed in the sitemap
  ([Describe pages to search engines and link previews](/recipes/search-and-link-previews)).
- `title:` and `description:` may be worked out from the parameters, so
  each note's search result shows its own title and summary.

The body of the page is the note's Markdown:

```wf
// src/pages/NotePage.wf
            Markdown(n.body)
```

`Markdown` renders headings, lists, quotes, emphasis and links, at build
time and live. It escapes the text first, so HTML in a note is shown, not
run ([Elements](/learn/06-elements)). Below the note, `related` lists the three
newest notes that share a tag with it — a `derived` value like any other.

**Check it:** click a note's title. Its page shows the whole note, and the
browser tab shows its title followed by `— Field Notes`. After `wf build`,
`build/notes/` holds seven folders, one per note.

## Step 7: List the tags, and write a page in Markdown

The Tags page groups the notes under each tag:

```wf
// src/pages/Tags.wf
        Grid(columns: { base: 1, md: 2 }, gap: .md, align: .start) {
            for tag in allTags by tag {
                derived filed = notes.filter(n => n.tags.includes(tag)).sortBy(n => n.date).reverse()
```

- A layout prop takes one value per breakpoint: one column on a phone, two
  from `md` up. It compiles to a media query, so the first paint is already
  right ([Styling](/learn/13-styling)).
- A `derived` value inside a `for` is worked out for each item.

The About page is not a `.wf` file at all. `src/about.md` is a page: its
front matter names its path, title, description and layout, and the rest
is its Markdown:

```markdown
---
path: /about
title: About — Field Notes
description: Who keeps this notebook, why it exists, and how the site is built.
layout: Sheet
---
# About
```

**Check it:** `/tags` shows one card per tag, in one column on a narrow
window and two on a wide one. `/about` shows the About page in the same
column as the others.

## Step 8: Keep the reader's saved notes

A store keeps the notes this reader saves:

```wf
// src/stores/Saved.wf
/// The notes this reader has saved for later, kept in their browser.
store Saved {
    persist slugs: [String] = []

    derived count = slugs.length
```

`persist` keeps the list in the browser across visits. There is no
account, and nothing is sent anywhere ([Stores](/learn/11-stores)).

The button that saves a note says whether it is pressed, the way assistive
technology reads it:

```wf
// src/components/SaveButton.wf
/// Saves a note for later, or takes it off the saved list.
component SaveButton(_ slug: String, title: String) {
    use Saved

    Button(if Saved.slugs.includes(slug) { "Saved" } else { "Save" },
        aria-pressed: Saved.slugs.includes(slug),
        aria-label: if Saved.slugs.includes(slug) { "Saved: {title}" } else { "Save: {title}" },
        class: "save-button").sm.outlined {
        on click { Saved.toggle(slug) }
    }
}
```

`aria-pressed` follows the state, and `styles.css` styles the pressed
button with `[aria-pressed="true"]`, so the look and the meaning are one
attribute ([Accessibility](/about/accessibility)). The Saved page lists
`notes.filter(n => Saved.slugs.includes(n.slug))`, and the navbar's badge
shows `Saved.count`.

**Check it:** click **Save** on a card. It reads **Saved**, and the navbar
shows a `1` badge beside **Saved**. Reload the page: the note is still
saved, and `/saved` lists it.

## Step 9: Test it, and run the checks a static site needs

A test reads the project's `data` file, as any page does
([Testing](/learn/16-testing)):

```wf
// tests/NoteFinder.wf
test "a search that matches nothing says so, and clears" {
    NoteFinder(notes)
    type "zeppelin" into "Search the notes"
    expect "Nothing matches"
    expect "0 of 7 notes"
    click "Clear the search"
    expect "7 of 7 notes"
    expect not "Nothing matches"
}
```

The project has six tests. Run them, check with warnings counted as
failures, build, and load the result in a browser:

```bash
wf test
wf check --deny-warnings
wf build
wf verify
```

`wf verify` loads every route of the built site in a headless Chrome —
each note's page at its `paths:` value — and fails on an error, a missing
file or a page that draws nothing ([Command line](/reference/cli)).

**Check it:** `wf test` reports `6 passed`, `wf build` reports `SSG:
pre-rendered static pages`, and `wf verify` ends with `0 problem(s)`.
`build/` is ready for any static host.

## What you built

- A static build, with canonical addresses, a sitemap and link previews
  ([Describe pages to search engines and link previews](/recipes/search-and-link-previews)).
- Typed data read from a JSON file at build time ([Fetching data](/learn/15-data)).
- A shell, and a layout every page names
  ([Pages and routing](/learn/05-pages-and-routing)).
- A page per note from one `:slug` page and `paths:`, and a page written in
  Markdown ([Write a page as a Markdown file](/recipes/markdown-pages)).
- A search and a filter that work in pre-rendered HTML
  ([Static sites and SPAs](/about/static-or-single-page)).
- A reader's saved list, with a pressed state assistive technology reads
  ([Accessibility](/about/accessibility)).
