# Set cache and security headers

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/cache-and-security-headers

This recipe sets the HTTP headers a host sends with a WebFluent build: how
long a browser may keep each file, and the security headers that only work
as real headers.

You need a host that lets you set headers, or one that reads `_headers`
(Netlify, Cloudflare Pages). The hosting recipes, such as
[Serve a site with nginx](/recipes/serve-with-nginx), show where each host takes
them.

With `build.csp` on, this is the `build/_headers` file a build writes:

```text
/*
  Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; font-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; form-action 'self'
  X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
  Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
  X-Frame-Options: DENY
```

## How it works

1. `/*` applies the headers under it to every path of the site.
2. `Content-Security-Policy` is the same policy every page already carries
   as a `<meta>` tag, plus `frame-ancestors`, which a browser ignores in a
   `<meta>` tag ([Security](/about/security#the-content-security-policy)).
3. `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy` and `X-Frame-Options` only
   work as real HTTP headers, so they are in this file and nowhere else.

The build writes no cache headers: those are yours to set, by the kind of
file.

## Set cache headers

To let browsers keep files without serving a stale site, set
`Cache-Control` by the kind of file:

| Files | Cache-Control | Why |
|---|---|---|
| HTML, `app.js`, `pages/*`, `styles.css`, `theme.js`, `js/*` (your own scripts), `elements.js` | `no-cache` (revalidate every time) | their names do not change between builds |
| `sw.js` | `no-cache` | a stale worker holds a stale site ([Make a site work offline](/recipes/work-offline)) |
| resized images (`hero.<hash>.960.webp`) | `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` | the name changes when the file does |
| `public/` files | your choice | they keep the names you gave them |

`no-cache` still lets the browser keep a copy. The browser asks the server
each time, and a `304 Not Modified` answer means it does not download the
file again.

## Set security headers

Netlify and Cloudflare Pages read `build/_headers` as it is. On any other
host, set the same headers in its configuration, as the hosting recipes
show: [nginx](/recipes/serve-with-nginx), [Apache](/recipes/serve-with-apache),
[Caddy](/recipes/serve-with-caddy) and [Vercel](/recipes/deploy-to-vercel). Serve the site over HTTPS, and turn
on HSTS once you are sure HTTPS works everywhere.
[Review a site's security before you deploy](/recipes/review-security) has the full checklist.

After the deploy, [check the headers it sends](/recipes/check-a-deploy).



---

# Call WF from a script

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/call-wf-from-a-script

The runtime is `window.WF`. A script under `src/`, the console, or a
library's callback can call it. This page has a button that copies the
page's address, and the script it calls says so with the runtime's toast:

**Needs:** the script `src/share.js`, shown below.

```wf
page Article(path: "/article", title: "Slow roasting", description: "Why we take eleven minutes over it.") {
    Heading("Slow roasting").h1
    Text("Eleven minutes, and why it matters.")
    Button("Copy the link") { on click { shareLink() } }
}
```

The script is a plain file under `src/`
([Call your own JavaScript](/recipes/call-your-own-script)):

```js
// src/share.js
/**
 * Copy this page's address, and say so in a toast.
 */
async function shareLink() {
  try {
    await navigator.clipboard.writeText(location.href);
    WF.toast("Link copied", "success");
  } catch (e) {
    WF.toast("Could not copy the link", "danger");
  }
}
```

## How it works

- `WF` is on `window` once `app.js` has run, so any script may call it
  while the page is open. `WF.toast(message, tone, ms)` shows a toast in
  a tone (`"info"` by default) for `ms` milliseconds (3000 by default).
- Other calls a script makes the same way: `WF.navigate("/about")` moves
  to another route, and `WF.storeSnapshot("Cart")` reads what a store
  holds. The [runtime reference](/reference/runtime) lists every
  function.
- A build keeps only the runtime modules its code reaches, and it reads
  your scripts under `src/` for that too: the `WF.toast` written in
  `src/share.js` keeps the toast module in the build, though no `.wf` code
  uses it.

> [!WARNING]
> A call the build cannot read is not counted: a script in `public/` or
> from another origin, a `WF[name]` built at run time, or the console. If
> it reaches a module nothing else uses, set `"build": { "runtime": "full" }`,
> or the call fails in the browser.

A script from another origin must be listed in `meta.scripts`, which widens
the policy for it. The build's CSP check refuses an inline `<script>`
([Security](/about/security#the-content-security-policy)).

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| `WF.toast is not a function` (or another runtime function) | The build left the module out: write the call in a script under `src/`, or set `"build": { "runtime": "full" }` |
| `WF is not defined` | The script ran before `app.js`: call `WF` from an event, a callback or a `wf:render` listener, not at the script's top level |



---

# Call your own JavaScript

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/call-your-own-script

Some things are easier to write in JavaScript: a pointer effect, a
measurement, glue around a library. Put the function in a `.js` file under
`src/`, and your pages call it by name. You need a WebFluent project
([Getting started](/learn/01-getting-started)); the script is a plain
browser script, with no `import`, no `export` and no build step.

**Needs:** the script `src/tilt.js`, shown below.

```wf
page Gallery(path: "/gallery", title: "Gallery", description: "Cards that lean.") {
    state max = 15

    Heading("Gallery").h1
    Card(class: "tilt",
         mount: (n) => initTilt(n, max),
         update: (tilt) => tilt.setMax(max),
         cleanup: (tilt) => tilt.destroy()) {
        Text("Move the pointer over me.")
    }
    Slider(bind: max, min: 0, max: 45, label: "How far")
}
```

This script tilts an element toward the pointer, and returns a handle the
page can update and destroy. Write it the way you would write any file a
`<script src>` loads:

```js
// src/tilt.js
/**
 * Tilt an element toward the pointer.
 * @param {HTMLElement} node
 * @param {number} [max] how far, in degrees
 */
function initTilt(node, max = 15) {
  const move = (e) => {
    const r = node.getBoundingClientRect();
    const x = (e.clientX - r.left) / r.width - 0.5;
    node.style.transform = `rotateY(${x * max}deg)`;
  };
  node.addEventListener("pointermove", move);
  return {
    setMax(m) { max = m; },
    destroy() { node.removeEventListener("pointermove", move); },
  };
}
```

## How it works

The page hands the card to `initTilt` with `mount:`, changes how far it
tilts with `update:` as the reader moves the slider, and removes the
listener with `cleanup:` when the page leaves
([Hand an element to a script](/recipes/hand-an-element-to-a-script)). The build
treats the script this way:

- **The file runs as written.** The build copies it to `build/js/tilt.js`
  byte for byte and links it with `<script defer>` on every page, before the
  compiled code. A stack trace points at your own line.
- **Its names are in scope.** Every top-level `function`, `class`, `const`,
  `let` and `var`, and anything assigned to `window.x`, is a name your `.wf`
  code can call directly. What a function or an IIFE keeps inside stays
  private, as it does in the browser.
- **A call is checked.** `initTilt(n, 1, 2)` is a `T10` error where it is
  written, because the function takes one or two arguments. Its JSDoc types
  the arguments ([Type a script with JSDoc](#type-a-script-with-jsdoc)). A
  name the file does not declare is still a `T13`.
- **A class is constructed.** WebFluent has no `new`. A call to a class a
  script declares compiles to `new`.
- **One name has one meaning.** Two scripts that declare the same name, or
  a script name that is also a component, a store, a `const`, or a name the
  language or the browser owns (`format`, `log`, `fetch`), is an error that
  names both.
- **An ES module is refused.** A file with a top-level `import` or `export`
  cannot run from a `<script src>`, so the build stops and says so. Load a
  published module from the config instead
  ([Load a library from a CDN](/recipes/library-from-a-cdn)).

The tools know your scripts too: `wf serve` rebuilds when a script changes,
`wf audit` lists what each one declares, `wf types` prints each function's
signature, and the editor completes, documents and jumps to them.

## Type a script with JSDoc

To have calls checked against a function's types, describe the function in
a JSDoc comment. JSDoc is a comment, so the file stays exactly what the
browser runs. The checker reads it this way:

| JSDoc | WebFluent |
|---|---|
| `string` · `number` · `boolean` | `String` · `Number` · `Bool` |
| `object` · `{ a: T }` | `Map`, or a shape of the fields written |
| `T[]` · `Array<T>` | `[T]` |
| `?T` · `T \| null` · `[name]` | `T?`, or a parameter a call may leave out |
| `Promise<T>` | `T`, as an action that awaits it reads it |
| `(v: T) => R` | a function: you may pass an action or a lambda |
| `HTMLElement`, anything else | `Any` |

With no comment at all, every parameter is `Any`, so adding a script never
breaks a build. Each tag only narrows what a call may pass. `@returns` types
the result.

## Let a script report, and keep the class in WebFluent

When the way an element looks depends on something only a script can see
(an intersection, a scroll position, a library's event), hand the script an
action. An action is a plain function at run time. The script calls it, and
the class stays in a `class:` the compiler can read.

This page sets `is-visible` on the card while it is on screen:

```wf
page Story(path: "/story", title: "Story", description: "It fades in.") {
    state visible = false
    action setVisible(v: Bool) { visible = v }

    Heading("Story").h1
    Card(class: { "is-visible": visible },
         mount: (n) => watchVisible(n, setVisible),
         cleanup: (w) => w.destroy()) {
        Text("Here I am.")
    }
}
```

This script reports whether an element is on screen:

```js
// src/visible.js
/**
 * Say whether `node` is on screen, each time that changes.
 * @param {HTMLElement} node
 * @param {(v: boolean) => void} onChange
 */
function watchVisible(node, onChange) {
  const io = new IntersectionObserver(([e]) => onChange(e.isIntersecting));
  io.observe(node);
  return { destroy: () => io.disconnect() };
}
```

Each class has one owner. A class that `class:` names belongs to
WebFluent, and a class a script adds with `classList.add` belongs to the
script: `class:` only ever takes off what it put on.

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| `T13`: nothing declares the function | Check that the file is under `src/` and declares the name at its top level, not inside another function |
| `T10` on a call that looks right | Count the parameters the function declares; a JSDoc `[name]` or a default value lets a call leave one out |
| The build stops on a top-level `import` or `export` | Remove them and declare the names at the top level; a published module loads from `meta.scripts` instead ([Load a library from a CDN](/recipes/library-from-a-cdn)) |
| An error that names your script and a component, store or `const` | Rename one of the two: a name has one meaning in a project |



---

# Draw a chart from a library

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/chart-from-a-library

A charting library such as Chart.js wants a canvas and gives back a chart
object. This page hands a canvas to the library, shows new figures when the
reader switches years, and destroys the chart when the page leaves. You
need a WebFluent project, and the scripts below saved under its `src/`.

**Needs:** the script `src/sales-chart.js` and the `meta.scripts` setting,
both shown below.

```wf
page Sales(path: "/sales", title: "Sales", description: "Sales by quarter, as a bar chart.") {
    state lastYear = false
    derived values: [Number] = if lastYear { [9, 14, 11, 13] } else { [12, 19, 7, 15] }

    Heading("Sales").h1
    Switch(bind: lastYear, label: "Show last year")
    Host(tag: "canvas", role: "img", aria-label: "Sales by quarter",
         mount: (canvas) => drawSales(canvas, values),
         update: (chart) => showSales(chart, values),
         cleanup: (chart) => chart.destroy())
}
```

The page calls two functions of a plain script under `src/`, typed with
JSDoc:

```js
// src/sales-chart.js
/**
 * A bar chart of `values`, one bar a quarter, drawn on `canvas`.
 * @param {HTMLCanvasElement} canvas
 * @param {number[]} values
 */
function drawSales(canvas, values) {
  return new Chart(canvas, {
    type: "bar",
    data: {
      labels: ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
      datasets: [{ label: "Sales", data: values }],
    },
  });
}

/**
 * Show new figures on a chart that `drawSales` made.
 * @param {Chart} chart
 * @param {number[]} values
 */
function showSales(chart, values) {
  chart.data.datasets[0].data = values;
  chart.update();
}
```

The library itself loads from a CDN, through `meta.scripts` in
`webfluent.app.json`:

```json
{ "meta": {
    "scripts": ["https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/chart.js@4.4.1/dist/chart.umd.min.js"]
} }
```

## How it works

- **The library loads first.** The build links each `meta.scripts` entry
  with `<script defer>`, in order, before your own scripts and the compiled
  code, so `Chart` exists when `drawSales` runs. It also widens the
  Content-Security-Policy by the CDN's origin, so the policy that ships
  beside the page does not block the library. The compiler never fetches
  the file, so `.wf` code never calls `Chart` directly: your script does.
- **Your script is a plain browser script.** The build copies
  `src/sales-chart.js` to `build/js/` as written and puts its top-level
  names in scope, so the page calls `drawSales` and `showSales` by name.
  Its JSDoc types each call: `values` must be a list of numbers, and a
  call with the wrong number of arguments is a `T10` error
  ([Call your own JavaScript](/recipes/call-your-own-script)). `Chart` and
  `HTMLCanvasElement` are types WebFluent does not know, so they read as
  `Any`.
- **`Host` makes the canvas.** `Host(tag: "canvas", …)` is a bare node for
  somebody else's code. `role: "img"` and `aria-label:` give the chart a
  name a screen reader announces, since a canvas has no text.
- **`mount:` draws the chart.** It runs when the canvas is made, and what
  it returns, the `Chart` object, is the handle `update:` and `cleanup:`
  receive ([Hand an element to a script](/recipes/hand-an-element-to-a-script)).
- **`update:` follows the data.** It reads `values`, so it runs again
  whenever the switch changes `values`, and `showSales` gives the existing
  chart the new figures instead of drawing a new one.
- **`cleanup:` destroys the chart** when the page leaves, so nothing the
  library set up outlives the canvas.

## Variations

To pin the library to the exact file you tested, add its subresource
integrity hash to `meta.integrity`, keyed by the same URL. The build
writes it on the tag with `crossorigin="anonymous"`, and a library from
another origin without one draws a `D05` warning. The compiler never
fetches the file to work the hash out; your CDN lists it, or compute it
from a copy of the file:

```bash
openssl dgst -sha384 -binary chart.umd.min.js | openssl base64 -A
```

The other ways an entry in `meta.scripts` can load (`async`, after the
page, as a module, or with `globals` your `.wf` code calls directly) are
in [Load a library from a CDN](/recipes/library-from-a-cdn).

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| `mount failed ReferenceError: Chart is not defined` in the console | The library did not load: check the URL in `meta.scripts`, and that the page was rebuilt after the config changed |
| The chart draws once and never changes | Make `update:` read the state the chart shows; an `update:` that reads nothing never runs again |
| Two charts on one canvas after a route change | Destroy the chart in `cleanup:` |



---

# Check a deploy

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/check-a-deploy

This recipe is the list to go through after each deploy, on any host: the
mistakes it catches pass every check on your own machine.

You need the deployed site's address.

- Open a deep link directly and reload it. A 404 means the host does not
  fall back to `index.html` (a single-page build), or `base_path` is wrong.
- View a page's source. In a static build, the page's text is in the HTML.
- Check the response headers in the browser's network panel.
- Run a link-preview debugger on a page, and submit `sitemap.xml` to the
  search engines' consoles.

The same checks from a terminal, with your site's address in `SITE` and a
page other than the home page in place of `/docs`:

```bash
SITE=https://example.com
curl -sI "$SITE/docs" | head -1                     # HTTP/2 200, not 404
curl -s "$SITE/docs" | grep -o '<h1[^>]*>[^<]*'     # a static build: the heading is in the HTML
curl -sI "$SITE/" | grep -iE 'content-security-policy|x-frame-options|cache-control'
curl -s "$SITE/sitemap.xml" | head                  # absolute addresses under meta.site_url
```

Each line prints something when the deploy is right: a `200` status, the
page's `<h1>` and its text, the three headers, and the first entries of the
sitemap. An empty line is the check that failed.

For the link preview, paste a page's address into the
[Facebook Sharing Debugger](https://developers.facebook.com/tools/debug/)
or [LinkedIn's Post Inspector](https://www.linkedin.com/post-inspector/);
for the sitemap, submit `$SITE/sitemap.xml` in
[Google Search Console](https://search.google.com/search-console) and
[Bing Webmaster Tools](https://www.bing.com/webmasters).

## How it works

- A deep link loaded directly is the one request the host answers without
  the router: the home page can work while every other address is a 404.
- A static build pre-renders every page, so its text should be in the
  HTML the host sends ([Static sites and SPAs](/about/static-or-single-page)).
- The headers show whether the host sends what `build/_headers` holds
  ([Set cache and security headers](/recipes/cache-and-security-headers)).
- A link preview and the sitemap use the absolute addresses
  `meta.site_url` names
  ([Describe pages to search engines and link previews](/recipes/search-and-link-previews)).

Before the next deploy, `wf verify` loads every page of the build in
headless Chrome and catches a script error, a failed request or a blank
page before it ships ([Install wf on a build machine](/recipes/install-wf-in-ci)).



---

# Build a confirm dialog

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/confirm-dialog

Before a reader deletes something, ask them. This component wraps an
`AlertDialog` with **Cancel** and **Confirm** buttons and tells the page which
one was pressed, so every destructive action on the site asks the same way:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
component Confirm(_ title: String, visible: Bool, danger: Bool = false) {
    event confirm()
    event cancel()
    slot
    AlertDialog(visible: visible, title: title) {
        children
        Row(gap: .sm, justify: .end) {
            Button("Cancel") { on click { emit cancel() } }
            Button("Confirm", tone: if danger { .danger } else { .primary }) { on click { emit confirm() } }
        }
    }
}

page Account(path: "/", title: "Account", description: "Close your account.") {
    state asking = false
    state gone = false
    Heading("Account").h1
    Button("Delete account").danger { on click { asking = true } }
    Confirm("Delete your account?", visible: asking, danger: true) {
        on confirm { gone = true  asking = false }
        on cancel { asking = false }
        Text("Everything goes. This cannot be undone.")
    }
    if gone { Alert("Account deleted.").info }
}
```

## How it works

- `Confirm` takes the question as its positional `title`, whether it shows
  as `visible`, and a `danger` prop that turns the confirm button red.
  `tone:` picks the button's case from a condition instead of a fixed flag.
- It declares two [events](/learn/10-components#events), `confirm` and
  `cancel`, and each button fires one with `emit`. The component decides
  nothing; the page does.
- `slot` declares a default [slot](/learn/10-components#slots), and
  `children` places it inside the dialog. The caller's block fills it, so
  the question's detail is the caller's to write.
- The page owns `asking`. **Delete account** sets it, and both handlers
  clear it, which closes the
  [dialog](/learn/08-events#overlays-modals-dialogs-toasts-and-menus).
- An `AlertDialog` is one to a screen reader, read with its body. Escape
  closes it as **Cancel** would, and a press beside it does not: an answer
  is a button.

## One question, from a handler

When the question is asked once, from one handler, `await ask(…)` draws the
alert dialog itself and is the answer:

```wf
page Account(path: "/", title: "Account", description: "Close your account.") {
    state gone = false
    Heading("Account").h1
    Button("Delete account").danger {
        on click {
            if await ask("Delete your account?", detail: "Everything goes. This cannot be undone.", yes: "Delete", danger: true) {
                gone = true
            }
        }
    }
    if gone { Alert("Account deleted.").info }
}
```

The focus starts on **Cancel**, the answer that loses nothing, and goes
back to the button once it is answered.



---

# Connect two readers' pages

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/connect-two-readers

A `peer` opens a WebRTC data channel straight from one reader's page to
another's, so messages travel between them with no server relaying them.
This page signals over a `broadcast` channel, so it connects two tabs of one
browser: open `/room?host=1` in one tab and `/room` in another.

**Needs:** nothing besides the page; open it in two tabs of one browser.

```wf
page Room(path: "/room", title: "Room", description: "Two readers, one line.") {
    state heard = ""
    channel lobby = broadcast("room") { on message(m) { link.signal(m) } }
    peer link = rtc(signal: m => lobby.post(m), initiator: query.host == "1") {
        on message(m) { heard = m.text }
    }

    Heading("Room").h1
    match link {
        connecting { Text("Waiting for the other side…").muted }
        open       { Button("Wave") { on click { link.send({ text: "hello" }) } } }
        closed(c)  { Text("They left.") }
        error(e)   { Alert(e.message).danger }
    }
    Text(heard)
}
```

## How it works

The language supplies the channel, not a server. Before two pages can
connect, they must tell each other how — an offer, an answer, and the
network routes each can be reached by. This exchange is called
*signalling*.

- **`signal: m => lobby.post(m)`** sends this side's signalling messages out,
  over whatever connection the app already has — here the `lobby`
  [channel](/recipes/talk-between-tabs).
- **`link.signal(m)`**, in the lobby's `on message`, hands the peer what the
  other side sent.
- **`initiator: query.host == "1"`** makes the tab opened with `?host=1` the
  side that makes the offer. Exactly one side does.
- **`match link`** reads the peer like a socket: `connecting`, `open`,
  `closed(c)`, `error(e)`.
- **`link.send(value)`** sends a message, and holds it until the channel
  opens; **`on message(m)`** in the peer's block hears the other side's.

When a page leaves, it closes its peer, and the other side reads `closed`
at once rather than when the connection times out.

| Option | Does |
|---|---|
| `signal:` | Required. A function handed each message the other side must receive. |
| `initiator:` | Whether this side makes the offer. Exactly one side does. |
| `ice:` | The servers that help two readers on different networks find each other: `[{ urls: "stun:…" }]`. None by default, which connects readers on the same network only. |
| `ordered:` | `false` for a channel that may deliver messages out of order. |

## Variations

### Connect readers on different machines

Between two readers on different machines, the signal rides the app's own
socket or `api` instead of a `broadcast` channel, and `ice:` names a STUN
server so readers behind different networks can find each other:

```wf
page Call(path: "/call", title: "Call", description: "Two readers, two machines.") {
    state heard = ""
    socket relay = ws("wss://example.com/signal") { on message(m) { link.signal(m) } }
    peer link = rtc(signal: m => relay.send(m), initiator: query.host == "1",
                    ice: [{ urls: "stun:stun.example.com:3478" }]) {
        on message(m) { heard = m.text }
    }

    Heading("Call").h1
    match link {
        open { Button("Wave") { on click { link.send({ text: "hello" }) } } }
        else { Text("Connecting…").muted }
    }
    Text(heard)
}
```



---

# Copy to the clipboard

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/copy-to-the-clipboard

A **Copy** button saves the reader selecting a link by hand. To copy text,
call the browser's clipboard from an action and say when it worked:

```wf
page Share(path: "/share", title: "Share", description: "Copy the link.") {
    state copied = false
    state failed = false
    action copy(text: String) {
        copied = false
        failed = false
        try {
            await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text)
            copied = true
        } catch e {
            failed = true
        }
    }
    Heading("Share").h1
    Button("Copy the link") { on click { copy(location.href) } }
    if copied { Toast("Copied").success }
    if failed { Toast("Could not copy. Select the address and copy it by hand.").danger }
}
```

## How it works

- `navigator.clipboard` and `location` are browser globals, used as written
  with no prefix.
- `writeText` returns a promise, so the
  [action](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity#actions-and-locals) awaits
  it. `await` makes the action async, and `copied` is set only once the
  text is on the clipboard.
- The browser may refuse: the page is not focused, it is not served over
  HTTPS, or the reader denied the permission. The promise then rejects, the
  `catch` sets `failed`, and the reader is told to copy by hand instead of
  seeing nothing.
- The button's click handler calls `copy` with the page's own address.
- A `Toast` shows once, when its branch is drawn. The action sets `copied`
  and `failed` back to `false` before it starts, so the branch is drawn again
  on every click and a second copy shows a second toast. Without that,
  `copied` would stay `true` and the second click would show nothing.



---

# Count a number to its new value

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/count-a-number

Make a figure arrive rather than jump — a total, a score, a balance — by
giving its element `count:` with a length of time. Press **Load** and the
revenue counts from `$0.00` to `$1,200.00`:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Revenue(path: "/", title: "Revenue", description: "A figure that counts up.") {
    state revenue = 0
    Heading("Revenue").h1
    Text(format(revenue, .currency), count: "600ms")
    Button("Load") { on click { revenue = 1200 } }
}
```

## How it works

- `count: "600ms"` counts the number to each new value over 600ms, easing
  out as it gets there.
- The first value is shown as it is, so a page does not open by counting
  up from nothing. Every later value is counted to from the one before.
- Each step is formatted the way the first was: a currency counts as a
  currency ([`format`](/reference/built-ins#format)).

A reader who asked for reduced motion sees the number at its new value at
once ([Respect reduced motion](/recipes/motion-defaults#respect-reduced-motion)).

# Count down

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/count-down

A countdown is a number that drops once a second until it reaches zero. To
build one, change a state in an `every` timer:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Countdown(path: "/", title: "Countdown", description: "Ten seconds, counted down.") {
    state left = 10
    every(1000) { if left > 0 { left = left - 1 } }
    Heading("Countdown").h1
    Progress(value: 10 - left, max: 10)
    Text(if left == 0 { "Done" } else { "{left}s" })
}
```

## How it works

- `left` is a [`state`](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity#state) holding
  the seconds that remain.
- [`every(1000)`](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity#timers) runs its
  block every 1000 milliseconds. The `if` stops the count at zero.
- The `Progress` bar and the `Text` both read `left`, so they repaint on
  every tick. The text says **Done** at zero.

The timer stops when the page leaves, so a reader who navigates away
leaves no interval running.



---

# Add a dark-mode switch

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/dark-mode-switch

Let the reader pick a light look, a dark one, or whatever their system
prefers, and keep that choice across visits. The switch needs a dark theme
named in `webfluent.app.json`:

**Needs:** the `theme` setting below in `webfluent.app.json`. The starter
already declares `theme Night` in `src/theme.wf` and a `ThemeToggle`
component that does this; replace `src/theme.wf` with this code's themes,
and its `Settings` page replaces the starter's `src/pages/Settings.wf`.

```json
{ "theme": { "name": "Light", "dark": "Night" } }
```

This program declares both themes and a settings page with three buttons,
the current choice drawn solid and the others outlined:

```wf
theme Light {
    color-background: #FFFFFF
    color-text: #0F172A
}

theme Night {
    color-background: #0B1220
    color-surface: #111827
    color-text: #E5E7EB
    color-text-muted: #9CA3AF
    color-border: #1F2937
}

page Settings(path: "/settings", title: "Settings", description: "How the site looks.") {
    Heading("Settings").h1
    Row(gap: .sm) {
        Button("Light", outlined: theme != "light") { on click { setTheme("light") } }
        Button("Dark", outlined: theme != "dark") { on click { setTheme("dark") } }
        Button("Match the system", outlined: theme != "system") { on click { setTheme("system") } }
    }
}
```

## How it works

- **Two themes.** `Night` names only the tokens that change in the dark;
  every token it leaves out keeps its value. The config's `theme.dark` says
  which theme is the dark one ([Styling](/learn/13-styling#dark-mode)).
- **`setTheme`** takes `"light"`, `"dark"` or `"system"`, and the choice is
  kept across visits. With `"system"`, the dark theme applies whenever the
  reader's system prefers dark (`prefers-color-scheme: dark`).
- **`theme`** reads the choice, and stays current. A `Bool` prop given a
  condition follows it, so `outlined: theme != "light"` outlines every
  button but the chosen one.



---

# Debounce a search

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/debounce-a-search

A search box that asks the server on every key sends a request per letter.
To wait until the reader stops typing, keep what they typed apart from
what you search for, and copy one to the other once they pause:

**Needs:** a server that answers `/api/search?q=…` with a list of results.
It claims `/`: paste it into a new project, or replace the starter's
`src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Search(path: "/", title: "Search", description: "Search as you type, without a request per key.") {
    state typed = ""
    state q = ""
    resource hits = fetch("/api/search?q={q}")
    Heading("Search").h1
    Input(bind: typed, placeholder: "Search", aria-label: "Search") {
        on input(debounce: 300.ms) { q = typed }
    }
    if q != "" {
        match hits {
            loading { Spinner.sm }
            error(e) { Text(e.message).danger }
            ready(list) { Text("{list.length} results for {q}") }
        }
    }
}
```

## How it works

- `typed` follows the input on every key, through `bind:`. `q` is what the
  page searches for, and only the handler writes it.
- `debounce: 300.ms` runs the handler once the `input` events have stopped
  coming for 300 ms, so a word typed quickly is one run, with the last of
  them. A wait still pending when the page leaves is dropped.
- The [resource](/learn/15-data#show-a-request-with-resource) splices
  `q` into its address, so it asks again each time `q` changes — once per
  pause, not once per key. It also asks once as the page opens, for
  `/api/search?q=`, before anything is typed; the `if q != ""` shows
  nothing of that answer, so the server only has to answer it quickly
  (an empty list will do).

For something that should run while the events keep coming, only less often
— a scroll position, a window being resized — write `throttle:` instead:
`on scroll(e, throttle: 100.ms) { … }` runs at once, then at most once
every 100 ms, and once more where the scrolling stopped. Both are in
[Events](/learn/08-events#how-often-a-handler-runs).



---

# Deploy to Cloudflare Pages

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/deploy-to-cloudflare-pages

This recipe has Cloudflare Pages build a WebFluent site on every push and
serve it, with the security headers the build writes.

You need a Cloudflare account and a Pages project connected to the
repository; the build command installs `wf` as
[Install wf on a build machine](/recipes/install-wf-in-ci) shows.

In the Pages project's build settings, set the build command:

```bash
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/master/install.sh | WF_VERSION=v6.1.0 bash && ~/.webfluent/bin/wf build
```

and set the build output directory to `build`.

For a single-page build, also add `public/_redirects` with this line:

```text
/*  /index.html  200
```

## How it works

1. The build command installs `wf` and builds the site, the same command
   [Deploy to Netlify](/recipes/deploy-to-netlify) uses. Cloudflare Pages serves
   the `build` folder.
2. The build copies `public/_redirects` to the root of `build/`. Its line
   answers every path with `index.html`, so a reload on a deep link
   reaches the single-page build's router.
3. Cloudflare Pages reads `_headers` and `_redirects` the same way Netlify
   does, so the security headers apply with no further setting.

## Check it

Check the response headers in the browser's network panel, as for
Netlify, and open a deep link directly. Then go through
[Check a deploy](/recipes/check-a-deploy).

# Deploy to GitHub Pages

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/deploy-to-github-pages

This recipe publishes a WebFluent site to GitHub Pages from a GitHub
Actions workflow, which builds the site on every push to `main`. GitHub
serves a project site under `https://<you>.github.io/<repo>/`, so the build
must know that sub-path.

You need the project in a GitHub repository; the workflow installs `wf` as
[Install wf on a build machine](/recipes/install-wf-in-ci) shows.

Set the sub-path, the site's address, `clean_urls` and `ssg` in
`webfluent.app.json`:

```json
{
    "build": { "ssg": true, "base_path": "/<repo>", "clean_urls": "file" },
    "meta": { "site_url": "https://<you>.github.io/<repo>" }
}
```

GitHub Pages serves files and nothing else: it has no rewrite that sends
every address to `index.html`. `"ssg": true` writes a file for every
page, so a reader who reloads `/<repo>/tasks`, or opens a link to it, gets
that page. A project made with `wf init -t spa` has `"ssg": false`; keep
it that way only if you also add the `404.html` step below.

Then add `.github/workflows/pages.yml`:

```yaml
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/master/install.sh | WF_VERSION=v6.1.0 bash
      - run: ~/.webfluent/bin/wf build
      # Only for a single-page build ("ssg": false): GitHub serves
      # 404.html for an address it has no file for, so the app loads there
      # and its router draws the page.
      # - run: cp build/index.html build/404.html
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: build
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
```

Finally, in the repository's **Settings → Pages**, set the source to
**GitHub Actions**, and push to `main`.

## How it works

1. `build.base_path` prefixes every link, every asset and the router's
   paths with `/<repo>`, and `meta.site_url` is the address the canonical
   links and the sitemap name. Write paths from the site's root as if
   there were no prefix: `Link("About", to: "/about")` links to
   `/<repo>/about`.
2. GitHub Pages answers `/contact` with a `301` redirect to `/contact/`.
   `"clean_urls": "file"` (or `"directory"`) makes the canonical address of
   every page one it serves without a redirect
   ([Keep addresses from redirecting](/recipes/search-and-link-previews#keep-addresses-from-redirecting)).
3. The workflow checks out the repository, installs a pinned `wf`, builds
   the site, uploads `build/` as the Pages artifact and deploys it. The
   `pages: write` and `id-token: write` permissions are what
   `actions/deploy-pages` needs.

GitHub Pages serves `404.html` for a path it has no file for. A static
build writes one when the project has a page on `path: "*"`; a page on a
`:param` route needs its values listed in `paths:` to have files of its own
([Data files](/learn/15-data)). GitHub Pages ignores
`_headers`, but the Content-Security-Policy still ships as a `<meta>` tag in
every page.

## Check it

Open the URL the workflow's deploy step prints, then open a page other
than the home page directly and reload it. With `clean_urls` set, the
address stays as you typed it, with no redirect. Then go through
[Check a deploy](/recipes/check-a-deploy).



---

# Deploy to Netlify

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/deploy-to-netlify

This recipe has Netlify build a WebFluent site on every push and serve it,
with the security headers the build writes.

You need a Netlify account and the project in a repository Netlify can
read; the build command installs `wf` as
[Install wf on a build machine](/recipes/install-wf-in-ci) shows.

Add `netlify.toml` at the project's root:

```toml
[build]
  command = "curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/master/install.sh | WF_VERSION=v6.1.0 bash && ~/.webfluent/bin/wf build"
  publish = "build"
```

For a single-page build, also add `public/_redirects` with this line:

```text
/*  /index.html  200
```

Then connect the repository in Netlify, or push to the branch it deploys.

## How it works

1. `command` installs `wf` and builds the site; `publish` tells Netlify to
   serve the `build/` folder.
2. The build copies `public/_redirects` to the root of `build/`. Its line
   answers every path with `index.html` and a `200`, so a reload on
   `/users/42` reaches the single-page build's router.
3. Netlify reads `_headers` from the build, so the security headers apply
   with no further setting
   ([Set cache and security headers](/recipes/cache-and-security-headers)).

## Check it

In the browser's network panel, select the page's document request. Its
response headers include `Content-Security-Policy` and
`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, which came from `_headers`. Then go
through [Check a deploy](/recipes/check-a-deploy).



---

# Deploy to Vercel

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/deploy-to-vercel

This recipe has Vercel build a WebFluent site on every push and serve it.
Vercel does not read the `_headers` file the build writes, so the headers
go in `vercel.json`.

You need a Vercel account and the project in a repository Vercel can read;
the build command installs `wf` as
[Install wf on a build machine](/recipes/install-wf-in-ci) shows.

Add `vercel.json` at the project's root. This one is for a single-page
build:

```json
{
  "buildCommand": "curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/master/install.sh | WF_VERSION=v6.1.0 bash && ~/.webfluent/bin/wf build",
  "outputDirectory": "build",
  "headers": [
    {
      "source": "/(.*)",
      "headers": [
        { "key": "X-Content-Type-Options", "value": "nosniff" },
        { "key": "Referrer-Policy", "value": "strict-origin-when-cross-origin" },
        { "key": "X-Frame-Options", "value": "DENY" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "rewrites": [{ "source": "/(.*)", "destination": "/index.html" }]
}
```

## How it works

1. `buildCommand` installs `wf` and builds the site; `outputDirectory`
   tells Vercel to serve `build/`.
2. `headers` sets the security headers on every path. Vercel does not read
   `_headers`, so copy every header the build wrote in `build/_headers`
   into this list, including the `Content-Security-Policy` line
   ([Set cache and security headers](/recipes/cache-and-security-headers#set-security-headers)).
3. `rewrites` answers every path with `index.html`, so a reload on a deep
   link reaches the single-page build's router.

## Variations

For a static build, leave out `rewrites`: each page has its own file, and
an unknown path should be a 404.

## Check it

Compare the response headers in the browser's network panel with
`build/_headers`. Each header in the file should be there. Then go through
[Check a deploy](/recipes/check-a-deploy).



---

# Build a Docker image

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/docker-image

This recipe packs a WebFluent site into a Docker image that serves it with
nginx, for a host that runs containers.

You need Docker on the machine that builds the image. The image installs
`wf` itself, as [Install wf on a build machine](/recipes/install-wf-in-ci)
shows.

Add a `Dockerfile` at the project's root:

```dockerfile
FROM debian:stable-slim AS build
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl ca-certificates
RUN curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/master/install.sh | WF_VERSION=v6.1.0 bash
WORKDIR /site
COPY . .
RUN /root/.webfluent/bin/wf build

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=build /site/build /usr/share/nginx/html
```

Build and run the image:

```bash
docker build -t site .
docker run -p 8080:80 site
```

## How it works

1. The first stage, `build`, installs `curl`, installs `wf` into
   `/root/.webfluent/bin/`, copies the project in and builds it to
   `/site/build`. `WF_VERSION` pins the release, so the image builds the
   same way until you change it.
2. The second stage starts from `nginx:alpine` and copies only the built
   site into nginx's document root. `wf` and the project's sources stay
   behind in the first stage.
3. `docker run -p 8080:80` serves the site on port 8080 of your machine.

## Variations

To use the settings from [Serve a site with nginx](/recipes/serve-with-nginx),
copy them into the second stage as `/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf`. When
TLS ends in front of the container, write `listen 80;` in place of the
`listen 443 ssl http2;` line. The second stage then reads:

```dockerfile
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=build /site/build /usr/share/nginx/html
```

Here `nginx.conf` is that `server` block, beside the `Dockerfile`, with its
`root` changed to `/usr/share/nginx/html`.

## Check it

Open `http://localhost:8080` and a deep link, and check the headers with
`curl -I http://localhost:8080/`. Then go through
[Check a deploy](/recipes/check-a-deploy).



---

# Drive an animation yourself

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/drive-an-animation

Play an animation when something happens, not only when an element
arrives: a card that pulses as the pointer reaches it. Call
`animate(element, name, duration)` from a handler, with a `ref:` handle on
the element:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Hover(path: "/", title: "Hover", description: "A card that pulses on hover.") {
    Heading("Hover").h1
    Card(ref: panel) {
        on mouseenter { animate(panel, "pulse", "400ms") }
        Text("Point at me.")
    }
}
```

## How it works

- `ref: panel` gives the page a handle on the card's element.
- `animate(panel, "pulse", "400ms")` plays the built-in `pulse` animation
  on it for 400ms, each time the pointer enters the card.
- `animate` returns a handle that plays as soon as it is made, and its
  `play()`, `cancel()` and `finished` are yours.

## Variations

### Replay an element's own animation

A flag plays once, when the element arrives. To play an animation the
element already carries again, from the start, call
`replayAnimation(element, name)`:

```wf
page Replay(path: "/", title: "Replay", description: "A card that fades in again on hover.") {
    Heading("Replay").h1
    Card.outlined.fadeIn {
        on mouseenter(e) { replayAnimation(e.currentTarget, "fadeIn") }
        Text("Point at me.")
    }
}
```



---

# Make a desktop app with Electron

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/electron-app

This recipe ships a WebFluent project as an Electron app: the build runs
in a Chromium shipped inside the app, and a page calls a Node.js side for
what a browser cannot do — open a folder dialog, read a file on disk,
start a process. Nothing in the language changes; a page reaches Node
through a plain script under `src/`, with one typed function per thing it
asks for ([Call your own JavaScript](/recipes/call-your-own-script)). For a
native side in Rust and the system's own web view instead, see
[Make a desktop or phone app with Tauri](/recipes/tauri-app).

You need a WebFluent project that builds with `wf build`, and Node.js
with npm.

These are the files of an Electron app, beside `src/`. First, the build
settings in `webfluent.app.json`:

```json
{
    "build": { "compress": false },
    "meta": { "sitemap": false }
}
```

Install Electron and electron-builder in the project's folder:

```bash
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev electron electron-builder
```

Point `package.json` at the main process, and add the scripts that run and
package the app:

```json
{
    "main": "electron/main.js",
    "scripts": {
        "start": "electron .",
        "dist": "wf build && electron-builder"
    },
    "build": { "files": ["electron/**", "build/**"] }
}
```

The main process opens the window, serves the build to it, and answers
the page's calls:

```js
// electron/main.js
const { app, BrowserWindow, dialog, ipcMain, net, protocol } = require("electron");
const fs = require("node:fs");
const path = require("node:path");
const { pathToFileURL } = require("node:url");

const BUILD = path.join(__dirname, "..", "build");

// To the page, app://localhost is an ordinary origin: absolute paths,
// fetch and its security policy work as they do on a site.
protocol.registerSchemesAsPrivileged([
  { scheme: "app", privileges: { standard: true, secure: true, supportFetchAPI: true } },
]);

const isFile = (p) => fs.statSync(p, { throwIfNoEntry: false })?.isFile() ?? false;

// A file of the build; a route the router draws gets index.html.
function serve(request) {
  const file = path.join(BUILD, decodeURIComponent(new URL(request.url).pathname));
  const found =
    file.startsWith(BUILD + path.sep) &&
    ([file, path.join(file, "index.html")].find(isFile) ??
      (path.extname(file) ? null : path.join(BUILD, "index.html")));
  return found
    ? net.fetch(pathToFileURL(found).href)
    : new Response("Not found", { status: 404 });
}

function openWindow() {
  const win = new BrowserWindow({
    width: 1000,
    height: 700,
    webPreferences: { preload: path.join(__dirname, "preload.js") },
  });
  // Packaged, the window shows the build; while you work, `wf serve`.
  win.loadURL(app.isPackaged ? "app://localhost/" : "http://localhost:3000/");
}

app.whenReady().then(() => {
  protocol.handle("app", serve);

  ipcMain.handle("greet", (_event, name) => `Hello, ${name}!`);
  ipcMain.handle("start-sync", (event) => {
    for (const done of [25, 50, 75, 100]) {
      // … a quarter of the work …
      event.sender.send("sync-progress", done);
    }
  });
  ipcMain.handle("pick-folder", async (event) => {
    const win = BrowserWindow.fromWebContents(event.sender);
    const { canceled, filePaths } = await dialog.showOpenDialog(win, {
      properties: ["openDirectory"],
    });
    return canceled ? null : filePaths[0];
  });

  openWindow();
  app.on("activate", () => {
    if (BrowserWindow.getAllWindows().length === 0) openWindow();
  });
});

app.on("window-all-closed", () => {
  if (process.platform !== "darwin") app.quit();
});
```

The preload script hands the page exactly what it may ask for:

```js
// electron/preload.js
const { contextBridge, ipcRenderer } = require("electron");

const events = ["sync-progress"];

contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld("native", {
  greet: (name) => ipcRenderer.invoke("greet", name),
  startSync: () => ipcRenderer.invoke("start-sync"),
  pickFolder: () => ipcRenderer.invoke("pick-folder"),
  onEvent: (name, handler) => {
    if (!events.includes(name)) throw new Error(`No event called ${name}`);
    const listener = (_event, payload) => handler(payload);
    ipcRenderer.on(name, listener);
    return () => ipcRenderer.removeListener(name, listener);
  },
});
```

And one script under `src/` gives the pages typed names for each call:

```js
// src/native.js — what electron/preload.js exposed, under the names the pages call.
/**
 * Whether the page is inside the app, rather than a browser tab.
 * @returns {boolean}
 */
function inApp() {
  return "native" in window;
}

const outside = () => Promise.reject(new Error("This needs the desktop app."));

/**
 * @param {string} name
 * @returns {Promise<string>}
 */
function greet(name) {
  return inApp() ? window.native.greet(name) : outside();
}

/** Start syncing; how far it has got arrives as `sync-progress`. */
function startSync() {
  return inApp() ? window.native.startSync() : outside();
}

/**
 * Ask for a folder; `null` when the reader cancels.
 * @returns {Promise<?string>}
 */
function pickFolder() {
  return inApp() ? window.native.pickFolder() : Promise.resolve(null);
}

/**
 * Hear an event the native side emits, until the function it returns is called.
 * @param {string} name
 * @param {(payload: any) => void} handler
 * @returns {() => void}
 */
function onEvent(name, handler) {
  return inApp() ? window.native.onEvent(name, handler) : () => {};
}
```

## How it works

### Prepare the build for a desktop

The same project builds for the web and for a desktop. Two keys in
`webfluent.app.json`, and one to leave out, drop what only a website needs:

- **`build.compress: false`** — the shell packs the folder into the app, so
  a `.gz` file beside every file would ship every file twice.
- **`meta.sitemap: false`** — writes no `sitemap.xml` or `robots.txt`;
  nothing crawls an app. You can leave `meta.site_url` and the link-preview
  tags unset too.
- **Leave `offline` out** — the files are already on the machine, so a
  service worker has nothing to keep.

A single-page build and a static build both work
([Static sites and SPAs](/about/static-or-single-page)), and addresses stay as they
are. The main process answers a path the build has no file for with
`index.html`, so reloading the window on `/settings` shows the settings
page.

An app is often used with no network, and a font named in `meta.fonts`
comes from another origin. To make a font always available, put the file in
`public/` and declare it with `@font-face` in a `.css` file under `src/`
([Styling](/learn/13-styling)).

### Set up Electron

1. `npm init -y` writes a `package.json`, and `npm install` adds Electron
   and electron-builder to it as development dependencies.
2. Electron's two files go in a folder called `electron/`. Do **not**
   put them under `src/`: every `.js` file under `src/` is linked into the
   pages, and these files run in Node, outside the pages.
3. `"main"` in `package.json` points Electron at the main process, and
   `npm start` runs `electron .`.
4. The main process opens the window and serves the build to it. A
   `file://` address would break the build's absolute addresses (there,
   `/app.js` is the root of the disk), so the build is served from an
   `app://` origin of its own. `protocol.handle("app", serve)` answers each
   request with the file of `build/` it names, the folder's `index.html`,
   or — for a path with no extension, a route the router draws —
   `build/index.html`. Packaged, the window loads `app://localhost/`;
   while you work, `http://localhost:3000/`.

### Call Node from a page

A page has no Node in it. The *preload script* runs beside the page and
hands it exactly what it may ask for: one function per channel, never
`ipcRenderer` itself. Each `ipcMain.handle` in the main process answers
one channel: `greet` returns a value, `start-sync` reports its progress as
`sync-progress` events, and `pick-folder` opens the system's folder
dialog. `onEvent` lets a page hear only the events the preload script
lists.

`src/native.js` takes the place of the three scripts of the Tauri recipe.
It keeps their names, so the `Hello`, `Sync` and `Library` pages of
[Make a desktop or phone app with Tauri](/recipes/tauri-app#call-a-rust-command)
run in Electron without a change. `inApp()` is false in a browser tab —
`wf serve` opened in a browser, `wf test`, `wf verify` — and each function
answers there instead of throwing, so every page still loads.

### Run the Electron app while you work

Run the dev server and the app in two terminals. In the first:

```bash
wf serve
```

In the second:

```bash
npm start
```

Saving a `.wf` file rebuilds and reloads the window. A change under
`electron/` needs the app restarted.

The page's security policy needs nothing added: `app://localhost` is the
page's own origin, as `http://localhost:3000` is while you work.

### Package the Electron app

Electron Forge and electron-builder both package an app from
`package.json`. Whichever you use, run `wf build` first, and make sure the
package holds `electron/` and `build/`; `src/` is not needed at run time.
With electron-builder, `npm run dist` does both: its `dist` script runs
`wf build`, then `electron-builder`, and `build.files` names the two
folders the package holds.

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | What to check |
|---|---|
| Every native call fails with `This needs the desktop app.` | The page is open in a browser tab, not the app |
| A packaged Electron app shows an empty window | The package is missing `build/`, or `wf build` did not run before packaging |
| The app's text falls back to another font offline | The font comes from `meta.fonts`; put the file in `public/` and declare it with `@font-face` |



---

# Use environment values, and keep secrets out

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/environments-and-secrets

Read a setting that changes between environments (an API's address, a
feature switch) with `env.NAME`, give it a value per environment, and keep
a private value such as an API key out of what readers download.

This page reads the API's address and a feature switch, and falls back to
defaults when nothing sets them:

**Needs:** an API that answers `/api/rows`, and the values set as [Set a
value](#set-a-value) shows. It claims `/`: paste it into a new project, or
replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
const API = env.PUBLIC_API ?? "/api"
const FEATURES = { billing: env.PUBLIC_BILLING == "on" }

page Rows(path: "/", title: "Rows", description: "Rows from the API.") {
    resource rows = fetch("{API}/rows")
    Heading("Rows").h1
    if FEATURES.billing { Link("Billing", to: "/billing") }
    match rows {
        loading { Spinner }
        error(e) { Text(e.message).danger }
        ready(r) { Text("{r.length} rows") }
    }
}

page Billing(path: "/billing", title: "Billing", description: "Plans and invoices.") {
    Heading("Billing").h1
}
```

## How it works

`env.PUBLIC_API` is the value of `PUBLIC_API`, fixed when the site is
built. A name that nothing sets reads as nothing (`null`), so `??` supplies
the default. Keep the values in `const`s at the top of the file, as above,
so every page reads them from one place.

The sections below set the values, keep the private ones out of the bundle,
and build once per environment.

## Set a value

You can set a value in three places. When two set the same name, the later
one in this list wins:

1. **The config's `env` map**, committed with the project:

   ```json
   { "env": { "PUBLIC_API": "/api", "PUBLIC_BILLING": "off" } }
   ```

2. **A `.env` file** beside `webfluent.app.json`, which you do not commit.
   `wf init` adds `.env` to `.gitignore`. Each line is `NAME=value`. A line
   that starts with `#` is a comment, a line may start with `export `, and a
   value may be in single or double quotes:

   ```bash
   PUBLIC_API=http://localhost:8080/api
   PUBLIC_BILLING=on
   ```

3. **The shell** that runs the build, for CI and one-off builds:

   ```bash
   PUBLIC_API=https://api.example.com wf build
   ```

   The shell supplies a name that begins `PUBLIC_`, or a private name the
   config or `.env` already declares. It does not bring in every variable
   the build happens to run with, such as `HOME`.

   A name that `public_env` makes public without the prefix takes its
   value from the config or `.env` only — `public_env` is part of the
   project, and a project you cloned could list `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`
   there to publish your shell's value. To let the shell supply one, name
   it in `WF_ALLOW_SHELL_ENV`, comma-separated:

   ```bash
   WF_ALLOW_SHELL_ENV=ANALYTICS_ID ANALYTICS_ID=UA-2 wf build
   ```

> [!NOTE]
> Versions before 4.1 read only the config's `env` map.

## Keep a private value out of the bundle

The build replaces `env.NAME` with its value in the JavaScript and HTML
that every reader downloads. That is right for an API address and wrong for
an API key. So a page, a component, a store or an `api` block may read only
a name that says it is public:

- a name that begins with **`PUBLIC_`**, or
- a name listed in the config's **`public_env`**.

In this config, `env.PUBLIC_API` and `env.ANALYTICS_ID` are public, and
`env.STRIPE_SECRET` is private:

```json
{
  "env": { "PUBLIC_API": "/api/v1", "ANALYTICS_ID": "UA-1", "STRIPE_SECRET": "sk_…" },
  "public_env": ["ANALYTICS_ID"]
}
```

A page may read `env.PUBLIC_API` and `env.ANALYTICS_ID`. Reading
`env.STRIPE_SECRET` from a page is a compile error
([`E108`](/errors/E108)) that names the file and the line.

A private value is still available to [server rendering](/recipes/render-a-template),
which runs on a server, where a secret stays secret. It never reaches the
bundle: the build writes only public values into it.

> [!CAUTION]
> Adding a name to `public_env` publishes its value to every reader of the
> site, and every build says so with a warning naming it. A secret that a
> third party needs belongs in a request your server makes, not in a page
> ([Security](/about/security#secrets-stay-out-of-the-bundle)).

## Name your own values something other than `env`

`env` is the language's name for these settings, and nothing else may use
it. A `state`, a prop, a route parameter, a loop item or a top-level `const`
called `env` is an error
([`E118`](/errors/E118)). For a
value that says which stage a page is about, use a name such as `target` or
`stage`.

## Build once per environment

To deploy the same source to several environments, run one build per
environment, each with its own values:

```bash
wf build                                              # .env on your machine
PUBLIC_API=https://staging.example.com/api wf build   # staging
PUBLIC_API=https://api.example.com wf build           # production
```

In CI, set the variables on the job's build step:

```yaml
- run: ~/.webfluent/bin/wf build
  env:
    PUBLIC_API: https://api.example.com
    PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID: ${{ vars.ANALYTICS_ID }}
```

Each build overwrites `build/`, so deploy what one build wrote before
running the next, each to its own host ([Ship](/recipes#ship)).

## Change other settings per deploy

A few settings outside `env` also change between deploys:

| Setting | What it is |
|---|---|
| `build.base_path` | The sub-path the site is served under. The build prefixes every link, asset and route with it ([Ship](/recipes#ship)) |
| `meta.site_url` | The site's absolute address, for canonical links, the sitemap and sharing tags |
| `theme.tokens` | Design tokens a pipeline supplies, on top of the theme: `{ "theme": { "tokens": { "color-primary": "#8B5CF6" } } }` |

These settings live in `webfluent.app.json`. There is no separate config
file per environment. A pipeline that needs different settings writes the
file before it builds; `wf config set` edits it from a script:

```bash
wf config set build.base_path /staging
```

## Audit what the project reads

To list every `env` name the project has, run `wf audit`:

```bash
wf audit
```

It prints each name, where it is read, and whether it is public, beside
everything else the site trusts ([Review a site's security before you deploy](/recipes/review-security)).
Run it before a release, and when you review a change that adds a name.

# Open a box to the height of its content

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/expand-to-content

CSS cannot animate to `height: auto`, so a box of details that should slide
open to whatever height its text needs takes `.expand`. Press **Details**
and the box opens; press it again and it closes:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Details(path: "/", title: "Details", description: "A box that opens smoothly.") {
    state open = false
    Heading("Details").h1
    Button("Details") { on click { open = !open } }
    show open {
        Stack(animate: .expand) { Text("As much text as there is.") }
    }
}
```

## How it works

- `show open` toggles whether the box is visible, and the box animates as
  it appears and goes.
- `animate: .expand` measures the height `auto` would give, animates to
  that number, then hands the height back, so the box keeps growing with
  its content.
- `.expand` on the way in is `.collapse` on the way out, so the box needs
  no `exit:`.

A reader who asked for reduced motion sees the box open at once
([Respect reduced motion](/recipes/motion-defaults#respect-reduced-motion)).



---

# Keep filters in the address

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/filters-in-the-address

A filter held in a `state` is lost on reload and missing from a link the
reader shares. To make it survive a reload, a shared link and the back
button, read it from `query` instead:

```wf
const PRODUCTS = [
    { name: "Kettle", price: 39 },
    { name: "Apron", price: 18 },
    { name: "Mug", price: 9 },
]

page Products(path: "/products", title: "Products", description: "Everything we sell.") {
    derived sort = query.sort ?? "name"
    derived shown = if sort == "price" {
        PRODUCTS.sortBy(p => p.price)
    } else {
        PRODUCTS.sortBy(p => p.name)
    }
    Heading("Products").h1
    Row(gap: .sm) {
        Link("By name", to: "/products?sort=name")
        Link("By price", to: "/products?sort=price")
    }
    for p in shown by p.name {
        Text("{p.name}: ${p.price}")
    }
}
```

Choose **By price** and the list reorders to Mug, Apron, Kettle, and the
address becomes `/products?sort=price`. Reload the page or share the link,
and it opens sorted by price.

## How it works

- [`query`](/learn/05-pages-and-routing#query-strings-and-fragments)
  is the address's query string as a map: `query.sort` is `"price"` for
  `?sort=price`, and null when the address has no `sort`.
- `sort` is a [`derived`](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity#derived)
  value, so `??` gives it a default and it follows the address. `shown`
  is derived from `sort`, so the list reorders whenever the address does.
- Each choice is a `Link` to the same page with another query. A query
  string is not part of the route, so `/products?sort=price` is still the
  `Products` page; only `sort` changes.

To change the query from an action instead of a link, call
`navigate("/products?sort=price")`.



---

# Hand an element to a script

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/hand-an-element-to-a-script

A library that draws into an element (a chart, a map, an editor, an
effect) needs the element when it is made, new values while it lives, and
a chance to stop when it goes. The three lifetime props give it each, on
any element or component call. This page hands a paragraph to a script
that types a greeting into it, retypes it when the name changes, and stops
its timer when the paragraph leaves:

**Needs:** the script `src/typewriter.js`, shown below.

```wf
page Welcome(path: "/welcome", title: "Welcome", description: "A greeting a script types out, letter by letter.") {
    state name = "reader"
    state typing = true

    Heading("Welcome").h1
    Input(bind: name, label: "Your name")
    Switch(bind: typing, label: "Type the greeting")
    if typing {
        Host(tag: "p",
             mount: (node) => startTypewriter(node, "Hello, {name}."),
             update: (writer) => writer.retype("Hello, {name}."),
             cleanup: (writer) => writer.stop())
    }
}
```

The script is a plain file under `src/`
([Call your own JavaScript](/recipes/call-your-own-script)):

```js
// src/typewriter.js
/**
 * Type `text` into `node`, one letter every 60 ms.
 * @param {HTMLElement} node
 * @param {string} text
 */
function startTypewriter(node, text) {
  let shown = 0;
  const timer = setInterval(() => {
    if (shown < text.length) node.textContent = text.slice(0, ++shown);
  }, 60);
  return {
    retype(next) { text = next; shown = 0; node.textContent = ""; },
    stop() { clearInterval(timer); },
  };
}
```

## How it works

- `mount: (node) => …` runs each time the element is made: the first
  paint, a route change, an `if` branch arriving, a list item added. What
  it returns is the *handle* the other two receive. Here the handle is the
  object with `retype` and `stop`.
- `update: (handle) => …` runs again whenever the state it reads changes.
  It reads `name`, so typing in the field retypes the greeting.
- `cleanup: (handle) => …` runs when the element leaves (its page, its
  branch or its list item), so nothing a library made outlives it. Turning
  the switch off removes the branch, and `stop` clears the timer.

A `mount:` that throws removes itself and logs the error; the page stays
up.

To get a bare node for a library, use `Host`, as this page does. It has
the same lifetime: `Host(tag: "canvas", …)` makes the element the library
wants. It makes a `div` by default, or a `span`, `canvas`, `svg`,
`section`, `figure`, `pre`, `p`, `ul` or `table`.

## Variations

The three props work on every element, not only `Host`:
`Card(mount: (n) => initTilt(n))` hands the card itself to a script. On a
component call, they belong to the component's root element, unless the
component declares a prop of that name itself.

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| `mount failed` in the console, and the element is empty | The script threw on mount; the message after it is the script's own error |
| `V10` on a `Host` | Use one of the tags `Host` makes; any other is a `div` |
| A timer or listener keeps running after the page changes | Stop it in `cleanup:`; the handle `mount:` returned is what `cleanup:` receives |

# Install wf on a build machine

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/install-wf-in-ci

This recipe installs `wf` on a machine that builds the site for you — a CI
runner, or the build step of a host such as Netlify — and runs the build
there. Every hosting recipe uses it.

You need a project that builds with `wf build` on your own machine, and a
build machine with `curl` and `bash`.

```bash
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/master/install.sh | WF_VERSION=v6.1.0 bash
~/.webfluent/bin/wf build
```

## How it works

1. The install script downloads `wf` into `~/.webfluent/bin/`. `WF_VERSION`
   pins the release it installs, so a new release cannot change a deploy
   without you knowing.
   `-f` makes `curl` fail on an error from the server instead of piping
   the error page to `bash`; `--proto '=https' --tlsv1.2` refuses to fetch
   the script over anything but HTTPS.
2. `~/.webfluent/bin/wf build` builds the project in the current folder
   and writes the whole site to `build/`. The full path works even where
   the install has not put `wf` on the `PATH` yet.

A static build writes each page as its own `index.html` (`/contact` is
`contact/index.html`). A page whose `path` is `*` is written to the root as
`404.html`, which is the file most static hosts serve for a path they have
no file for.

## Variations

Without `WF_VERSION`, the script installs the latest release:

```bash
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/master/install.sh | bash
```

To find the latest release, the script asks GitHub's API, which limits how
often one address may ask. A shared CI runner often hits that limit, and
the install stops with "could not determine the latest version". A pinned
`WF_VERSION` never asks, which is one more reason every hosting recipe
pins it.

You can also build on your own machine and upload `build/`. It is only
files.

## Prepare the site before the first deploy

Do these once, before the first deploy:

1. Set `meta.site_url` in `webfluent.app.json` to the address the site will
   have. If the site lives under a sub-path (`/docs`), also set
   `build.base_path`.
2. Decide between a static build and a single-page build
   ([Static sites and SPAs](/about/static-or-single-page)). A single-page build
   needs the host to answer every path with `index.html`.
3. Build the site and load it in a real browser:

   ```bash
   wf build
   wf verify
   ```

   `wf verify` loads every page in headless Chrome and fails on a script
   error, a failed request or a blank page.

After the deploy, [check it](/recipes/check-a-deploy).



---

# Keep writes made offline

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/keep-writes-made-offline

Keep the reader's changes when the network drops, and send them when it
comes back. This needs offline support turned on
([Make a site work offline](/recipes/work-offline)), with `"sync": true` in its
config:

**Needs:** `offline` with `"sync": true` in `webfluent.app.json`, below,
and a site served over HTTPS ([Make a site work
offline](/recipes/work-offline)).

```json
{ "offline": { "precache": ["/"], "sync": true } }
```

This page tells the reader how many changes are waiting to be sent:

```wf
page Notes(path: "/notes", title: "Notes", description: "Notes that save offline.") {
    Heading("Notes").h1
    if network.queued > 0 {
        Text("{network.queued} change(s) will be sent when you are back online").muted
    }
}
```

## How it works

With `sync` on, a write — any method but `GET` and `HEAD`, made through
`fetch` or an `api` — that fails because the network is gone is kept
instead of thrown. The call resolves with nothing, so what the page showed
stays shown.

`network.queued` is how many writes are waiting. Show it, as the page
above does, so the reader knows their changes are safe.

### What is kept

Only a write that failed for want of a network is kept: the browser says it
is offline, or the site's own server could not be reached. A request to
another origin that is refused while the browser is online — a CORS
refusal, a closed port — fails as it would without `sync`.

A credential is never stored with a kept write. What an `api`'s
`on request` hook adds — an `Authorization` header from the session — is
added again when the write is sent, by the hook as it is then: a write made
before a logout goes out with no one's token, never the old one. A write
whose call carries a credential header itself (`headers: { "Authorization":
token }`) cannot be kept without it, so it is not kept, and its call fails
as it would without `sync`.

A `File` body is not kept, and its call fails as it would without `sync`.

### When it is sent

When the connection returns, the kept writes are sent in order:

- by Background Sync, where the browser has it, so a closed tab still sends
  them;
- by the page otherwise, the next time it is open.

A server that answers has the write, even if it refuses it. A server that is
down, or asks the client to wait, keeps the write waiting for later.

A write whose service adds credentials with its hook is sent by a page that
has that service open, so the worker leaves it — and the writes after it,
to keep them in order — for the next such page.

### Forget the kept writes

To forget every kept write — when the reader logs out, for example — call
`WF.clearQueued()` from one of the project's scripts.



---

# Make a page work with a keyboard and a screen reader

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/keyboard-and-screen-reader

The built-ins already render the markup assistive technology expects, and
the compiler reports what it can see in that markup
([Accessibility](/about/accessibility)). What is left is yours: a name
for every control that matches what a sighted reader sees, and a keyboard
path through any element you turned into a control. This page has a
labelled search field, an icon-only button, and a card that acts as a
button:

```wf
page Plans(path: "/plans", title: "Plans", description: "Choose a plan.") {
    state q = ""
    state chosen = ""
    Heading("Plans").h1
    Input(bind: q, label: "Search the plans", hint: "Try “team” or “solo”").search
    IconButton(icon: "close", label: "Clear the search") { on click { q = "" } }
    Button("Search", aria-label: "Search the plans") { on click { log(q) } }
    Card(role: "button", tabindex: "0") {
        on click { chosen = "Team" }
        on key("Enter") { chosen = "Team" }
        on key("space") { chosen = "Team" }
        Text("Team plan")
    }
    Text("Chosen: {chosen}")
}
```

## How it works

- **A visible `label:`, not a placeholder.** `label:` is a real
  `<label for>`, and `hint:` is tied to the control with
  `aria-describedby`. A placeholder disappears as soon as the reader types,
  so prefer a label; `A03` warns of an `Input` with neither.
- **An icon-only control has a name.** `label:` on an `IconButton`, or
  `aria-label:` on anything else, is read aloud and never shown (`A02`).
- **An `aria-label` begins with the visible words.** Someone who says
  "click Search" to voice control then reaches the right button. One that
  does not contain them is an `A15`: a `Button("Save", aria-label: "Submit
  the form")` should say `aria-label: "Save the note"`.
- **A custom control needs a role, a place in the tab order, and keys.**
  Use `Button` whenever you can. When an element must act as one, as the
  `Card` here does, give it `role: "button"`, `tabindex: "0"` and handlers
  for the keys a button answers to, Enter and Space. Without `tabindex`,
  the card cannot be reached with Tab; without the key handlers, reaching
  it does nothing.

## Check it with assistive technology

The compiler's checks are a floor. Before you ship a page, use it the way
its readers do:

1. **Use only the keyboard.** Put the mouse away. Tab through the page,
   open and close every menu and dialog, and submit every form. Focus is
   always visible and never lost.
2. **Use a screen reader.** VoiceOver (macOS: ⌘F5), NVDA (Windows, free) or
   TalkBack (Android). Listen to the page's list of headings and landmarks,
   and to what a form says when it fails.
3. **Zoom to 200%**, and narrow the window. Nothing needs horizontal
   scrolling.
4. **Turn on reduced motion** in your system settings, and reload. Nothing
   moves.

Part of this can be automated. `wf test`'s `click "Save"` and
`type "…" into "Email"` find controls by the name a reader sees, the way
assistive technology does, so a test that passes is a page someone can
operate ([Test a page](/recipes/test-a-page)).

## A checklist

- `wf check` reports no `A` warnings.
- Every picture's alt text says what it shows, and decorative ones have
  `alt: ""`.
- Every link and button says what it does without the text around it.
- Every control has a visible label, and every `aria-label` contains the
  visible words.
- Colour is never the only way something is said.
- Every custom control is reachable with Tab and works with Enter and
  Space.
- The page works with only a keyboard, with a screen reader, at 200% zoom,
  and with reduced motion.



---

# Add keyboard shortcuts and a command palette

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/keyboard-shortcuts

An app a reader uses every day earns shortcuts: a key to save, and one
key that opens a list of every command, which they filter by typing and
run with Enter. This page answers Ctrl+S (⌘S on a Mac) and opens its
palette on Ctrl+K (⌘K):

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. Paste it into a file under
`src/pages/` and open `/notes`.

```wf
type Command { id: String, label: String, keys: String }

const COMMANDS: [Command] = [
    Command(id: "new", label: "New note", keys: "mod+n"),
    Command(id: "save", label: "Save", keys: "mod+s"),
    Command(id: "dark", label: "Switch to dark", keys: ""),
    Command(id: "light", label: "Switch to light", keys: ""),
]

page Notes(path: "/notes", title: "Notes", description: "Notes, with a command palette on Ctrl+K.") {
    state open = false
    state search = ""
    state said = "Press Ctrl+K (⌘K on a Mac) for commands."
    derived shown = COMMANDS.filter(c => c.label.toLowerCase().includes(search.toLowerCase()))

    action run(id: String) {
        open = false
        search = ""
        if id == "dark" { setTheme("dark") }
        if id == "light" { setTheme("light") }
        said = "Ran “{COMMANDS.find(c => c.id == id)?.label ?? id}”."
    }

    on key("mod+k", e) {
        e.preventDefault()
        open = true
    }
    on key("mod+s", e) {
        e.preventDefault()
        run("save")
    }

    Heading("Notes").h1
    Text(said)
    Button("Commands") { on click { open = true } }

    Modal(visible: open, title: "Commands") {
        on close { open = false }
        Input(bind: search, label: "Find a command", autofocus: true).search {
            on keydown(e) {
                if e.key == "Enter" && shown.length > 0 { run(shown[0].id) }
            }
        }
        Stack(gap: .xs) {
            for c in shown by c.id {
                Button(c.label).full {
                    on click { run(c.id) }
                    if c.keys != "" { Text(keyLabel(c.keys)).muted.sm }
                }
            }
            if shown.length == 0 { Text("No command matches.").muted }
```
