  `[x](javascript\:alert\(1\))` is checked as the `javascript:alert(1)` URL
  it says, and drawn as its words.

Where a backslash is shown as written:

- before anything that is not ASCII punctuation, as in `C:\Users`;
- in a code span or a fence, where nothing is Markdown;
- at the end of a paragraph's, a heading's or a list item's last line,
  which has no line after it to break to.

A fence's language takes escapes too: `c\+\+` after the backticks is `c++`.

## Variations

### Show text somebody else wrote with `.inert`

Documentation from a language server, a `///` comment or a package's
readme is text somebody else wrote. It often has HTML entities in it, and
links and pictures that should not be followed or fetched from where you
show it. To show it, add `.inert`:

```wf
page Hover(path: "/", title: "Hover", description: "Documentation from a language server.") {
    state docs = "Returns a list of &lt;T&gt; &mdash; see [the guide](https://example.com/guide).\n\n![build](https://ci.example.com/badge.svg)"
    Heading("Hover").h1
    Markdown(docs).inert
}
```

It draws one paragraph, `Returns a list of <T> — see the guide.`, with no
link in it, and leaves the badge out. Under `.inert`:

- **Entities are decoded, then escaped.** `&lt;color&gt;` shows as
  `<color>`, and a `<script>`, written out or encoded, is shown as text. In
  `` `code` `` and in a fence an entity stays as written, as CommonMark
  leaves it. The named entities are the ones documentation is written
  with — `&lt;` `&gt;` `&amp;` `&quot;` `&apos;` `&nbsp;`, the dashes,
  quotes and arrows, and a few signs — and any numeric entity works
  (`&#60;`, `&#x3C;`).
- **A link is drawn as its words**, with no `<a>`.
- **A picture is left out**, with the space after it. A paragraph of
  nothing but pictures is left out with them.
- **Everything else is drawn as plain `Markdown` draws it**: paragraphs,
  fences, `code`, `**strong**`, `*em*` and `_em_`, headings, lists, quotes,
  rules and backslash escapes. A language server escapes its documentation
  this way: the CSS one writes `margin\-top` and
  `&lt;length\-percentage&gt;\{1,4\}`, which `.inert` shows as `margin-top`
  and `<length-percentage>{1,4}`. An escaped `&` begins no entity:
  `\&lt;` shows the four characters `&lt;`.

`inert:` also takes a value, `Markdown(docs, inert: untrusted)`, and
follows it. Plain `Markdown` is unchanged: an entity in it shows as it was
written, so a page that wrote `&lt;` to mean those four characters still
shows them.



---

# Reorder a list by dragging

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/reorder-by-dragging

To let the reader put a list in their own order, make each row something
they can pick up with `drag:`, and something another row can be dropped on
with `on receive`. This page lists today's jobs; drag a row above or below
another to move it, or use its arrow buttons:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. Paste it into a file under
`src/pages/` and open `/order`.

```wf
type Job { id: String, title: String }

page Order(path: "/order", title: "Today's order", description: "Drag the jobs into the order you will do them.") {
    state jobs: [Job] = [
        Job(id: "brief", title: "Write the brief"),
        Job(id: "call", title: "Call the printer"),
        Job(id: "proofs", title: "Check the proofs"),
    ]

    action move(id: String, target: String, position: String) {
        let moving = jobs.find(j => j.id == id)
        if moving == null { return }
        let rest = jobs.filter(j => j.id != id)
        let at = rest.findIndex(j => j.id == target)
        let index = if position == "after" { at + 1 } else { at }
        jobs = [...rest.slice(0, index), moving, ...rest.slice(index)]
    }

    action step(id: String, offset: Number) {
        let from = jobs.findIndex(j => j.id == id)
        let to = from + offset
        if to < 0 || to >= jobs.length { return }
        move(id, jobs[to].id, if offset > 0 { "after" } else { "before" })
    }

    Heading("Today's order").h1
    Stack(gap: .sm, role: "list") {
        for job, i in jobs by job.id {
            Card(drag: job.id, dropValue: job.id, role: "listitem") {
                on receive(d) { move(d.value, job.id, d.position) }
                Row(gap: .sm, align: .center) {
                    Icon("grid")
                    Text("{i + 1}. {job.title}")
                    Spacer
                    IconButton(icon: "chevron-up", label: "Move {job.title} up", disabled: i == 0).sm {
                        on click { step(job.id, -1) }
                    }
                    IconButton(icon: "chevron-down", label: "Move {job.title} down", disabled: i == jobs.length - 1).sm {
                        on click { step(job.id, 1) }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

## How it works

- `drag: job.id` makes each `Card` something the reader can pick up: with a
  mouse, by moving it a few pixels; with a finger or a pen, by holding it
  still for a moment. While it moves, the runtime draws a ghost of the row
  and a line where it would land, and Escape puts it back.
- `on receive(d)` on the same `Card` makes every row a place to drop one.
  `d.value` is the dropped row's `drag:` value (the job's `id`), and
  `d.position` is `"before"` or `"after"`: which half of this row the
  pointer was over.
- `move` takes the job out of the list and puts it back next to the row it
  was dropped on. It builds a new list rather than changing the old one in
  place, so everything that reads `jobs` draws again. The `for … by job.id`
  keeps each row's nodes and moves them, so nothing is redrawn from
  scratch.
- Dragging needs a pointer. The arrow buttons do the same move from the
  keyboard, and their labels name the job (`Move Write the brief up`), so a
  screen reader says which row each one moves. The first row's up button
  and the last row's down button are disabled.
- `role: "list"` and `role: "listitem"` tell a screen reader the cards are
  a list, and how many items it has.

The new order lasts as long as the page is open. To keep it across visits,
make the list a `persist` instead of a `state`:
`persist jobs: [Job] = [ … ]`.

## Variations

- **Drop onto a row, not between rows**: add `dropInside: true` to the
  `Card`. A drop over the row's middle then has `d.position == "inside"`,
  which is how a file tree moves a file into a folder.
- **A strip across the page**, such as tabs: give each item
  `dropAxis: .x`, so `before` and `after` are its left and right halves.
- **Two lists that must not mix**: give the rows of each its own
  `dragGroup: "todo"` and `dragGroup: "done"`. A row is dropped only on a
  row of its group.
- **Show where it will land as it moves**: `dropValue: job.id`, already on
  each row, names it. Add `on dragmove(d)` to the `Card`: the dragged row
  hears `d.over`, the `dropValue` of the row under the pointer (`null` over
  nothing), and can show it.

To check the arrow buttons, write a test that clicks one
([Test a page](/recipes/test-a-page)):

```wf no-check
test "a job moves down" {
    Order
    expect "1. Write the brief"
    click "Move Write the brief down"
    expect "1. Call the printer"
    expect "2. Write the brief"
}
```

That test needs the page above in the same project, so it is not compiled
on its own here.



---

# Make navigation responsive

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/responsive-navigation

A row of links fits a laptop but not a phone. To show the links on a wide
screen and a menu button that opens them on a narrow one, branch on
`viewport`:

**Needs:** nothing besides this code. It is a whole project's `app` and
pages: paste it into a new project, replacing `src/App.wf` and the
starter's pages.

```wf
app {
    state open = false
    if viewport.md {
        Row(gap: .md) {
            Link("Home", to: "/")
            Link("Docs", to: "/docs")
            Link("Pricing", to: "/pricing")
        }
    } else {
        IconButton(icon: "menu", label: "Open navigation", aria-expanded: open, aria-controls: "nav-menu") {
            on click { open = !open }
        }
        show open {
            Stack(gap: .sm, animate: .slideDown, id: "nav-menu") {
                on click { open = false }
                Link("Home", to: "/")
                Link("Docs", to: "/docs")
                Link("Pricing", to: "/pricing")
            }
        }
    }
    Router
}

page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "Navigation that fits the screen.") { Heading("Home").h1 }
page Docs(path: "/docs", title: "Docs", description: "How it works.") { Heading("Docs").h1 }
page Pricing(path: "/pricing", title: "Pricing", description: "What it costs.") { Heading("Pricing").h1 }
```

On a wide window the three links sit in a row above every page. Narrow the
window and they give way to a menu button; press it and the links slide
down beneath it.

## How it works

- [`viewport.md`](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity#the-browser-as-values)
  is true while the window is at least the `md` breakpoint wide. The
  runtime updates it when a breakpoint is crossed, so the `if` swaps the
  row for the button as the window narrows.
- On a narrow screen, the `IconButton` toggles `open`. Its `label:` is the
  button's accessible name, since the icon has no text, and
  `aria-expanded: open` tells a screen reader whether the menu it controls
  (`aria-controls`, the `Stack`'s `id`) is open.
- `show open` keeps the links in the page and hides them while `open` is
  false. `animate: .slideDown` plays as they appear, and a click on a link
  closes the menu again.
- The navigation is in `app`, around the `Router`, so every page shows it
  and `open` lives on from page to page.

The pre-rendered page does not know the window's width, so what depends on
`viewport` is drawn once the page is live. For layout alone — a row that
becomes a column — prefer
[responsive values](/learn/13-styling#responsive-values), which are
right in the first paint.

The three pages are there so every link lands on one; in a site of your
own the links name the pages you have.



---

# Review a site's security before you deploy

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/review-security

The compiler refuses most of what would make a page unsafe on every build
([Security](/about/security)). What it cannot see — what the project
chose to trust, the host's headers, the server's checks — is a review, and
`wf audit` prints what that review asks for:

```bash
wf audit
```

## How it works

`wf audit` lists:

- every `Unsafe.*`, and whether it is sanitised;
- the project's own scripts, and the names each declares;
- every origin the pages load from;
- everything written to the reader's machine, and where;
- every `env` name, and whether it is public;
- the policy this build ships;
- what the compiler itself depends on.

Add `--json` to get the same report for a tool. `wf audit` only reports; it
never fails a build.

## Before you deploy

- Run `wf audit`, and read all of it.
- Set `"csp": true`, and make sure the build passes its own check.
- Check that `_headers` reaches your host, or set the same headers
  another way ([Set cache and security headers](/recipes/cache-and-security-headers)).
- Serve over HTTPS, with HSTS.
- Keep the session in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie — not in
  `persist` ([Sign in with a session cookie](/recipes/sign-in-with-a-session-cookie)).
- Read no non-public `env` name in a page (the build refuses one).
- Make sure every `Unsafe.Html` is sanitised, or provably your own
  markup ([Show HTML from outside the project](/recipes/show-html-from-outside)).
- Check authorisation on the server for every request, not with
  `guard:`.
- Have the server check uploads: the type from the file's bytes, not its
  name; a size limit it enforces itself; a stored name it generates, never
  the one it was given; and storage nothing is served from.

After the deploy, [check the headers it sends](/recipes/check-a-deploy).



---

# Animate route changes

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/route-transitions

Fade or slide from one page to the next, on every route change, by giving
the `Router` a `transition:` and a `duration:` in `app`:

**Needs:** nothing besides the code, which is a whole project's `app` and
pages: paste it into a new project, replacing `src/App.wf` and
`src/pages/Home.wf`.

```wf
app {
    Navbar {
        Navbar.Brand { Link("Motion", to: "/") }
        Navbar.Links { Link("Home", to: "/")  Link("About", to: "/about") }
    }
    Router(transition: .fade, duration: "200ms")
}

page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "The front page.") { Heading("Home").h1 }
page About(path: "/about", title: "About", description: "Who we are.") { Heading("About").h1 }
```

## How it works

- `transition:` is `.fade`, `.slide` or `.none` (the next page replaces the
  last at once). `duration:` is how long the change takes.
- On each route change the old page plays out and the new one in; then
  focus and scroll settle and the new title is announced.
- Where the browser has the View Transitions API, the change plays through
  it: the browser's own crossfade, or the slide the engine's stylesheet
  defines for `[data-wf-transition="slide"]`. Your own
  `::view-transition-*` rules in a project stylesheet may restyle either.
  In other browsers, a class-based animation plays instead.

A reader who asked for reduced motion gets no route transition: the next
page replaces the last at once
([Respect reduced motion](/recipes/motion-defaults#respect-reduced-motion)).

## Variations

### Slide instead of fade

`.slide` slides the old page out and the new one in:

```wf
app {
    Navbar {
        Navbar.Brand { Link("Motion", to: "/") }
        Navbar.Links { Link("Home", to: "/")  Link("About", to: "/about") }
    }
    Router(transition: .slide, duration: "250ms")
}

page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "The front page.") { Heading("Home").h1 }
page About(path: "/about", title: "About", description: "Who we are.") { Heading("About").h1 }
```

# Run a script in a worker

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/run-a-worker

A `worker` runs a script of your site beside the page, off its thread, so
slow work — a language service, a parser, anything that would make typing
stutter — never holds up the page. It is held like a socket: owned by what
opened it, and stopped when that leaves. Here a store holds one for the
whole app, and a page shows what it reports:

**Needs:** the worker's script at `public/workers/css.js`, which [How it
works](#how-it-works) shows. It claims `/`: paste it into a new project,
or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
store Lang {
    state problems: [Map] = []
    state restarts = 0
    worker css = spawn("/workers/css.js", restart: 1, timeout: 5000) {
        on message(m) { if m.type == "diagnostics" { problems = m.items } }
        on restart(e) { restarts = restarts + 1 }
    }
    action complete(text: String, at: Number) {
        return await css.request("complete", { text: text, at: at }, { supersede: true })
    }
    action check(text: String) { css.send({ method: "check", params: { text: text } }) }
}

page Editor(path: "/", title: "Editor", description: "A worker beside the page.") {
    Heading("Editor").h1
    match Lang.css {
        open     { Text(if Lang.css.pending > 0 { "Checking…" } else { "Checked" }) }
        error(e) { Alert("The CSS service stopped: {e.message}").danger }
        else     { Text("Stopped") }
    }
    Text("{Lang.problems.length} problems, {Lang.restarts} restarts")
    Button("Complete") { on click { Lang.complete("a { col", 7) } }
    Button("Check") { on click { Lang.check("a { col") } }
}
```

## How it works

The worker's side is a plain script under `public/` — the one place,
besides a project script, where you write JavaScript by hand:

```js
// public/workers/css.js
self.onmessage = ({ data }) => {
  const { id, method, params, cancel } = data;
  if (cancel !== undefined) return;                       // a newer request took over
  if (method === "complete") self.postMessage({ id, result: complete(params) });
  if (method === "check") self.postMessage({ type: "diagnostics", items: check(params.text) });
};
```

- **`worker css = spawn("/workers/css.js", …)`**, declared in the store,
  starts the script when the store is first read and stops it with the
  store.
- **`restart: 1`** and **`timeout: 5000`** say how often a crashed worker is
  started again and how long a request may wait for its answer.
- **`match Lang.css`** reads the worker's `.state`: `open`, `error` (the
  `error(e)` arm) or `closed`. **`Lang.css.pending`** is how many requests
  are out.

The page and the worker talk in three ways:

- **Ask and wait: `.request(method, params)`.** It posts
  `{ id, method, params }` and returns a promise of what the worker posts
  back as `{ id, result }`. A reply of `{ id, error }` rejects it, with the
  error's `message` and its `data`. A request not answered within
  `timeout:` fails — 10 seconds when unset, or `{ timeout }` on the
  request. With `{ supersede: true }`, a newer request of the same method
  fails the older one, and the worker is posted `{ cancel: id }`. The
  store's `complete` action asks this way.
- **Tell: `.send(value)`.** It posts the value and expects nothing. The
  store's `check` action tells this way.
- **Listen: messages with no `id`.** What the worker posts without an `id`
  is a message: `on message(m)` hears it, and `.last(kind)` is the last of
  a kind, by its `type` or its `method`. The `diagnostics` the script posts
  arrive this way.

A worker that crashes — an error nothing in it caught — fails every request
that was out and is started again, up to `restart:` times, running
`on restart(e)` each time. Past that it is `error`, and `on error(e)` runs.
`.restart()` starts it again by hand, and `.close()` stops it.

Pass `type: .module` to start a module worker. The script is a file of the
site, so it is asked for under the base path, and a name `public/` does not
have is a `D01`.



---

# Describe pages to search engines and link previews

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/search-and-link-previews

The build writes each page's head — its title, description, canonical
link, Open Graph and Twitter tags, JSON-LD and icons — from the page's
attributes and the `meta` settings in `webfluent.app.json`, so what a search
result or a shared link shows is set where the page is declared. This blog
has a home page with its own sharing image, a page per post that adds tags
of its own, and a thanks page kept out of search:

**Needs:** `src/posts.json` and the pictures it names in `public/`, and
`meta.site_url` in `webfluent.app.json`, each shown below. It claims `/`
and the name `Home`: paste it into a new project, or replace the starter's
`src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
type Post { slug: String, title: String, summary: String, cover: String, date: String, body: String }

const SITE = "https://acme.example"

data posts: [Post] = "posts.json"

page Home(path: "/", title: "Acme", description: "Tools for small teams.", image: "/og-default.png", image_alt: "The Acme logo on a blue field") {
    Heading("Acme").h1
    for p in posts by p.slug {
        Link(p.title, to: "/posts/{p.slug}")
    }
}

page PostPage(path: "/posts/:slug", slug: String, type: "article", paths: posts.map(p => p.slug),
              title: "{posts.find(p => p.slug == slug)?.title ?? slug} — Acme",
              description: "{posts.find(p => p.slug == slug)?.summary ?? "A post from the blog."}") {
    derived post = posts.find(p => p.slug == slug)
    head {
        meta(property: "og:image", content: "{SITE}{post?.cover ?? "/og-default.png"}")
        meta(property: "article:published_time", content: post?.date ?? "")
    }
    if let p = post {
        Image(src: p.cover, alt: p.title)
        Heading(p.title).h1
        Text(format(p.date, .date, "long")).muted
        Markdown(p.body)
    }
}

page Thanks(path: "/thanks", title: "Thanks", description: "Your message reached us.", noindex: true) {
    Heading("Thanks").h1
}
```

The posts are a JSON file the build reads, `src/posts.json`; a list of one
is enough to try it:

```json
[
  {
    "slug": "hello",
    "title": "Hello, world",
    "summary": "Why we started Acme, and what we make.",
    "cover": "/covers/hello.png",
    "date": "2026-03-05",
    "body": "We make *tools* for small teams."
  }
]
```

Put the pictures it names in `public/` (`public/og-default.png`,
`public/covers/hello.png`), and set `meta.site_url` as the config below
does. Built, `posts/hello/index.html` is titled "Hello, world — Acme",
its description is the post's summary, and its `og:image` is
`https://acme.example/covers/hello.png`.

## How it works

Each page's `title:` and `description:` are its `<title>` and the snippet a
search result shows; `image:` and `image_alt:` are its sharing card's
picture; `type: "article"` marks a post; `noindex: true` keeps a page out of
search. The rest comes from `meta` in `webfluent.app.json`. A config that
fills in every site-wide setting:

```json
{
  "meta": {
    "title": "Acme",
    "description": "Tools for small teams.",
    "lang": "en",
    "site_url": "https://acme.example",
    "site_name": "Acme Inc.",
    "owner": "organization",
    "same_as": ["https://github.com/acme"],
    "image": "/og-default.png",
    "image_alt": "The Acme logo on a blue field",
    "favicon": "/favicon.svg",
    "touch_icon": "/apple-touch-icon.png",
    "sitemap": true,
    "fonts": ["https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter&display=swap"],
    "stylesheets": ["/print.css"]
  }
}
```

What the build writes into each page's head:

- **`<title>` and `<meta name="description">`**, from the page's `title:`
  and `description:`. The description is the snippet a search result shows
  and a link preview quotes; keep it under about 150 characters.
- **A canonical link and `og:url`**, when `site_url` is set. A relative
  canonical is worse than none, so without `site_url` the build writes
  none.
- **Open Graph and Twitter card tags**: `og:title`, `og:description`,
  `og:image` (the page's `image:` or the site's), `og:type` from `type:`
  (`website` or `article`), `og:site_name`, and `og:locale` in the form
  Open Graph reads — `meta.lang` `en` is `en_US`, `en-GB` is `en_GB`, `ar`
  is `ar_AR` — with an `og:locale:alternate` for each other locale.
- **The image's size and description**: `og:image:width` and
  `og:image:height`, read from the file when the image is in `public/` (one
  on another origin is not fetched, so its card states no size), and
  `og:image:alt` and `twitter:image:alt` from the page's `image_alt:`, or
  `meta.image_alt` for the site's image. A sharing image is best at
  1200×630.
- **JSON-LD**: the site's owner, a `WebSite` it publishes, a `WebPage` or
  `Article`, and a `BreadcrumbList` derived from the route's segments. Each
  breadcrumb is a page a reader can open; a level no route answers is left
  out.
- **`hreflang` alternates** for the page and each of its translations
  (`translates:`), each at its own address and in its own `lang:`, with
  `x-default` for the one in the site's language
  ([A page in its own language](/recipes/site-in-two-languages)).
- **The icons**: `<link rel="icon">` for `favicon` (typed, so an SVG is
  read as one) and `<link rel="apple-touch-icon">` for `touch_icon`. Each
  is linked from the site's root under the `base_path`
  (`/my-site/favicon.svg`), so it stays right when the router moves the
  page to another address.
- **`<meta name="robots" content="noindex">`**, and no sitemap entry, for a
  `noindex: true` page.

### Add tags for one page

To add tags of a page's own — an article's cover, its publication date —
write them in `head { }` ([Pages and routing](/learn/05-pages-and-routing#per-page-head-tags)).
`PostPage` above sets its own Open Graph image from the post. A link
preview fetches the image from another site, so its address must be
absolute: `{SITE}` puts the site's origin in front of the post's
site-relative cover. A tag written in `head { }` takes the place of the
one the build would write, so the page carries one `og:image`.

The `title:` and `description:` of a `:param` page may name its
parameters — `title: "{slug} — Blog"` — and each pre-rendered file, and the
live page's tab, has that route's value. The title may also splice an
expression over the parameters and the program's constants and data, as
`PostPage`'s does, and so may the description. The build works it out for
each file, and the router again on each visit. `image:` is written as it
stands, so a picture that depends on the parameter goes in `head { }`.
Anything else the head should say about the entry goes in `head { }`, as
above; the runtime keeps those tags current as the parameter changes.

### Say who the site belongs to

The JSON-LD names the site's owner: `meta.site_name`, published as an
`Organization` unless `meta.owner` says it is a person. To publish a
personal site, name the person, what they do and where else they are:

```json
{
  "meta": {
    "site_url": "https://ada.example",
    "site_name": "Ada Lovelace",
    "owner": "person",
    "job_title": "Analyst",
    "same_as": ["https://github.com/ada", "https://www.linkedin.com/in/ada/"]
  }
}
```

The JSON-LD then holds a `Person` (`@id` `…/#person`) with `jobTitle` and
`sameAs`. The `WebSite`'s `publisher` and every `WebPage`'s `about` point
at it. An organisation's `WebSite` names it as `publisher` too, and takes
`same_as` for its profiles.

To say anything else schema.org allows about a person or an organisation,
add it to `meta.owner_details`. It is merged into the node as written:

```json
{
  "meta": {
    "owner_details": {
      "alternateName": "Augusta Ada King",
      "worksFor": [{ "@type": "Organization", "name": "Analytical Engines" }],
      "alumniOf": { "@type": "CollegeOrUniversity", "name": "University of London" },
      "knowsAbout": ["Mathematics", "Computing"],
      "knowsLanguage": ["en", "fr"]
    }
  }
}
```

What the node is — `@type`, `@id`, `name`, `url` — and what `job_title` and
`same_as` write come from those settings; setting one in `owner_details`
is `E111`.

> [!WARNING]
> Structured data has to agree with what the pages show, and the build
> cannot check that. State in `owner_details` only what the site says too.

### Preload fonts served from the site

A font named by a `@font-face` in a project `.css` file is found only once
`styles.css` has arrived and been read. To fetch it with the page instead,
list it in `meta.preload`:

```json
{ "meta": { "preload": ["/fonts/inter-latin.woff2"] } }
```

```css
/* src/fonts.css */
@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  font-weight: 400 800;
  font-display: swap;
  src: url("/fonts/inter-latin.woff2") format("woff2");
}
```

Each path becomes a `<link rel="preload">` in every page's head, ahead of
the stylesheets, with `as` taken from its extension: `font`, `style`,
`script` or `image`. A font preload also carries `crossorigin`, without
which the browser fetches the font twice.

Serving the fonts from `public/` instead of a font service also takes a
third-party stylesheet and two connections out of the way of the first
paint. A path on another origin is `E111`: the policy the build ships
would refuse it.

### Keep addresses from redirecting

A static build writes `/contact` as `contact/index.html`. Most static
hosts — GitHub Pages among them — answer `/contact` with a `301` redirect
to `/contact/`. A canonical link, a sitemap entry and every link that names
`/contact` then name an address that redirects, which a search engine reads
as "not this page". To fix it, set `build.clean_urls` to one of two values:

```json
{ "build": { "ssg": true, "clean_urls": "file" } }
```

- **`"file"`** keeps `/contact` and writes `contact.html` beside
  `contact/index.html`, which the host serves for `/contact` directly. The
  page then addresses its scripts and sheets from the site's root
  (`/app.js`, under the `base_path`), so the one file reads the same from
  either address.
- **`"directory"`** names every route with its slash: the canonical link,
  `og:url`, the sitemap, the breadcrumbs, the `hreflang` alternates, and
  every `Link(to:)`, `Sidebar.Item(to:)` and `navigate()` whose target is
  one of the site's pages (`/contact` becomes `/contact/`). A file such as
  `/cv.pdf`, another origin, or an address worked out whole at run time is
  left as written.

Unset, the addresses are `/contact` and the files `contact/index.html`.
That is right for a host that serves the directory without a redirect:
Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, and Vercel with `cleanUrls`.

## A checklist for being found

- Set `meta.site_url`. Without it there are no canonical links, no sitemap
  and no absolute sharing URLs.
- Give every page a `title:` and a `description:` of about 150 characters.
  `S01`–`S03` warn when one is missing or too long.
- Pre-render with `build.ssg: true`, so the text is in the HTML.
- Use one `h1` per page, with headings in order (`A11`, `A12`).
- Give every shared page an `image:`, or set `meta.image` for the site — at
  1200 × 630 pixels, which suits most previews — in `public/`, so its size
  is in the card, with an `image_alt:` (or `meta.image_alt`) that says what
  it shows.
- On GitHub Pages and hosts like it, set `build.clean_urls`, so the
  canonical address never redirects.
- For a personal site, set `meta.owner: "person"`, with `job_title`,
  `same_as` and, for the rest of who they are, `owner_details`.
- Serve web fonts from `public/`, named in `meta.preload`, instead of a
  font service's stylesheet.
- Set `noindex: true` on pages that should not be found: sign-in, thanks,
  drafts.
- Check the result: view a built page's source, and paste a URL into a
  link-preview debugger.



---

# Send a message as the page unloads

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/send-on-unload

`beacon(url, data)` records that something happened even when the reader
is leaving — an analytics event, a "reader left" signal. A `fetch` started
as the page unloads is cancelled; a beacon is delivered. This checkout page
sends one when the reader leaves it, whether they close the tab, go to
another site or switch away:

```wf
page Checkout(path: "/checkout", title: "Checkout", description: "Pay for the order.") {
    state paid = false

    on visibilitychange {
        if document.visibilityState == "hidden" {
            beacon("/analytics", { event: "left-checkout", paid: paid })
        }
    }

    Heading("Checkout").h1
    Button("Pay").primary { on click { paid = true } }
}
```

## How it works

`beacon` posts a small body with `navigator.sendBeacon`, which the browser
delivers even as the page unloads, where a `fetch` would be cancelled. It
returns nothing to wait for: the page goes on, and so may the reader.

`on visibilitychange`, written at the top of the page, listens on the
document for as long as the page shows. The page turns `hidden` whenever
the reader leaves it: closing the tab, following a link to another site,
switching tabs or apps, or locking the phone. That is the last moment a
page can count on, and the one browsers recommend for this; `unload` and
`beforeunload` often never fire on a phone. Because a hidden page may come
back, the beacon can be sent more than once for one visit: count visits on
the server, or keep a `state sent = false` and send only the first time.
Going to another page of the same site does not hide the document, so it
sends nothing; the listener stops with the page.

### Send on a click instead

To record a step the reader takes, send the beacon from the handler. The
request still arrives if the click also takes the reader away:

```wf
page Pay(path: "/pay", title: "Pay", description: "Pay for the order.") {
    Heading("Pay").h1
    Button("Pay").primary { on click { beacon("/analytics", { event: "checkout", value: 42 }) } }
}
```



---

# Serve a site with Apache

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/serve-with-apache

This recipe serves a WebFluent build with Apache, configured by an
`.htaccess` file that ships with the build.

You need an Apache host with `mod_rewrite` and `mod_headers`, and a
`build/` folder from `wf build`
([Install wf on a build machine](/recipes/install-wf-in-ci)).

Put this in `public/.htaccess`:

```apache
Options -MultiViews
RewriteEngine On
# A single-page build:
# RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
# RewriteRule ^ /index.html [L]
ErrorDocument 404 /404.html
Header always set X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
Header always set X-Frame-Options "DENY"
Header always set Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
```

Then upload `build/` to the site's document root.

## How it works

1. The build copies `public/.htaccess` to the root of `build/`, so it
   lands in the document root with the site.
2. For a single-page build, uncomment the two rewrite lines: a path that
   is no file is answered with `index.html`, where the router draws the
   page.
3. `ErrorDocument 404 /404.html` serves the page whose `path` is `*`.
4. The `Header` lines send security headers the build writes to
   `build/_headers` ([Set cache and security headers](/recipes/cache-and-security-headers#set-security-headers)).

## Variations

Compress the text files one of two ways:

- Turn on `mod_deflate`, which compresses on the way out. This is the
  simplest, and covers every text file.
- Serve the `.gz` files the build wrote, so Apache compresses nothing
  itself. `Options MultiViews` does not do it: content negotiation only
  runs when the file asked for does not exist, and `app.js` does. Add these
  lines after `RewriteEngine On`, before the single-page lines, as Apache's
  own `mod_deflate` documentation does it:

  ```apache
  # The build's app.js.gz for app.js, when the browser accepts gzip
  RewriteCond "%{HTTP:Accept-Encoding}" "gzip"
  RewriteCond "%{REQUEST_FILENAME}.gz" -s
  RewriteRule "^(.*)\.(css|js)$" "$1.$2.gz" [QSA]

  # Sent with the right type, and not compressed a second time
  RewriteRule "\.css\.gz$" "-" [T=text/css,E=no-gzip:1]
  RewriteRule "\.js\.gz$" "-" [T=text/javascript,E=no-gzip:1]

  <FilesMatch "\.(css|js)\.gz$">
      Header append Content-Encoding gzip
      Header append Vary Accept-Encoding
  </FilesMatch>
  ```

  This covers the scripts and stylesheets, the largest files. Pages are
  asked for by their folder (`/contact/`), which the rule cannot see as a
  file, so leave `mod_deflate` on for HTML.

## Check it

`curl -I` a page and check for `X-Content-Type-Options`,
`X-Frame-Options` and `Referrer-Policy`. With the `.gz` rules,
`curl -sI -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" https://example.com/app.js` answers
`Content-Encoding: gzip` and `Content-Type: text/javascript`. Open a path that does not exist and check that you get
the site's `404.html`. Then go through [Check a deploy](/recipes/check-a-deploy).



---

# Serve a site with Caddy

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/serve-with-caddy

This recipe serves a WebFluent build with Caddy, which also gets and
renews the site's TLS certificate.

You need a server running Caddy, and a `build/` folder from `wf build`
([Install wf on a build machine](/recipes/install-wf-in-ci)).

Add a site block to the `Caddyfile`:

```text
example.com {
    root * /var/www/site
    encode gzip
    file_server {
        precompressed gzip
    }
    try_files {path} {path}/ {path}.html /index.html
    header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff
}
```

Then upload `build/` to `/var/www/site` and reload Caddy.

## How it works

1. `root` is the folder the build is uploaded to.
2. `precompressed gzip` serves the `.gz` files the build wrote; `encode
   gzip` compresses on the way out what has none.
3. `try_files` decides what a path reaches: the file, the folder's
   `index.html`, the `.html` file `clean_urls: "file"` writes, and last
   `/index.html`, the single-page fallback.
4. `header` sends a security header; add the others from
   `build/_headers` the same way
   ([Set cache and security headers](/recipes/cache-and-security-headers#set-security-headers)).

## Variations

For a static build, remove `/index.html` from the end of `try_files`, so
an unknown path is a 404.

## Check it

Open a deep link directly and reload it, then check the headers with
`curl -I`. Then go through [Check a deploy](/recipes/check-a-deploy).



---

# Serve a site with nginx

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/serve-with-nginx

This recipe serves a WebFluent build from a server of your own with nginx:
the precompressed files the build wrote, its 404 page, and the cache and
security headers.

You need a server running nginx with a TLS certificate for the site, and a
`build/` folder from `wf build`
([Install wf on a build machine](/recipes/install-wf-in-ci)).

Put the security headers in a file of their own, so every block that
needs them can include them:

```nginx
# /etc/nginx/snippets/site-headers.conf
add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff always;
add_header Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin always;
add_header X-Frame-Options DENY always;
# add_header Content-Security-Policy "…as in build/_headers…" always;
```

Then add this `server` block, and pick the `try_files` line for your kind
of build:

```nginx
server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    server_name example.com;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;
    root /var/www/site;

    gzip_static on;                          # serve the .gz files the build wrote
    include snippets/site-headers.conf;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ $uri.html =404; # a static build
        # try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;  # a single-page build
    }
    error_page 404 /404.html;

    location = /sw.js {
        include snippets/site-headers.conf;
        add_header Cache-Control "no-cache";
    }

    # Pictures the build resized and renamed: hero.4a6178a1.960.webp, hero.4a6178a1.jpg
    location ~* "\.[0-9a-f]{8}(\.[0-9]+)?\.(webp|avif|jpe?g|png|gif)$" {
        include snippets/site-headers.conf;
        add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable";
    }
}
```

Upload the build with any tool — for example, `rsync` — and reload nginx:

```bash
rsync -a --delete build/ server:/var/www/site/
```

## How it works

1. `root` is the folder the build is uploaded to.
2. `gzip_static on` sends the `.gz` file the build wrote beside a text
   file when the browser accepts gzip, so nginx compresses nothing itself.
3. `try_files` decides what a path reaches. In a static build, `/contact`
   is `contact/index.html` (`$uri/`) or, with `clean_urls: "file"`,
   `contact.html` (`$uri.html`); anything else is a 404. In a single-page
   build, every path falls back to `index.html`, where the router draws the
   page.
4. `error_page 404 /404.html` serves the page whose `path` is `*`.
5. `sw.js` is never cached without asking. The pictures the build resized
   and renamed (`img/hero.<hash>.<width>.webp`, and the original as
   `img/hero.<hash>.jpg`) are cached for a year, since a changed picture
   gets a new name. A file of `public/` keeps the name you gave it, so it is
   left to the browser's usual checks: a new `/logo.png` reaches readers at
   once ([Set cache headers](/recipes/cache-and-security-headers#set-cache-headers)).
6. The `add_header` lines are the security headers the build writes to
   `build/_headers`. Copy the `Content-Security-Policy` line from that file
   into the commented line to send the policy as a header too.
7. nginx drops the server's `add_header` lines in any `location` that has
   an `add_header` of its own. That is why the two locations that set
   `Cache-Control` include the headers file again: without it, `sw.js` and
   the pictures would be sent with no security headers.
8. `ssl_certificate` and `ssl_certificate_key` name the certificate the
   `listen 443 ssl` line needs; the paths above are where Certbot puts
   them.

`rsync -a --delete` makes the server's folder match `build/`, removing
files an older build left behind.

## Check it

`curl -I` a page and check the headers. Ask for a compressed copy and check
that nginx sends the build's `.gz` file:

```bash
curl -sI -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" https://example.com/app.js
```

The response has `Content-Encoding: gzip`. Then go through
[Check a deploy](/recipes/check-a-deploy).



---

# Listen to server-sent events

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/server-sent-events

A `stream` receives a one-way flow of events from a server — prices,
progress, a log — over server-sent events. Use it when the server talks and
the page only listens; for two-way messages, [open a socket](/recipes/open-a-socket).
This page shows the latest price as it arrives:

**Needs:** a server that sends events named `price` from `/events`.

```wf
page Prices(path: "/prices", title: "Prices", description: "Live prices.") {
    state price = 0
    stream ticks = sse("/events", events: ["price"])
    effect { if let p = ticks.last("price") { price = p } }

    Heading("Prices").h1
    match ticks {
        open { Text("Price: {price}") }
        else { Text("Connecting…").muted }
    }
}
```

## How it works

- **`stream ticks = sse("/events", events: ["price"])`** opens the stream
  when the page is drawn and closes it when the reader leaves. `events:`
  names the event types to listen for; only those names are listened to.
- **`ticks.last("price")`** is the latest event of that name. Each event
  name is kept apart, so it is the last price and not the last event of any
  kind; `ticks.last()` is the last unnamed message. The `effect` copies it
  into `price` each time a new one arrives.
- **`match ticks`** reads the stream's state, with the same arms as a
  socket: `connecting`, `open`, `closed(c)`, `error(e)`, or an `else`.

`ticks.messages` holds the messages in order — the last 500, or as many as
`keep:` says. A message whose data parses as JSON arrives as a value.

The browser reconnects a stream on its own and resumes from the last event
id the server sent. Pass `credentials: true` to send the site's cookies
with the request.



---

# Carry an element across a route change

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/shared-element

Have the browser carry one element from one page to the next — a cover
picture in a list of posts that grows into the article's header — instead
of fading it out and back in. Give it the same `shared:` name on both
pages:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
type Post { id: String, slug: String, title: String, cover: String }

const posts: [Post] = [
    Post(id: "1", slug: "slow-roasting", title: "Slow roasting", cover: "/roast.jpg"),
]

page Blog(path: "/", title: "Blog", description: "Every post.") {
    Heading("Blog").h1
    for post in posts by post.id {
        Link(to: "/p/{post.slug}") {
            Image(src: post.cover, alt: post.title, shared: "cover-{post.id}")
            Text(post.title)
        }
    }
}

page Article(path: "/p/:slug", title: "Post", description: "One post.", slug: String) {
    if let post = posts.find(p => p.slug == slug) {
        Heading(post.title).h1
        Image(src: post.cover, alt: post.title, shared: "cover-{post.id}")
    } else {
        Heading("Not found").h1
    }
}
```

## How it works

- The `Blog` page draws each cover with `shared: "cover-{post.id}"`, and
  the `Article` page draws the same post's cover under the same name.
- When the route changes from one to the other, the browser moves the
  element from its old place and size to its new one.
- Both elements must carry the same name, and only one element on a page
  may carry each name — which is why the name here includes the post's
  `id`. If the two pages give it different names, or two elements on one
  page carry the same name, the element crossfades instead of moving.



---

# Show a carousel

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/show-a-carousel

Show pictures or panels one at a time, with buttons to move between them
and, if you want, advancing on their own. Wrap each slide in a
`Carousel.Slide` inside a `Carousel`.

This page shows three photographs that advance every five seconds:

**Needs:** `one.jpg`, `two.jpg` and `three.jpg` in `public/`. It claims
`/`: paste it into a new project, or replace the starter's
`src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Gallery(path: "/", title: "Gallery", description: "Three pictures.") {
    Heading("Gallery").h1
    Carousel(label: "Recent work", autoplay: true, interval: 5000) {
        Carousel.Slide { Image(src: "/one.jpg", alt: "A bridge at dusk") }
        Carousel.Slide { Image(src: "/two.jpg", alt: "The harbour from above") }
        Carousel.Slide { Image(src: "/three.jpg", alt: "Rain on the market") }
    }
}
```

## How it works

- **Each `Carousel.Slide` is one slide**, shown one at a time.
- **The controls come with it.** A carousel has a named previous button, a
  named next button, and a dot per slide.
- **`label:` names it.** Its `label:` names the region for screen readers.
  It is a `region` described as a carousel, unless you set its `role:` or
  `aria-roledescription:` yourself.
- **`autoplay` advances it** every `interval:` milliseconds. With
  `autoplay`, the carousel also has a button that stops it. It pauses while
  the pointer or the keyboard focus is on it, and it does not advance at
  all for a reader who asked for reduced motion.



---

# Show another page in a frame

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/show-a-page-in-a-frame

Show another page inside yours (a video player, a map, a preview your app
builds) with `Frame`, and hear what that page posts back.

This page embeds a video player and a preview of the site's own, and shows
what the preview sends back. The player is on another origin, so the
config names it in `meta.frame`; without it, the page's
Content-Security-Policy blocks the frame and it stays blank:

**Needs:** the `meta.frame` setting below in `webfluent.app.json`, and a
page at `/preview/` for the second frame to show.

```json
{ "meta": { "frame": ["https://www.youtube-nocookie.com"] } }
```

```wf
page Talk(path: "/", title: "The talk", description: "The launch talk, and what the preview says.") {
    state heard = ""
    Heading("The talk").h1
    Frame(src: "https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/dQw4w9WgXcQ", title: "The launch talk", allow: "fullscreen")
    Frame(src: "/preview/", title: "Preview", sandbox: "allow-scripts") {
        on message(m) { heard = m.data }
    }
    Text(heard)
}
```

## How it works

- `title:` says what the frame shows. A screen reader announces a frame by
  its title, and a frame without one draws an `A17` warning.
- `on message(m)` hears what the framed page posts with
  `window.parent.postMessage(…)`, and nothing that any other page posts.
  `m.data` is what it sent.
- `sandbox:` limits what the framed page may do: `"allow-scripts
  allow-forms"` allows scripts and forms, and an empty string allows
  nothing.
- `allow:` names the browser features the framed page may use.

A frame from another origin must be named in `meta.frame`, or the page's
Content-Security-Policy refuses it ([Security](/about/security)).
The build and `wf check` do not warn about a missing one: the frame is
simply blank in the browser. `meta.frame` takes origins only
(`https://www.youtube-nocookie.com`), not paths.

### Frame your own pages

A page of your own site (`src: "/preview/"`) needs no extra setting. The
site's pages are served refusing to be framed by anyone
(`X-Frame-Options: DENY`). A project that places a `Frame` with a
site-relative `src:` is served `SAMEORIGIN` instead, both by `wf serve` and
in the `_headers` file a build writes. Your site may frame its own pages,
and no other site may.

## Variations

### Draw HTML you give the frame

To draw HTML instead of loading an address (an example a page renders, or a
preview of what a reader is writing), use `srcdoc:`. This page previews a
note as the reader types it:

```wf
page Preview(path: "/preview-note", title: "Preview", description: "A note, drawn as it will look.") {
    state note = "Hello"
    Heading("Preview").h1
    Input(bind: note, label: "Note")
    Frame(srcdoc: "<p>{note}</p>", title: "The note, drawn", sandbox: "")
}
```

The frame draws the HTML sandboxed as `sandbox:` says, so `sandbox: ""`
draws it with no script and no reach into your page. HTML from a value with
no `sandbox:` is given `sandbox=""` — what a value holds is somebody else's
document, scripts and all — and the build names it with a `V03`. A value
that reads state draws the new HTML each time it changes, and the
pre-rendered page has the HTML before any script runs.

A frame's `on message` hears what its own document posts, from the origin
that document has: its address's, or the opaque `"null"` of a sandbox
without `allow-same-origin`. A page the frame was navigated to is no
longer its own.

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | Why, and what to do |
|---|---|
| `A17` on a `Frame` | Add a `title:` that says what the frame shows |
| A frame from another site stays blank | Its origin is not in `meta.frame`, so the policy blocks it |



---

# Show an icon

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/show-an-icon

Draw an icon with `Icon("name")`: one of 83 built-in SVG icons, drawn inline
in the current text colour, so it follows the theme. Use it beside text, on
an icon-only button or in a sidebar.

This page shows icons on their own, on an icon-only button, and in a
sidebar:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Inbox(path: "/", title: "Inbox", description: "Messages, with icons.") {
    Heading("Inbox").h1
    Row(gap: .sm) {
        Icon("mail")
        Icon("bell").lg.primary
        IconButton(icon: "close", label: "Close the inbox")
    }
    Sidebar {
        Sidebar.Item(to: "/", icon: "home") { Text("Home") }
    }
}
```

## How it works

- `Icon("mail")` draws the icon named `mail`. The `.sm` and `.lg` flags
  size it, and a tone flag such as `.primary` colours it.
- `IconButton` is a button that shows only an icon. Its `label:` is its
  accessible name for screen readers, and also its tooltip unless you give
  it a `title:`.
- `Sidebar.Item` takes an `icon:` too.

## The built-in icons

These are the 83 built-in icons:

- **General**: `home`, `menu`, `search`, `close`, `user`, `settings`,
  `check`, `plus`, `minus`, `edit`, `trash`, `star`, `heart`, `mail`,
  `bell`, `download`, `upload`, `eye`, `link`, `calendar`, `filter`, `info`,
  `warning`, `arrow-left`, `arrow-right`, `chevron-down`, `chevron-right`,
  `chevron-left`, `logout`, `copy`, `sun`, `moon`.
- **For an editor or a tool**: `folder`, `folder-plus`, `folder-off`,
  `file`, `file-plus`, `refresh`, `alert-circle`, `clock`, `dot`, `diff`,
  `book`, `git-pull-request`, `pin`, `git-branch`, `more-horizontal`,
  `window-minimize`, `window-maximize`, `outline`, `help-circle`,
  `collapse-all`, `locate`, `chevron-up`, `globe`, `external-link`,
  `panel-down`, `panel-up`, `code`, `monitor`, `git-commit`, `play`,
  `layers`, `insert`, `grid`, `list`, `square`, `pill`, `image`, `sparkle`,
  `lock`, `type`, `pointer`, `reach`, `frame`, `line`,
  `pipette`, `comment`, `hand`, `zoom`, `ruler`, `eye-off`, `unlock`.

A name that is not in the list draws as the word itself, and the compiler
warns with `V08`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The build keeps only the glyphs your program names. If an icon's name
> arrives at run time, set `"build": { "runtime": "full" }` so every glyph
> ships.

## Use an icon that is not built in

For an icon that is not built in, put an SVG file in `public/` and show it
with `Image(src: "/icons/rocket.svg", alt: "")`.

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | Why, and what to do |
|---|---|
| An icon shows as a word | The name is not one of the built-in icons (`V08`), or it arrives at run time and the build left its glyph out. Use a listed name, or set `build.runtime` to `"full"` |

# Show code on a page

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/show-code

`Code` shows code: inline inside a sentence, or as a block, coloured by its
language. This page mixes inline code into a sentence and shows two
coloured blocks:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Snippets(path: "/", title: "Snippets", description: "Code on the page.") {
    Heading("Snippets").h1
    Text("Run ")  Code("wf serve")  Text(" to start.")
    Code("page Home(path: \"/\") {\n    Text(\"Hi\")\n}", language: "wf").block
    Code("$ wf build", language: "bash").block
}
```

## How it works

- **`Code("…")`** is inline code. Placed between two `Text`s, it reads as
  part of the sentence.
- **`Code("…").block`** is a block, for code over several lines.
- **`language:`** colours it — `wf`, `json`, `bash` or `css`. The colouring
  is done at build time and in the browser alike, with the theme's
  `syntax-*` tokens, and a `Markdown` fence in one of those languages is
  coloured the same way.

# Show HTML from outside the project

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/show-html-from-outside

Every string an element shows goes in as text, so `"<p>"` in your data is
shown as `<p>`. Sometimes the content really is HTML: a CMS body, the
output of a Markdown renderer of your own, an email. This page fetches a
post and shows its HTML body as markup:

```wf
type Post { title: String, body: String }

api Backend(base: "/api") {
    get post(slug: String) at "posts/:slug" -> Post
}

page PostPage(path: "/p/:slug", title: "Post", description: "One post.", slug: String) {
    resource post = Backend.post(slug: slug)
    match post {
        ready(p) {
            Heading(p.title).h1
            Unsafe.Html(sanitize(p.body))
        }
        else { Skeleton }
    }
}
```

## How it works

- `sanitize(html)` keeps only what an allow-list names: a fixed set of
  elements and, for each, a fixed set of attributes. It keeps no
  `<script>`, `<style>`, `<iframe>` or `<form>`, and no `on*` attribute,
  and every `href` and `src` goes through the same scheme check as every
  other URL. A dropped element keeps its text.
- `Unsafe.Html(markup)` puts the result in as markup. The build prints a
  `V03` at each one, saying whether its markup went through `sanitize`,
  and `wf audit` lists them all.
- `sanitize` runs at build time as well as in the browser, from the same
  allow-list, so a pre-rendered page shows the sanitised body at once.

> [!CAUTION]
> Use `Unsafe.Html(raw)` without `sanitize` only for markup **your project
> produced**. Anything that arrived from outside goes through `sanitize`.

[Security](/about/security#one-door-for-markup) says why markup has
one door, and what the allow-list keeps out.

## Variations

- **Markup a project script inserts**: a script under `src/` that sets
  `innerHTML` with markup from outside the project passes it through
  `WF.sanitize(…)` first ([Call WF from a script](/recipes/call-wf-from-a-script)).
- **Markdown instead of HTML**: `Markdown(text)` escapes any HTML in the
  text and needs no `Unsafe` ([Render Markdown](/recipes/render-markdown)).



---

# Show what the network is doing

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/show-the-network

`network` tells a page whether it is online, how fast the line is and
whether the reader asked to save data, so the page can change what it does
on a slow line or none at all. This inbox warns when the browser is offline
and when data saver is on:

```wf
page Inbox(path: "/inbox", title: "Inbox", description: "Your messages.") {
    Heading("Inbox").h1
    if !network.online { Alert("You are offline — changes are queued.").warning }
    if network.saveData { Text("Data saver is on.").muted }
}
```

## How it works

Like `viewport`, `network` is a browser value that keeps itself current:
each `if` that reads it is drawn again when the connection changes, with
nothing to subscribe to.

| Member | What it is |
|---|---|
| `network.online` | Whether the browser has a connection |
| `network.effectiveType` | How fast it is: `4g`, `3g`, … |
| `network.saveData` | Whether the reader asked to save data |
| `network.downlink` | The estimated bandwidth, in megabits per second |
| `network.queued` | How many writes wait for the connection, when the site works offline ([Offline](/recipes/keep-writes-made-offline)) |



---

# Sign in with a session cookie

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/sign-in-with-a-session-cookie

A token kept in the page can be read by any script that reaches it. To sign
a reader in without holding a token at all, let the server set a session
cookie, describe the service with `credentials: .sameOrigin`, and keep the
signed-in user in a store:

**Needs:** a server that answers the `/api` endpoints the `api` block
names and sets the session cookie. The code declares `type User` and an
`app`, as the starter does: paste it into a new project, replacing
`src/App.wf` and the starter's `src/stores/auth.wf`.

```wf
type User { id: String, name: String }

api Auth(base: "/api") {
    credentials: .sameOrigin
    get me() -> User
    post signIn(body: Map) -> User
        errors { 401 -> Map }
    post signOut()
}

store Session {
    state user: User? = null
    state checked = false
    derived signedIn = user != null
    action load() {
        try { user = await Auth.me() } catch e { user = null }
        checked = true
    }
    action signIn(email: String, password: String) {
        user = await Auth.signIn(body: { email: email, password: password })
        navigate("/account")
    }
    action signOut() {
        await Auth.signOut()
        user = null
        Auth.me.invalidate()
        navigate("/")
    }
}

page SignIn(path: "/sign-in", title: "Sign in", description: "Sign in to your account.", noindex: true) {
    state email = ""
    state password = ""
    state problem = ""
    validate email { required  email }
    validate password { required }
    action send() {
        problem = ""
        try { await Session.signIn(email, password) } catch e { problem = "That email and password do not match." }
    }
    Heading("Sign in").h1
    if problem != "" { Alert(problem).danger }
    Form(bind: form) {
        on submit { send() }
        Input(bind: email, label: "Email").email
        Input(bind: password, label: "Password").password
        Button("Sign in", type: .submit, disabled: send.pending).primary
    }
}

page Account(path: "/account", title: "Your account", description: "Your account.", guard: !Session.checked || Session.signedIn, redirect: "/sign-in") {
    use Session
    // The guard is read when the route opens, which on a reload is before
    // `load` has answered; this sends the reader on once it has.
    effect { if Session.checked && !Session.signedIn { navigate("/sign-in") } }
    Heading("Your account").h1
    if !Session.checked { Spinner }
    if let u = Session.user {
        Text("Signed in as {u.name}")
        Button("Sign out") { on click { Session.signOut() } }
    }
}
```

The app asks the server who is signed in once, when the site opens, in
`src/App.wf`:

```wf
app {
    use Session
    Session.load()
    Router
}
```

## How it works

- `Auth` [describes the service](/learn/15-data#describe-a-service-with-api).
  `credentials: .sameOrigin` sends the session cookie with every call, so
  the page holds no token. `errors { 401 -> Map }` types what a refused
  sign-in answers.
- The `Session` [store](/learn/11-stores#a-first-store) holds the
  user, or `null`, and `signedIn` is derived from it. `load` asks the
  server who is signed in, `signIn` and `signOut` call the service and
  move the reader on with `navigate`.
- The server sets the cookie when a sign-in succeeds, with a header such as
  `Set-Cookie: session=…; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=1209600`.
  `HttpOnly` keeps it from every script, `SameSite=Lax`
  from another site's form, and `Secure` off plaintext connections.
- `Auth.me.invalidate()` on sign-out drops what the endpoint cached, so
  the next reader of the tab is not shown the last one's. Do the same for
  every endpoint whose answer is one reader's: an answer cached under one
  `Authorization` header is never served for another, but a cookie cannot
  be read, so the cache cannot tell one cookie's reader from the next.
- The `SignIn` page validates its two fields and calls `Session.signIn`
  in a `try`, so a wrong password shows an `Alert` instead of throwing.
  `send.pending` disables the button while the request runs, and
  `noindex: true` keeps the page out of search results.
- `Session.load()` at the top of `app` runs once, when the site opens: a
  reader who comes back with a session cookie is signed in again, and
  `checked` turns true when the server has answered either way.
- The `Account` page has a [guard](/learn/05-pages-and-routing#guards).
  A guard is read once, when the route opens, so it lets the page through
  while `checked` is still false, and the `effect` sends a signed-out
  reader to `/sign-in` as soon as the answer arrives. Until then the page
  shows a `Spinner`.

The session is an httpOnly cookie the server sets, so the page never holds
a token. `guard:` hides the page from a reader who is signed out, and the
server still checks every request
([Security](/about/security#where-a-session-belongs)).



---

# Publish a page in each language

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/site-in-two-languages

Have a search engine find your site in each of its languages. `t()` and
`setLocale` translate a page in the browser, at one address, and a search
engine indexes what that address's HTML says, which is the default locale.
A site that wants each language found writes each page once per language,
at an address of its own, and says how the pages are joined.

This site is written in Arabic, with its home page in English at `/en`.
The site's language, its address and a static build go in
`webfluent.app.json`. Without `meta.lang` the site's pages are taken to be
in English, and without `meta.site_url` there is no absolute address for
the alternates:

**Needs:** the settings below in `webfluent.app.json`. It claims `/` and
the name `Home`: paste it into a new project, or replace the starter's
`src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```json
{
    "build": { "ssg": true },
    "meta": { "lang": "ar", "site_url": "https://example.com" }
}
```

Then the pages:

```wf
page Home(path: "/", title: "منذر عمر", description: "مهندس خلفيات.") {
    Heading("مرحباً").h1
}

page HomeEn(path: "/en", title: "Monzer Omer", description: "Engineer.",
            lang: "en", translates: Home) {
    Heading("Hello").h1
}
```

## How it works

- **`lang:`** is the language the page is written in. A page without one
  is in the site's (`meta.lang`, or `default_locale`). The page is written
  `<html lang="en">`, with `dir="rtl"` for a language written right to
  left, and its `og:locale` and its JSON-LD's `inLanguage` say the same.
  The router sets `lang` and `dir` on `<html>` when it shows the page, and
  puts back the site's (or the locale the reader chose) on a page without
  one.
- **`translates:`** names the page this one is a translation of. Pages
  joined this way — `HomeFr` may translate `Home` too — each list all of
  them as `hreflang` alternates, at their own addresses and canonical to
  themselves, with `x-default` for the one in the site's language, and
  each names the others' languages as `og:locale:alternate`.
- **A `:param` page's translation is matched by its parameters:**
  `/en/posts/:slug` for `/posts/:slug`, filled with the same `slug`.

A `translates:` that names no page, or two translations of one page in one
language, is `R05`.



---

# Pass a store's value to a component

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/store-value-as-a-prop

A component that needs only one value from a store can take it as a prop
instead of using the store. That keeps the component reusable outside that
store: a test or another page can hand it any number:

**Needs:** nothing besides the code. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
store Cart { state count = 0 }

component CartBadge(count: Number) {
    if count > 0 { Badge("{count}").primary }
}

page Shop(path: "/", title: "Shop", description: "Everything we sell.") {
    use Cart
    Heading("Shop").h1
    Row(gap: .sm, align: .center) {
        Button("Add to cart") { on click { Cart.count = Cart.count + 1 } }
        CartBadge(count: Cart.count)
    }
}
```

No badge shows while the cart is empty. Press **Add to cart** and a badge
reading 1 appears beside the button, and counts up with every press.

## How it works

- `CartBadge` declares a `count` [prop](/learn/10-components#props) and
  knows nothing about `Cart`.
- The page reads the [store](/learn/11-stores#a-first-store) after
  `use Cart` and passes `Cart.count` down.
- A prop that reads state stays live inside the component, so the badge
  repaints when `Cart.count` changes. The button changes it here; in a shop
  of your own, an action of the store would.



---

# Talk to the site's other tabs

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/talk-between-tabs

A `channel` keeps tabs of the same site in step — a cart, a sign-in, a
setting. Every tab that opens a channel of the same name hears what the
others post, with no server involved. This shop keeps its cart count the
same in every tab:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page; open it in two tabs. It claims `/`:
paste it into a new project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf`
with it.

```wf
store Cart {
    state count = 0
    action add() { count = count + 1 }
    action merge(m: Map) { count = m.items }
}

page Shop(path: "/", title: "Shop", description: "A cart every tab agrees on.") {
    use Cart
    channel cart = broadcast("cart") { on message(m) { Cart.merge(m) } }

    Heading("Shop").h1
    Text("{Cart.count} in the cart")
    Button("Add to cart") { on click { Cart.add()  cart.post({ items: Cart.count }) } }
}
```

## How it works

- **`channel cart = broadcast("cart")`** joins the channel named `cart`. A
  channel is a page's for as long as the page shows.
- **`cart.post(value)`** sends a value to every other tab on the channel.
  Here the button adds to the cart, then posts the new count.
- **`on message(m)`**, in the channel's block, hears what another tab
  posted, and hands it to the store's `merge` action.

Open the page in two tabs and add to the cart in one: the other tab's count
follows. A tab does not hear its own posts, and both tabs must be on the
same origin. `cart.last` is the last message another tab posted. A
channel's state is `open`, or `closed` in a browser without
`BroadcastChannel`.



---

# Make a desktop or phone app with Tauri

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/tauri-app

This recipe ships a WebFluent project as a Tauri app: the build runs in
the system's own web view, and a page calls a Rust side for what a browser
cannot do — read a file on disk, open a folder dialog, show a
notification. Nothing in the language changes; a page reaches Rust through
a plain script under `src/`, with one typed function per command
([Call your own JavaScript](/recipes/call-your-own-script)). For a native side in
JavaScript on Node.js instead, see
[Make a desktop app with Electron](/recipes/electron-app).

You need a WebFluent project that builds with `wf build`, Rust, and the
system libraries listed in Tauri's
[prerequisites](https://tauri.app/start/prerequisites/).

These are the settings a Tauri app needs. In `webfluent.app.json`:

```json
{
    "build": { "compress": false },
    "meta": { "sitemap": false, "connect": ["ipc:", "http://ipc.localhost"] }
}
```

The commands that make the Rust side and run the app:

```bash
cargo install tauri-cli --version "^2" --locked
cargo tauri init --app-name notes --window-title Notes \
    --frontend-dist ../build --dev-url http://localhost:3000 \
    --before-dev-command "wf serve" --before-build-command "wf build"
cargo tauri dev
```

And two keys in the `src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` that `cargo tauri init`
writes:

```json
{
    "identifier": "com.example.notes",
    "app": { "withGlobalTauri": true }
}
```

## How it works

The steps below take these settings in order, then add what a page calls:
a Rust command, an event, a plugin.

### Prepare the build for a desktop

The same project builds for the web and for a desktop. Two keys in
`webfluent.app.json`, and one to leave out, drop what only a website needs:

- **`build.compress: false`** — the shell packs the folder into the app, so
  a `.gz` file beside every file would ship every file twice.
- **`meta.sitemap: false`** — writes no `sitemap.xml` or `robots.txt`;
  nothing crawls an app. You can leave `meta.site_url` and the link-preview
  tags unset too.
- **Leave `offline` out** — the files are already on the machine, so a
  service worker has nothing to keep.

`meta.connect` is for the security policy; see
[Allow Tauri requests in the security policy](#allow-tauri-requests-in-the-security-policy).

A single-page build and a static build both work
([Static sites and SPAs](/about/static-or-single-page)), and addresses stay as they
are. Tauri answers a path the build has no file for with `index.html`, so
reloading the window on `/settings` shows the settings page.

An app is often used with no network, and a font named in `meta.fonts`
comes from another origin. To make a font always available, put the file in
`public/` and declare it with `@font-face` in a `.css` file under `src/`
([Styling](/learn/13-styling)).

### Set up Tauri

1. `cargo install tauri-cli` installs the Tauri CLI, once per machine.
2. `cargo tauri init`, run in the project's folder, writes `src-tauri/`
   beside `src/`: the Rust side, its `Cargo.toml` and `tauri.conf.json`.
   Its flags point Tauri at `build/` for the app, at `wf serve` on port
   3000 while you work, and at the `wf` commands that make each.
   WebFluent never reads `src-tauri/`, and Tauri runs the two `wf`
   commands in the project's folder.
3. Two keys in `src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` change:
   - **`identifier`** — a reverse-domain name of your own. `cargo tauri
     build` refuses the default, `com.tauri.dev`.
   - **`withGlobalTauri`** — puts Tauri's JavaScript API on
     `window.__TAURI__`, every plugin's API included, so a plain script uses
     it with no `import` and no npm.

Leave `app.security.csp` at `null`: every page already carries its own
policy (see [Allow Tauri requests in the security policy](#allow-tauri-requests-in-the-security-policy)).

### Run the Tauri app while you work

`cargo tauri dev` runs `wf serve` and opens the app's window on it. Saving
a `.wf` file rebuilds and reloads the window, and a build that fails shows
its error over the page, as it does in a browser ([CLI](/reference/cli)).
Saving a Rust file rebuilds the app. If `dev.port` is not `3000`, change
`devUrl` to match.

To build the installers, run:

```bash
cargo tauri build
```

This command runs `wf build`, embeds `build/` in the binary, and writes the
installers under `src-tauri/target/release/bundle/`.

### Call a Rust command

A *command* is a Rust function a page may call. Write it in
`src-tauri/src/lib.rs` and list it in `run()`. This file has two commands:
`greet` returns a value, and `start_sync` returns at once and reports its
progress as events:

```rust
use tauri::Emitter;

#[tauri::command]
fn greet(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("Hello, {name}!")
}

#[tauri::command]
fn start_sync(app: tauri::AppHandle) {
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        for done in [25, 50, 75, 100] {
            // … a quarter of the work …
            let _ = app.emit("sync-progress", done);
        }
    });
}

// in run(), before .run(…):
//     .invoke_handler(tauri::generate_handler![greet, start_sync])
```

A page calls a command through a script that names it. Write one function
per command, typed with JSDoc, so `.wf` code calls `greet(name)` like any
other function and the checker holds every call to its types:

```js
// src/native.js
/**
 * Whether the page is inside the app, rather than a browser tab.
 * @returns {boolean}
 */
function inApp() {
  return "__TAURI__" in window;
}

/**
 * Call a Rust command. What its `Err` holds arrives as an `Error`.
 * @param {string} command
 * @param {object} [args]
 * @returns {Promise<any>}
 */
function invoke(command, args) {
  if (!inApp()) return Promise.reject(new Error("This needs the desktop app."));
  return window.__TAURI__.core.invoke(command, args).catch((err) => {
    throw new Error(typeof err === "string" ? err : JSON.stringify(err));
  });
}

/**
 * @param {string} name
 * @returns {Promise<string>}
 */
function greet(name) {
  return invoke("greet", { name });
}

/** Start syncing; how far it has got arrives as `sync-progress`. */
function startSync() {
  return invoke("start_sync");
}
```

Three rules hold for every command:

- **Arguments are named.** A command's parameters are the keys of the
  object, in camelCase: a Rust `note_id` is `{ noteId }`.
- **A result is a promise.** A command that returns `Result<T, E>` resolves
  with the `T`. Its `Err` rejects, and `invoke` turns it into an `Error`,
  so a page's `catch e` reads `e.message`.
- **`inApp()` is false in a browser tab** — `wf serve` opened in a browser,
  `wf test`, `wf verify` — where there is no native side. Each function
  answers there instead of throwing, so every page still loads.

The page awaits the function in an action and shows the reply:

```wf
page Hello(path: "/", title: "Hello", description: "Says hello from Rust.") {
    state name = ""
    state reply = ""

    action ask() {
        try {
            reply = await greet(name)
        } catch e {
            reply = e.message
        }
    }

    Heading("Hello").h1
    if !inApp() {
        Alert("Open this in the app to talk to Rust.").info
    }
    Input(bind: name, label: "Your name")
    Button("Greet").primary { on click { ask() } }
    Text(reply)
}
```

In the app, typing `Ada` and pressing **Greet** shows `Hello, Ada!`. In a
browser tab, the page shows the alert, and **Greet** shows `This needs the
desktop app.`

### Listen for events from Rust

`start_sync` returns at once and reports as it goes, with `app.emit(…)`. A
page hears an event for as long as it shows, so tie the listener to the
page's lifetime: `mount:` starts it, and `cleanup:` stops it when the page,
branch or item leaves. First, wrap Tauri's `listen` in a script:

```js
// src/events.js
/**
 * Hear an event the native side emits, until the function it returns is called.
 * @param {string} name
 * @param {(payload: any) => void} handler
 * @returns {() => void}
 */
function onEvent(name, handler) {
  if (!inApp()) return () => {};
  const listening = window.__TAURI__.event.listen(name, (e) => handler(e.payload));
  return () => { listening.then((stop) => stop()); };
}
```

Then hand the listener an action. This page shows a progress bar that
fills as the events arrive:

```wf
page Sync(path: "/sync", title: "Sync", description: "How far the sync has got.") {
    state done = 0
    state problem = ""

    action setDone(n: Number) { done = n }
    action start() {
        try {
            await startSync()
        } catch e {
            problem = e.message
        }
    }

    Stack(gap: .md,
          mount: (n) => onEvent("sync-progress", setDone),
          cleanup: (stop) => stop()) {
        Heading("Sync").h1
        Progress(value: done, max: 100)
        Text("{done}%")
        Button("Sync now") { on click { start() } }
        Text(problem)
    }
}
```

Pressing **Sync now** moves the bar through 25, 50, 75 and 100%.

### Use a Tauri plugin

A dialog, the file system, notifications, the clipboard, opening a link in
the browser: each is a Tauri plugin. To add one, run the CLI. It adds the
crate, the line in `run()`, and the plugin's default permission in
`src-tauri/capabilities/default.json`:

```bash
cargo tauri add dialog
```

With `withGlobalTauri` on, the plugin's API is on
`window.__TAURI__.dialog`. Wrap what a page uses, as with a command:

```js
// src/dialogs.js
/**
 * Ask for a folder; `null` when the reader cancels.
 * @returns {Promise<?string>}
 */
function pickFolder() {
  if (!inApp()) return Promise.resolve(null);
  return window.__TAURI__.dialog.open({ directory: true });
}
```

This page asks for a folder and shows the one the reader picked:

```wf
page Library(path: "/library", title: "Library", description: "Where the notes are kept.") {
    state folder = ""

    action choose() {
        let picked = await pickFolder()
        if picked != null {
            folder = picked
        }
    }

    Heading("Library").h1
    Button("Choose a folder") { on click { choose() } }
    if folder != "" {
        Text("Notes are kept in {folder}.")
    } else {
        Text("No folder yet.").muted
    }
}
```

A plugin's call fails until its permission is granted. `cargo tauri add`
grants the default set. Name anything beyond it — for example, a path the
`fs` plugin may read — in the same capabilities file.

### Allow Tauri requests in the security policy

With `build.csp` on — as it is for a project `wf init` makes — every page
says where it may send requests ([Security](/about/security)). Tauri sends
each call as a request: to `http://ipc.localhost` on Windows and Android,
and to `ipc://localhost` on macOS, Linux and iOS. Name both in
`meta.connect`, the second as its scheme alone, which is how a policy names
an app's own scheme:

```json
{ "meta": { "connect": ["ipc:", "http://ipc.localhost"] } }
```

Other settings follow the same pattern:

- **A protocol of your own** (`register_uri_scheme_protocol`) is named the
  same way. For a frame the app fills from it, write `"frame": ["myapp:",
  "http://myapp.localhost"]`; a frame's `src` may then use that scheme.
- **WebAssembly**: a page that compiles it adds `"wasm": true`.
- **Style elements**: a page whose scripts write `<style>` elements adds
  `"style_elements": true`.

## Variations

### Run it on a phone

The same project runs on Android and iOS. Make the phone's side once, then
run it while you work (`ios` in place of `android`, on a Mac):

```bash
cargo tauri android init
cargo tauri android dev
```

- **The dev server.** `wf serve` listens to this machine only. To let the
  phone reach it, make `beforeDevCommand` `wf serve --host 0.0.0.0` and
  point `devUrl` at the machine's address on the network
  ([CLI](/reference/cli)).
- **No window chrome.** A phone has no title bar: draw one only on a
  desktop.
- **Edge to edge.** The page is drawn under the phone's own bars, so pad
  the app's frame by `env(safe-area-inset-*)`, once a script sets
  `viewport-fit=cover` on the viewport tag.
- **Back.** Android's back gesture goes back through the router's history.
  To close an open sheet first, take the gesture with Tauri's
  `app.onBackButtonPress` from the same script, in an effect that gives it
  back.
- **Plugins.** Capabilities are split by `"platforms"`, and a phone-only
  plugin (haptics, a barcode scanner) is registered under `#[cfg(mobile)]`.

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | What to check |
|---|---|
| Every native call fails with `This needs the desktop app.` | The page is open in a browser tab, not the app — or `withGlobalTauri` is off, so `window.__TAURI__` is missing |
