| A Tauri call is blocked by the security policy | `meta.connect` names both `ipc:` and `http://ipc.localhost` |
| A Tauri plugin's call fails | Its permission is not granted in `src-tauri/capabilities/default.json` |
| `cargo tauri build` refuses to run | `identifier` in `tauri.conf.json` is still `com.tauri.dev` |
| The Tauri window shows nothing while you work | `devUrl` does not match `dev.port` |
| The app's text falls back to another font offline | The font comes from `meta.fonts`; put the file in `public/` and declare it with `@font-face` |



---

# Test a page

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/test-a-page

A test renders a component or a whole page, acts on it the way a reader
does — typing, clicking, pressing keys — and checks the text the page
shows. This shopping list has a component that counts, a page that adds
items, and three tests:

**Needs:** a `tests/` folder beside `src/`, and a Chrome or Chromium on
the machine for the tests that click (or `WF_CHROME` naming one). The block
holds three files; the comment above each says where it goes.

```wf
// src/components/Count.wf
component Count(_ n: Number) {
    Text(if n == 1 { "1 thing to buy" } else { "{n} things to buy" })
}

// src/pages/Shopping.wf
page Shopping(path: "/shopping", title: "Shopping", description: "What to buy.") {
    state items: [String] = ["Milk"]
    state draft = ""

    Heading("Shopping").h1
    Count(items.length)
    Form {
        on submit(e) {
            e.preventDefault()
            if draft != "" { items = items.concat([draft]) }
            draft = ""
        }
        Input(bind: draft, label: "Item")
        Button("Add", type: .submit).primary
    }
    for item in items by item { Text(item) }
}

// tests/shopping.wf
test "one thing reads in the singular" {
    Count(1)
    expect "1 thing to buy"
    expect not "things"
}

test "adding an item lists it and counts it" {
    Shopping
    expect "1 thing to buy"
    type "Bread" into "Item"
    click "Add"
    expect "Bread"
    expect "2 things to buy"
}

test "an empty item is not added" {
    Shopping
    click "Add"
    expect "1 thing to buy"
}
```

Run them:

```bash
wf test
```

```text
  new   tests/shopping.wf — one thing reads in the singular (snapshot written)
  ok    tests/shopping.wf — adding an item lists it and counts it (in a browser)
  ok    tests/shopping.wf — an empty item is not added (in a browser)
3 passed, 0 failed, 1 snapshot(s) written
```

## How it works

- `wf test` runs every `test "…" { }` under `tests/`. A build ignores
  them, so they never reach the site.
- A test's body is drawn like a page's: `Count(1)` places the component,
  and `Shopping`, a page with no route parameter, is placed by its name.
  The project's components, stores, types and constants are all in reach.
- `expect "…"` checks the text a reader would see, with white space
  collapsed the way a browser lays it out, never the markup.
  `expect not "…"` checks that it is absent.
- A test with a step that acts — `click`, `type … into`, `press` — is
  built into a real page and run in headless Chrome, so the handler runs,
  the state changes and the page draws again. `type "Bread" into "Item"`
  finds the field by its label, and `click "Add"` the button by its text:
  by what a reader sees, so a test also catches a control that lost its
  name.
- A test that only looks needs no browser. It is rendered and compared
  with a snapshot, `tests/__snapshots__/shopping/<test name>.html`, written
  the first time it runs. When a change is meant, `wf test --update`
  writes the snapshots again; commit them with the code.
- A handler that throws fails the test, so a broken click is caught even
  when the text happens to match.

## Variations

- **Seed the state**: `test "…"(data: { items: ["a", "b"] }) { … }` starts
  the body's state, or a store by its name, with that data.
- **Close a dialog**: `press "Escape"` closes the open `Modal` or `Dialog`;
  `press "Enter" in "Search"` presses a key in one named field.
- **One file**: `wf test tests/shopping.wf` runs only that file's tests.
- **Every page in a browser**: `wf verify` loads each route of the built
  site and fails on a script error, a failed request or a page that drew
  nothing ([Testing](/learn/16-testing#check-every-page-with-wf-verify)).
- **In CI**: run `wf check`, `wf test` and `wf build` in that order
  ([Install wf on a build machine](/recipes/install-wf-in-ci)).

A key step names a key as the browser names it (`"Enter"`, `"Escape"`,
`"a"`), or a combination as `on key(…)` writes one: `press "mod+k"` holds ⌘
on a Mac and Ctrl elsewhere, so a shortcut is tested by pressing it.



---

# Translate a site

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/translate-a-site

Show a site in the reader's language: one file of messages per locale,
`t("key")` wherever text goes, and a switch that changes the language on the
spot, right to left included. To start a new project this way, see
[Start a project translated](#start-a-project-translated).

This program has a language picker in its navigation bar and a home page
whose heading, count and button are translated. It reads the translation
files that [Set up the translation files](#set-up-the-translation-files)
shows:

**Needs:** the `i18n` setting and the translation files that [Set up the
translation files](#set-up-the-translation-files) shows. The code is a
whole project's `app` and home page, and declares `type User`, as the
starter does: paste it into a new project, replacing `src/App.wf` and
`src/pages/Home.wf`.

```wf
type User { name: String }

app {
    state chosen = locale
    Navbar {
        Navbar.Brand { Link("i18n", to: "/") }
        Navbar.Links {
            Link(t("nav.home"), to: "/")
            Link(t("nav.about"), to: "/about")
        }
        Navbar.Actions {
            Select(bind: chosen, label: t("nav.language")) {
                on change { setLocale(chosen) }
                Select.Option("English", value: "en")
                Select.Option("العربية", value: "ar")
                Select.Option("Español", value: "es")
            }
        }
    }
    Router
}

page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "The home page.") {
    state user = User(name: "Sam")
    state items: [String] = ["a", "b", "c"]
    Heading(t("welcome", { name: user.name })).h1
    Text(t("items", { count: items.length }))
    Button(t("actions.save")).primary
    Text("Locale: {locale}, direction: {dir}")
    if locale == "ar" { Text("النسخة العربية") }
}

page About(path: "/about", title: "About", description: "About the site.") {
    Heading(t("nav.about")).h1
}
```

## How it works

### Set up the translation files

List the site's locales in `webfluent.app.json` under `i18n`.
`default_locale` names the language the site is written in, and `dir` the
directory that holds the files:

```json
{
  "i18n": {
    "default_locale": "en",
    "locales": ["en", "ar", "es"],
    "dir": "src/translations"
  }
}
```

Then put one file per locale in that directory — `en.json`, `ar.json`,
`es.json`. Each is a flat map of keys to messages; by convention a key has
dots in it to group related messages. This is `src/translations/en.json`:

```json
{
  "nav.home": "Home",
  "nav.about": "About",
  "nav.language": "Language",
  "welcome": "Welcome, {name}!",
  "items.one": "{count} item",
  "items.other": "{count} items",
  "actions.save": "Save"
}
```

And this is `src/translations/ar.json`, with the six plural forms Arabic
uses:

```json
{
  "nav.home": "الرئيسية",
  "nav.about": "حول",
  "nav.language": "اللغة",
  "welcome": "أهلاً، {name}!",
  "items.zero": "لا عناصر",
  "items.one": "عنصر واحد",
  "items.two": "عنصران",
  "items.few": "{count} عناصر",
  "items.many": "{count} عنصراً",
  "items.other": "{count} عنصر",
  "actions.save": "حفظ"
}
```

And `src/translations/es.json`, whose words have the two forms English has:

```json
{
  "nav.home": "Inicio",
  "nav.about": "Acerca de",
  "nav.language": "Idioma",
  "welcome": "¡Bienvenido, {name}!",
  "items.one": "{count} elemento",
  "items.other": "{count} elementos",
  "actions.save": "Guardar"
}
```

A locale with no file, and a key one locale has and another lacks, are
build warnings (`I03`). At run time a key missing from the reader's locale
falls back to the default locale's message, and only then to the key itself.

### Translate text with `t()`

To show a message in the reader's language, call `t("key")` wherever a
string goes, as `Home` does above. Pass a map as the second argument to
fill placeholders and to pick a plural form.

In English the home page reads **Welcome, Sam!**, **3 items** and a **Save**
button; in Arabic, **أهلاً، Sam!**, **3 عناصر** and **حفظ**.

How `t()` behaves:

- **It follows the locale.** `t("key")` is the message for the current
  locale, and every call is evaluated again when the locale changes.
- **It fills placeholders.** `t("key", { name: value })` replaces each
  `{name}` in the message with the map's value.
- **A `count` picks the plural form.** The form comes from the locale's
  CLDR plural rules, which the browser's `Intl.PluralRules` follows too:
  Arabic has `zero`, `one`, `two`, `few`, `many` and `other`; English has
  `one` and `other`; Japanese has only `other`. A count of exactly 0 uses
  `key.zero` wherever the file has one, in any language, so English can say
  "No files" rather than "0 files". Without the form it wants, `t()` falls
  back to `key.other`, then to `key`.
- **A key's forms all come from one language** — the reader's, when its
  file has the key at all, otherwise the default locale's. It never mixes
  one form from each.
- **The pre-rendered page is already translated.** The build resolves `t`
  for the default locale when it pre-renders a page, by the same rules, so
  the HTML is in the default language, its counts in that language's forms.

> [!WARNING]
> Never build a sentence from pieces (`t("greeting") + name`). Word order
> differs between languages. Put a placeholder in the message, so a
> translator can move it.

### Switch the locale

To let the reader change language, call `setLocale(code)`. The `app` above
puts a language picker in the navigation bar, and `Home` shows the current
locale and direction.

`locale` is the current locale's code, and `dir` is `"ltr"` or `"rtl"`.
An `app` block may declare `state` as a page does, as `chosen` is above.
It starts as `locale`, so a reader who chose Arabic on an earlier visit
finds العربية already selected.

On a switch, the runtime sets `<html lang>` and `<html dir>`. A locale is
right to left when its language is: Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu, Pashto,
Sindhi, Central Kurdish, Uyghur, Yiddish, Dhivehi, Kashmiri, Syriac,
Aramaic and N'Ko — with any region, so `ar-EG` is too. A site whose default
locale is one of them is written `<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">` from the
start, before any script runs.

`meta.lang` may name a region of the default locale's language (`en-GB` for
`en`); otherwise the default locale is the page's language.

The built-ins use logical CSS properties (`margin-inline-start`, not
`margin-left`), so their layouts mirror with no work on your side. Use
logical properties in your own `style { }` blocks too.

### Choose the locale a page opens in

A page opens in `default_locale`, with two exceptions:

1. **The address names a locale.** `?lang=<code>`, for one of the
   configured locales, opens the page in it: `/about?lang=ar` is the Arabic
   page, for a link you share. It does not change the reader's kept
   choice. It is not an address a search engine indexes: its HTML, and its
   canonical link, are the default locale's, so the build lists no `?lang=`
   address as an `hreflang` alternate. To have each language found, give
   it pages of its own ([A page in its own language](/recipes/site-in-two-languages)).
2. **The reader chose a locale before.** `setLocale(code)` keeps the code
   in the reader's `localStorage`, under `wf:locale`, and every page loaded
   after that opens in it, on this visit and the next. Choosing
   `default_locale` again forgets it.

So a static site, which loads each page afresh, keeps the reader's language
from page to page, and a language switch can be a pair of buttons:

```wf
app {
    Navbar {
        Navbar.Brand { Link("i18n", to: "/") }
        Navbar.Actions {
            Button("English") { on click { setLocale("en") } }
            Button("العربية") { on click { setLocale("ar") } }
        }
    }
    Router
}
```

The runtime does not guess from the browser's language. Nothing is kept
until the reader chooses, so a first visit gets the `?lang=` locale or the
default, and a search engine's crawler the default. To start a first visit in the
browser's language, keep whether the reader has chosen in a store with
`persist`, and until they have, call
`setLocale(navigator.language.slice(0, 2))` from an `effect` in the app.

A static build pre-renders every page once, in the default locale; another
locale is applied as the page loads. So a search engine indexes only the
default locale's text. For each language to be found, give it pages of
its own ([A page in its own language](/recipes/site-in-two-languages)).

### Format numbers and dates for the locale

`format` and `ago` follow the current locale
([Expressions](/reference/expressions)). `format(1234.5, .currency, "EUR")` is
`€1,234.50` in `en` and `1.234,50 €` in `de`; `ago(date)` says
"il y a 3 jours" in `fr`. The pre-rendered page uses a table of the common
locales' separators and currency symbols, and the live page uses the
browser's `Intl` and corrects any difference.

To choose the digits a locale writes, add the Unicode extension to its
code:

- `setLocale("ar-u-nu-arab")` reads the `ar` table and writes `format` —
  a date pattern too, its AM/PM in the locale's words — `ago` and every
  count in Arabic-Indic digits (١١ ملفًا).
- `setLocale("ar-u-nu-latn")` writes them in 0–9, whatever the browser's
  Arabic would pick.
- Bare `ar` leaves the digits to the browser.

A count is prose, so it takes the locale's digits. Another number spliced
into a message — a line number, a version — stays as it is. The document's
`lang` is the language, `ar`, whatever digits the code names.

### Translate long-form text

For a paragraph or a page of prose:

- Under `"literals": true`, `Markdown("…")` written in place is words like
  any other text: its whole source, `**` and all, is the key.
- Text inside a `.md` page is not passed through `t`. Keep one Markdown
  file per locale, each with its own `path`, `lang` and `translates` in
  its front matter, or keep the text in the translation file under a key
  and render `Markdown(t("about.body"))`.

## Start a project translated

To begin a new project in several languages, pass `--locales` to `wf init`,
with the default locale first:

```bash
wf init my-app --locales en,ar
```

This works for the `spa` and `static` templates. The new project has:

- the `i18n` config above, and `meta.lang` set to the default locale;
- every visible string of the starter passed through `t("…")`;
- a language switch with one entry per locale;
- a file for each locale in `src/translations/`. The default locale's holds
  the starter's English, which its pages and tests are written in. Arabic
  holds the starter's Arabic. Any other locale starts as a copy of the
  English, for you to translate.

Each locale is a language tag (`en`, `ar`, `pt-BR`). `--locales ar,en`
makes Arabic the default, so the page is right to left from the first
paint. From Rust, the same is
`webfluent::init::create_with(dir, name, &Options { template, locales })`.

## Check what each locale lacks

To see the translations as a table, run `wf translations`:

```bash
wf translations
wf translations --missing ar
wf translations --unused
wf translations --plurals
```

| Command | What it prints |
|---|---|
| `wf translations` | Each locale, the plural forms its rules use, and how many keys it lacks, a form it lacks, or a placeholder that differs from the default locale's |
| `--missing ar` | What Arabic lacks |
| `--unused` | The keys nothing names |
| `--plurals` | CLDR's plural rules: every locale's forms |
| `--json` | The whole table: each key with its message in every locale, and every place a `t()` names it |

From Rust the table is `webfluent::i18n::table` (with the `internals` feature, outside semver), which can also write one
message back into its file with every other byte as it was.

## Checklist

- Every visible string goes through `t`, including `label:`,
  `placeholder:` and `aria-label:` values.
- No sentence is built from parts (`t("x") + name`); a placeholder lets a
  translator reorder it.
- Every count has its plural forms, even in English, and a `zero` where
  "none" reads better as a sentence.
- `wf translations --missing <locale>` lists nothing for any locale.
- You have tried the site once in a right-to-left locale, and checked:
  - alignment, and icons that imply a direction (arrows);
  - any `left` or `right` in your own CSS;
  - a Latin code or figure inside Arabic text, which needs a left-to-right
    run of its own (`direction: ltr; unicode-bidi: isolate`) to keep its
    parts in order.
- If each language should be found by search, each has pages of its own,
  with `lang:` and `translates:`, and `wf check` reports no `R05`.



---

# Translate by the words as written

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/translate-by-the-words

Translate a project that was written in one language from the start,
without inventing keys or wrapping every string in `t()`: each string a
reader sees is looked up in the reader's table by its own words. Turn it on
with `"literals": true` in the `i18n` config:

**Needs:** the `i18n` setting below, and the translation files [How it
works](#how-it-works) shows. It claims `/`: paste it into a new project,
or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```json
{ "i18n": { "default_locale": "en", "locales": ["en", "ar"], "literals": true } }
```

This page keeps its English words, and a reader in Arabic sees them
translated:

```wf
page Problems(path: "/", title: "Problems", description: "What the checks found.") {
    state report = { count: 3, files: 11 }
    Heading("Problems").h1              // المشاكل, for a reader in ar
    Text("{report.count} missing")      // one key, `{count} missing`
    Text("{report.files} files")        // 11 ملفًا, for a reader in ar
}
```

## How it works

Every string a reader sees is looked up by its text as written: an
element's text, and props such as `label:`, `title:`, `placeholder:`,
`aria-label:` and `alt:`. The Arabic table, `src/translations/ar.json`,
maps the English words to their translation:

```json
{
  "Problems": "المشاكل",
  "{count} missing": "{count} مفقودة",
  "{files} files.zero": "لا توجد ملفات",
  "{files} files.one": "ملف واحد",
  "{files} files.two": "ملفان",
  "{files} files.few": "{files} ملفات",
  "{files} files.many": "{files} ملفًا",
  "{files} files.other": "{files} ملف"
}
```

How the text becomes a key:

- **A splice of a plain path is a placeholder.** It is named for the
  path's last part, so `"{report.count} missing"` is the key
  `{count} missing`. A splice of anything more, such as `"{n + 1} more"`,
  keeps the text as written.
- **Each branch of an `if` is its own key** when the text chooses between
  them.
- **A value shown by its name** — a `derived` or `state` — is looked up
  only when its name says it is words, such as `countText` or
  `emptyLabel`. Shown words that neither rule covers draw an `I05` warning.
- **What is not words is left alone:** an icon's name, `Code(…)`, and a
  component named `Kbd`.
- **A list of words is translated word by word.** A `labels:` prop, which
  holds one word for each option of a control whose options are values,
  is looked up item by item: `Segmented(options: ["2", "4"], labels: ["2
  spaces", "4 spaces"])` on your own `Segmented` component.

The default locale's messages are the words themselves, so its file may be
empty. `wf translations` counts each string as a key in use, and lists what
another locale has not translated as missing.

An empty `en.json` shows `{files} files` as written, so an English reader
sees `11 files`, and `1 files` for one. To get "1 file" right, give
`en.json` its two forms:

```json
{ "{files} files.one": "{files} file", "{files} files.other": "{files} files" }
```

### Count by the number in the text

A literal with one number spliced into it picks its plural form by that
number, as `"{report.files} files"` does. The key's plural forms are keys
too, as for `count` with `t()`: `{files} files.one`, `{files} files.other`
and the rest, as in the table above.

The default locale gives its forms the same way — `"{files} files.one":
"{files} file"` — where its words differ by count. With two numbers in the
text, neither is taken as the count: the message is looked up as written.



---

# Tween a property when state changes

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/tween-on-change

Animate a style property as state changes it — a panel growing taller, a
colour shifting — rather than an element arriving. Add a `transition { }`
block that names the property and how long it takes. Press **Toggle** and
the card grows to show the rest of its text:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Tween(path: "/", title: "Tween", description: "A panel that grows.") {
    state open = false
    Heading("Tween").h1
    Card {
        style { max-height: {if open { "20rem" } else { "3rem" }}; overflow: hidden }
        transition { max-height: 250ms ease-in-out }
        Button("Toggle") { on click { open = !open } }
        Text("Long content that reveals itself.")
    }
}
```

## How it works

- The `style { }` value of `max-height` reads `open`, so it follows the
  state: `3rem` closed, `20rem` open ([Styling](/learn/13-styling)).
- `transition { max-height: 250ms ease-in-out }` tweens that property
  whenever its value changes, over 250ms. Each line names a property, then
  its length and easing; a design token may stand for either.
- An element's block is ordered `style`, then `transition`, then its
  handlers and children.

A reader who asked for reduced motion gets no tween: the card changes
height at once
([Respect reduced motion](/recipes/motion-defaults#respect-reduced-motion)).



---

# Show validation messages on a form

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/validation-messages

A form should say what is wrong beside the field that is wrong, before the
reader submits it. To check a form as the reader fills it in, put a
`validate` block beside each state:

**Needs:** nothing besides the page. It claims `/`: paste it into a new
project, or replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Signup(path: "/", title: "Sign up", description: "Make an account.") {
    state email = ""
    state password = ""
    state confirm = ""
    state sent = false
    validate email { required  email "Enter a valid email" }
    validate password { required  minLength(8) "At least 8 characters" }
    validate confirm { matches(password) "The passwords differ" }
    Heading("Sign up").h1
    Form(bind: form) {
        on submit { sent = true  form.reset() }
        Input(bind: email, name: "email", label: "Email").email
        Input(bind: password, name: "password", label: "Password").password
        Input(bind: confirm, name: "confirm", label: "Confirm password").password
        Button("Create account", type: .submit, disabled: !form.valid).primary
    }
    if sent { Alert("Welcome aboard.").success }
}
```

## How it works

- Each [`validate`](/learn/14-forms#validate-a-field) block names a
  state and lists its rules. A rule may take a message after it; without
  one, the rule's own is used.
- `matches(password)` holds `confirm` to whatever `password` is now.
- The control bound to a state shows that state's message. Each control
  shows its own message when the reader leaves it, with the accessible
  wiring an `error:` gets.
- `Form(bind: form)` hands the page a handle: `form.valid` disables the
  button until every rule passes, and `form.reset()` clears the form after
  a submit.
- A submit that fails moves focus to the first problem and does not run
  the `on submit` handler.

[Forms](/learn/14-forms) lists every rule.



---

# Add video and audio

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/video-and-audio

Show a video with `Video(src:)` and play sound with `Audio(src:)`, with the
browser's own playback controls, captions for the video and a transcript for
the recording.

This page plays a demo with captions and a talk with its transcript, both
from `public/`:

**Needs:** `demo.mp4`, `demo.en.vtt`, `demo.jpg`, `talk.mp3` and
`talk.txt` in `public/`. It claims `/`: paste it into a new project, or
replace the starter's `src/pages/Home.wf` with it.

```wf
page Media(path: "/", title: "Media", description: "The demo and the launch talk.") {
    Heading("Media").h1
    Video(src: "/demo.mp4", captions: "/demo.en.vtt", poster: "/demo.jpg").controls
    Audio(src: "/talk.mp3", transcript: "/talk.txt").controls
}
```

## How it works

- The `.controls` flag shows the browser's playback controls.
- `captions:` names a WebVTT file. The build writes it as a `<track>`, so a
  reader who cannot hear the video can follow it.
- `transcript:` names a text file. The build draws it as a link beneath the
  player.
- `poster:` names the picture a video shows before it plays.

Give every video captions and every recording a transcript. A `Video`
without `captions:`, and an `Audio` without `transcript:`, each draw an
`A09` warning.

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | Why, and what to do |
|---|---|
| `A09` on a `Video` or `Audio` | Add `captions:` to the video or `transcript:` to the recording |



---

# Make a site work offline

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/recipes/work-offline

Keep a site working when the network is gone: the build writes a service
worker, `sw.js`, that stores the site's pages on the reader's device, and a
page that was not stored shows a fallback page of your own.

Before you start:

- **Serve the site over HTTPS**, or from `localhost`. Browsers run service
  workers only from a secure origin.
- **Serve `sw.js` fresh.** The page registers the worker with
  `updateViaCache: "none"`, so the browser asks for it on every visit — but
  a CDN in front can still hold a copy. Give `sw.js` the header
  `Cache-Control: no-cache` ([Cache and security headers](/recipes/cache-and-security-headers#set-cache-headers)).
- **Deploy everything in `build/` together.** The worker's version is a
  hash of every file the build wrote, so deploying half a build confuses it.

Add `offline` to `webfluent.app.json`:

**Needs:** the `offline` setting below, a site served over HTTPS (or from
`localhost`), and a page at `/` for the fallback page to link to.

```json
{ "offline": {
    "precache": ["/", "/docs/*"],
    "fallback": "/offline",
    "cache": { "/api/*": "network-first" },
    "sync": true
} }
```

The `fallback` is an ordinary page of your site. This one tells the reader
what happened:

```wf
page Offline(path: "/offline", title: "Offline", description: "Shown when a page was not stored.") {
    Heading("You are offline").h1
    Text("This page was not saved for offline use. It will load when you are back online.")
    Link("Go to the home page", to: "/")
}
```

## How it works

With `offline` in the config, the build writes `sw.js` beside the pages.
Each key says what it keeps and how:

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| `precache` | The routes a first visit stores, as globs. `"/"` by default. Each route is stored with its own chunk and stylesheet, and the shell with them. |
| `fallback` | A page's `path`, shown for a route that was not stored. |
| `cache` | How a path the build did not write — an API, say — is fetched: `network-first`, `cache-first`, `stale-while-revalidate` or `network-only`. A path not named passes through untouched. |
| `sync` | Keep a write made with no network and send it later ([Keep writes made offline](/recipes/keep-writes-made-offline)). |

A stored route loads with no network at all. When there is a network, a
navigation still goes to it first, so a page that changed is never served
stale while the server is there to ask.

## What the worker keeps

What a `cache` entry fetches is kept in the worker's runtime store, the 200
most recently fetched answers, for the next reader of the device — so an
answer that is one reader's is never kept: one the server marks
`Cache-Control: no-store` or `private`, one asked for with an
`Authorization` header, and one that varies by `Cookie` or `Authorization`.
Mark what is personal `private` and it stays off the device.

Two sites on one origin under different `base_path`s keep apart: each has
its own stores, kept writes and `persist` values (`wf:/shop:cart`), and
neither deletes, serves or sends the other's. A site at the root keeps the
names it always had, and one under a base path reads a value kept under the
old name once and keeps it under the new one.

> [!NOTE]
> Under `wf serve` the worker removes itself. A page answered from its own
> store would hide every edit you make.

## Test it offline

Because `wf serve` removes the worker on purpose, test the built output with
a plain static server. Build the site and serve `build/`:

```bash
wf build
python3 -m http.server -d build
```

Then, in the browser:

1. Open the site. In the developer tools, open
   **Application → Service workers** and check the worker is activated.
2. In the **Network** panel, tick **Offline** and reload. Stored routes
   load; every other route shows the `fallback` page.
3. Make a write, then untick **Offline**. The write goes out, and
   `network.queued` drops to zero.

`wf verify` runs against the built output too, and the repository's own
browser tests hold the whole flow to a real Chrome.

## Troubleshooting

- **An upload made offline fails.** A `File` body is never kept: the call
  fails as it would without `sync`. Ask the reader to try again online.
- **A write arrives at the server minutes late.** That is the design: a kept
  write is sent once it can be. Make the server's endpoints safe to receive
  late, and idempotent where a retry could repeat one.
- **The API the site needs does not work offline.** What `cache` does not
  name passes straight through to the network. Give the API a
  `network-first` or `stale-while-revalidate` entry.
- **A page that loaded offline yesterday has to be fetched again.** The
  browser decides how much it keeps, and can evict the store under storage
  pressure. The next visit with a network stores it again.
- **Readers keep getting the old version.** Something in front of the site
  caches `sw.js`. Serve it with `Cache-Control: no-cache`.
- **Nothing is stored when you test with `wf serve`.** The dev server
  removes the worker. Test the output of `wf build` with a static server.



---

# WebFluent for HTML and CSS authors

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/coming-from/html-css

If you write HTML and CSS by hand, WebFluent keeps what you know and takes
away the repetition: elements come designed and accessible, a page's head
is written for you, and a layout is a `Row` or a `Grid` instead of a class
and a rule. Your CSS still works — any `.css` file under `src/` is part of
the build.

## The map

| Concept | HTML & CSS | WebFluent |
|---|---|---|
| A page | `index.html` with `<head>`, `<title>` and `<body>` | `page Home(path: "/", title: "Home", description: "…") { … }` |
| A heading | `<h1>Welcome</h1>` | `Heading("Welcome").h1` |
| A paragraph | `<p>Hello</p>` | `Text("Hello")` |
| A link | `<a href="/about">About</a>` | `Link("About", to: "/about")` |
| A picture | `<img src="/team.jpg" alt="The team">` | `Image(src: "/team.jpg", alt: "The team")` |
| A button | `<button class="btn btn-primary">Save</button>` | `Button("Save").primary` |
| A list | `<ul><li>One</li></ul>` | `List { List.Item { Text("One") } }` |
| A table | `<table><thead>…</thead><tbody>…</tbody></table>` | `Table { Table.Head { … } Table.Body { … } }` |
| A form field | `<label for="e">Email</label><input id="e" type="email">` | `Input(bind: email, label: "Email").email` |
| A row with flexbox | `<div class="row">` and `.row { display: flex; gap: 16px }` | `Row(gap: .md) { … }` |
| A grid | `.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) }` | `Grid(columns: 3, gap: .md) { … }` |
| A responsive grid | a `@media` rule per breakpoint | `Grid(columns: { base: 1, md: 3 })` |
| Inline styles | `style="padding: 2rem"` | `style { padding: 2rem }` in the element's block |
| Hover and focus | `.card:hover { … }` | `style { &:hover { … } }` |
| A stylesheet | `<link rel="stylesheet" href="site.css">` | any `.css` file under `src/` |
| CSS variables | `--brand: #0F766E` and `var(--brand)` | a `theme` of design tokens, read as `$color-primary` |
| Dark mode | `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` | a second theme, named as `"dark"` in the config |
| A script | `<script src="app.js"></script>` | a plain `.js` file under `src/`, its functions called by name |
| Meta tags | `<meta name="description">`, Open Graph tags | the page's `title:` and `description:`, and `meta` in the config |

## Things that work differently

**Elements are checked.** An `Image` with no `alt:` is a warning (`A01`), a
`Link` to a page that does not exist is an error (`R01`), and a flag the
element does not have (`Button("Save").primray`) stops the build. What you
would have caught with a validator and an accessibility audit, the
compiler catches on every build.

**Text is text.** Every string goes in as text, so a `<` in it is shown,
not parsed. Markup you did not write goes through `Unsafe.Html(sanitize(…))`,
which the build reports each time; inline `onclick` handlers do not compile
— a handler is `on click { … }` in the element's block.

**The head is written for you.** Each page's title, description, canonical
link, Open Graph and Twitter tags, structured data, a sitemap and
`robots.txt` come from the page and the config
([Describe pages to search engines and link previews](/recipes/search-and-link-previews)).

**Your CSS is welcome, scoped by you.** A `.css` file under `src/` is bundled
after the built-ins' rules, so yours win; `class:` on any element adds your
classes. A `style { }` block is for the one element it is on.

**A site, not a pile of files.** Pages share a header and footer through
`app` (or a `layout:`), a value shared by pages is a `store`, and repeated
markup is a `component` with typed props.

## A component, ported

A card that shows a person, in HTML and CSS and in WebFluent.

```html
<div class="card">
  <img class="avatar" src="/ada.jpg" alt="Ada Lovelace">
  <div>
    <h2>Ada Lovelace</h2>
    <p class="muted">Analyst</p>
  </div>
</div>

<style>
  .card { display: flex; gap: 12px; align-items: center; padding: 16px;
          border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 8px; }
  .avatar { width: 48px; height: 48px; border-radius: 50%; }
  .muted { color: #666; }
</style>
```

```wf
page Team(path: "/", title: "Team", description: "Who we are.") {
    Heading("Team").h1
    Person("Ada Lovelace", role: "Analyst", photo: "/ada.jpg")
}

component Person(_ name: String, role: String, photo: String) {
    Card.outlined {
        Row(gap: .sm, align: .center) {
            Avatar(src: photo, alt: name)
            Stack {
                Heading(name).h2
                Text(role).muted
            }
        }
    }
}
```

- **No class names to invent.** `Card.outlined`, `Avatar` and `.muted` come
  designed, and follow the theme.
- **One component, many people.** `Person` is placed with each person's
  props; the compiler checks every call.



---

# WebFluent for LaTeX and Typst authors

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/coming-from/latex

WebFluent prints PDFs and slide decks from the same language it builds
websites with, with no TeX installation and no browser. If you know LaTeX
or Typst, the shapes are familiar — a document, headings, a table of
contents, page headers and footers — but the layout is the web's: rows,
stacks and grids, styled with CSS.

## The map

| Concept | LaTeX / Typst | WebFluent |
|---|---|---|
| The paper | `\documentclass[a4paper]{article}` / `#set page(paper: "a4")` | `Document(size: "A4", margin: "20mm") { … }` |
| Title and author | `\title{…}\author{…}` / `#set document(title: …)` | `Document(title: "Q1 report", author: "Acme")` |
| A section | `\section{Results}` / `= Results` | `Heading("Results").h2` (the title is the `h1`) |
| A subsection | `\subsection{Method}` / `== Method` | `Heading("Method").h3` |
| A paragraph | a blank line between paragraphs | `Text("…")`, or `Markdown("…")` for several |
| Bold and italic | `\textbf{x}`, `\emph{x}` / `*x*`, `_x_` | `Text("x").bold`, `Text("x").italic`, or `**x**` in `Markdown` |
| A list | `itemize` / `- item` | `List { List.Item { Text("…") } }` |
| The contents | `\tableofcontents` / `#outline()` | `TableOfContents(levels: 2)` |
| A new page | `\newpage` / `#pagebreak()` | `PageBreak` |
| Keep together | `\begin{minipage}` / `block(breakable: false)` | `style { break-inside: avoid }` |
| Headers and footers | `fancyhdr` / `#set page(header: …)` | `Header { … }`, `Footer { Text("Page {page} of {pages}") }` |
| A table | `tabular` / `#table(…)` | `Table { Table.Head { … } Table.Body { … } }` |
| A figure | `\includegraphics{chart.png}` / `#image("chart.png")` | `Image(src: "/chart.png", alt: "…")` |
| A chart | `pgfplots` | `Chart(kind: .bar, data: SALES, x: "month", y: "web")` |
| A macro | `\newcommand{\price}[1]{…}` / `#let price(x) = …` | `component Price(_ amount: Number) { … }` |
| Data | `\input{data}`, `datatool` / `#let data = json("data.json")` | `data sales = "sales.json"`, or a `const` |
| Fonts | `fontspec` / `#set text(font: …)` | a `.ttf` or `.otf` under `fonts/`, named in `font-family` |
| Slides | Beamer frames / Touying | `Presentation { Slide { … } }`, with `"output_type": "slides"` |
| Building | `pdflatex`, `latexmk` / `typst compile` | `wf build`, with `"output_type": "pdf"` in the config |

## Things that work differently

**The layout is CSS.** A document is laid out from the same HTML and CSS a
web page would get: `Row`, `Stack` and `Grid` place things side by side,
and a `style { }` block or a `.css` file styles them. There are no TeX boxes
and glue to tune.

**Breaking across pages is a rule, not a command.** Paragraphs keep two
lines on each side of a break, a heading moves with what follows it, and a
table repeats its header row on every page it continues on. Ask for the
rest with `break-inside: avoid` and `PageBreak`.

**There is no math typesetting.** A formula is a picture or an SVG you
place with `Image`. There is no bibliography system either; references are
text you write.

**Arabic and right-to-left work out of the box.** A document whose `lang`
is `ar`, `he`, `fa` or `ur` is laid out right to left, and shaping comes
with it — no extra packages.

**One source, three outputs.** The page that prints as a PDF can also be a
web page, and a `Presentation` is a deck from the same components
([PDF and slides](/learn/17-pdf-and-slides)).

## A component, ported

A short report with a footer and a table, in LaTeX and in WebFluent.

```latex
\documentclass[a4paper]{article}
\usepackage{fancyhdr}
\pagestyle{fancy}
\cfoot{Page \thepage}
\title{Quarterly report}
\author{Acme Studio}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\section{Sales}
Revenue grew in every region.
\begin{tabular}{lr}
Region & Revenue \\
North & \$2.4M \\
South & \$1.9M \\
\end{tabular}
\end{document}
```

```wf
page Report(path: "/", title: "Quarterly report", description: "Sales for the quarter.") {
    Document(size: "A4", title: "Quarterly report", author: "Acme Studio") {
        Footer { Text("Page {page} of {pages}").muted.sm.center }
        Heading("Quarterly report").h1
        Text("Acme Studio").muted
        Heading("Sales").h2
        Text("Revenue grew in every region.")
        Table(caption: "Revenue by region") {
            Table.Head { Table.Row { Table.Cell("Region")  Table.Cell("Revenue") } }
            Table.Body {
                Table.Row { Table.Cell("North")  Table.Cell("$2.4M") }
                Table.Row { Table.Cell("South")  Table.Cell("$1.9M") }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

- **The footer is an element**, drawn on every page, with `page` and
  `pages` in scope.
- **The table is the web's table**, broken between rows and with its header
  repeated when it spans pages.



---

# WebFluent for React developers

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/coming-from/react

Most of what you know from React carries over: components with props,
state, a router and shared stores. The difference to hold on to is that
WebFluent is a compiler with typed markup, not a library: a component's body
runs once, and only the text, attribute or style that reads a changed value
updates. There are no hooks, no dependency arrays and no setters.

## The map

| Concept | React | WebFluent |
|---|---|---|
| A value that changes | `const [n, setN] = useState(0)` | `state n = 0` |
| Changing it | `setN(n + 1)` | `n = n + 1` |
| A value worked out from others | `const total = useMemo(() => sum(items), [items])` | `derived total = items.sum()` |
| A side effect | `useEffect(() => { start(); return () => stop() }, [id])` | `effect { start(id)  cleanup { stop() } }` |
| A handle on an element | `const box = useRef(null)` … `box.current.focus()` | `Input(bind: q, ref: box)` … `box.focus()` |
| A component | `function Card({ title }) { … }` | `component Card(_ title: String) { … }` |
| What the caller puts inside | `{props.children}` | `children` |
| A callback prop | `onChange={(v) => setLast(v)}` | `event change(value: Number)`, handled as `on change(value) { last = value }` |
| A controlled input | `value={q} onChange={(e) => setQ(e.target.value)}` | `Input(bind: q, label: "Search")` |
| State shared across pages | `createContext`, Redux, Zustand | `store Cart { … }`, read as `Cart.items` after `use Cart` |
| A route | `<Route path="/users/:id" element={<User />} />` | `page User(path: "/users/:id", id: String) { … }` |
| Showing something conditionally | `{open && <Panel />}` | `if open { Panel }` |
| A list | `{items.map((i) => <li key={i.id}>{i.name}</li>)}` | `for i in items by i.id { Text(i.name) }` |
| Fetching | TanStack Query's `useQuery({ queryKey: ["users"], queryFn })`, or `useEffect` + `fetch` | `resource users = fetch("/api/users")`, read with `match users { … }` |
| Styling | `className`, CSS modules, Tailwind | flags (`Button("Save").primary`), `style { }` on the element, design tokens |
| A test | Testing Library: `render`, `fireEvent.click`, `getByText` | `test "…" { click "Save"  expect "Saved" }` |

## Things that work differently

**It is a compiler, not a library.** There is no virtual DOM and no
re-render. Each text, attribute or style that reads a state follows it on
its own, and a component's body runs once, when it is placed. That is why
there are no hooks and no rules about calling them in order.

**The markup is typed.** The compiler knows the props, flags, events and
slots of every built-in and of every component you declare.
`Button("Save").primray` does not build, and neither does a handler for an
event the component never fires (`E103`). An unknown prop on your own
component is `C02`, not a silent pass-through.

**Pages own their routes.** There is no route table. Each `page` names its
`path:`, and the compiler builds the router from them, ordered by
specificity, so the order you declare pages in cannot hide a route.

**No imports, no npm.** Every file under `src/` is part of one program, so a
component declared anywhere is usable everywhere. A JavaScript library is a
URL in `meta.scripts`, and your own JavaScript is a plain `.js` file under
`src/` whose functions `.wf` code calls by name
([Call your own JavaScript](/recipes/call-your-own-script)).

**The build is the site.** Pre-rendering, code splitting, image resizing, a
sitemap, link previews and a Content-Security-Policy come from `wf build`,
with no plugins to choose. There is no server rendering on each request: a
site is static files and a browser runtime, talking to your API.

**Text is text.** The only way to put markup on a page is `Unsafe.Html(…)`,
which the build flags every time, and inline handlers and `javascript:`
URLs do not compile ([Security](/about/security)).

**Using it inside a React app.** Publish components as custom elements and
place their tags in JSX
([Publish components as custom elements](/recipes/publish-custom-elements)).

## A component, ported

The same counter, in React and in WebFluent. It starts at a number the
caller passes, counts up on a click, shows a badge when the count is even,
and tells the caller about each change.

```jsx
function Counter({ start = 0, onChange }) {
  const [n, setN] = useState(start);
  const even = useMemo(() => n % 2 === 0, [n]);
  return (
    <div className="row">
      <button onClick={() => { setN(n + 1); onChange?.(n + 1); }}>+</button>
      <span>{n}</span>
      {even && <span className="badge">even</span>}
    </div>
  );
}
```

```wf
page Scores(path: "/", title: "Scores", description: "A counter that reports each change.") {
    state last = 0
    Heading("Scores").h1
    Counter(start: 2) { on change(value) { last = value } }
    Text("Last change: {last}")
}

component Counter(start: Number = 0) {
    event change(value: Number)
    state n = start
    derived even = n % 2 == 0
    Row(gap: .sm, align: .center) {
        Button("+") { on click { n = n + 1  emit change(n) } }
        Text("{n}")
        if even { Badge("even").info }
    }
}
```

- **No hooks and no dependency arrays.** `derived` knows what it reads.
- **No setter.** You assign: `n = n + 1`.
- **No `className`.** `Badge` comes designed, and `.info` is a flag the
  compiler checks.
- **The event is declared.** A caller that handles `on chnage` gets `E103`
  at build time, instead of a handler that never runs.



---

# WebFluent for Svelte developers

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/coming-from/svelte

If you write Svelte, WebFluent will feel close: it is also a compiler, state
is a plain assignment, and only what reads a changed value updates. What
WebFluent adds is a typed markup: every element, prop, flag, event and slot
is checked at build time, and the components come designed.

## The map

| Concept | Svelte | WebFluent |
|---|---|---|
| A value that changes | `let n = $state(0)` | `state n = 0` |
| Changing it | `n += 1` | `n = n + 1` |
| A value worked out from others | `let total = $derived(sum(items))` | `derived total = items.sum()` |
| A side effect | `$effect(() => { start(); return stop })` | `effect { start()  cleanup { stop() } }` |
| A handle on an element | `<input bind:this={box}>` | `Input(bind: q, ref: box)` |
| A component | a `.svelte` file | `component Card(_ title: String) { … }` |
| Props | `let { title, tone = "calm" } = $props()` | `component Card(_ title: String, tone: Tone = .calm)` |
| What the caller puts inside | `{@render children()}` | `children` |
| A snippet the component draws | `{@render row(item)}` | `slot row(item: Todo)`, filled as `row(todo) { … }` |
| An event | a callback prop, `onchange?.(n)` | `event change(value: Number)`, `emit change(n)` |
| Two-way binding | `<input bind:value={q}>` | `Input(bind: q, label: "Search")` |
| Shared state | a store or a `.svelte.js` module | `store Cart { … }`, read as `Cart.items` after `use Cart` |
| A route | SvelteKit `src/routes/users/[id]/+page.svelte` | `page User(path: "/users/:id", id: String) { … }` |
| `{#if}` | `{#if open}<Panel />{:else}<p>…</p>{/if}` | `if open { Panel } else { Text("…") }` |
| `{#each}` | `{#each items as i (i.id)}<li>{i.name}</li>{/each}` | `for i in items by i.id { Text(i.name) }` |
| `{#await}` | `{#await promise}…{:then data}…{:catch e}…{/await}` | `match users { loading { … } ready(list) { … } error(e) { … } }` |
| A class that follows state | `class:done={todo.done}` | `class: { "done": todo.done }` |
| Transitions | `transition:fade` | `.fadeIn`, `exit: .fadeOut` |
| A test | Vitest with Testing Library: `render`, `fireEvent.click`, `getByText` | `test "…" { click "Save"  expect "Saved" }` |

## Things that work differently

**The elements are typed too.** `svelte-check` types your props and the
expressions in your markup; WebFluent also knows every built-in's flags,
events and slots. `Button("Save").primray` does not build, and neither
does a handler for an event the component does not fire (`E103`).

**Elements come designed.** `Button`, `Card`, `Table`, `Modal` and the rest
are built in, with their accessibility work done, and a flag picks a variant
(`.primary`, `.lg`). Your own look is a theme of design tokens and a
`style { }` on the element.

**Pages own their routes.** There is no `src/routes` folder: each `page`
names its `path:`, and the compiler builds the router from every page,
ordered by specificity.

**No imports.** Every file under `src/` is part of one program, so a
component declared anywhere is usable everywhere.

**Fetching is a value.** A `resource` is read with `match`, and repeats when
a state its address reads changes; an `api` block describes a service once,
so every call is typed, cached and cancellable.

**The build is the site.** Pre-rendering, code splitting, image resizing and
a Content-Security-Policy come from `wf build`; there is no server to run.

## A component, ported

The same counter, in Svelte and in WebFluent. It starts at a number the
caller passes, counts up on a click, shows a badge when the count is even,
and tells the caller about each change.

```svelte
<script>
  let { start = 0, onchange } = $props();
  let n = $state(start);
  let even = $derived(n % 2 === 0);
  function inc() { n += 1; onchange?.(n); }
</script>

<div class="row">
  <button onclick={inc}>+</button>
  <span>{n}</span>
  {#if even}<span class="badge">even</span>{/if}
</div>
```

```wf
page Scores(path: "/", title: "Scores", description: "A counter that reports each change.") {
    state last = 0
    Heading("Scores").h1
    Counter(start: 2) { on change(value) { last = value } }
    Text("Last change: {last}")
}

component Counter(start: Number = 0) {
    event change(value: Number)
    state n = start
    derived even = n % 2 == 0
    Row(gap: .sm, align: .center) {
        Button("+") { on click { n = n + 1  emit change(n) } }
        Text("{n}")
        if even { Badge("even").info }
    }
}
```

- **The same reactivity**, spelled `state` and `derived`.
- **The event is declared**, so a caller's misspelled handler is a build
  error rather than a prop nobody reads.
- **No `class`.** `Badge` comes designed, and `.info` is checked.



---

# WebFluent for Vue developers

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/coming-from/vue

Vue's single-file components, refs, computed values, slots and `v-model`
all have a close match in WebFluent. The difference to hold on to is that
WebFluent is a compiler with typed markup: there is no `.value`, no
template language beside the script, and every prop, slot and event is
checked at build time.

## The map

| Concept | Vue | WebFluent |
|---|---|---|
| A value that changes | `const n = ref(0)` | `state n = 0` |
| Changing it | `n.value++` | `n = n + 1` |
| A value worked out from others | `const total = computed(() => sum(items.value))` | `derived total = items.sum()` |
| A side effect | `watchEffect((onCleanup) => { start(); onCleanup(stop) })` | `effect { start()  cleanup { stop() } }` |
| A handle on an element | `<input ref="box">` … `box.value.focus()` | `Input(bind: q, ref: box)` … `box.focus()` |
| A component | a `.vue` file with `<script setup>` and `<template>` | `component Card(_ title: String) { … }` |
| Props | `defineProps({ title: String })` | `component Card(_ title: String, tone: Tone = .calm)` |
| The default slot | `<slot />` | `children` |
| A named slot | `<slot name="trailing" />` | `slot trailing`, filled as `trailing { … }` |
| A scoped slot | `<slot :item="item" />` | `slot row(item: Todo)`, filled as `row(todo) { … }` |
| An event | `defineEmits(["change"])`, `emit("change", n)` | `event change(value: Number)`, `emit change(n)` |
| `v-model` | `<input v-model="q">` | `Input(bind: q, label: "Search")` |
| Shared state | `provide`/`inject`, Pinia | `store Cart { … }`, read as `Cart.items` after `use Cart` |
| A route | vue-router `{ path: "/users/:id", component: User }` | `page User(path: "/users/:id", id: String) { … }` |
| `v-if` / `v-else` | `<Panel v-if="open" /><p v-else>…</p>` | `if open { Panel } else { Text("…") }` |
| `v-show` | `<Panel v-show="open" />` | `show open { Panel }` |
| `v-for` | `<li v-for="i in items" :key="i.id">{{ i.name }}</li>` | `for i in items by i.id { Text(i.name) }` |
| Class bindings | `:class="{ done: todo.done }"` | `class: { "done": todo.done }` |
| Transitions | `<Transition name="fade">` | `.fadeIn`, `exit: .fadeOut` |
| Fetching | `<Suspense>` with an async `setup`, or VueUse's `useFetch("/api/users")` | `resource users = fetch("/api/users")`, read with `match users { … }` |
| A test | Vitest with Vue Test Utils: `mount`, `trigger("click")`, `text()` | `test "…" { click "Save"  expect "Saved" }` |

## Things that work differently

**One file, one language.** A component is declared in `.wf` with its
state, its markup and its handlers together; there is no `<template>`, no
`<script>` block and no `.value` to remember. A component's body runs once,
and only what reads a changed value updates.

**The markup is typed.** The compiler knows the props, flags, events and
slots of every built-in and of every component you declare. A misspelled
prop, an unknown flag (`Button("Save").primray`) or a handler for an event
the component does not fire stops the build, with the fix suggested.

**Pages own their routes.** There is no router file. Each `page` names its
`path:`, and the compiler builds the router from every page.

**No imports.** Every file under `src/` is part of one program, so a
component declared anywhere is usable everywhere, and two declarations of
one name are an error.

**Styles are on the element.** A `style { }` block is CSS for that element,
with design tokens (`$surface`) and nesting (`&:hover`); there is no
`<style scoped>`, and what a selector over many elements needs goes in a
`.css` file under `src/`.

**Using it inside a Vue app.** Publish components as custom elements and
use their tags in a template
([Publish components as custom elements](/recipes/publish-custom-elements)).

## A component, ported

The same counter, in Vue and in WebFluent. It starts at a number the caller
passes, counts up on a click, shows a badge when the count is even, and
tells the caller about each change.

```vue
<script setup>
import { ref, computed } from "vue";
const props = defineProps({ start: { type: Number, default: 0 } });
const emit = defineEmits(["change"]);
const n = ref(props.start);
const even = computed(() => n.value % 2 === 0);
function inc() { n.value++; emit("change", n.value); }
</script>

<template>
  <div class="row">
    <button @click="inc">+</button>
    <span>{{ n }}</span>
    <span v-if="even" class="badge">even</span>
  </div>
</template>
```

```wf
page Scores(path: "/", title: "Scores", description: "A counter that reports each change.") {
    state last = 0
    Heading("Scores").h1
    Counter(start: 2) { on change(value) { last = value } }
    Text("Last change: {last}")
}

component Counter(start: Number = 0) {
    event change(value: Number)
    state n = start
    derived even = n % 2 == 0
    Row(gap: .sm, align: .center) {
        Button("+") { on click { n = n + 1  emit change(n) } }
        Text("{n}")
        if even { Badge("even").info }
    }
}
```

- **No `.value`.** A state is read and assigned by its name.
- **`derived` replaces `computed`**, and knows what it reads.
- **The event is declared** where the component is, and checked where it is
  handled.

# Accessibility

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/about/accessibility

This essay is about the accessibility a WebFluent page has before you do
anything, the part the compiler checks on every build, and the part that
stays yours: building pages people can use with a keyboard, a screen
reader, voice control, zoom or reduced motion.

Most inaccessible pages were not made that way on purpose. A `<div>` with
a click handler looks like a button and is not one; a field whose label is
a placeholder looks labelled until the reader types. Each is a small
mistake that a checklist would catch, and checklists are read once.

WebFluent moves as much of the checklist as it can out of your hands. The
built-ins render the markup assistive technology expects, the router and
forms manage focus, and the compiler reports what it can see as a finding
with a code, on every build. That leaves the work no tool can do (meaning,
wording, order) and frees your attention for it.

## What the built-ins do

You get these behaviours without asking, as long as you use the built-in
elements rather than rebuilding them:

- **Semantic elements.** A `Button` is a `<button>`, a `Link` an `<a>`,
  `Heading(…).h2` an `<h2>`. `Header` and `Footer` are landmarks,
  and so is a `Section` given an `aria-label`. A `Table` is a `<table>`
  whose head cells are `<th scope="col">`, a `List` is a `<ul>` or `<ol>`,
  and the page's content is a `<main>`.
- **A skip link.** It is first in the tab order, visible when focused, and
  jumps past the navigation to the content.
- **Route changes that behave like page loads.** Focus moves to the new
  page's heading, the scroll returns to the top, and the new title is
  announced.
- **Labelled fields.** `label:` is a real `<label for>`. `hint:` and the
  error are tied to the control with `aria-describedby`. An error sets
  `aria-invalid` and is announced when it appears ([Forms](/learn/14-forms)).
- **Forms that point at the problem.** A submit that fails moves focus to
  the first field with an error and announces it.
- **Dialogs that hold focus.** `Modal` and `Dialog` are real `<dialog>`
  elements: the rest of the page is inert, Escape closes them, and focus
  returns to what opened them.
- **Focus held where you ask.** Any other element holds focus with
  `trapFocus: open` — a find bar, a panel. Focus moves in, Tab and
  Shift+Tab go round inside it, a click outside brings focus back, and when
  `open` turns false, focus returns to where it was.
- **Menus with the keys people expect.** The arrow keys move and skip a
  disabled item, Home and End jump to the ends, Enter and Space choose,
  ArrowRight opens a submenu and ArrowLeft leaves it, and Escape closes the
  innermost menu and returns focus. A check item is a `menuitemcheckbox`
  with `aria-checked`; an item's shortcut is its `aria-keyshortcuts`.
- **Splitters you can move without a mouse.** A `Splitter` is a
  `separator` with its size as `aria-valuenow`. It takes focus, the arrow
  keys move it, Home and End go to its ends, and Enter resets it.
- **Announcements.** A `Toast` is spoken politely. To announce anything
  else, call `WF.announce(text)`.
- **The active link.** The link to the current page carries
  `aria-current="page"`.
- **Reduced motion.** A reader who asked for it gets no animation at all,
  and a carousel does not play on its own ([Motion](/recipes/motion-defaults#respect-reduced-motion)).
- **Visible focus.** Every interactive built-in shows a focus ring for the
  keyboard (`:focus-visible`), but not on every click.

## What the compiler checks

The compiler checks every page for the mistakes it can see in the markup,
and reports each as a warning on every build and in the editor. Each code
has a full entry, with a fix, in [Diagnostics](/errors#accessibility),
and `wf explain CODE` prints it in your terminal.

| Code | What it checks |
|---|---|
| `A01` | Every `Image` has `alt:` (an empty one for a decorative picture) |
| `A02` | Every `IconButton` has a `label:` |
| `A03`, `A04` | Every `Input` has a label or at least a placeholder (prefer a label); every `Checkbox`, `Radio`, `Switch`, `Slider` and `Textarea` has a label |
| `A05`, `A06`, `A07` | Buttons, links and headings have text |
| `A08` | Every `Modal`, `Dialog`, `AlertDialog` and `Sheet` has a `title:` (a `Sheet` may have a `label:`) |
| `A09` | A video has captions and controls; audio has a transcript |
| `A10` | A table has a header row |
| `A11`, `A12` | No heading level is skipped, and each page has exactly one `h1` |
| `A13` | The theme's text and background colours meet WCAG AA contrast |
| `A14` | A `role:` holds children of the roles it requires |
| `A15` | A control's `aria-label` contains its visible text, for voice control |
| `A16` | No literal `id:` is shared by several elements, in a loop or a reused component |
| `A17` | Every `Frame` has a `title:` |
| `A18` | Every `Popover` drawn as a dialog has a `label:` |

For example, this button's `aria-label` does not contain the word it
shows, so a voice-control user who says "click Save" may not reach it:

```wf expect=A15
page Editor(path: "/", title: "Editor", description: "Write a note.") {
    Heading("Editor").h1
    Button("Save", aria-label: "Submit the form")
}
```

The fix is to start the `aria-label` with the visible words:
`aria-label: "Save the note"`.

## What the compiler cannot check

The compiler can see markup; it cannot see meaning. These are still yours:

- **Alt text that says what the picture shows**, in its context. "Photo"
  passes `A01` and helps nobody.
- **Link text that says where it goes.** Twelve "Read more" links pass
  `A06`.
- **An order that makes sense.** The reading order is the source order. Do
  not rearrange it visually with `order:` or absolute positioning.
- **Colour that is not the only signal.** An error in red also says so in
  words; a chart has labels.
- **The contrast of your own styles.** `A13` checks the theme's tokens, not
  a colour written directly in a `style { }` block.
- **Custom controls.** A `Card` made clickable with `on click` is not a
  button to a keyboard until it has a role, a place in the tab order and
  key handlers.
- **Time limits.** A `Toast` disappears. Anything the reader must act on
  belongs in an `Alert` that stays.

Each of these is a judgement about what a page means to the person using
it, which is why no build can make it. What a tool can do is make the
judgement cheaper:
[Make a page work with a keyboard and a screen reader](/recipes/keyboard-and-screen-reader)
names every control so it matches what a sighted reader sees, turns a card
into a control a keyboard can reach, and then checks the page the way its
readers use it — with only a keyboard, a screen reader, 200% zoom and
reduced motion — ending with a checklist. Because `wf test` finds a
control by the name a reader sees, as assistive technology does, a test
that clicks through a page is also a test that someone can operate it.

## Next

[Forms and validation](/learn/14-forms): bind controls to state, validate what the reader types, upload files, and show what the server said.



---

# Contributing

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/about/contributing

This page is for working on WebFluent itself: the compiler, the
runtime, the editor support or this guide. It tells you how to build and
test the project, where each part lives, and what to update when you change
one.

The project holds itself to the rule it holds programs to: what can be
checked is checked, by a test, on every push. The registry, the error
pages, the components reference and every example in this guide are tied
to the compiler, so a change that leaves one of them behind fails a test
instead of drifting. Most of what follows is where those ties are, so you
know which ones a change will pull.

WebFluent is one Rust crate — the compiler and the `wf` binary — with a
language server beside it, editor extensions, a small JavaScript runtime
and this guide, all in one repository:
[github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent).

## Before you start

You need:

- Rust 1.92 or later (the crate uses the 2024 edition).
- Node.js 20, for the runtime's tests and the browser suites.
- Chrome or Chromium, for the browser suites.

Clone the repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent
cd WebFluent
```

## Build and test

Build the compiler, then run the Rust tests, the runtime's tests and the
lints that CI runs:

```bash
cargo build
cargo test --workspace
node --test tests/js/*.test.mjs
cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings
```

The browser suites check what only a real browser can — a service worker,
WebRTC, layers, keys, gestures and more. They drive the release build, so
build it first, then run them from `tests/browser`:

```bash
cargo build --release
cd tests/browser
npm ci
npm test
```

`npm test` runs sixteen suites, starting with `offline.mjs` and `peer.mjs`;
each is also a script you can run alone, such as `node offline.mjs`. CI
runs all of it on every push, and a few browser suites more.

## The repository

Each part of the project has its own folder. Under `src/`, the compiler is
in layers, bottom first; a module uses only its own layer and the ones
above it in this list, which `tests/module_layers.rs` holds it to:

```text
src/
  base/                      spans, text helpers, the file systems a build reads and writes
  diagnostics/               every finding's code (codes.rs), fixes and output; the error types
  syntax/                    lexer/, parser/, the .wfx layout/, the printers and the formatter
  registry/                  every built-in's props, cases, flags, events, slots, parts
  project/                   config, themes/ (tokens and the built-ins' CSS), i18n, scripts, data, media
  check/                     sema/ (names, the type checker), linter/, validation, scopes, edits
  web/                       codegen/ (JS, HTML, CSS, the pre-rendered page, SEO), runtime/modules/, motion
  paged/                     the PDF and slides engine
  template/                  the template engine behind `wf render`
  build/                     `wf build` as a library call, its cache, assets, the service worker
  tools/                     migrate, test, verify, audit, studio, agent, init, generate, docs
  cli/                       each `wf` command
crates/wf-lsp/               the language server
editors/                     VS Code, Zed and the Tree-sitter grammars: submodules, each its own repository
md-docs/                     this guide
site/                        the documentation site, written in WebFluent
tests/                       Rust integration tests, tests/js (runtime), tests/browser (Chrome)
spec/                        design notes and plans
```

The editors live in their own repositories — [tree-sitter-webfluent](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/tree-sitter-webfluent),
[webfluent-zed](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/webfluent-zed) and [webfluent-vscode](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/webfluent-vscode) — linked here as submodules under `editors/`. Building and
testing the compiler needs none of them. To work on one, or to run the
checks that hold them to the compiler (`just zed-check`), check them out:

```bash
git submodule update --init
```

A change there is committed and pushed in its own repository; then the
submodule's new commit is committed here (`git add editors/zed`).

## The pipeline

A source file passes through these stages, in order:

```text
.wf / .wfx → lexer → parser → lower → semantic checks → type checker → linters → code generators
                                                                                 ├─ JavaScript + HTML + CSS
                                                                                 └─ PDF / slides
```

Every stage reads the **registry** for what a built-in takes. So a prop
added there is known at once to the checker, the linters, the language
server, `wf docs` and the
[components reference](/reference).

## Change a built-in's props or flags

1. Edit the built-in's entry in `src/registry/builtins.rs`.
2. Update its CSS in `src/project/themes/` and its code generation in
   `src/web/codegen/`.
3. Rewrite the [components reference](/reference) from
   the registry, with the command below.

```bash
cargo xtask site
```

## Change the grammar

A change to the grammar touches every place that reads or writes source:

- the parser, in `src/syntax/parser/v2.rs`;
- the formatter and the `.wfx` layout;
- the printer, in `src/syntax/print.rs`;
- both Tree-sitter grammars, in [tree-sitter-webfluent](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/tree-sitter-webfluent) (checked out here as the
  `editors/tree-sitter-webfluent` submodule).

The guide's own code blocks are the grammar's test corpus.
`tests/printer_corpus.rs` prints every statement of every project in the
repository back in its place and holds it to the same tree, and
`tests/reprint_corpus.rs` holds every edit to changing only its own bytes.

## Change the runtime

Edit or add a module in `src/web/runtime/modules/`, and add a test for it in
`tests/js/`. The manifest that says what reaches each module,
`src/web/runtime/modules/manifest.json`, is written by a Rust test, so you do
not edit it by hand.

## Add a diagnostic

1. Give the finding a code, a severity and a title in
   `src/diagnostics/codes.rs`.
2. Write its page, `md-docs/errors/<CODE>.md`: what the reader sees, why,
   and the fix, with a program in a `wf expect=CODE` block that draws the
   code. The test suite compiles every example and checks that it draws its
   code, and a code with no page fails a test. The
   [Diagnostics](/errors) index lists every page.

## Change this guide

The guide lives in `md-docs/`, one file per chapter, in a folder for its
kind of page (`learn/`, `recipes/`, `about/`, `reference/`, `errors/`,
`coming-from/`), and is the source of the documentation site:
`cargo xtask site` writes the site's chapter pages, the book's chapter list,
the components reference and the search index from it, and
`cargo xtask site --check` says whether they are current. Each chapter
starts with front matter naming its number, its kind, its route, its group
in the sidebar, the line under its title and its search description.
"How we write", §8 of `plans/docs-redesign/README.md`, holds the rules
every page follows, and `tests/docs_parse.rs` checks the ones a test can
read.

The test suite holds the guide to the compiler:

- every `wf` code block parses, type-checks and compiles without a
  warning;
- every `wf expect=CODE` block draws that code;
- every link between chapters, and every anchor, resolves;
- every declaration, keyword, built-in, browser value, built-in function,
  config key, command and diagnostic code appears in it;
- the tokens chapter is the baseline, and the configuration chapter's
  defaults are the compiler's;
- the site's pages are what the generator writes from the guide.

Words after `wf` in a fence say how a block is checked: `expect=CODE`
(it must draw that code), `fixed` (the corrected program after one),
`page` and `live` (built, previewed, and editable by the reader),
`files=a,b` (one file of a multi-file example), and `no-check` (not
compiled, for a block the prose says is not a program). The full list is
`Fence` in `tests/common/mod.rs`.

## Release a version

[`RELEASING.md`](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/blob/master/RELEASING.md) in the repository lists the steps: one
tag builds the binaries, the packages and the editor extensions.

## Next

[Why WebFluent](/about/why): why the language exists, and the choices it makes.
