# How reactivity works

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/about/how-reactivity-works

This essay explains what WebFluent does when a value changes: how a
`state` knows who reads it, why only those readers redraw, and how
branches, lists and refreshed data keep the nodes they already drew.

The claim it defends: a page should be drawn once, and after that a
change should touch exactly the nodes that read what changed. Everything
below is the machinery that makes that true, and the price it charges.

## What a page compiles to

This page has a value that changes, a value worked out from it, and a
button that changes it.

```wf
page Home(path: "/", title: "Count", description: "A counter.") {
    state count = 0
    derived double = count * 2
    Heading("Count").h1
    Text("{count} doubled is {double}")
    Button("Add one") { on click { count = count + 1 } }
}
```

`wf build` turns it into one function that runs once, when the route is
shown. Here it is, laid out for reading:

```js
function Page_Home(params) {
  const _count = WF.signal(0);
  const _root = document.createDocumentFragment();
  const _double = WF.computed(() => _count() * 2);
  _root.appendChild(WF.el("h1", { className: "wf-heading" }, "Count"));
  _root.appendChild(WF.el("p", { className: "wf-text" },
    () => `${_count()} doubled is ${_double()}`));
  const button = WF.el("button", { className: "wf-btn", type: "button" }, "Add one");
  button.addEventListener("click", () => { _count.set(_count() + 1); });
  _root.appendChild(button);
  return _root;
}
```

There is no render function that runs again, no tree of descriptions to
compare with the last one, and no component that re-renders. The heading
is a plain `<h1>` made once. The paragraph's text is the one thing that
can change, and it is handed to `WF.el` as a function: that function is
what will run again.

## A signal knows who reads it

`WF.signal(0)` returns a getter. Calling it returns the value, and, if an
effect is running at that moment, adds that effect to the signal's list of
readers. That is the whole trick of dependency tracking: nothing is
declared, because reading is declaring.

The function the paragraph was given becomes an effect over one text node.
Its first run reads `_count()` and `_double()`, so both now list it. When
the button calls `_count.set(1)`, the signal compares the new value with
the old one (`!==`), and, since they differ, runs the effects that read it.
The text node gets its new text. The `<h1>`, the button and the rest of
the page are not touched, because nothing about them read `count`.

An effect listens to exactly what its last run read. Each run takes it off
every signal it was listed on, and the run lists it again. So an effect
whose condition stopped reading a value stops running for that value, and
the set of dependencies is always the true one, not one you wrote down.

## A derived value is an effect that writes a signal

`derived double = count * 2` compiles to `WF.computed`: a signal of its
own, kept current by an effect that reads `count`. When `count` changes,
that effect runs, writes `double`, and the write runs `double`'s readers
in turn. A derived value that works out to the same value as before
(`count > 0` while `count` goes from 3 to 4) stops there: its signal
compares, sees no change, and its readers do not run.

Two consequences follow:

- A derived value is eager. It is worked out when what it reads changes,
  not when something reads it, so reading it costs nothing.
- It cannot be assigned. It has one source, its expression, and the
  compiler refuses an assignment to it (`X01`).

## One change, one ordered run

A change does not redraw at once and then again for every dependent; it
collects every effect it reaches and runs them in one pass, oldest first.
The order matters. A branch is made before what it draws, so when an `if`
closes and a `derived` it guarded changes in the same click, the branch
runs first, takes its contents away, and the effects inside it are
disposed of before they can read a value that no longer makes sense for
them.

An effect that writes what it reads comes back into the same pass. One
that settles does so in a run or two. One that never settles would loop
forever; the compiler refuses the ones it can see (`X02`), and the runtime
stops any other after 100 runs, with a warning under `wf serve`.

## Values are replaced, not mutated

A signal notices a change by comparing identities. If code pushed onto
the list a `state` holds, the list would be the same object, and nothing
would redraw. So WebFluent never lets that happen silently:
`items[i].done = v`, `form.name = v` or `items.sort()` written as a
statement compile to the state given a copy with that place changed.
Reading `items.sort(…)` in an expression sorts a copy. You write the
change the way you think of it, and the signal still sees a new value.

## A branch tracks its condition, and nothing else

An `if` compiles to `WF.when`, an effect that reads only the condition.
The branch's body is drawn with tracking turned off, so a value the body
reads does not make the whole branch draw again; it makes the one node
that reads it update, as anywhere else. The branch draws again only when
the condition flips.

Everything the body made belongs to the branch. Effects, timers from
`every` and `after`, event listeners on the window, handles from `ref:`:
each is created inside a scope, and when the branch leaves, the scope runs
every cleanup it collected. A signal that outlives the branch, such as a
store's state, has the branch's effects taken off its list, so it does not
keep their nodes alive. That is why a page in WebFluent does not leak a
timer when you navigate away from it: the page is a scope too.

## A keyed list moves rows instead of rebuilding them

This page has a list, a count worked out from it, and a branch.

```wf
type Todo { id: String, title: String, done: Bool = false }

page Todos(path: "/", title: "Todos", description: "A list that keeps its rows.") {
    state todos: [Todo] = [Todo(id: "1", title: "Milk"), Todo(id: "2", title: "Bread")]
    state draft = ""
    derived left = todos.filter(item => !item.done).length

    Heading("Todos").h1
    Text("{left} left")
    Input(bind: draft, label: "New todo")
    Button("Add") { on click { todos = todos.concat([Todo(id: uuid(), title: draft)])  draft = "" } }
    for todo in todos by todo.id {
        Checkbox(bind: todo.done, label: todo.title)
    }
    if left == 0 {
        Text("All done.")
    }
}
```

`for … by todo.id` compiles to `WF.each` with a key. Each row is drawn
once and filed under its key. When the list changes, the runtime walks the
new list: a key it has seen keeps its nodes and is moved into place if it
moved; a new key is drawn; a key that is gone is disposed of and removed.
A checkbox that has focus keeps it while rows are added or removed around it, because
it is the same element.

A keyed `for` is also *live*. Its body reads the item through an accessor,
a small signal of its own, so a new value under the same key reaches the
row's nodes in place: the label's text node updates, and nothing else in
the row is redrawn. Without `by`, the runtime has no way to tell one row
from another, and rebuilds the list whole on every change; the compiler
warns when that would lose state (`U09`).

## A refresh keeps what did not change

Data from a server makes the same promise harder to keep, because every
response is new objects. A resource that asks again on an interval would
otherwise hand the list a fresh array of fresh rows every 30 seconds.

```wf
type Server { id: String, name: String, status: String }

page Servers(path: "/", title: "Servers", description: "Every server, kept current.") {
    resource servers: [Server] = fetch("/api/servers", on: .interval(30.seconds))
    Heading("Servers").h1
    match servers {
        loading { Text("Loading…") }
        error(e) { Text(e.message) }
        ready(list) {
            for s in list by s.id { Text("{s.name}: {s.status}") }
        }
    }
}
```

Before the answer to a refresh is stored, the runtime lays it over what
was there: a row with the same `id` that is equal to the old one is
replaced by the old object, and a list in which nothing changed is the old
list. Then the ordinary machinery does the rest. The `ready` arm stays
drawn, since the arm is still `ready`. The list, handed the same array,
has nothing to do. A server whose status changed gives a new object under
the same key, and its row's text node updates. An answer that changed
nothing redraws nothing.

## What it costs

Fine-grained reactivity is not free. Its costs are the reasons for most
of the rules you meet in the book:

- **A value read once is read once.** A `state` that starts from `now` or
  `viewport` takes the value it had when the page opened and never moves
  (`X06`). Only a `derived`, or text that reads the value, follows it.
- **Identity is the change.** A list changed in place behind the
  compiler's back, by your own script, is not a change. Hand a script an
  action, and let the action assign.
- **Keys are your job.** The runtime cannot guess which row is which. A
  `by` that names what identifies the item, not its position, is what
  lets a row keep its focus and its state.

In return, a click costs what it changes and nothing more, a page needs no
memoization to stay fast, and what you see in the source, the place a
value is read, is the place the page updates.

For the language side of this, read
[State and reactivity](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity) and
[Control flow](/learn/09-control-flow). The functions named here are
listed in the [runtime API](/reference/runtime).



---

# Security

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/about/security

This essay sets out WebFluent's security model: what the compiler
guarantees about every page it writes, what no compiler can guarantee, and
the decisions it leaves to you.

A web page is a program you hand to a stranger's machine, and its strings
come from everywhere: a form, a URL, a CMS, a database, another service.
Most security bugs are one mistake, a string that arrives somewhere it
becomes *code* instead of *content*. Advice against that mistake has been
written for twenty years, and the mistake is still the most common one,
because advice has to be followed on every line and a deadline only has
to win once.

So WebFluent does not advise. It makes the safe spelling the only one the
compiler accepts, and names the one door that is not safe so a review can
find it. What follows is the list of those guarantees, the places they
stop, and what lies on the other side of each.

## What the compiler guarantees

These are properties of the output, not advice. You do not have to turn
them on.

- **Text is text.** Every string an element shows goes in as a text node.
  `"<script>"` in your data can never become a script. The one exception
  has `Unsafe` in its name ([One door for markup](#one-door-for-markup)).
  An `html:` argument on an element is an attribute called `html`, as any
  argument an element does not declare is (`C04`), and never markup.
- **No inline handlers.** Events are bound with `addEventListener`.
  `Button("x", onclick: expr)` is a compile error, because an `on*`
  attribute is the one place a browser runs an attribute's value. Write
  `on click { }` instead. `style:` is refused the same way (`E106`): a
  value from data would be the element's whole inline style. A
  `style { }` block sets one property at a time.
- **An attribute holds its value.** A `class:` from data, a page title from
  a route parameter or front matter, a chart's or a QR code's colour: each
  is escaped for where it is written, and a colour must be a colour
  (`#0F766E`, `red`, `rgb(…)`, `var(--x)`) or the default is drawn. A
  design token whose value holds `<`, `{`, `}` or `;` is left out of the
  stylesheet, so a theme cannot close a rule and open another.
- **No URL a browser would run.** `href:`, `src:`, `to:`, `poster:` and
  `navigate()` take a URL whose scheme is `http`, `https`, `mailto`, `tel`,
  `sms` or `ftp`, or a URL with no scheme at all. The compiler refuses a
  literal where you write it, and the runtime refuses a value that exists
  only at run time at the moment it is used. A page may never point at
  `javascript:`, `data:`, `vbscript:`, `blob:` or `file:`.
- **Except a picture in its address.** A `data:image/png;base64,…` or
  `data:image/svg+xml,…` URL is allowed where a picture is drawn: an
  `Image`'s or an `Avatar`'s `src:`, a Markdown picture, and an `<img>` that
  `sanitize` keeps. An `<img>` never runs what it shows, not even an SVG's
  scripts. A link, a frame or a form never takes one, and `data:text/html`
  is not a picture.
- **No handle on your page.** A link with `target:` carries
  `rel="noopener noreferrer"`, so the page it opens cannot navigate yours;
  `sanitize` adds both to such a link whatever its `rel` said, and keeps
  `opener` on none.
- **`navigate()` stays on the site.** A value the page was handed —
  `navigate(query.next ?? "/")` after a sign-in — goes to a page of the
  site; an address on another origin (`//elsewhere.example`) is refused, and
  the reader stays where they are. Leave the site with a `Link`.
- **A frame drawing HTML from a value runs none of it.** A
  `Frame(srcdoc: value)` with no `sandbox:` is given `sandbox=""`, and the
  build names it (`V03`). Its `on message` hears only what that frame's
  own document posts, from the origin that document has, not a page it
  navigated to.
- **A page's `head { }` points nowhere a browser runs.** Its `src:` and
  `href:` go through the scheme check at build time and in the browser. A
  `script(src:)` must be written out, and a refresh may not take its
  address from a value (`E107`): either would let whoever controls the
  value choose what the page runs or where the reader goes.
- **Markdown is escaped first.** `Markdown(text)` shows any HTML in the
  text instead of running it. Its links and pictures go through the same
  scheme check as every other URL: a link to a `javascript:` URL is drawn
  as its words, with no link, at build time and in the browser alike. So is
  one that puts a backslash before its colon (`javascript\:`), which
  Markdown reads as the colon it escapes. For text somebody else wrote,
  such as a language server's documentation, `Markdown(text).inert` draws
  no link or picture at all ([Render Markdown](/recipes/render-markdown)).
- **A `Secret` cannot escape.** It may not be shown, spliced into a string,
  logged or persisted. Each is a `T12`, reported at the line that does it.
- **A non-public `env` name cannot be read from a page.** See
  [Secrets stay out of the bundle](#secrets-stay-out-of-the-bundle).
- **A build stays in its project.** `data`, `image`, `api … from` and
  `i18n.dir` name paths inside the project; an absolute path or a `..` is
  an error. A link that points out of the project, at nothing, or back on
  itself is left out of every walk with a warning. A `build.output` outside
  the project, or a link inside it, is refused unless the command line says
  `--allow-output-outside`, and the build removes only the `.gz` files it
  wrote itself. A cloned project cannot make `wf build` read or delete
  files elsewhere on your machine.

## What it cannot guarantee

Some decisions are outside the compiler's reach:

- **What your server does with what you send it.** Injection into a SQL
  query, a template or a shell happens on the other side of the wire.
- **Whether a reader may see a thing.** `guard:` on a page hides a route;
  it does not authorise anything. Authorisation is the server's answer, and
  the server checks it on every request.
- **A dependency you add yourself.** A `<script>` in `public/`, a font from
  another origin, an embed — each is code you choose to trust.
- **Your hosting.** HTTPS, HSTS, cookie flags and rate limits are the
  host's job.

## One door for markup

Sometimes the content really is HTML: a CMS body, the output of a Markdown
renderer of your own, an email. There is one way to show it, and it takes
two calls, `Unsafe.Html(sanitize(body))`, because they do different jobs:

- `Unsafe.Html(markup)` puts markup in as markup. Its name lets a review
  find every one with a search for `Unsafe`, and the build prints a `V03`
  at each, saying whether the markup went through `sanitize`.
- `sanitize(html)` is an **allow-list**: a fixed set of elements and, for
  each element, a fixed set of attributes. A tag nobody has thought of is
  dropped, not permitted. It keeps no `<script>`, `<style>`, `<iframe>` or
  `<form>`, and no `on*` attribute, and every `href` and `src` goes through
  the same scheme check as every other URL. A dropped element keeps its
  text, so removing a `<font>` does not remove the sentence inside it.

`sanitize` runs at build time as well as in the browser, from the same
allow-list. A pre-rendered page therefore shows the sanitised body at once,
not an empty box that fills in when the script loads.

`Unsafe.Html` without `sanitize` is for markup the project itself produced;
anything that arrived from outside goes through `sanitize`.
[Show HTML from outside the project](/recipes/show-html-from-outside)
is a page that does it.

## Where a session belongs

`persist` writes to `localStorage` or `sessionStorage`. **Neither is a
place for a session token.** Any script that reaches your page can read
both, and that is the whole payload of a cross-site scripting bug: without
a readable token the bug is a defacement; with one it is an account
takeover.

A session belongs in an **httpOnly cookie** the server sets, and each of
its flags closes one door:

- `HttpOnly` puts the cookie out of reach of every script, including yours.
- `SameSite=Lax` stops another site's form from riding on it.
- `Secure` keeps it off plaintext connections.

The browser sends the cookie with each request, so the page needs no token
at all: an `api` with `credentials: .sameOrigin` sends it with every call.
[Sign in with a session cookie](/recipes/sign-in-with-a-session-cookie)
builds the whole flow, including what to forget when the reader signs out.

A page *may* keep what a page may show: a display name, a theme, a
preference. If a value would matter to someone who stole it, it belongs
behind a request.

The compiler enforces the part it can. Declare a token as a `Secret`, and
keeping it with `persist` is a `T12`:

```wf expect=T12
page Account(path: "/", title: "Account", description: "Your account.") {
    persist _token: Secret = ""
    Heading("Account").h1
}
```

## Secrets stay out of the bundle

`env.NAME` is replaced by its value **at build time**, and the value lands
in the JavaScript the browser downloads. That is right for an API's base
address and wrong for an API key. So a page, a component, a store or an
`api` block may read only a name that is public: one that begins `PUBLIC_`,
or one that `public_env` in the config lists. Any other name is an `E108`
compile error naming the file and the line, and every build warns of each
`public_env` name it bundles, since its name does not say so.

`public_env` comes with the project, so it cannot reach into the shell of
whoever builds it: a name it lists without the `PUBLIC_` prefix takes its
value from the config or `.env`, and from the shell only when
`WF_ALLOW_SHELL_ENV` names it.

A private value is still there for `wf render`, which runs on a server
where a secret stays secret
([Render a template](/recipes/render-a-template)). A secret that has to
reach a third party belongs in a request your server makes, not in a page.
[Use environment values, and keep secrets out](/recipes/environments-and-secrets)
sets values, lists public ones, and builds once per environment.

## Uploads are checked on the server

A `File` from `FileUpload` is a handle on a file on the reader's machine.
`accept:` and `.size` help the reader pick the right file. They are **not**
checks: both live in the page, and a page is the attacker's to rewrite.

The server decides what it accepts. It reads the type from the file's
bytes, not its name; enforces a size limit itself; generates the stored
file's name, never using the one it was given; and stores uploads
somewhere nothing is served from.

## The Content-Security-Policy

A Content-Security-Policy (CSP) tells the browser which scripts, styles,
images and connections a page may use. `"build": { "csp": true }` ships
one, and a project `wf init` creates has it on. The build then writes:

- a `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">` in every page, right
  after `<meta charset>`: a meta policy governs only what the browser
  parses after it, so it stands before the title, the sharing tags and a
  page's own `head { }` tags, which a page's data reaches;
- a `_headers` file for hosts that read one (Netlify, Cloudflare Pages;
  other hosts ignore it — on Vercel the headers go in `vercel.json`, see
  [Deploy to Vercel](/recipes/deploy-to-vercel), and
  [Set cache and security headers](/recipes/cache-and-security-headers)
  covers the rest).

`frame-ancestors` is only in `_headers`, because a browser ignores it in a
meta tag. A policy that carried it there would say one thing and do
another.

The policy is `'self'` throughout, with no `'unsafe-inline'` for scripts:
the compiler writes external files and binds events with
`addEventListener`, so nothing needs it. The build widens it by exactly the
origins that `meta.fonts`, `meta.stylesheets` and `meta.scripts` declare,
so the policy never blocks a font or library you declared. Your own scripts
under `src/` are served from the site itself and need nothing added.

### Who may frame a page

By default no other site may frame your pages. `_headers` says
`frame-ancestors 'none'` and `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, and `wf serve` sends
the same, so nobody can lay your page under theirs to trick a reader into
clicking it.

A project that frames a page of its own — a `Frame` whose `src:` is
site-relative, such as `Frame(src: "/preview/", title: "Preview")` — is
relaxed to its own origin and no further: `frame-ancestors 'self'` and
`X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`. A `Frame` of another origin's page changes
nothing here; that is `meta.frame`'s `frame-src`, below.

### What else a page may reach

Anything beyond that is named, origin by origin: `meta.connect` for the
origins a page sends requests to, `meta.img` for images, `meta.frame` for
frames, each joining its directive of the policy, plus an app's own
schemes, `meta.wasm` for WebAssembly and `meta.style_elements` for scripts
that write `<style>`. Each widens the policy by exactly what it names, and
no more. [Allow other origins in the security policy](/recipes/allow-other-origins)
sets each one.

### The build checks its own output

**The build holds every page to the policy it ships.** It reads each HTML
file back and stops on anything the policy would block: an inline
`<script>`, a `<style>`, a `style=` attribute, an `on*` attribute, a
script or stylesheet from an origin the policy never named or from an
address that names no place (`data:`, `javascript:`), a `<base>`, or a
refresh that sends the reader to another site. It reads the HTML as a
browser does — names in any case, attributes apart by white space or a
`/`, values quoted or not. A policy is a promise about what a page
contains; without this check, the browser would enforce it and show a
blank page. A page the check refuses is removed from the output, so a
deploy that ignores the failed build does not publish it.

A page's own `head { script(src: …) }` or stylesheet `link` is added on the
live page, after the HTML is written, so the compiler checks it where you
write it instead: one from an origin the config does not declare is an
`E902` on that line.

One thing is allowed rather than refused: a `style { }` value that **reads
state** is written on the element, because it has nowhere else to go. When
a build emits one, `style-src` gains `'unsafe-inline'` and the build names
the pages that caused it, so the stricter policy is one edit away. A
literal in a `style { }` block is already a shared class and costs nothing.

## Code you choose to trust

A `.js` file under `src/` runs on every page exactly as written. The
compiler reads its names; it does not rewrite or sandbox it. It is code you
trust, like the rest of `src/`. What it puts in the page with `innerHTML`
is markup, so markup from outside the project goes through
`WF.sanitize(…)` there too.

A file from another origin — a library, a stylesheet, a font — is code
that origin can change after you read it. It belongs in `meta.scripts`,
`meta.stylesheets` or `meta.fonts` with an integrity hash in
`meta.integrity`, so a change at that origin cannot reach your readers; the
build warns (`D05`) about one without
([Allow other origins in the security policy](/recipes/allow-other-origins#variations),
[Load a library from a CDN](/recipes/library-from-a-cdn)).

## What a review reads

Everything the compiler cannot refuse is something the project chose to
trust, so a review starts from a list of those choices. `wf audit` prints
it — every `Unsafe.*`, every script, origin and stored value, every `env`
name, the policy — and never fails a build.
[Review a site's security before you deploy](/recipes/review-security)
reads it, and goes through the checklist for the build, the host and the
server.

## Next

[What a build ships](/about/what-a-build-ships): what a build already does to be fast, and how to see what it weighs.



---

# Static or single-page

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/about/static-or-single-page

This essay compares the two shapes a WebFluent build takes: a static
site, with a pre-rendered HTML file for every route, and a single-page
app, with one shell that draws every page in the browser.

The usual framing makes this a choice of framework: one for content
sites, another for apps, and a migration when a site turns out to be
both. WebFluent treats it as a setting. The same source builds either
shape, one key in the config, `build.ssg`, picks it, and you can change
your mind on any day without touching a page. What is worth deciding is
not which tool to use but what the reader should get first: the text, or
the app.

The sections below say what each shape writes, how a static page comes to
life, what the build can know when it pre-renders, and what each shape
asks of a host.

## Two shapes of build

`build.ssg` decides what `wf build` writes:

| What differs | Static (`"ssg": true`) | Single-page (`"ssg": false`) |
|---|---|---|
| What is written | One HTML file per route — `index.html`, `about/index.html`, `posts/hello/index.html` — each the page's first paint | One `index.html` shell; the router draws every page in the browser |
| First paint | Immediate: the text is in the HTML | After the script loads and runs |
| Search engines and link previews | See the real page | See the shell (with its title and tags) until they run the script |
| Moving between pages | A real page load | Instant, with no reload; focus and scroll handled, the title announced |
| The host | Any static host, as it is | Must answer every path with `index.html` (the "SPA fallback") |
| Interactive | Yes, once the script *hydrates* the page in place | Yes |

The source is the same either way. Only the output changes.
`"output_type": "static"` means the same as `"ssg": true`, and a build with
`ssg` set to `false`, or left out, is single-page. `wf init -t static`
starts a project with `ssg` on and `wf init -t spa` one with it off; either
can change its mind at any time without the source changing.

## When to choose each

**Choose static** for anything people find by searching or share by link:
marketing sites, docs, blogs, shops. The text is in the HTML, so search
engines and link previews see the real page.

**Choose single-page** for an app behind a sign-in, where every page is
personal and moving between pages fast matters more than the first paint.
Choose it too when your host cannot serve a file per route.

## Hydration

A static page is readable before any script runs. When `app.js` arrives,
it *hydrates* the page: it draws the page beside the one already there,
then takes the painted one over in place.

What happens to each part of the page:

- An element nothing holds on to stays exactly as it was painted. Its
  attributes are brought up to date; it is never moved or drawn again.
- An element that a handler, an effect, a `ref` or a widget holds is put
  where the painted one stood, inside the painted parent.
- Text that a signal keeps current changes inside the painted element.

The reader never sees the page flash or redraw, and keeps their scroll
position, their focus and anything they had selected. The page's largest
paint stays the first one, which is what a search engine's speed score
measures.

Under `wf serve`, the runtime compares the page it took over with the one
it drew, and says so in the console when they differ. A difference is a
WebFluent bug, never yours.

## What the static paint knows

The *static paint* is the HTML the build pre-renders for a page. To paint
it, the build evaluates the page as far as it can know the values:

| Source | In the pre-rendered HTML |
|---|---|
| Literals, `const`, `data`, `image`, `env` | Painted |
| `state` initial values, and `derived` values over them | Painted |
| Stores, from their initial values | Painted |
| Components | Expanded, with props substituted and slots filled |
| `t("…")` | In the default locale |
| `format`, `ago`, the list and string helpers | Computed, with a built-in table of locales |
| `resource` and `api` calls | The `loading` arm; the live page fetches and replaces it |
| `await fetch` in an action | Nothing, until the action runs |
| `viewport`, `query`, `hash`, `theme`, `network` | Unknown — a condition on them is drawn once the page is live |
| Anything read from `window`, `document`, `localStorage` | Unknown |

For the first paint to be right, prefer what the build can see:

- **Data files over fetches** for content that changes only when you
  deploy ([Fetching data](/learn/15-data)).
- **[Responsive values](/learn/13-styling#responsive-values) over `viewport`**
  for layout.

## Routes with no single file

A page on a `:param` route, such as `/posts/:slug`, is one page in the
source and any number of addresses on the site, so a static build has no
single file to write for it. It can only pre-render the values it is told
about, at build time: `paths:` on the page lists them — from a `data` file,
a `const` or a literal list — and the build writes one painted file per
value, each with its own title, and lists them in the sitemap
([Pre-render a page for each item](/recipes/pre-render-each-item)). A
value nobody listed has no file, so the host answers it with the site's
404 page. A single-page build has none of this to decide: its router draws
any value in the browser.

The same reasoning gives the 404 page its file. A page on the `*` route is
drawn by the router for any address no page claims, and a static build
also writes it as `404.html`, which most static hosts serve for a path they
have no file for
([Show your own page for an unknown address](/recipes/not-found-page)).

## What each shape asks of a host

A static build asks almost nothing: any host that serves files serves it.
A single-page build has one file, `index.html`, so every path a reader
might open — `/users/42` — has to reach it, and the host needs a rule that
answers every path with `index.html`. Without it the home page works, but
a reload on any other address is a 404. Each host's rule is one line, and
each deploy and server recipe in the [Ship recipes](/recipes#ship)
has it.

Two settings adapt a build to where it is served, whichever its shape.
`build.base_path` serves the site under a sub-path, such as a GitHub Pages
project site, and prefixes every link, asset and route with it, so the
source still writes paths from the site's root
([Deploy to GitHub Pages](/recipes/deploy-to-github-pages)).
`build.clean_urls` keeps every canonical address one the host serves
without redirecting `/contact` to `/contact/`
([Keep addresses from redirecting](/recipes/search-and-link-previews#keep-addresses-from-redirecting)).

## Next

- [Markdown pages](/recipes/markdown-pages) and
  [search and link previews](/recipes/search-and-link-previews): what
  the build writes for search engines.
- [Deploy to GitHub Pages](/recipes/deploy-to-github-pages), or any host in the [recipes](/recipes): put either shape on a host.



---

# What a build ships

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/about/what-a-build-ships

This essay is about what `wf build` writes, and why a WebFluent site is
fast by default rather than by effort.

Most slow sites are not slow because someone chose to make them slow. They
are slow because every library, component and font arrived for a good
reason, and nothing ever weighed the total. A framework cannot weigh it
for you: it does not know which of its features your program uses, so it
ships them all and leaves the pruning to a bundler that reads JavaScript
it did not write.

A compiler that reads the whole program can do better. It knows which
runtime modules the code it generated calls, which built-ins' rules the
pages use, and which design tokens something names, so a build ships those
and nothing else. Your part is smaller: look at what it writes, set a
limit that warns you when it grows, and avoid the few patterns no compiler
can fix.

## What the build already does

You get these without setting anything:

- **Only the runtime you use.** The *runtime* is the JavaScript the
  compiled pages call. It is a set of modules, and a build keeps only the
  ones its code reaches, and of those only the functions its calls reach.
  A single-page build of one page of static text is an `app.js` of
  about 5 kB, 1.9 kB gzipped.
- **Short names.** A minified build shortens the runtime's own names, its
  top-level ones and each function's locals. What your pages call keeps
  its name.
- **A chunk per page.** `build.split` (on by default) writes each page's
  code and styles as their own files, loaded the first time its route is
  shown. A site of one page is not split: its code is all in
  `app.js`.
- **Pre-rendered HTML.** With `build.ssg`, each page's HTML is written at
  build time, so the first paint needs no script.
- **One pruned stylesheet.** It holds the rules of only the built-ins you
  use, and only the design tokens something names.
- **Precompressed files.** A `.gz` file sits beside every text file, for a
  host that serves it. `wf serve` sends the same bytes, so Lighthouse run
  against the dev server measures what a deploy sends.
- **Images at every width**, with `width` and `height` so nothing shifts, a
  placeholder while they load, the first image eager and the rest lazy
  ([Add a picture](/recipes/add-a-picture)).
- **Minified output.** `build.minify` (on by default) strips comments and
  white space.

## See what a build weighs

To see the size of everything a build writes, run the build with
`--stats`:

```bash
wf build --stats
```

This is the output for the project `wf init -t spa` makes, trimmed (the
exact numbers move a little from release to release):

```text
  What it weighs
    app.js                               49.4 kB  (16.7 kB gzipped)
    styles.css                           26.5 kB  (5.0 kB gzipped)
    pages/Settings.js                     8.8 kB  (2.2 kB gzipped)
    pages/Profile.js                      5.6 kB  (1.5 kB gzipped)
    pages/Tasks.js                        4.2 kB  (1.3 kB gzipped)
    pages/Home.js                         3.5 kB  (1.1 kB gzipped)
    …
    total                                99.7 kB

  Runtime: 19 of 44 modules, 123.5 kB of 406.7 kB kept, 110.7 kB with its names shortened (before minifying)
    core          26.3 kB  always
    router        13.9 kB  WF.router
    form          12.7 kB  WF.form
    motion        12.6 kB  enter:
    each          10.6 kB  WF.each
    store          9.1 kB  WF.store
    keep           8.9 kB  WF.persist
    field          2.7 kB  WF.field
    …
    left out: keys format offline peer scalars text slot browser host …

  Tokens: 30 nothing in the output names, left out
```

Read it in three parts:

- **What it weighs** lists every text file with its gzipped size. The
  starter's form brings in `form` and `field`, its store brings in `store`
  and `keep`, its second page brings in `router`, and its entry animations
  bring in `motion`.
- **Runtime** lists each module with what the build kept of it — the
  functions the program reaches — and what reached it. When a module you
  did not expect is in the build, look here first.
- **Tokens** counts the design tokens the build left out because nothing
  names them.

Each build records its sizes in `.wf-sizes.json` beside the project, so the
next `--stats` shows how each file moved since the last build (for example,
`+20 B`).

The project's own scripts are listed by their path under `js/`, such as
`js/tilt.js` ([Call your own script](/recipes/call-your-own-script)). The build
copies them as written: it does not minify a file it promises to ship byte
for byte.

## Set a size budget

To be warned when a file grows past a size, name its gzipped limit in
`build.budget`:

```json
{ "build": { "budget": { "app.js": "40 kB", "styles.css": "30 kB", "pages/Home.js": "10 kB" } } }
```

Any output may have a budget, including a page's chunk and one of your own
scripts under `js/`. A build over budget prints a warning and goes on. A CI
job that should fail on it can read the same numbers.

## Time pages in a browser

To measure how fast each page paints, build the site and run `wf verify`
with a budget in milliseconds:

```bash
wf build && wf verify --budget 800
```

`wf verify` loads every route in headless Chrome. For each route it prints
the first contentful paint, the number of nodes in the document, and the
bytes and requests it took. `--budget 800` fails a route whose first paint
is slower than 800 ms. Lighthouse and the browser's performance panel work
on the build as on any other site.

## Avoid what makes a site slow

These are the patterns that slow a WebFluent site down, and what to do
instead:

| Pattern | Why it is slow | Do this instead |
|---|---|---|
| A large `data` file | `data posts = "posts.json"` is inlined into the bundle, so a 2 MB file is 2 MB of JavaScript | Keep build-time data to what pages show. Fetch the rest, or split it across pages that each read one file |
| A waterfall of fetches | A resource whose URL depends on another's answer waits for that answer | Ask for both at once, or have the server send them together |
| Layout decided by `viewport` | `viewport` is unknown until the script runs, so the page paints one branch and then swaps it | Use [responsive values](/learn/13-styling#responsive-values), which are CSS |
| `"runtime": "full"` | It ships every module | Use it only when a hand-written script calls `WF` in ways the build cannot see, or an icon's name arrives at run time |
| Web fonts | Each weight is a download | Use `display=swap` and few weights, or the baseline's system fonts |
| An unkeyed list that changes | `for item in items` rebuilds the list | Key it: `for item in items by item.id` moves the nodes that stayed |
| Pictures the build cannot process | An SVG, a URL or a path built at run time is used as written: one size, no placeholder | Use a literal `src:` into `public/`, or declare the picture with `image` ([Add a picture](/recipes/add-a-picture)) |

## Next

[Static or single-page](/about/static-or-single-page): the two shapes a build takes, and what each one gives a reader.



---

# Why WebFluent

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/about/why

This essay argues for WebFluent: why a language for websites, PDFs and
slide decks should exist when JavaScript frameworks already do the job, and
what it gives up to be what it is.

The argument in one line: a website is a program whose mistakes are found
by its readers, and most of those mistakes can be found by a compiler
first, if the language is designed so that the compiler can see them.

## What breaks a website

Here is a page with a counter, the smallest program that has every part a
site has: an address, text, state, and something the reader does.

```wf
page Home(path: "/", title: "Hello", description: "A first WebFluent page.") {
    state count = 0
    Container {
        Heading("Hello, world").h1
        Text("You have clicked {count} times.")
        Button("Click me").primary { on click { count = count + 1 } }
    }
}
```

Now count the ways the same page goes wrong in a typical stack. A class
name misspelled in the markup does nothing. A prop a component does not
take is ignored. A field read from a record that does not have it is
`undefined`, and the page shows `undefined`. A value that may be `null`
crashes the page only for the reader whose data has a gap. A link to a
route that was renamed is a 404 that nobody sees until a reader follows
it. None of these is a hard problem. Each one is a problem the toolchain
had all the information to report, and did not.

WebFluent starts from the other end. Every word in a program resolves to
one declaration the compiler knows: a built-in in the registry, or a
component, store, type or page the project declares. A word that resolves
to nothing is an error, not a no-op.

```wf expect=E103
page Home(path: "/", title: "Hello", description: "A first WebFluent page.") {
    Button("Save").primry
}
```

The build stops on that line, says that `Button` has no flag `primry`, and
lists the ones it takes. The browser never sees the page.

## One lexeme, one meaning

The compiler can only check what it can read, so the grammar is built for
reading. Each kind of word means one thing:

- A lowercase keyword declares: `page`, `component`, `store`, `state`,
  `derived`, `action`, `type`, `enum`, `api`.
- A capitalised name is an element or a type: `Button`, `Todo`.
- `.primary` after a call sets a `Bool` prop or picks the case of an enum
  prop, and nothing else.
- `name: value` passes a prop. A block is the element's children.
  `on click { }` is a handler. `style { }` is CSS.

There is no second spelling for any of these, no attribute that is
sometimes a prop and sometimes markup, no string that is sometimes a
template. That is a constraint on the author, and it is the reason the
compiler, the linters, the formatter and the language server can all read
one registry and agree. When the editor offers you the flags of a `Button`
after a dot, it is reading the same table the build refuses `primry` from.

The cost is real: you cannot invent syntax, and a library cannot extend
the grammar. A component you write is called exactly as a built-in is, and
that is the extension point the language offers.

## Refuse what would fail in the browser

A compiler that stopped at spelling would be a linter. WebFluent's goes
further, because most of what fails in a browser is a type error or a
reactivity error in disguise:

- A value that may be `null`, read as if it were not, is `T04`. An
  `if let`, a `??` or a `!= null` check narrows it.
- A `state` that reads `now` once and so never ticks is `X06`; the fix the
  compiler offers is `derived`.
- An effect that writes what it reads, and so never settles, is `X02`.
- A link to a path no page answers is `R01`.
- A `Secret` shown, logged, spliced into a URL or kept with `persist` is
  `T12`.
- A page the build's own Content-Security-Policy would block is `E902`;
  the build reads its output back and holds it to the policy it ships.

Each finding has a code, a place, a hint and, where there is one right
answer, a fix the editor applies. The bet is that a project with no
findings is a project whose pages load, and `wf verify` exists to test the
bet: it opens every route in a real browser and fails on an uncaught error,
a failed request or a page that drew nothing.

Types make most of this possible, and they are optional. A value the
checker cannot work out is `Any`, which agrees with everything, so a
program that declares no types checks as it always would. Every annotation
you add narrows what the checker can say.

## Secure by construction, not by advice

The same idea applies to security. Advice such as "escape your output" or
"never put a token in `localStorage`" is agreed to in every review and hard to
follow on every line. WebFluent turns the advice into properties of the
output: every string an element shows is a text node; markup goes in only
through `Unsafe.Html`, which is named so a review finds it; an `href:`
whose scheme a browser would run is refused where it is written; an `env`
name that is not public cannot be read from a page. The
[security essay](/about/security) lists each guarantee and what is still yours.

## One source for the web and for paper

A team that publishes a site usually publishes documents too: an invoice,
a report, the slides for the quarter. These tend to live in a second
toolchain, with a second set of styles that drifts from the first.

WebFluent lays a PDF out from the same HTML and CSS the page would get, by
its own paged engine, with no browser and no external tool. A `Card` in a
PDF looks like the `Card` on the site, a theme's tokens reach both, and a
`Presentation` makes a deck from the same components. The same templates
render with JSON data from Rust or Node on a server. One language, one
look, one set of checks.

## Fine-grained, with no virtual DOM

A `state` is a signal. What reads it is what redraws: the text node that
splices `{count}`, an attribute, a branch. Nothing re-renders a component
to find out what changed, so there is no virtual DOM to diff and no memo
to forget. [How reactivity works](/about/how-reactivity-works) follows a click
from the handler to the text node it changes.

## One binary

`wf` is the compiler, the dev server, the formatter, the test runner and
the template renderer; its sibling `wf-lsp` is the language server, built
from the same compiler. There is no `node_modules`, no
bundler, and no configuration to write before the first page. A build
writes only the runtime modules the program reaches and only the component
rules it uses, so a page of text ships a few kilobytes of script. The
[essay on what a build ships](/about/what-a-build-ships) shows the numbers.

## What it gives up

A language with opinions is the wrong tool for some work:

- **A framework's ecosystem.** There is no package of WebFluent
  components to install from npm. Any browser library can be used from a
  plain script under `src/` or a `meta.scripts` entry, but you write the
  binding yourself.
- **Rendering per request.** A WebFluent site is static files and a
  browser runtime; your server stays your server. The template engine
  renders HTML and PDFs with data on a server, but it runs no handlers
  after the render.
- **Freedom of syntax.** One spelling for each thing means none of your
  own.

If those costs are acceptable, what you get in return is a site whose
mistakes the compiler finds before your readers do.

## Where to go from here

- To learn the language, start with
  [Your first page](/learn/01-getting-started).
- Coming from a framework, read
  [Coming from React](/coming-from/react) (or Vue, or Svelte) first.
- To look a fact up, use the [reference](/reference).
- This guide describes WebFluent 6. [Upgrading](/errors/upgrading) lists what
  each release changed.



---

# Expressions

https://webfluent.monzeromer.dev/reference/expressions

An expression is anything that has a value: a prop's value, a condition,
the right side of a `state` or a `derived`, or the inside of `{…}` in a
string. Remember one thing: wherever WebFluent wants a value, any
expression in this chapter can stand there, and it stays live when it reads
state.

In this chapter:

- literals, including the literals of the language's own types;
- interpolation, and how a splice formats its value;
- operators and their precedence;
- `if` and `match` used as values;
- fields, calls, lambdas and the methods of strings, lists and numbers;
- `format` and `ago`, regular expressions, design tokens as values;
- `await`, constants, and the functions the language adds.

## A first example

This page works out a total from state and shows it. It uses a list
literal, a lambda, a method, arithmetic, an `if` expression and a
formatted splice:

```wf
page Basket(path: "/basket", title: "Basket", description: "What the basket holds.") {
    state prices = [4.5, 12, 3.5]
    state member = true
    derived subtotal = prices.sum()
    derived total = if member { subtotal * 0.9 } else { subtotal }
    Heading("Basket").h1
    Text("{prices.length} items, {total:.currency}")
    Text(if member { "Member price" } else { "Join to save 10%" }).muted
}
```

The page shows `3 items, $18.00` and `Member price`:

- `[4.5, 12, 3.5]` is a list literal, and `prices.sum()` is one of the
  helpers lists have.
- `if member { … } else { … }` is a value: the block that runs gives it.
- `{total:.currency}` is a splice that formats its value as money.

When `member` or `prices` changes, `subtotal`, `total` and both texts
follow.

## Literals

A literal writes a value directly. This page declares one of each of the
everyday kinds:

```wf
page Literals(path: "/literals", title: "Literals", description: "One value of each kind.") {
    state label = "Draft"                         // String
    state count = 42                              // Number
    state ratio = 3.14                            // Number
    state open = true                             // Bool
    state note: String? = null                    // null
    state sizes = [1, 2, 3]                       // [Number]
    state owner = { name: "Sam", age: 30 }        // a map with those fields
    state slug = /^[a-z]+$/i                      // a regular expression
    state accent = $primary                       // a design token
    Heading("Literals").h1
    Text("{label} {count} {ratio} {open} {sizes.length} {owner.name}")
    Text("{note ?? \"none\"} {slug.test(label)} {accent}")
}
```

How each kind behaves:

- **Strings** are double-quoted and read the escapes `\n`, `\t`, `\r`,
  `\\`, `\"`, `\{` and `\}`. A raw string `#"…"#` and a block string
  `"""…"""` are in
  [Language basics](/learn/04-language-basics#three-ways-to-write-one).
- **Lists and maps** may span lines and take a trailing comma. A map
  literal has the shape it was written with, so the checker can read
  `owner.name` and refuse a misspelled field.
- **`null`** is the absence of a value. Only a type that ends in `?`
  holds it.

The language's own types have literals too
([Types](/learn/12-types#the-types-the-language-brings-with-it)):

```wf
page Typed(path: "/typed", title: "Typed", description: "Literals of the built-in types.") {
    state due: Date = @2026-03-14             // a Date
    state opens: Time = @09:30                // a Time
    state at: DateTime = @2026-03-14T09:30Z   // a DateTime
    state wait: Duration = 90.minutes         // a Duration: ms, seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks
    state price: Money = €12.99               // Money, in minor units; $ and £ too
    state brand: Color = #0F766E              // a Color
    Heading("Typed").h1
    Text("{due} {opens} {at} {wait.minutes()} {format(price)} {brand}")
}
```

## Interpolation

`"{expr}"` puts the value of an expression into a string. Anything that
shows text accepts one, and the text follows the state it reads:

```wf
page Greeting(path: "/greeting", title: "Greeting", description: "Text built from state.") {
    state name = "Sam"
    state count = 3
    derived noun = if count == 1 { "item" } else { "items" }
    Heading("Hello, {name}").h1
    Text("You have {count} {noun}")
    Text("Total: {format(count * 9.99, .currency)}")
    Text("Next: {count + 1}")
}
```

The page shows `Hello, Sam`, `You have 3 items`, `Total: $29.97` and
`Next: 4`.

Any expression may go inside `{…}`: a call, a method chain, an `if`, even a
string of its own. `"{n ?? "none"}"` and `"{if ok { "yes" } else { "no" }}"`
both work. The rules:

- The group must close on the same line.
- A splice opens with a name, a `(` or a `[`. Anything else in braces —
  `"{key: value}"` in prose, a fragment of code, `"{"` alone — stays text.
- For a long expression, declare a `derived` value and splice its name, as
  `noun` above. It reads better and the checker names it in a message.

### Showing a value a particular way

A splice may say how to show its value: `{value:.style}`, or
`{value:.style(option)}`. It is `format(value, .style, option)` written
where the value is read.

```wf
page Receipt(path: "/receipt", title: "Receipt", description: "An order, formatted.") {
    state total = 1234.5
    state count = 1235
    state shipped = "2026-03-05T10:00:00Z"
    state discount = 0.256
    Heading("Receipt").h1
    Text("Total: {total:.currency}")            // Total: $1,234.50
    Text("{count:.integer} items")              // 1,235 items
    Text("Shipped {shipped:.date(long)}")       // Shipped March 5, 2026
    Text("Saved {discount:.percent(1)}")        // Saved 25.6%
}
```

The styles and their options are those of `format`, listed under
[`format` and `ago`](#format-and-ago). The value is an expression like any
other, so `{order.total:.currency}` and `{rows.sum():.compact}` both work.

> [!WARNING]
> A splice must open with a name, a `(` or a `[`, so `"{0.256:.percent}"`
> shows as written. Give the number a name first — `derived ratio = 0.256`,
> then `{ratio:.percent}` — or wrap it: `{(0.256):.percent}`.

## Operators

The operators, by kind:

| Kind | Operators |
|---|---|
| Arithmetic | `+ - * / %`, unary `-` |
| Comparison | `== != < <= > >=` (`!==` too) |
| Logic | `&& \|\| !` |
| Null | `??` fallback, `?.` optional chain |
| Range | `a..b` (exclusive), `a..=b` (inclusive) |
| Spread | `[...a, x]`, `{ ...m, key: v }` |
| Grouping | `( )` |

This page uses most of them:

```wf
page Scores(path: "/scores", title: "Scores", description: "Two numbers compared.") {
    state home = 7
    state away = 2
    state player: Map? = null
    Heading("Scores").h1
    Text("{home + away} {home - away} {home * away} {home / away} {home % away}")
    Text(if home > away && away != 0 { "Home leads" } else { "Away leads" })
    Text(player?.name ?? "No player picked")
    for round in 1..=3 { Badge("Round {round}") }
}
```

How they behave:

- `+` joins strings when either side is a `String`, and adds numbers
  otherwise. Arithmetic on anything else is a `T18`.
- `==` compares values. Two records with the same fields are not `==`
  unless they are the same object, so compare their ids.
- Against a `null` literal, `==` and `!=` also match a value that is
  absent, such as a query key the address does not have.
- `a ?? b` is `b` when `a` is `null`. `a?.b`, `a?.m()` and `a?.[i]` read
  through a `null` and give `null` instead of failing.
- A range is the whole numbers from `a` up to `b`, without `b` for `..` and
  with it for `..=`.

Precedence, strongest first: `!`, unary `-` and `await`; then `* / %`;
`+ -`; the comparisons; `==` and `!=`; `&&`; `||`; `??`; and ranges last. So
`1..n + 1` is `1..(n + 1)`, and `a ?? b || c` is `a ?? (b || c)`. The full
table is in [Grammar](/reference/grammar#expressions).

## Choosing a value

`if` and `match` are expressions when they stand where a value is
expected. Each arm's block is its value:

```wf
enum Level { low, mid, high }

page Grades(path: "/grades", title: "Grades", description: "A score, graded.") {
    state score = 72
    state level: Level = .mid
    derived grade = if score >= 90 { "A" } else if score >= 70 { "B" } else { "C" }
    derived tone = match level { .low { "calm" } .mid { "steady" } else { "loud" } }
    Heading("Grade {grade}").h1
    Text("The room is {tone}")
    Badge(grade, tone: if score >= 70 { .success } else { .danger })
}
```

The rules:

- An `if` with no `else` is `null` when its condition fails.
- `if let x = v { a } else { b }` binds `x` when `v` is not `null`.
- A `match` on an enum, as a value or as a statement, needs an arm for
  every case or an `else` (`T15`). One that covers every case needs no
  `else`.
- A case with a payload binds one name in a `match` expression:
  `match status { .failed(reason) { reason } else { "" } }`.

## Fields, calls and methods

A field is read with `.`, an item with `[i]`, and a method is called with
`.name(…)`. This page filters, maps and joins a list of records:

```wf
type Todo { id: String, title: String, done: Bool = false }

page Todos(path: "/todos", title: "Todos", description: "A list, filtered and joined.") {
    state todos: [Todo] = [Todo(id: "1", title: "milk"), Todo(id: "2", title: "eggs", done: true)]
    state search = "M"
    derived open = todos.filter(todo => !todo.done)
    derived titles = todos.map(todo => todo.title.capitalize())
    derived hits = todos.filter(todo => todo.title.toLowerCase().includes(search.toLowerCase()))
    derived first = todos.first()
    derived summary = titles.join(", ")
    Heading("{todos.length} todos").h1
    Text("{open.length} open, {hits.length} match: {summary}")
    if let f = first { Text("First: {f.title}") }
}
```

A lambda is written `x => expr`, `(a, b) => expr` or `() => expr`. Its body
is one expression; when it must do more, it calls an action. To return a
map, write the parameters in parentheses: `(x) => { key: x }`. A
parameter's type comes from what the method expects, so `todo` above is a
`Todo`.

A member something declares wins over a helper of the same name. A store
may name an action `preview`, `first` or `truncate`: `OpenFiles.preview(path)`
calls that action, with its arguments, from a page or from another store,
and a worker's `css.last(kind)` is the worker's own `last`. The helpers
below are for lists and strings.

### String methods

`length`, `trim()`, `trimStart()`, `trimEnd()`, `toLowerCase()`,
`toUpperCase()`, `capitalize()`, `truncate(n)`, `dedent()`, `lines()`,
`words()`, `includes(s)`, `startsWith(s)`, `endsWith(s)`, `indexOf(s)`,
`lastIndexOf(s)`, `slice(a, b)`, `substring(a, b)`, `charAt(i)`, `at(i)`,
`replace(a, b)`, `replaceAll(a, b)`, `split(sep)`, `padStart(n, c)`,
`padEnd(n, c)`, `repeat(n)`, `normalize()`, `localeCompare(other)`,
`match(re)`, `search(re)`.

`dedent()` takes the common indentation off a block of text — the
indentation a string carried in from a file or an API keeps and a reader
does not want. `lines()` splits a text by line ending, and `words()` by
runs of whitespace.

### List methods

`length`, `map(f)`, `filter(f)`, `find(f)`, `findIndex(f)`, `some(f)`,
`every(f)`, `includes(x)`, `indexOf(x)`, `reduce(f, init)`, `join(sep)`,
`slice(a, b)`, `concat(other)`, `reverse()`, `sort(f)`, `sortBy(f)`,
`groupBy(f)`, `unique()`, `take(n)`, `first()`, `last()`, `sum()`,
`flatMap(f)`, and, in an action or a handler, `push(x)` and `remove(i)`.

`sortBy`, `groupBy`, `unique`, `take`, `first`, `last`, `sum`,
`capitalize`, `truncate`, `dedent`, `lines` and `words` are WebFluent's
own; the rest are the browser's. Every one of them also runs at build time,
so the pre-rendered page shows the result. [Built-ins](/reference/built-ins#list-methods)
says what each returns.

On a state, `sort` and `reverse` read in an expression work on a copy, so
reading a sorted list never changes the list. As a statement, `push`,
`remove` and `sort` give the state a new list, so whatever reads it
repaints.

### Number methods

`toFixed(n)`, `toPrecision(n)`, `toString()`. To convert, use
`Number("12")` for a string to a number, and `"{n}"` or `String(n)` for a
number to a string. `Math.round`, `Math.max` and the rest are available as
`Math.*`.

## `format` and `ago`

`format(value, .style, option)` writes a number, a date or money as text in
the reader's locale. The locale is the i18n locale when the project has
one, and the document's language otherwise. This page shows each style:

```wf
page Formats(path: "/formats", title: "Formats", description: "Every style of format.") {
    state price = 1234.5
    state ratio = 0.256
    state visitors = 1200000
    state when = "2026-03-14T09:30:00"
    Heading("Formats").h1
    Text(format(price, .currency))                 // $1,234.50
    Text(format(price, .currency, "EUR"))          // €1,234.50
    Text(format(ratio, .percent))                  // 26%
    Text(format(ratio, .percent, 1))               // 25.6%
    Text(format(price, .decimal, 1))               // 1,234.5
    Text(format(visitors, .integer))               // 1,200,000
    Text(format(visitors, .compact))               // 1.2M
    Text(format(when, .date))                      // Mar 14, 2026
    Text(format(when, .date, "long"))              // March 14, 2026
    Text(format(when, .time))                      // 9:30 AM
    Text(format(when, .datetime))                  // Mar 14, 2026, 9:30 AM
    Text(format(when, "EEEE d MMMM yyyy, HH:mm"))  // Saturday 14 March 2026, 09:30
    Text(ago(when))                                // 3 days ago
    Text(format(when, .relative))                  // the same
}
```

The styles, and the option each takes:

| Style | Gives | Option |
|---|---|---|
| `.number` (the default) | `1,234.5` | — |
| `.integer` | `1,235` | — |
| `.decimal` | `1,234.50` | places, `2` when omitted |
| `.currency` | `$1,234.50` | the currency code, `"USD"` when omitted |
| `.percent` | `26%`, of a fraction | places, `0` when omitted |
| `.compact` | `1.2K`, `1.2M` | — |
| `.date`, `.time`, `.datetime` | `Mar 14, 2026`, `9:30 AM` | `"short"`, `"medium"`, `"long"` or `"full"` |
| `.relative` | `3 days ago` | — |

A pattern string in place of a style writes a date with these letters:
`yyyy yy MMMM MMM MM M dd d EEEE EEE HH H hh h mm ss a`. A `Money` value
needs no style: `format(price)` writes it in its own currency.

`ago(date)` gives the distance from now in words: `now` under 45 seconds,
then `5 minutes ago`, `yesterday`, `in 2 days`. `ago(date, moment)`
measures from a moment of your own.

The pre-rendered page formats with a built-in table of the common locales
and currencies. Once the page's script runs, the browser's `Intl` takes
over and corrects any difference. A change of locale redraws every
formatted text.

## Regular expressions

`/…/flags` is a regular expression. This page checks an address as the
reader types it:

```wf
page Signup(path: "/signup", title: "Sign up", description: "An address, checked as it is typed.") {
    state email = ""
    derived valid = /^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$/.test(email)
    derived domain = email.split("@").last() ?? ""
    Heading("Sign up").h1
    Input(bind: email, label: "Email")
    if email != "" && !valid { Text("That does not look like an email.").danger.sm }
    Text("Domain: {domain}")
}
```

What each use gives:

- `re.test(s)` is a `Bool`.
- `s.match(re)` and `re.exec(s)` are a `[String]?`: the match and its
  groups, or `null`.
- `s.replace(re, "x")` and `s.replaceAll(re, "x")` are a `String`;
  `s.split(re)` is a `[String]`; `s.search(re)` is a `Number`.

## Tokens as values

`$name` names a design token from the theme ([Styling](/learn/13-styling)). In
a style it becomes the token's CSS variable. As a value it is a reference
to that variable, so a prop or a state that takes a colour takes a token:

```wf
page Callout(path: "/callout", title: "Callout", description: "A border coloured by a token.") {
    state accent = $primary
    Heading("Callout").h1
    Card {
        style { border-left: 4px solid {accent} }
        Text("The border takes its colour from the theme.")
    }
}
```

When the theme changes `color-primary`, the border changes with it.

As a value there is no property to say which group a short name belongs
to, so `$primary` is read as the one group that has it, the colours:
`$color-primary`. A short name several groups have (`$md` is a spacing, a
radius and a shadow) is written in full: `$spacing-md`.

## `await`

`await` waits for a promise inside an action or a handler, and makes the
action asynchronous. While a call of it runs, `name.pending` is `true`:

```wf
page Report(path: "/report", title: "Report", description: "Rows loaded on request.") {
    state rows: [Map] = []
    state note = ""
    action load() {
        rows = await fetch("/api/rows")
        let answer = await fetch("/api/note", { method: "GET" })
        note = answer.text ?? ""
    }
    Heading("Report").h1
    Button("Load", disabled: load.pending) { on click { load() } }
    Text("{rows.length} rows, note: {note}")
}
```

`fetch(url, options)` returns the parsed JSON body, or throws when the
response fails. `options` is a map with `method`, `headers` and `body`; a
map given as `body` is sent as JSON. `await` outside an action, a handler,
a timer or a hook is a `T17`. [Fetching data](/learn/15-data) has `resource`, the
declarative way to load data.

## Constants

`const` declares a value for the whole project. Every page, component and
store reads it by name, and the build inlines it into the bundle:

```wf
const MAX_ROWS = 50
const PAGE_SIZE: Number = 20
const API = env.PUBLIC_API_URL ?? "/api"

page Settings(path: "/settings", title: "Settings", description: "The limits this site runs with.") {
    Heading("Settings").h1
    Text("Up to {MAX_ROWS} rows, {PAGE_SIZE} a page, from {API}")
}
```

A constant may carry a type, as `PAGE_SIZE` does. Assigning to one is an
`X01`. `env.NAME` reads a value fixed at build time — from the config's
`env` map, a `.env` file or the shell. A page may read only a public name,
one that begins `PUBLIC_` or that `public_env` lists;
[Environments and secrets](/recipes/environments-and-secrets) has the rules.

## Built-in functions

These functions are everything the language adds to what the browser
already has. Anything else followed by parentheses is a method, an action,
a component or one of the browser's own globals. [Built-ins](/reference/built-ins#functions)
has an entry for each.

| Name | Does |
|---|---|
| `log(x)` | Prints a value to the console |
| `navigate(path)` | Changes the route ([Pages and routing](/learn/05-pages-and-routing#links-and-navigation)) |
| `format(v, .style, opt)`, `ago(d)` | Formats a value ([above](#format-and-ago)) |
| `t("key", args)`, `setLocale("ar")` | Translates, and switches the locale ([Translate a site](/recipes/translate-a-site)) |
| `setTheme("dark")` | `"dark"`, `"light"` or `"system"`, kept across visits ([Styling](/learn/13-styling#dark-mode)) |
| `keyIs(e, "mod+s")`, `keyLabel("mod+s")` | Tests a key event against a shortcut, and writes a shortcut for this system |
| `every(ms) { }`, `after(ms) { }` | Timers ([State and reactivity](/learn/07-state-and-reactivity#timers)) |
| `animate(el, name, ms)`, `replayAnimation(el, name)` | Plays an animation by hand ([Motion](/recipes/drive-an-animation)) |
| `optimistic(holder, change)` | Shows a change before the server agrees ([Fetching data](/learn/15-data#show-a-change-before-the-server-agrees)) |
| `beacon(url, data)` | Sends data in a way that outlives the page ([Send on unload](/recipes/send-on-unload)) |
| `sanitize(html)` | Passes markup through an allow-list ([Security](/about/security#one-door-for-markup)) |
| `uuid()` | Makes a fresh `Uuid` ([Types](/learn/12-types#the-types-the-language-brings-with-it)) |
| `fetch(url, options)` | Sends a request, through the same engine as `api` ([Fetching data](/learn/15-data#fetch-on-demand-with-await-fetch)) |
| `ws(…)`, `sse(…)`, `broadcast(…)`, `rtc(…)`, `spawn(…)` | Open a socket, a stream, a channel, a peer or a worker, after `socket x =` and the rest ([Open a socket](/recipes/open-a-socket)) |

The browser's own globals need no prefix and compile to themselves:
`window`, `document`, `console`, `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, `JSON`,
`Math`, `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `clearTimeout`,
`clearInterval`, `parseInt`, `parseFloat`, `Array`, `Object`, `String`,
`Number`, `Boolean`, `Promise`, `Error`, `Map`, `Set`, `RegExp`,
`Infinity`, `NaN`, `undefined`, `encodeURIComponent`, `decodeURIComponent`,
`encodeURI`, `decodeURI`, `atob`, `btoa`, `fetch`, `alert`, `confirm`,
`prompt`, `requestAnimationFrame`, `cancelAnimationFrame`, `navigator`,
`location`, and the other platform names that
[Built-ins](/reference/built-ins#browser-globals) lists.

## Summary

| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"text {expr}"` | A string with a live value spliced in |
| `"{value:.style(option)}"` | A splice formatted as `format` would |
| `a ?? b`, `a?.b`, `a?.[i]` | A fallback for `null`, and reading through one |
| `a..b`, `a..=b` | A range, without and with its end |
| `[...xs, x]`, `{ ...m, key: v }` | A list or map spread into a new one |
| `if c { a } else { b }` | The value of the arm that runs |
| `match v { .case { a } else { b } }` | The value of the arm that matches |
| `x => expr`, `(a, b) => expr` | A lambda |
| `/pattern/flags` | A regular expression |
| `$name` | A design token |
| `await expr` | The result of a promise, in an action or a handler |
| `const NAME = expr` | A value the whole project reads |

[Grammar](/reference/grammar#expressions) has the full precedence table, and
[Built-ins](/reference/built-ins) every function, value and method.

## Next

[Styling](/learn/13-styling).
